### feedback_cross_language_pitfalls.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language design pitfalls
description: Three approaches the user rejected when designing SoraMech's cross-language wire format
type: feedback
originSessionId: e9ed70c7-2b63-425c-987c-6431040bedfb
---
When designing anything that touches the cross-language data path, avoid these three shapes — the user pushed back on each and the rejections are load-bearing for the architecture.

**1. Don't propose runtime "handles" that route operations back to the originating spec.**

**Why:** Real library functions in the wild (qsort, libcurl, anything from libc) expect actual native values — a real `int (*)(int,int)` function pointer, a real `char *` — not a SoraMech-issued id string. They can't be modified to participate in our runtime's routing scheme. The wire must carry data the destination spec can fully reconstruct into a native value, not opaque tokens.

**How to apply:** When a value seems hard to serialize (function pointers, coroutines, opaque pointers), decompose to data primitives (address + signature, bytecode + upvalues, ptr + length). If the destination needs a callable, the destination spec synthesizes one at reconstruction time (libffi trampoline for C, `ffi.cast` for LuaJIT). The "phone home" callback that the trampoline performs internally is fine — it's an artifact of the destination spec's reconstruction, not exposed in the wire format. What's forbidden is a wire primitive that says "operations on this value cross back to the source."

**2. Don't propose pair-wise language conversion paths (lua→c, c→lua, etc.).**

**Why:** N languages means N² conversion paths, which means adding a new language breaks the existing ones. The wire must use a language-agnostic intermediate (JSON) and every spec must implement only the two pair-symmetric callbacks (`to_json`, `from_json`). New language = implement those two functions, nothing else touches.

**How to apply:** Never write code that names two specific languages in a conversion context. Specs only ever see JSON on the wire. If a JSON primitive needs an extension (like `$function_pointer`), it lives in the universal JSON contract, not as a lua-spec-specific or c-spec-specific concept.

**3. Don't propose per-function annotations for type ambiguities (lengths, discriminators, callback signatures).**

**Why:** The user pointed out that "discriminator" is a vocab word the system has no general way to ask about. We can't prompt "which param is the length?" because that pairing convention lives in the function's English documentation, not its types. Asking the user to write annotations means asking them to know specialized vocabulary they didn't sign up for.

**How to apply:** When a function signature has ambiguous types (`char *` with no length, `union` with no tag, `void *` with no signature), expose each parameter as a separate input slot on the box. The user wires the slots according to the function's documentation — `p` from one source, `n` from another. The system never infers pairings; the user expresses them by wiring. If the destination needs a length and no length wire is provided, the wire compile fails with a plain-English fix-it message ("destination needs length, source provides only a pointer — wire a length input here").

**Common thread:** all three rejections are the same principle in different clothes — **SoraMech bends to the language, not the other way around.** Users write idiomatic code in their language. Libraries are used as-is. Specs are self-contained and pair-symmetric. The system stays out of the user's vocabulary.

```

### project_cross_language_wire.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language wire format
description: Dual-ring slot per port (native ring + JSON ring + ordering ring). JSON only at language borders. Per-edge classification at graph load; per-cell precision at runtime.
type: project
originSessionId: 5670858b-274f-49c4-89b8-a4b83ce33d7c
---
Design corrected 2026-05-21 — replaces the older "JSON always" framing.

**Each input slot is a dual-ring buffer.** Per port: one `ring_native` (consumer-language native bytes), one `ring_json` (JSON bytes from cross-language producers), and one `ring_order` of `(which_ring, idx)` tuples in arrival order. Allocate `ring_json` and `ring_order` lazily — same-language-only ports pay nothing for them.

**Push selects ring by per-edge bit.** Producer's spec writes native bytes to `ring_native` if `output_edge_native[j]` is true; otherwise calls `native_to_json` and writes to `ring_json`. Either way, pushes a `(which_ring, idx)` tuple to `ring_order`.

**Pop reads ordering ring first.** Dispatch pops `ring_order`, gets `(which_ring, idx)`, then pops the indicated cell. The consumer's spec receives `(input_data[i], input_native[i])` per input port and dispatches per flag — decode native or decode JSON.

**Why dual-ring instead of per-port classification.** Per-port (slot is all-JSON if any fan-in is cross-lang) is the pessimistic approximation — same-language values eat JSON cost on mixed-fan-in ports. Dual-ring is precise per cell: a port fed by one Lua box and one C box keeps the Lua cells native and JSON-encodes only the C-sourced cells.

**Why JSON for the cross-language ring (not pair-wise paths, not type-annotated raw bytes).** JSON's structure is self-describing — every language has a natural mapping for object/array/number/string/bool/null. Adding language K means K's spec implements its own `native_to_json` and `json_to_native`. N spec-pairs, not N² language-pair paths. The native ring's format is each spec's private choice — Lua may pick msgpack or `cjson.encode` or a custom binary form; C uses `memcpy` of the wrapper struct; Bash uses strings.

**Sentinel primitives for non-JSON-mappable values.** `$ref` (pointer + length into the large-value heap), `$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque` ("these bytes are language-X-internal"). Carried inside the JSON ring as object-shaped sentinels. Cross-language receivers that can't reconstruct fail at wire compile.

**`$function_pointer` reconstruction — wrapper binary + persistent subprocess (issue 318, amended 2026-05-22).** Earlier design had the consumer's spec FFI-cast the raw process-local address. Rejected: FFI is language-pair-specific, biases SoraMech toward the Lua↔C corner, breaks the N-not-N² rule. Replacement: at map-compile time the compiler asks the *producing* spec to compile the referenced function + its enumerable dependencies into a standalone wrapper binary on disk that speaks a small line protocol on stdio. The consumer spec spawns one persistent subprocess per `$function_pointer` it receives and talks to it over the same socket-like channel used for any out-of-process spec. Every language pays the same price; new languages only implement "compile a function to a wrapper binary" — no pair-wise FFI knowledge required.

**Spec `invoke` signature change.** Collapses `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` into one `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags: `int invoke(handle, ..., const int *input_native, int n_inputs, int output_native, void *out_buf, ...)`. The spec dispatches per input internally. This is the contract change that unblocks 306/307's typed marshalling.

**Two compile-time layers stack:**
- **Per-edge classification (issue 312, this design)** — graph loader computes `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` on each box; dispatch routes pushes accordingly. This issue is the wire-format design.
- **Same-language source merge (issue 313, research / blocked)** — concatenate every same-language box's source into one translation unit per language. Boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks; what 313 thins is the spec invocation overhead inside the merged region (direct call into the worker's `lua_State` instead of dlsym + marshal + bridge). The dual-ring slot machinery does NOT collapse — tasks still need slots to wait for sibling inputs. 313 makes the ring cells cheaper to read/write; it doesn't remove them.

**Three rejected design shapes** (kept here so they don't get reinvented):
1. **Handles back-routing to the owning spec** — library functions in the wild can't be modified to use SoraMech-shaped handles. Rejected.
2. **Pair-wise language paths** — every new language would have to grow N-1 translation paths against existing languages. Rejected. The dual-ring's "two rings per slot" is the dimension-cap that prevents this.
3. **Per-function discriminator / length annotations on the wire** — the system has no universal vocabulary to ask "is param 2 the length?" Rejected; the user expresses these by wiring two separate input slots.

**How to apply:** When discussing wire format, slot store shape, dispatch routing, or spec callbacks: think dual-ring (native, JSON, ordering) per slot, per-edge classification at push time, per-cell tag at pop time, JSON-only-at-borders, language-private native bytes everywhere else.

```

### project_custom_translation_specs.md

```markdown
---
name: Custom translation specs per port
description: Users can override the default native/JSON wire path on any input port for any reason — a knob in the wire format vocabulary (issue 246)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Per-port custom translation specs** let the user intervene at a specific input port and replace the default dual-ring decode path with user-written code. The override applies to that one port; the rest of the graph uses the default native-or-JSON path from issue 312.

**Motivating cases (any reason qualifies, not just cross-language):**
- Cross-language ambiguity the default specs can't infer: a C++ class with methods landing at a C box (drop methods? expose as fn pointers? restructure?), a `void *` carrying a libcurl handle, a union whose discriminator is on a separate wire.
- Same-language reshape: massaging a value into a different shape on its way in (rename fields, drop a layer, project a subset) without adding a transform box on the canvas.
- Validation / coercion: clamp a number, enforce a schema, fail loudly on unexpected shapes.

**How it composes with the dual-ring design:**
- The custom spec runs at *pop* time on the consumer side, after the ordering ring has been consulted and the cell has been read from the appropriate ring. The user's code receives the decoded value (native or JSON-decoded) and produces whatever the consumer's `invoke` will see.
- A port with a custom translation gets its own wire color in the editor (issue 245) — visible signal that this port doesn't use the default path.

**Why:** The default native/JSON contract covers the cases JSON's structure handles cleanly. Everything outside that needs a user escape hatch — *and* the same hatch is useful for purely-local "I want this input shaped differently" cases. One mechanism, many uses.

**How to apply:** When the design needs an override knob on the cross-language path, propose "custom translation spec on the destination port" rather than inventing per-function annotations, type discriminator metadata, or producer-side conversion hints (all three were rejected — see feedback_cross_language_pitfalls). The port is the unit of override; the spec is user code; the rest stays default.

```

### project_editor_visual_language.md

```markdown
---
name: Editor visual language for wires
description: Wire color in the canvas editor encodes language pairing across the edge, not just routing kind — a UI invariant future work should respect (issue 245)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Wires are colored by language pairing across the edge**, with a separate color for wires whose destination port carries a user-written custom translation (issue 246). Pre-245 wires were colored purely by routing kind (default slate-blue, comparator branches orange/blue/green).

**The pairing-based palette:**
- **Same-language hop** — the wire carries native bytes; default neutral color.
- **Cross-language hop (forest green, ~`#228b22`)** — different producer/consumer languages; runtime translates via JSON at the wire. The color is a standing reminder that encode + decode is happening on that hop.
- **Custom-translation hop** — a third distinct color signaling the destination port has a user-written translation spec overriding the default path.
- Branch-routing colors (orange/blue/green from comparator boxes) compose on top — routing kind and language pairing are orthogonal axes the editor must show simultaneously.

**Why:** The runtime treats same-lang and cross-lang hops very differently (dual-ring slot design, issue 312), but pre-245 the editor gave the box author no visual signal that the JSON translation step existed. It was invisible until someone read the dispatch code. Translation cost should be legible from the canvas.

**How to apply:** Any future editor work that touches wire rendering must preserve "color encodes language pairing." Don't propose recoloring schemes that overload the cross-language signal onto another concept. New routing concepts get new axes (line style, glyphs, animation) rather than stealing color. When discussing wire visuals, name both axes — routing kind AND language pairing — even if only one is changing.

```

### project_encapsulated_map.md

```markdown
---
name: Encapsulated map as box
description: A sub-map opens as a single box on a parent canvas. Data boxes marked externally-supplied become input ports; write boxes marked externally-consumed become output ports. The documented exception to single-output-per-box (issue 248, amended 2026-05-23)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**A map directory has two ways to be opened:** as the top-level graph (existing map-select UI), or as an **encapsulated box** on the currently-edited parent map (issue 248). Opening through the file browser while a parent map is open instantiates the sub-map as a single box on the parent's canvas.

**The encapsulation contract — symmetric input and output toggles:**
- **Inputs:** any `data` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-supplied" in its inspector. Each such box becomes a typed input port on the encapsulated box.
- **Outputs:** any `write` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-consumed" in its inspector. Each such box surfaces as a **distinct output port** on the encapsulated box. A write box with the toggle on can still write to its `path` if one is set — the file destination and the parent-wire destination are independent.

**Encapsulated maps are the documented exception to issue 218's "single output per box" rule.** They have *N* output ports — one per externally-consumed write box, where *N* may be zero (pure side-effect map), one, or many. Every other box kind still has exactly one output.

**Rejected earlier design (2026-05-21):** packing all write-box outputs into a single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, single wire out. Rejected 2026-05-23 because it would have repurposed file-writing machinery to emit strings into wires — substituting one mechanism for another. The symmetric toggle design preserves the `write` box's "terminate a value" semantics and treats the destination kind as a mode toggle.

**Why:** Encapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph. The parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals — it sees declared input ports, declared output ports, and known semantics. Sub-maps can be edited independently, reused across parents, and packaged once for distribution. This is the closest SoraMech gets to "user-defined functions" while staying graph-native.

**How to apply:** When discussing map composition, reuse, or "how do users build libraries of behavior" — encapsulation is the answer. Don't propose alternative function-abstraction mechanisms (named subgraphs as text references, macro-style inlining, blob-packed outputs) without explicitly weighing them against the symmetric-toggle shape. Both toggles (`externally-supplied` on data boxes, `externally-consumed` on write boxes) are the user-facing port-declaration mechanism — don't invent a separate "ports manifest" file.

```

### project_soramech.md

```markdown
---
name: SoraMech project context
description: Core architecture decisions, file layout, and execution model for SoraMech, across phase 2 (current) and phase 3 (designed)
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
SoraMech is a visual FSM/dataflow editor and execution engine at /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/.

**Why:** Primary use case is LLM orchestration on the SoraMind Alpine cluster. Strings flow between boxes like variables. History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.

**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**
- `src/006-server-main.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy. No runner management.
- Runner — phase 2: `src/007-runner-main.lua` (synchronous Lua). Phase 3: `soramech-pool` (C binary, designed in issues 301–311, not yet built).
- `assets/index.html` — vanilla JS canvas editor. Editor only — no run button. Compile button (issue 222) is a phase 2 placeholder; it triggers the phase 3 build pipeline (issue 219).

**Key architecture decisions (current truth):**
- Each box is its own JSON file in `boxes/<id>.json`. Connections written to BOTH endpoint files; loader validates both ends agree — hard error if not.
- **Single output wire per box** (issue 218 complete). No `outputs` array. The function returns one value; routing is by `from_branch` on the connection.
- **Comparator-based branching** (issue 210) — replaces the earlier `branch` box kind with named ports. A box may carry a `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires `lt`/`eq`/`gt` connections. No spec is invoked for comparators.
- **Iterator boxes** (issue 221) — pure routing primitives, no `ref`/`fn`. Dispatch layer cycles through `iterator_outputs` based on a per-task counter.
- **Phase 2 drivers** are shell scripts under `drivers/` (one process per call, stdout as channel). **Phase 3 language specs** are `.so` libraries under `langs/<name>/spec.so` loaded via `dlopen` (issue 303). Lua and C are in-process; Bash is out-of-process via Unix domain socket.
- Data files: per-map JSON in `data/`. Section-level `constant` flag. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.
- State/ephemeral: `tmp/` is a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Phase 2 writes `last-run.json` (single doc). Phase 3 writes `last-run.jsonl` (JSON Lines, issue 311) — decoupled from the editor, consumed by LLMs / CLI viewers / test harness.
- **Phase 3 runtime model**: C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool; per-task slots in process heap (issue 302) with refcounting and a separate large-value heap; dispatch layer (304) is the worker action; graph loader is C (305), no embedded Lua at the runner level. Phase 2's synchronous executor retires when phase 3 lands.

**How to apply:** When working on any component, respect the three-way separation. Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server. Map directory format is the only shared contract. The phase 2 driver model and the phase 3 spec model coexist conceptually (phase 2 is current, phase 3 is fully designed) but the runtime mechanism differs entirely; box JSON and the editor are unchanged across the cutover.

```

### project_threading.md

```markdown
---
name: threading_model
description: SoraMech's threading model — phase 2 synchronous, phase 3 SoraMech-owned C thread pool with per-port slots and language specs
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
**Phase 2 (current)**: synchronous executor in `src/004-executor.lua`. Single-threaded, sequential box execution. One driver shell-out per box call. The phase 2 path goes away when phase 3 lands — no fallback, no coroutine intermediate.

**Phase 3 (designed, not yet built)**: C pool runner with a SoraMech-owned thread pool. The 3d-rts pool at `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` is the **design reference**, not vendored — SoraMech owns its pool implementation so the spawn primitive, worker context, init barrier, and iterator-pinning extensions are all under our control. The architecture is fully specified across issues 301–313.

Key phase 3 concepts:
- **Per-input-port slots** (not per-task), allocated at graph load and durable for the run. Each slot is a ring buffer (`n_cells` cells of `cell_capacity` bytes). 1-cell slots use peek-not-drain (literals, single-push wires); N-cell slots use pop-and-drain (queued / multi-push wires). No per-slot refcounting — slot lifetime is the whole run.
- **Tasks are ephemeral**: spawned dynamically by the dispatch layer when a box's input set is ready. Tasks carry just `box_id` and a counter snapshot. Box state (counter, input slots, language handle) is durable.
- **Language specs** under `langs/<name>/spec.so`, loaded via `dlopen` at startup. Uniform `lang_spec_t`. No language is privileged.
- **Same-language fast path** (issue 312): wire format defaults to JSON, but two adjacent same-language boxes use the language's native serialization (Lua `lua_dump`, C struct memcpy). Compile-time wire classification picks the path.
- **In-process specs** (Lua, C) via `lua_pcall` / `dlsym`. **Out-of-process specs** (Bash) via Unix domain sockets to a persistent per-worker subprocess.
- **Dispatch layer** (304) is the worker-side action: pop inputs → branch on box mode → invoke spec → push to downstream input slots → end. No blocking, no wait lists; tasks spawn on input arrival and run to completion.
- **Iterator and comparator routing** in the dispatch layer. Comparator runs the function and routes by output value. Iterator skips the function and routes by per-box counter (atomic spawn-time increment). Iterator tasks parallelize across workers; ordering preserved via per-push counter tags on consumer slots.
- **No-null rule** (issue 230): every input port must be wired, given a literal, or marked optional. Compile fails on missing inputs.
- **Init barrier**: pool startup waits until every worker has run every spec's `init(worker_idx)` before submitting tasks. Avoids tasks landing on uninitialized handles.
- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program.
- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations tie up a worker. Pool size is the budget. Cooperative split (kickoff + check-done iterator) avoids holding a worker. See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.

**Effil is explicitly NOT used.** Coroutines are not used. The C pool is the chosen mechanism. 3d-rts is referenced as design inspiration, not vendored.

**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC: phase 2 is synchronous shell-out drivers; phase 3 is the SoraMech-owned C pool runner with `lang_spec_t`, per-port slot stores, and dispatch-layer routing. Never suggest effil. 3d-rts is a reference, not a dependency. Issues 301–313 carry the design.

```

  "message":{
    "content":"hello claude. Today, we're going to close out every single one of these issues. Then, we're going to go through the completed issue files one by one, and justify their existence. If they cannot be justified, they will be updated until they match the correct design. Then, we will hand them off to another project who will attempt to re-create what we've built from scratch using only the issue files as a guide. If they succeed, we will know that our issue files are in the correct format. If they fail, then either they did not fill in the gaps between issue files correctly, or the issue files are too clunky, obfuscated by technical details, or weighted down by development inertia that is of no use to a set of fresh eyes, and is simply there to justify our actions. Not ideal. In any of those cases, we should attempt to re-write the issue files until the design is solid. The issue files are the product, the source-code and implementation is just how we prove that it works.",
    "role":"user"
  },
  "permissionMode":"default"
}
```

    "content":"- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors (\"from now on when X\", \"each time X\", \"whenever X\", \"before/after X\") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions (\"allow X\", \"add permission\", \"move permission to\"), env vars (\"set X=Y\"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: \"allow npm commands\", \"add bq permission to global settings\", \"move permission to user settings\", \"set DEBUG=true\", \"when claude stops show X\". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.\n- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: \"rebind ctrl+s\", \"add a chord shortcut\", \"change the submit key\", \"customize keybindings\".\n- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.\n- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.\n- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. \"check the deploy every 5 minutes\", \"keep running /babysit-prs\"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.\n- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run (\"run this once at 3pm\", \"remind me to check X tomorrow\").\n- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).\nTRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.\nSKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.\n- frontend-design:frontend-design: Create distinctive, production-grade frontend interfaces with high design quality. Use this skill when the user asks to build web components, pages, or applications. Generates creative, polished code that avoids generic AI aesthetics.\n- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation\n- review: Review a pull request\n- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch",
    "skillCount":11
  }
}

      "content":"# 217 — Variadic ports and the language-spec variadic shape\n\n## Status\nopen — Part A and Part B mechanics are in the codebase; Part C is\nthe active design question\n\n## What this issue is now\n\nThe original issue was titled \"Concat box with per-input variadic\nports and auto-grow/shrink.\" That framing has aged out:\n\n- There is no dedicated **concat box kind**. `M.concat(sep, ...)`\n  lives in `libs/text.lua` and is invoked by any call box that\n  imports it. The variadic UI work was never specific to concat.\n- The original \"split returns a JSON-encoded array on the single\n  output wire\" story was a phase-2 transport assumption. Phase 3\n  (issue 312, same-language wire fast path) classifies each edge\n  and only JSON-encodes when crossing a language boundary. So\n  `M.split` returning a Lua array is correct in-language and the\n  runtime bridges if the downstream box is a different language.\n\nThe issue is now about the **editor's variadic-port mechanic** and\nhow it interacts with the **language spec** — specifically, what\nthe editor's `var` toggle means and what governs whether it's\noffered.\n\n## Part A — `libs/text.lua` *(shipped)*\n\n`libs/text.lua` ships `M.concat(sep, ...)`, `M.split(text, sep)`,\nand (via issue 237) `upper`, `lower`, `trim`, `replace`,\n`replace_first`, `contains`, `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `length`,\n`substring`. All are pure string operations consumed by call\nboxes; no special box kind exists.\n\n`M.split` is most useful paired with the iterator box (issue 221)\nso each part fans out to its own dispatch. Without the iterator\nit's just \"an array on a wire\" — legitimate but flat.\n\n## Part B — Editor variadic data model *(shipped)*\n\nA box JSON can carry a `variadic_inputs` array of base names; slots\nare stored as `<base>_<index>` in the `inputs` array. The inspector\n(`assets/js/004-inspector.js`) implements:\n\n- `make_variadic(port_name)` — turn a plain port into a one-slot\n  variadic group (`text` → `text_0`).\n- `unmake_variadic(base)` — collapse back to a single port.\n- `add_variadic_slot(base)` — append `<base>_<last+1>` (auto-grow).\n- `remove_variadic_slot(slot_name)` — delete and renumber.\n- `auto_grow_after_set(box, slot_name)` — append a new empty slot\n  when the user uses the current last slot.\n\nAuto-grow triggers on wire-connect and on value-set. Shrinking is\nexplicit-only — `×` button per slot. Wire-disconnect and value-\nclear do **not** shrink, deliberately, so transient editing\ndoesn't lose structure.\n\nThe schema (`src/001-schema.lua`) accepts `variadic_inputs` as an\noptional array of strings.\n\n## Part C — What `var` actually means *(active design)*\n\n### Wrong model (rejected)\n\nThe earlier framing said: regex-parse each source file in the\neditor, mark functions whose signatures end in `...` / `\"$@\"` /\n`va_list` as \"variadic-capable,\" and gate the `var` toggle on\nthat per-function flag.\n\nThat model collapses on contact with the project's vision:\n\n1. **It's not a per-function fact.** Every Lua function accepts N\n   positional args. `function f(a)` called with five args silently\n   keeps the first; `...` in the signature is the *author's choice\n   to capture extras*, not a runtime constraint. Bash is the same\n   — every function gets `\"$@\"` whether it touches it or not. C\n   through the dispatch wrapper (issue 304) is the same —\n   `argc`/`argv` is the universal call shape.\n2. **It centralises language knowledge in the editor.** Per-\n   language regex parsers in the editor are exactly the\n   ossification the `langs/<name>/` model exists to prevent.\n   Adding a new language would mean writing a new regex.\n3. **It locks the editor to a static source view.** A function the\n   user is in the middle of editing might briefly not have `...`\n   in the signature; the editor would flicker the toggle on/off.\n\n### Right model: variadic shape is a language fact\n\nThe language declares its calling-convention shape once, in\n`langs/<name>/spec.js`:\n\n```js\nexport const LANGUAGE_SPEC = {\n  name: 'lua',\n  file_ext: '.lua',\n  variadic_shape: 'positional',\n};\n```\n\n`variadic_shape: 'positional'` means the language accepts N\npositional args at call time, period. Every shipped language today\n(Lua, Bash, C) declares this. Future languages with different\nshapes (Python `**kwargs`, streaming generators, tagged unions)\ndeclare their own shape — the editor's variadic UI eventually\ngrows variants for them, but `positional` covers everything we\nship.\n\nA language that genuinely cannot accept variadic input declares\n`variadic_shape: 'none'`, and the editor disables the `var` toggle\nfor all its boxes. We don't have one of those today.\n\n### Editor behaviour under this model\n\n- The `var` toggle on a port is gated by **language**, not by\n  function. For every Lua / Bash / C box today, the toggle is\n  available.\n- The user is responsible for matching wired arity to the\n  function's intent. The editor surfaces what the source declares\n  (via `parser.js`'s named parameters) so the user can see the\n  arity the author wrote. If they wire five inputs to a function\n  whose body only reads the first, that's a user choice — same\n  class as wiring a string into a port the function treats as a\n  number. The runtime doesn't police it.\n- Compile-time (issue 309) and validator (issue 002) checks\n  surface obvious mismatches as documentation, not as gates.\n\n### What `parser.js` does and doesn't do\n\n`langs/<name>/parser.js` continues to enumerate functions in a\nsource file and extract named parameter and return names. That\nfeeds the file browser. It does **not** compute any per-function\nvariadic property — the early `variadic_tail` field was removed\nin this issue's pass.\n\n### Implementation status\n\n- `langs/lua/spec.js`, `langs/bash/spec.js`, `langs/c/spec.js` —\n  shipped. Each exports `LANGUAGE_SPEC` with `variadic_shape:\n  'positional'`.\n- `langs/lua/parser.js`, `langs/bash/parser.js` — shipped without\n  `variadic_tail`. Still produce inputs/outputs for the file\n  browser.\n- `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` — shipped. Asserts every\n  spec.js exports a valid `LANGUAGE_SPEC` with a known\n  `variadic_shape`.\n- Inspector consumption of `LANGUAGE_SPEC.variadic_shape` —\n  **not yet wired**. Today the `var` toggle is offered\n  unconditionally; the gate-by-language step is the remaining\n  work.\n\n### Remaining work\n\n1. `assets/js/004-inspector.js::mk_port_display` — load the active\n   box's language spec (the same dynamic-import pattern used for\n   lexers), and hide the `var` button when\n   `variadic_shape !== 'positional'`. Today every shipped language\n   is positional, so this is a future-proofing step rather than a\n   visible change.\n2. Inspector renders the parsed signature near the box header so\n   the user always sees the function's declared arity. This is the\n   documentation half of the design — replaces the rejected \"gate\n   the toggle per function\" approach with \"show the arity, let the\n   user judge.\"\n3. Update `docs/005-language-specs.md` with a \"language spec for\n   the editor\" section pointing at `spec.js` as the canonical\n   home for editor-facing language facts (variadic shape, future\n   additions).\n\n## Future development ideas\n\n### Variadic shapes that aren't `positional`\n\n- `keyed` — Python `**kwargs`, Ruby keyword splats. Slot model is\n  `(key, value)` pairs, user labels per slot, not auto-numbered.\n- `tagged` — Rust enum lists, Haskell heterogeneous lists. Per-\n  slot `(tag, value)`.\n- `stream` — generators, channels, iterators. One slot, queued.\n  Closer to issue 213's queued-input model than to positional\n  variadic.\n\nEach shape has its own auto-grow rule and inspector controls. The\nlanguage spec declares which shape applies; the editor renders\naccordingly. None of these are shipped — the positional shape\ncovers every language so far. Captured here so the design door\nstays open.\n\n### Outputs\n\nThe single-output rule (issue 218) is unchanged. Variadic is an\ninput-side concern.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `libs/text.lua` — Part A library functions\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — Part B variadic mechanics, future\n  home for the spec-driven `var` gate\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — accepts `variadic_inputs`\n- `langs/lua/spec.js`, `langs/bash/spec.js`, `langs/c/spec.js` —\n  the language-level `variadic_shape` declarations\n- `langs/lua/parser.js`, `langs/bash/parser.js` — function\n  enumeration (no per-function variadic detection)\n- `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` — spec.js contract tests\n- `issues/231-move-signature-parsers-into-langs.md` — moved\n  signature parsing into `langs/<name>/parser.js`\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — supersedes the\n  old \"JSON-encode every wire\" story Part A was framed against\n- `issues/221-iterator-box.md` — the canonical companion to\n  `M.split` for fan-out\n",

      "content":"# 232 — Test coverage map\n\n## Status\nongoing (test inventory; updated each time tests are added or\nremoved)\n\n## Why this exists\n\nThis issue is the project-wide answer to \"what's tested, what\nisn't, and what runs the tests.\" It folds together two earlier\nthreads:\n\n- **316** (now folded in here) — a cheap, build-free unit-test\n  runner script. Its scope lives under \"Test runners → Planned\"\n  below.\n- The parser-test work that opened this issue (Node-side tests\n  for `langs/<name>/parser.js`).\n\nA related but separate issue is **311** — phase-3 integration\ntests and the JSONL run-output format. 311's scope is the JSONL\nwriter + the `tests/maps/<name>/` fixtures driven through\n`soramech-pool`; the coverage of those fixtures shows up in the\n\"End-to-end fixtures\" section below, but the writer/format work\nstays in 311.\n\nWithout a coverage view, gaps accumulate silently: tests get\nwritten for the area someone happens to be touching, and the rest\ndrifts uncovered. The checklist below is that view, updated every\ntime tests are added or removed.\n\nEvery time a new test file lands or a test gap is closed, the\nchecklist below is updated. When a new module is added, a row goes\ninto the appropriate section showing it has no coverage yet.\n\n## How to read the table\n\n- `[x]` — has a dedicated test file (path in the row).\n- `[ ]` — no dedicated test; may be exercised indirectly through\n  integration fixtures, but not directly verified.\n- `[~]` — partially covered; only some surface area is tested.\n- `[—]` — intentionally untested (vendored library, thin entrypoint, etc.).\n\n## Editor side — JavaScript\n\nThe editor is a browser app served by `src/005-http-server.lua`.\nNo JS test runner was wired up before the work that opened this\nissue; the parser tests introduced one (Node's built-in\n`node:test`). Other JS modules can follow the same pattern when\nthey get tests.\n\n| Module | Coverage | Test file |\n|---|---|---|\n| `langs/lua/parser.js` | `[x]` | `tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs` |\n| `langs/bash/parser.js` | `[x]` | `tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs` |\n| `langs/c/parser.js` | `[—]` | not written yet; issue 231 makes it optional |\n| `langs/lua/spec.js` | `[x]` | `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` |\n| `langs/bash/spec.js` | `[x]` | `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` |\n| `langs/c/spec.js` | `[x]` | `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` |\n| `langs/lua/lexer.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `langs/bash/lexer.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `langs/c/lexer.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/001-canvas.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/002-boxes.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/003-api.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/004-inspector.js` | `[ ]` | — (variadic helpers are pure functions, prime unit-test candidates) |\n| `assets/js/005-app.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/006-wires.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/007-filebrowser.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `assets/js/008-source-view.js` | `[ ]` | — |\n\nHighest-value next targets: the variadic-slot helpers in\n`004-inspector.js` (pure functions, no DOM dependency, directly\nconsumed by issue 217's Part C inspector gate) and the lexer\nregistries in the language directories.\n\n## Lua libraries — `libs/*.lua`\n\n| Module | Coverage | Test file |\n|---|---|---|\n| `libs/soramech-data.lua` | `[x]` | `tests/003-data-test.lua` |\n| `libs/text.lua` | `[ ]` | — (issue 237 expanded the surface: concat, split, upper, lower, trim, replace, replace_first, contains, starts_with, ends_with, length, substring) |\n| `libs/files.lua` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `libs/ollama.lua` | `[—]` | requires a live Ollama endpoint; integration-level only |\n| `libs/dkjson.lua` | `[—]` | vendored third-party |\n\n`libs/text.lua` is the most important gap — every function is a\npure string operation with obvious edge cases (empty input, nil\ninput, no match, plain vs. pattern), exactly the shape unit tests\ncatch best.\n\n## Lua server side — `src/*.lua`\n\n| Module | Coverage | Test file |\n|---|---|---|\n| `src/001-schema.lua` | `[ ]` | — (validates box JSON; deserves direct accept/reject tests) |\n| `src/002-validate-map.lua` | `[ ]` | — (CLI map validator; only exercised via integration fixtures) |\n| `src/003-loader.lua` | `[ ]` | — |\n| `src/004-executor.lua` | `[~]` | exercised end-to-end via `tests/004-driver-test-runner.lua` and integration maps; no unit-level coverage |\n| `src/005-http-server.lua` | `[ ]` | — (GET/PUT boxes, connections, files, source) |\n| `src/006-server-main.lua` | `[—]` | thin entrypoint |\n| `src/007-runner-main.lua` | `[—]` | thin entrypoint |\n\nSchema and validator are the highest-value gaps — they are the\nlast line of defense against malformed map files and they're pure\nfunctions over JSON-shaped tables, very testable.\n\n## C runtime — `src/*.c`\n\nBest-covered area of the project; The single entry\n  point for \"run everything the build doesn't run.\" Folds Node-test\n  results into the same pass/fail counter as the integration checks.\n- `make test` — builds the C unit-test binaries, runs them, then\n  invokes `scripts/run-tests.sh`.\n\n### Planned — `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh` (folded in from issue 316)\n\nA cheap, build-free runner for the C unit-test binaries. `make\ntest` builds and runs everything; that's fine for \"ship it\"\nverification, awkward as a development loop:\n\n- The build phase prints `→ src/foo.c` for every file, dozens of\n  lines before the first test runs on a clean tree.\n- Tests run inside a Make recipe; one binary failing aborts the\n  recipe, so later binaries that would have run aren't reported.\n- Unit-test and integration-test output interleave in one stream.\n\nGoals for the new script:\n\n1. **Cheap.** No make recursion, no spec rebuilds, no integration\n   tests. Under a second on a current build.\n2. **Continues past failures.** Every binary runs; summary at the\n   bottom names what went wrong.\n3. **Pretty by default, mineable on request.** Per-binary one-line\n   status by default; `--quiet` prints only totals; `--verbose`\n   dumps each binary's full output.\n4. **Filterable.** `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh 009` runs only\n   binaries whose names start with `009`.\n\nConcept: glob `build/tests/<name>-test`, sort by filename (which\nsorts by the project's leading numeric index), run each in turn,\ncapture stdout/stderr, parse the binary's trailing\n`N passed, M failed` line for the verdict.\n\nOutput shape:\n```\n  009-slot-store-test                          16 / 16  ok\n  010-graph-loader-test                        13 / 13  ok\n  015-large-value-heap-test                     8 /  8  ok\n  ...\n  113 / 113 tests passed (14 binaries)\n```\n\nA failing binary prints its captured output below the summary\nline. Exit code is zero iff every binary passes; non-zero with the\ncount of failing binaries otherwise.\n\nConvention compliance per CLAUDE.md: hard-coded `${DIR}` at top\nwith arg override, all paths under `${DIR}`, each shell command on\nits own line, lives at `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh`.\n\nOpen question (from 316): should the script warn when a binary's\nsource is newer than the binary? Cheap (`stat` both sides), but\nthe default should be \"just run what's built\" — offer it as\n`--check-stale`.\n\n### Implementation steps for the new runner\n1. Write `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh` with the layout above.\n2. Verify it picks up every existing `build/tests/*-test` binary\n   and produces the expected totals.\n3. Verify `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh 015` filters to one binary.\n4. Verify `--quiet` and `--verbose` produce useful output.\n5. Provoke a failure (temporarily modify one test) and confirm\n   the failure is reported, exit code non-zero, captured output\n   visible.\n6. Add a `make quicktest` alias or document the script in the\n   Makefile's `help` target.\n\n## Suggested next test additions (ranked)\n\n1. **`libs/text.lua`** — pure-Lua tests next to\n   `tests/003-data-test.lua`. Issue 237's expansion left a wide\n   untested surface and consumers (issue 217 part C, issue 224)\n   are about to multiply.\n2. **`src/001-schema.lua`** — accept/reject tests for box JSON.\n   Cheap, and the schema gates everything the executor sees.\n3. **Inspector variadic helpers** (`assets/js/004-inspector.js`) —\n   `parse_variadic_name`, `is_variadic_slot`, `variadic_slots_for`,\n   `last_variadic_index`, `make_variadic`, `unmake_variadic`,\n   `add_variadic_slot`, `remove_variadic_slot`. All pure, all\n   feeding into the part-C work.\n4. **Lexer round-trips** for the three shipped languages — feed a\n   known source through `tokenize`, check the token stream.\n5. **`langs/c/parser.js`** — write it and its tests together when\n   issue 231 commits to a C parser.\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### 2026-05-19 — parser tests + Node runner integration\n\n`tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs` and `tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs`\nadded under Node's built-in `node:test`. They run via\n`scripts/run-tests.sh`, which gained a `parser_tests()` section\nthat calls `SORAMECH_DIR=\"$DIR\" node --test \"$tf\"` for each file\nand folds the result into the existing pass/fail summary.\n\n`SORAMECH_DIR=...` overrides the project root when running outside\nthe default install path. Argv would collide with `node --test`'s\nfile-list parsing, so an env var is the right channel.\n\nVerified failure detection by temporarily inverting a parser\ncheck — the relevant test failed as expected and the failure\nsurfaced through the shell runner.\n\n### 2026-05-19 — language-spec test, variadic_tail retired\n\nThe earlier pass added a `variadic_tail` field to both parsers\nalong with assertions in the parser tests. That model — per-\nfunction detection of variadic capability by source regex — was\nfundamentally wrong for the project's vision (every shipped\nlanguage already accepts N positional args at call time; \"is this\nfunction variadic\" is a question the runtime doesn't care about).\nSee issue 217's rewrite for the full reasoning.\n\nThe fix in this pass:\n\n- `variadic_tail` removed from `langs/lua/parser.js` and\n  `langs/bash/parser.js`. The parsers still extract named\n  parameters and outputs; the `...` token is still stripped from\n  inputs so the editor shows only named ports.\n- `tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs` and\n  `tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs` had their variadic_tail\n  assertions removed; they now lock the trimmed contract.\n- `langs/lua/spec.js`, `langs/bash/spec.js`, `langs/c/spec.js` —\n  new. Each exports `LANGUAGE_SPEC` with `variadic_shape:\n  'positional'`. This is the canonical home for editor-facing\n  language metadata.\n- `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` — new. Asserts every\n  spec.js exports a valid `LANGUAGE_SPEC` with a known\n  `variadic_shape`.\n\n10 / 10 passing in the full runner.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — the integration + JS test driver\n- `tests/232-lua-parser-test.mjs`, `tests/233-bash-parser-test.mjs`\n- `issues/completed/311-integration-tests-and-run-output.md` if\n  closed by then, otherwise `issues/311-…` — phase-3 integration\n  tests and JSONL format. ```json
{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"257d51a0-7788-4512-a6d0-192577054f1a",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-20T19:07:15.531Z",

  "toolUseResult":{
    "type":"text",
    "file":{
      "content":"# 233 — Unified `routing` schema for branching boxes\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Concept\n\nA \"branching box\" is a regular call box whose output, after the\nfunction runs, is sent to **one of several** downstream\ndestinations rather than to all of them. Same function, same\ninputs, same output value — only the routing decision differs.\nCurrently we have two flavors:\n\n- **Comparator**: routes the function's output by comparing it\n  to a stored threshold. Three fixed branches (`lt` / `eq` /\n  `gt`).\n- **Iterator**: routes the function's output to one of N branches\n  in round-robin fashion, advancing a counter on every call.\n\nThe two are the same shape (function runs → output gets routed)\nwith different rules for picking the branch. The current schema\nhas them as separate top-level fields (`comparand` and\n`iterator_outputs`), which makes them look like unrelated\nfeatures. They aren't.\n\n(For \"send the same value to multiple destinations,\" the user\njust pulls multiple wires out of a single output port — fan-out\nalready works on plain call boxes. No routing decision needed.)\n\n### Branch-level fan-out\n\nFan-out applies on a per-branch basis even for branched boxes. If\nthe comparator's `lt` port has three wires going to three\ndifferent consumers, then each time the routing decision picks\n`lt`, all three wires receive the value (a copy is pushed into\neach consumer's input slot). On a subsequent invocation that\npicks `eq`, only the wires hanging off the `eq` port fire.\n\nEach branch port acts like its own little plain-call output port\nwhen it fires. The routing decision picks **which branch** fires;\nthe branch's own fan-out picks **which consumers** receive the\nvalue when it does.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEvery call box carries a `routing` field. No implicit defaulting:\nplain boxes have `routing: { \"kind\": \"plain\" }`, the same way\nbranched boxes carry their own kind. Explicit and consistent —\nno \"what if I forget the routing field\" surprises at validation\ntime.\n\n```json\n{ \"id\": \"plain-call\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"...\", \"fn\": \"...\",\n  \"inputs\": [...],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" } }\n\n{ \"id\": \"score-router\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"src/score.lua\", \"fn\": \"score\",\n  \"inputs\": [...],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"comparator\", \"comparand\": 4 } }\n\n{ \"id\": \"round-robin\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"src/dispatch_msg.lua\", \"fn\": \"dispatch_msg\",\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"iterator\", \"n_outputs\": 3 } }\n```\n\nRouting kinds defined in this design: `plain`, `comparator`,\n`iterator`, `randomizer`, `weighted`, `distributor`. Of those,\n**this issue ships `plain`, `comparator`, and `iterator` only**\n— that's the surface area already in production, just unified\nunder one schema. The other three (`randomizer`, `weighted`,\n`distributor`) are designed below for context but split into\ntheir own follow-on issue files when this one is implemented, so\neach ships independently.\n\nThe `routing.kind` field picks which dispatch-layer rule decides\nthe branch. Schema validates the kind value and the kind-specific\nparameters together.\n\n**The function always runs**, regardless of routing kind. The\nfunction produces the value; routing decides where the value\ngoes.\n\n### kind=\"plain\"\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n```\n\nOne output port. The function's output value fans to every wire\nattached to that port unconditionally. No routing decision; the\ndispatch layer skips the branch picker and pushes to all wires.\n\nThis is the default for new boxes; the editor sets it\nautomatically when a box is created.\n\n### kind=\"comparator\"\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"comparator\", \"comparand\": \"<number>\" }\n```\n\nThree output ports: `lt`, `eq`, `gt` (fixed names; ports aren't\nrenameable per the editor's port-immutability rule). The\nfunction's output value is compared to `comparand`; the matching\nbranch fires.\n\n#### Multi-band comparator (planned brainstorm)\n\nThe current 3-branch lt/eq/gt design is a special case of \"value\nfalls into a numeric range, fire the corresponding branch.\" A\ngeneralization:\n\n```json\n\"routing\": {\n  \"kind\": \"comparator\",\n  \"thresholds\": [3, 7, 11, 17]\n}\n```\n\nFive output ports get named by the threshold positions —\n`below_3`, `between_3_7`, `between_7_11`, `between_11_17`,\n`above_17`. With `thresholds: [4]` this becomes the current\n3-branch lt/eq/gt (with `eq` being \"exactly 4\"), so the legacy\nshape is one configuration of the new one.\n\n**Equality bands via doubled thresholds.** Encode the current\n`eq` semantics by repeating a threshold value: `thresholds: [3, 3]`\nmeans \"less than 3, exactly 3, greater than 3\" — three bands, the\nmiddle one being a zero-width point that fires only on exact\nequality. With `thresholds: [3, 3, 7, 7]` you get five bands:\n`< 3`, `== 3`, `3 < x < 7`, `== 7`, `> 7`. The editor sees a\nlist of thresholds; the runtime sees doubled values as\n\"point bands.\"\n\nThis means the legacy 3-branch lt/eq/gt is exactly\n`thresholds: [c, c]` — the eq case is just a zero-width band at\nthe comparand. Behind the scenes the editor can present the\nsingle-comparand UI but store `[c, c]` so the dispatch layer has\none consistent representation.\n\nDefer the schema specifics — the single-comparand case ships\nfirst; multi-band is a follow-on once we have a use case that\nactually needs more than three.\n\n### kind=\"iterator\"\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"iterator\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n```\n\n`n_outputs` output ports, named conventionally (`out_0`, `out_1`,\n…). Every invocation reads the box's `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot\nvia `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)`; that index picks\nthe branch.\n\nThe function still runs and produces the routed value. Iterator\ndefaults the function to a passthrough identity if the user\nhasn't picked a `ref` / `fn` — but the user is free to attach\nany function whose output should be round-robin-distributed.\n\n### kind=\"randomizer\"\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"randomizer\", \"n_outputs\": 4 }\n```\n\nPicks a branch uniformly at random per invocation.\nImplementation: hash the counter-slot value into the branch\nindex, so the distribution is deterministic-given-seed but\nspread across branches.\n\n```c\nuint32_t i = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, UINT32_MAX);\nuint32_t branch = hash(i) % n_outputs;\n```\n\n`hash` is a cheap mixing function (xorshift, FNV); not\ncryptographic. The point is breaking up the monotonic counter so\nconsecutive calls don't go to consecutive branches.\n\n### kind=\"weighted\"\n\n```json\n\"routing\": {\n  \"kind\":    \"weighted\",\n  \"weights\": [0.8, 0.2]\n}\n```\n\nProbability-based distribution. With `[0.8, 0.2]` and two output\nports, 80% of invocations fire branch 0, 20% fire branch 1.\n\nImplementation: at compile time, weights are normalized into a\ncumulative table on a `0..PRECISION-1` integer scale (e.g.\n`PRECISION = 1000`). Per call:\n\n```c\nuint32_t r = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, PRECISION);\n// pre-computed cumulative: [0..799] → branch 0, [800..999] → branch 1\nuint32_t branch = lookup_band(r, cumulative_table);\n```\n\nSame counter-slot machinery as iterator and randomizer; the\ndifference is the mapping from counter to branch.\n\n**Inspector UI for weighted routing**: a horizontal slider with\nN knobs dividing it into N+1 segments — except really N segments\nsince each knob is the boundary between adjacent segments. A\nwider segment means a larger fraction of invocations flow down\nthat path. Below the slider, one line per output port:\n\n```\nout_0    [▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓░░░░░░░░░░░░]    80%\nout_1    [░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░▓▓▓▓]    20%\n```\n\nEach line shows the output port name on the left, a visual band\nin the middle indicating its slice of the distribution, and the\npercentage on the right. Adjusting the slider knobs updates the\npercentages live; the percentages are also editable directly\n(typing `30` into the right column shifts the relevant knob).\n\n### kind=\"distributor\" (load-aware)\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"distributor\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n```\n\nSends the value to the **least-busy** downstream consumer:\ninspects the fill levels of the input slots wired to each branch\nand picks the branch whose downstream slot has the fewest queued\nvalues.\n\nImplementation: dispatch action peeks the `tail - head` count on\neach downstream input slot and picks the minimum. Tied branches\nfall back to atomic-counter round-robin so ties don't always go\nto the same branch.\n\nThis is the only routing kind that's not purely\nself-contained — it reads downstream slot state — but it doesn't\nadd any new dispatch-layer concept beyond querying slot fill\n(which the slot store already knows).\n\n### Future kinds\n\nThe pattern is: any new routing kind plugs in at one place\n(`routing.kind` value + dispatch-layer branch picker). All\nexisting kinds and any future ones live entirely in the dispatch\nlayer + slot store + editor — never in language specs, never in\nuser-written functions.\n\n## Iterator + function: ships as \"function always runs\"\n\nIterator boxes always run their function. The dispatch action\nbecomes uniform across routing kinds:\n\n```\n1. Read inputs (pop / peek per port mode).\n2. Invoke spec (always — function runs regardless of routing kind).\n3. Pick branch via routing.kind:\n     comparator   → compare(output, comparand)\n     iterator     → slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)\n     randomizer   → hash(slot_read_inc(counter_slot, MAX)) % n_outputs\n     weighted     → cumulative lookup\n     distributor  → argmin(downstream fill)\n     (no routing) → fan to all outgoing wires\n4. Push function output to outputs[picked branch] (or all wires if\n   no routing).\n```\n\nA single dispatch path for all branching boxes; the routing rule\nplugs into step 3.\n\n## Schema migration\n\nFew enough existing maps that we can hand-migrate them. The\nloader does **not** carry a legacy-shape adapter; once this\nships, all map files are expected to use the `routing` field. If\na map with the old shape is opened, the schema validator rejects\nit and the user (or a one-off migration script) updates it.\n\nIf we end up wanting a one-off script, it walks `maps/<name>/boxes/*.json`\nand rewrites:\n- `comparand: X` → `routing: { kind: \"comparator\", comparand: X }`\n- `iterator_outputs: [...]` → `routing: { kind: \"iterator\", n_outputs: len(...) }`\n- everything else → no change\n\nBut for the current map count, manual edits are faster than\nwriting the script.\n\n## Inspector UI\n\nA `routing` selector in the inspector replaces the separate\n`compare` toggle and `iterator` toggle. The dropdown's options\nexpand as new routing kinds ship:\n\n```\nmode:    [plain ▾ | comparator | iterator]\n```\n\nPer-kind controls below the dropdown — for the kinds shipped in\nthis issue:\n- **plain**: nothing extra.\n- **comparator**: numeric `comparand` input. (Multi-band UI is\n  the brainstorm above, lands in its own issue.)\n- **iterator**: `n_outputs` integer input.\n\nOutput ports re-render to match the routing kind: 1 dot for\nplain, 3 fixed dots (lt/eq/gt) for comparator, N dots for\niterator. Port names follow the routing kind's convention; not\nuser-renameable (issue 224's read-only-port-name rule).\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\nThis issue ships `plain`, `comparator`, and `iterator` only —\nthe existing surface area unified under one schema. The other\nkinds get follow-on issue files (one per kind: randomizer,\nweighted, distributor, multi-band-comparator) opened when this\nissue is implemented.\n\n1. `src/001-schema.lua`: accept `routing` field with `kind` ∈\n   `{plain, comparator, iterator}`; reject legacy `comparand` /\n   `iterator_outputs`. Schema also rejects unknown `kind` values\n   so future kinds gate on their own implementation.\n2. `assets/js/004-inspector.js`: mode dropdown replacing the two\n   toggles; per-kind controls (none for plain, `comparand` input\n   for comparator, `n_outputs` for iterator).\n3. `assets/js/002-boxes.js`: render branches based on\n   `routing.kind`.\n4. `assets/js/006-wires.js`: connection's `from_branch` matches\n   the routing kind's port naming.\n5. Phase 3 dispatch (issue 304): branch on `routing.kind` for the\n   branch-selection step. Three rule paths shipped here; new\n   kinds add their own paths in their own issues.\n\nHand-migrate existing maps before merging. Open the follow-on\nissues for randomizer / weighted / distributor / multi-band\ncomparator at merge time so their designs aren't lost.\n\n## Why now\n\n- Editor inspector keeps gaining toggles per routing kind. A\n  unified mode dropdown scales linearly with kinds; separate\n  toggles don't.\n- Phase 3 dispatch will naturally have a \"select branch\" step;\n  routing it through `routing.kind` is the same code regardless\n  of whether we ship Level B now or refactor later.\n- The new routing kinds (randomizer, weighted, distributor) only\n  make sense in the unified schema. Adding them as separate\n  top-level fields would be unmaintainable.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — schema accepts new field\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — mode dropdown\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — branch rendering\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — branch matching\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — counter slot mechanism\n  used by iterator / randomizer / weighted\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer's branch\n  picker dispatches on `routing.kind`\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Distributor under fan-out**: if a branch wire goes to\n  multiple consumers (fan-out), the \"fill level\" of that branch\n  is ambiguous. Use the max of the consumers' fills, or the sum,\n  or something else. Probably max — the bottleneck is the\n  slowest consumer.\n- **Multi-band comparator threshold edges**: `x == threshold`\n  goes to which side of the cut? Lean toward \"less-than-or-equal\"\n  for consistency. Need to nail down before implementation.\n- **Weighted ties**: floating-point weights summing to `1.0`\n  doesn't always discretize cleanly. Compile-time normalization\n  picks an integer scale (1000) and rounds; the last band\n  absorbs any leftover so the ranges always sum to PRECISION.\n\n## Level C example (deferred)\n\nThe big follow-on after this issue ships is a fully data-driven\nrouter: one dispatch path that reads a small rule expression\nfrom the box JSON and evaluates it. Example shape:\n\n```json\n\"routing\": {\n  \"kind\": \"rules\",\n  \"rules\": [\n    { \"when\": \"output < 3\",                   \"to\": \"small\" },\n    { \"when\": \"output >= 3 and output < 7\",   \"to\": \"medium\" },\n    { \"when\": \"output >= 7\",                  \"to\": \"large\" }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\nThe dispatch layer ships a small expression evaluator (a few\ndozen lines: variables = `output`, `counter`, `fill[i]`;\noperators = comparisons, boolean conjunction, arithmetic). Every\nexisting routing kind reduces to a \"rules\" expression:\n\n- comparator → three rules with `when: output < c / output == c / output > c`\n- iterator → one rule using `counter % N` as the band index\n- randomizer → one rule using `hash(counter) % N`\n- weighted → cumulative-band rules\n\nThe benefit: one code path in dispatch instead of five. Custom\nrouting without writing a spec callback or modifying user\nfunctions. The cost: a small evaluator (still entirely in C, no\nspec involvement).\n\nWorth pursuing once Level B has shipped and we have real maps\nusing the kinds — at that point the consolidation is concrete\nrather than speculative. Open as a separate issue when ready.\n",
      "numLines":418,

The\n109\tfunction's output value is compared to `comparand`; the matching\n110\tbranch fires.\n111\t\n112\t#### Multi-band comparator (planned brainstorm)\n113\t\n114\tThe current 3-branch lt/eq/gt design is a special case of \"value\n115\tfalls into a numeric range, fire the corresponding branch.\" A\n116\tgeneralization:\n117\t\n118\t```json\n119\t\"routing\": {\n120\t  \"kind\": \"comparator\",\n121\t  \"thresholds\": [3, 7, 11, 17]\n122\t}\n123\t```\n124\t\n125\tFive output ports get named by the threshold positions —\n126\t`below_3`, `between_3_7`, `between_7_11`, `between_11_17`,\n127\t`above_17`. With `thresholds: [4]` this becomes the current\n128\t3-branch lt/eq/gt (with `eq` being \"exactly 4\"), so the legacy\n129\tshape is one configuration of the new one.\n130\t\n131\t**Equality bands via doubled thresholds.** Encode the current\n132\t`eq` semantics by repeating a threshold value: `thresholds: [3, 3]`\n133\tmeans \"less than 3, exactly 3, greater than 3\" — three bands, the\n134\tmiddle one being a zero-width point that fires only on exact\n135\tequality. With `thresholds: [3, 3, 7, 7]` you get five bands:\n136\t`< 3`, `== 3`, `3 < x < 7`, `== 7`, `> 7`. The editor sees a\n137\tlist of thresholds; the runtime sees doubled values as\n138\t\"point bands.\"\n139\t\n140\tThis means the legacy 3-branch lt/eq/gt is exactly\n141\t`thresholds: [c, c]` — the eq case is just a zero-width band at\n142\tthe comparand. Behind the scenes the editor can present the\n143\tsingle-comparand UI but store `[c, c]` so the dispatch layer has\n144\tone consistent representation.\n145\t\n146\tDefer the schema specifics — the single-comparand case ships\n147\tfirst; multi-band is a follow-on once we have a use case that\n148\tactually needs more than three.\n149\t\n150\t### kind=\"iterator\"\n151\t\n152\t```json\n153\t\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"iterator\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n154\t```\n155\t\n156\t`n_outputs` output ports, named conventionally (`out_0`, `out_1`,\n157\t…). Every invocation reads the box's `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot\n158\tvia `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)`; that index picks\n159\tthe branch.\n160\t\n161\tThe function still runs and produces the routed value. Iterator\n162\tdefaults the function to a passthrough identity if the user\n163\thasn't picked a `ref` / `fn` — but the user is free to attach\n164\tany function whose output should be round-robin-distributed.\n165\t\n166\t### kind=\"randomizer\"\n167\t\n168\t```json\n169\t\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"randomizer\", \"n_outputs\": 4 }\n170\t```\n171\t\n172\tPicks a branch uniformly at random per invocation.\n173\tImplementation: hash the counter-slot value into the branch\n174\tindex, so the distribution is deterministic-given-seed but\n175\tspread across branches.\n176\t\n177\t```c\n178\tuint32_t i = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, UINT32_MAX);\n179\tuint32_t branch = hash(i) % n_outputs;\n180\t```\n181\t\n182\t`hash` is a cheap mixing function (xorshift, FNV); not\n183\tcryptographic. The point is breaking up the monotonic counter so\n184\tconsecutive calls don't go to consecutive branches.\n185\t\n186\t### kind=\"weighted\"\n187\t\n188\t```json\n189\t\"routing\": {\n190\t  \"kind\":    \"weighted\",\n191\t  \"weights\": [0.8, 0.2]\n192\t}\n193\t```\n194\t\n195\tProbability-based distribution. With `[0.8, 0.2]` and two output\n196\tports, 80% of invocations fire branch 0, 20% fire branch 1.\n197\t\n198\tImplementation: at compile time, weights are normalized into a\n199\tcumulative table on a `0..PRECISION-1` integer scale (e.g.\n200\t`PRECISION = 1000`). Per call:\n201\t\n202\t```c\n203\tuint32_t r = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, PRECISION);\n204\t// pre-computed cumulative: [0..799] → branch 0, [800..999] → branch 1\n205\tuint32_t branch = lookup_band(r, cumulative_table);\n206\t```\n207\t\n208\tSame counter-slot machinery as iterator and randomizer; the\n209\tdifference is the mapping from counter to branch.\n210\t\n211\t**Inspector UI for weighted routing**: a horizontal slider with\n212\tN knobs dividing it into N+1 segments — except really N segments\n213\tsince each knob is the boundary between adjacent segments. A\n214\twider segment means a larger fraction of invocations flow down\n215\tthat path. Below the slider, one line per output port:\n216\t\n217\t```\n218\tout_0    [▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓░░░░░░░░░░░░]    80%\n219\tout_1    [░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░▓▓▓▓]    20%\n220\t```\n221\t\n222\tEach line shows the output port name on the left, a visual band\n223\tin the middle indicating its slice of the distribution, and the\n224\tpercentage on the right. Adjusting the slider knobs updates the\n225\tpercentages live; the percentages are also editable directly\n226\t(typing `30` into the right column shifts the relevant knob).\n227\t\n228\t### kind=\"distributor\" (load-aware)\n229\t\n230\t```json\n231\t\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"distributor\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n232\t```\n233\t\n234\tSends the value to the **least-busy** downstream consumer:\n235\tinspects the fill levels of the input slots wired to each branch\n236\tand picks the branch whose downstream slot has the fewest queued\n237\tvalues.\n238\t\n239\tImplementation: dispatch action peeks the `tail - head` count on\n240\teach downstream input slot and picks the minimum. Tied branches\n241\tfall back to atomic-counter round-robin so ties don't always go\n242\tto the same branch.\n243\t\n244\tThis is the only routing kind that's not purely\n245\tself-contained — it reads downstream slot state — but it doesn't\n246\tadd any new dispatch-layer concept beyond querying slot fill\n247\t(which the slot store already knows).\n248\t\n249\t### Future kinds\n250\t\n251\tThe pattern is: any new routing kind plugs in at one place\n252\t(`routing.kind` value + dispatch-layer branch picker). All\n253\texisting kinds and any future ones live entirely in the dispatch\n254\tlayer + slot store + editor — never in language specs, never in\n255\tuser-written functions.\n256\t\n257\t## Iterator + function: ships as \"function always runs\"\n258\t\n259\tIterator boxes always run their function. The dispatch action\n260\tbecomes uniform across routing kinds:\n261\t\n262\t```\n263\t1. Read inputs (pop / peek per port mode).\n264\t2. Invoke spec (always — function runs regardless of routing kind).\n265\t3. Pick branch via routing.kind:\n266\t     comparator   → compare(output, comparand)\n267\t     iterator     → slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)\n268\t     randomizer   → hash(slot_read_inc(counter_slot, MAX)) % n_outputs\n269\t     weighted     → cumulative lookup\n270\t     distributor  → argmin(downstream fill)\n271\t     (no routing) → fan to all outgoing wires\n272\t4. Push function output to outputs[picked branch] (or all wires if\n273\t   no routing).\n274\t```\n275\t\n276\tA single dispatch path for all branching boxes; the routing rule\n277\tplugs into step 3.\n278\t\n279\t## Schema migration\n280\t\n281\tFew enough existing maps that we can hand-migrate them. The\n12\tinspector still owns the name, and the dot still works as a\n13\twire-grab target even though wiring into a port with a literal\n14\tvalue would severs that literal on connect.\n15\t\n16\tWhat the user reading the map can see at a glance:\n17\t\n18\t```\n19\t●  \"hello world\"\n20\t```\n21\t\n22\tThe port's variable name (`text`, `prompt`, whatever it is in\n23\tthe underlying function signature) is invisible on the canvas.\n24\tA reader has to open the inspector to recover the binding.\n25\t\n26\t## Intended behavior\n27\t\n28\tA port with a literal value rendered in three pieces, in three\n29\tpositions, in this order left-to-right:\n30\t\n31\t```\n32\ttext   ·   \"hello world\"\n33\t```\n34\t\n35\t- **Port name** (`text`) — moved to the LEFT of the box's edge,\n36\t  in the gutter just outside the box body. This is the\n37\t  variable's identity, and 235's value-takes-over rendering\n38\t  hid it. Pulling it out to the left puts the name back in\n39\t  plain sight WITHOUT giving up the value display.\n40\t- **Nodule** — a smaller, denser dot sitting where the regular\n41\t  port dot would. About half the radius of a wired port's dot.\n42\t  Visual marker only — it advertises \"this port is bound\" the\n43\t  same way the regular dot advertises \"this port can be wired.\"\n44\t  Color match its kind, same as the regular dot, so the eye\n45\t  reads it as a port without confusion.\n46\t- **Literal value** (`\"hello world\"`) — to the RIGHT of the\n47\t  nodule, same position the regular port name occupies on a\n48\t  wired port. Truncation rules from 235 still apply (24-char\n49\t  limit with ellipsis, tooltip for the full value).\n50\t\n51\tA wired port stays exactly as it is today — full-size dot,\n52\tname to its right, no left-of-box-edge label.\n53\t\n54\t### Wire-connect targeting disabled\n55\t\n56\tA literal-bound port is no longer a valid drag-target for\n57\twires. `Boxes.hit_test_port` excludes literal-bound input ports\n58\tfrom its hit search, so:\n59\t\n60\t- The cursor over a nodule does NOT highlight the port for a\n61\t  wire-grab.\n62\t- The user cannot start drawing a wire from / to a literal-bound\n63\t  port. To rebind, they clear the literal value in the inspector\n64\t  first; the port then renders as a wirable dot again.\n65\t\n66\tToday, dropping a wire onto a port with a literal value silently\n67\tclears the literal (per the existing inspector code, line ~656\n68\tin `004-inspector.js`). That behavior was a defensible\n69\tcompromise pre-239 because the value was the only visible\n70\tstate — losing it to a wire was reversible by re-typing.\n71\tPost-239 the user is explicitly indicating \"this is bound, no\n72\twires,\" so we honor that instead of dropping a value on accident.\n73\t\n74\t### Why this is better than the 235-only rendering\n75\t\n76\t- The user reading a map sees BOTH the variable identity and\n77\t  the bound value, on one line, without inspector lookup.\n78\t- The nodule is unambiguously \"not a wire target,\" so the user\n79\t  doesn't waste a drag attempt only to learn the literal was\n80\t  silently cleared.\n81\t- The left-of-edge name uses canvas gutter space that is\n82\t  currently empty, so the box body's horizontal budget is\n83\t  unaffected.\n84\t\n85\t### Edge cases\n86\t\n87\t- **Multiple ports with literals**: each gets its own left-of-\n88\t  edge name. Boxes with several literal-bound ports show a\n89\t  cleanly-stacked column of names in the gutter.\n90\t- **Variadic slot with a literal**: same rule as any other\n91\t  port. The variadic group's auto-grow / hide-empty-trailing\n92\t  rules from issue 217 are unaffected.\n93\t- **Port name long enough to collide with the left-of-edge\n94\t  gutter of an adjacent box**: clip with ellipsis at the box's\n95\t  max gutter width (TBD constant; ~12 monospace chars at\n96\t  10px gives ~72 world-px gutter, which is fine for typical\n97\t  identifiers). Tooltip on hover for the full name, same as\n98\t  235's value tooltip.\n99\t\n100\t## Suggested implementation steps\n101\t\n102\t1. `assets/js/002-boxes.js`:\n103\t   - Add a `port_is_literal_bound(box, i)` helper. Returns true\n104\t     when the port has a value AND no incoming wire. (The same\n105\t     three-state check `port_label_text` already does — pull it\n106\t     into a shared helper.)\n107\t   - In `draw_box`'s input-port loop: when literal-bound, draw\n108\t     the nodule (half-radius, same fill/stroke style as a normal\n109\t     dot) instead of the full dot; render the port name to the\n110\t     LEFT of the dot position (textAlign right, with the box's\n111\t     world x as the right edge); the value label drawing\n112\t     continues unchanged (235 path).\n113\t   - `hit_test_port`: skip ports that are literal-bound on\n114\t     inputs. The output side is unaffected (outputs don't carry\n115\t     literal values).\n116\t2. `assets/js/006-wires.js::create_connection`: the\n117\t   sever-literal-on-connect path in 004-inspector.js becomes\n118\t   unreachable because the literal port can't be a drag target.\n119\t   It can stay as a defensive guard in case some other code\n120\t   path forces a connection.\n121\t3. Tests: extend the 235 case set with two new cases:\n122\t   - \"wire attached, literal present\" → still renders as wired\n123\t     (wire wins, no nodule).\n124\t   - \"literal only\" → renders nodule + left-name + right-value.\n125\t\n126\t## Open questions\n127\t\n128\t- **Nodule radius**: half (3px world) is a starting guess. Visual\n129\t  weight will tell us if it should be smaller; refine after\n130\t  shipping. Constant in 002-boxes.js so it's a one-line change.\n131\t- **Gutter clip width**: 12 chars at 10px is a guess. Could be\n132\t  expressed as a fraction of `BOX_W` to scale if BOX_W ever\n133\t  changes. Probably not worth parameterizing today.\n134\t- **Inspector indication of \"this port is literal-bound\"**: the\n135\t  inspector already shows the value field; that's the only\n136\t  binding state. No additional UI needed there — the canvas is\n137\t  the place where the visual rule applies.\n138\t\n139\t## Relevant files\n140\t\n141\t- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — `draw_box` input-port path,\n142\t  `hit_test_port`, helpers\n143\t- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — sever-on-connect guard\n144\t- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — sever-on-set guard (still\n145\t  fires when the user sets a literal through the inspector\n146\t  while a wire is attached; the wire-into-literal direction is\n147\t  the one this issue closes off)\n148\t- `issues/completed/235-literal-value-replaces-port-name-on-canvas.md`\n149\t  — the predecessor; the value-on-canvas rule this issue\n150\t  retains, the dot-stays-the-same-size rule this issue\n151\t  supersedes\n152\t"

```json
{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"f0649c30-66f9-4f78-a128-4949e3a589a7",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-20T19:07:25.753Z",
