      "content":"# 303 — Language runtime spec: pluggable per-language invocation\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nEach language has an ad-hoc driver script (`drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`,\n`drivers/c.sh`). The driver is invoked per box call: spawn a process, run\nthe function, read stdout, exit. Adding a new language means writing a new\ndriver script and modifying the executor to know about it.\n\nThere is no shared interface, no persistent runtime, and no way for a user\nto add a language without touching SoraMech internals.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe language runtime spec is the user-extensible interface that defines how\na language's functions are invoked from inside the thread pool. Every\nlanguage goes through this interface — there is no special path for any\nlanguage. Lua is a spec. C is a spec. Bash is a spec. A user adding Python\nwrites another spec.\n\nThe pool runner does not know how to \"run a Lua function.\" It knows how to\ncall `lang->invoke(...)`. The Lua spec is the thing that knows how to run a\nLua function.\n\nThe user provides the bridging code. SoraMech does not transpile, rewrite,\nor convert box source between languages. If the user wants Rust, the user\nwrites a Rust spec.\n\n## The interface\n\nEach language spec is a C library that exports a single symbol:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;       // \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ...\n    const char *file_ext;   // \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\" — for box file resolution\n\n    // Once-per-worker. Returns an opaque handle stored in worker_ctx.\n    // Called at pool startup, before any tasks run.\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n\n    // Once-per-worker. Called at pool shutdown.\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n\n    // Optional: called once per box source file at map load.\n    // For languages that compile (C → .so), this is where compilation\n    // happens. For languages that don't (Lua, Bash), this is NULL.\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n\n    // The invocation. Inputs are arrays of (bytes, size) pairs,\n    // already read from slots by the dispatch layer. The spec writes\n    // its return value into out_buf and sets *out_size.\n    //\n    // Returns 0 on success, nonzero on error.\n    int   (*invoke)(void *handle,\n                    const char *file_path,\n                    const char *fn_name,\n                    const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes, int n_inputs,\n                    void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n\nextern lang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec;\n```\n\nThe spec library is built as a `.so` and loaded by the pool runner at\nstartup via `dlopen` / `dlsym`. The runner iterates `langs/*/spec.so`,\nloads each, and registers it under its `name`.\n\n## Slot access boundary\n\nSpecs do not see slot IDs. The dispatch layer (issue 304) reads input\nvalues from slots into raw byte buffers, hands them to `invoke`, receives\nthe output bytes, and writes them to the output slot. This decouples\nspecs from slot internals — a spec only deals with values.\n\nIf a future language wants zero-copy access (e.g. memory-mapping a slot\ndirectly into a Python bytearray), the interface can be extended. Do not\nadd it preemptively.\n\n## Per-language layout\n\nSpecs live under `langs/<name>/`:\n\n```\nlangs/lua/\n    spec.c              ← implements lang_spec_t (handles → lua_State)\n    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so             ← built artifact\n\nlangs/bash/\n    spec.c              ← bridges to bash-server.sh via Unix domain socket\n    bash-server.sh      ← persistent subprocess started by spec.init\n    Makefile\n\nlangs/c/\n    spec.c              ← uses dlopen/dlsym; compile = gcc -shared -fPIC\n    Makefile\n\nlangs/python/           ← user-added; not shipped\n    spec.c\n    Makefile\n```\n\nThe pool runner has no compiled-in knowledge of any specific language.\nEven Lua is loaded as a `.so` at startup. This keeps the boundary honest\n— there is no temptation to special-case the \"shipped\" languages.\n\n## Built-in specs (shipped, not privileged)\n\nSoraMech ships specs for:\n- **Lua** — handle is a `lua_State`. `invoke` calls `luaL_loadfile` (cached)\n  + `lua_pcall`. Args pushed as Lua strings; return read as Lua string.\n- **C** — handle is a small `dlopen` handle cache. `compile` runs\n  `gcc -shared -fPIC -o <out_path> <src_path>`. `invoke` does\n  `dlsym` + direct call.\n- **Bash** — handle is a Unix domain socket connected to a persistent\n  bash subprocess (`bash-server.sh`). `invoke` sends a framed request,\n  reads a framed response.\n\nThese are the reference implementations. They demonstrate the spec\ninterface for in-process FFI (Lua, C) and for out-of-process socket\nservers (Bash, and any future language whose runtime cannot be embedded).\n\n## Compilation\n\nThe optional `compile` hook runs at map load (or at editor compile-button\ntime, issue 219). For C, it produces a `.so` next to the source. For\nLua and Bash, no compilation step is needed; `compile` is `NULL`.\n\nCompilation outputs go in the map's `compiled/bin/` directory (issue\n222). The dispatch layer passes the compiled artifact path to `invoke`,\nnot the original source path, when a compiled artifact exists.\n\n## Iterator counter prepending\n\nThe iterator counter (issue 221) is prepended to the input array by the\ndispatch layer, not by the spec. From the spec's perspective, an\niterator box just has one extra input. The spec doesn't know which\ninput is the counter — that's a graph-level concept.\n\n## Errors crash the program\n\nA nonzero return from `invoke` is a fatal error. The dispatch layer\nprints the error context (box id, function name, language) to stderr\nand aborts the process. There is no recovery, no retry, no per-task\n\"failed\" state, no fallback. There are no timeouts on stalled tasks,\nno wait-list garbage collection, no failure propagation through the\ngraph.\n\nThe reasoning: a task that cannot produce a correct return value is a\nbug. Bugs do not belong in production. Building in detection and\nrecovery for bug states adds runtime cost and complexity to handle a\ncase that should not exist. If a bug surfaces in production, the\nprogram crashes loudly; the developer fixes the bug and redeploys.\n\nThe spec is still responsible for catching language-level errors (Lua\n`error()`, C signals it can intercept, Bash nonzero exit) and\ntranslating them into a nonzero return — so that the dispatch layer\nsees a clean signal instead of an undefined post-error state. Once\nreturned, the program ends.\n\n## User-facing documentation\n\nThe interface is published in `langs/lang-spec.h`, which every spec\nimplementation includes. That header is the source of truth for the\ncontract.\n\nUser-facing docs that mention the language spec system:\n- `README.md` — short paragraph in the features list pointing out that\n  any language can be added by writing a spec, with a one-line example\n  of what that means\n- `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) — the long-form guide\n  on writing a spec: walk through the Lua spec as a small reference,\n  show what `init` / `invoke` / `teardown` do, point at the C spec for\n  the `compile`-using case and the Bash spec for the\n  socket-server case\n- `docs/000-table-of-contents.md` — index entry for the new doc\n\nWithout these the spec system is invisible — users would never know it\nexists or how to extend it.\n\n## Open questions\n\n(none currently)\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Write `langs/lang-spec.h` — the public interface header.\n2. Write `langs/lua/spec.c` first. Lua is the easiest because it's already\n   our default language and the existing driver gives a reference behavior.\n3. Write `langs/c/spec.c` — adds `compile` callback, exercises the dlopen\n   path.\n4. Write `langs/bash/spec.c` + `langs/bash/bash-server.sh` — exercises\n   the out-of-process socket model. This is the proof that languages\n   without an embeddable runtime fit the same interface.\n5. Pool runner registry: `dlopen` every `langs/*/spec.so` at startup,\n   register by `name`. Box files are routed to specs by `file_ext`.\n6. Smoke test: a map with one Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all\n   running in the pool, all going through the spec interface. No\n   special-cased code paths.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`, `drivers/c.sh` — current ad-hoc\n  drivers, replaced by `langs/<name>/spec.c`\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool startup invokes\n  spec `init` per worker per language\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — dispatch layer reads slots and\n  passes raw bytes to specs (specs do not touch slots)\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — calls `invoke` per task\n- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — compile button\n  runs spec `compile` for every box\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — Option 1 (FFI) and Option 3 (Unix\n  socket) describe the two execution models specs implement\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Registry — 2026-05-12\n\n`src/011-spec-registry.{c,h}` scans a `langs/` directory, dlopens\nevery `<name>/spec.so` it finds with `RTLD_NOW | RTLD_LOCAL`, and\nexposes name + extension lookup plus enumeration. The three\nshipped stubs (lua/c/bash) load cleanly and round-trip through\n`spec_registry_get` and `spec_registry_for_ext`. Four unit tests\nin `tests/011-spec-registry-test.c` cover the load, missing dir,\nnull inputs, and accessor safety.\n\nDeferred: hooking `spec->init(worker_idx)` into the pool's\n`worker_main` between TLS setup and the init barrier. That's the\nfinal piece that makes 303 fully wired; lands in a follow-on once\na spec has a real `init` body to call (issue 306 onward).\n\n### Per-worker init / teardown helper — 2026-05-12\n\n`spec_registry_init_worker(r, worker_idx, handles, cap)` and the\nmatching `_teardown_worker` walk the registry, call each spec's\ninit/teardown, and stash handles in a caller-provided array.\nIndex in the array matches index in the registry. Specs with NULL\ninit contribute NULL handles; teardown skips NULL slots. A new\nunit test runs against the three shipped specs and now confirms\nthat the Lua spec's init returns a non-NULL `lua_State` while the\nstill-stub C and Bash specs leave their slots NULL.\n\nWhat's still ahead inside 303: actually calling the helper from\nthe pool's `worker_main` so each worker thread populates its\n`worker_ctx_t.handles[]` before crossing the init barrier. Small\nchange; lives in `libs/task-pool/pool.c` and needs the runner to\npass a `spec_registry_t *` into `pool_create` (or to a new\n`pool_init_specs` API). Lands in the next pass.\n\n### Pool worker hook — 2026-05-12\n\n`libs/task-pool/pool.{c,h}` grew a per-worker init callback:\n`pool_set_worker_init(p, cb, user)` and `pool_init_barrier` now\nreturns an int (0 ok, -1 if any worker's callback failed). The\ninit barrier became a three-stage handshake so callbacks\nregistered between `pool_create` and `pool_init_barrier` can't\nrace the workers — stage 1 parks workers until the barrier\nauthorises them, stage 2 runs each worker's callback, stage 3\nreleases everyone into the task loop.\n\n`tests/303-pool-spec-init-test.c` wires `spec_registry_init_worker`\ninto the pool callback (a two-line trampoline) and asserts that\nspawned tasks see a non-NULL `lua_State` in\n`pool_current_worker->handles[lua_idx]`, with each worker getting\nits own distinct state. The pool-internal callback test in\n`tests/301-pool-test.c` covers the success and failure paths\nwithout the registry. 303 is now functionally complete end to\nend — the registry loads specs, the helper inits them per\nworker, and the pool's worker_main calls them through the hook.\n",

Called at pool shutdown.\n45\t    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n46\t\n47\t    // Optional: called once per box source file at map load.\n48\t    // For languages that compile (C → .so), this is where compilation\n49\t    // happens. For languages that don't (Lua, Bash), this is NULL.\n50\t    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n51\t\n52\t    // The invocation. Inputs are arrays of (bytes, size) pairs,\n53\t    // already read from slots by the dispatch layer. The spec writes\n54\t    // its return value into out_buf and sets *out_size.\n55\t    //\n56\t    // Returns 0 on success, nonzero on error.\n57\t    int   (*invoke)(void *handle,\n58\t                    const char *file_path,\n59\t                    const char *fn_name,\n60\t                    const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes, int n_inputs,\n61\t                    void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n62\t} lang_spec_t;\n63\t\n64\textern lang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec;\n65\t```\n66\t\n67\tThe spec library is built as a `.so` and loaded by the pool runner at\n68\tstartup via `dlopen` / `dlsym`. The runner iterates `langs/*/spec.so`,\n69\tloads each, and registers it under its `name`.\n70\t\n71\t## Slot access boundary\n72\t\n73\tSpecs do not see slot IDs. The dispatch layer (issue 304) reads input\n74\tvalues from slots into raw byte buffers, hands them to `invoke`, receives\n75\tthe output bytes, and writes them to the output slot. This decouples\n76\tspecs from slot internals — a spec only deals with values.\n77\t\n78\tIf a future language wants zero-copy access (e.g. memory-mapping a slot\n79\tdirectly into a Python bytearray), the interface can be extended. Do not\n80\tadd it preemptively.\n81\t\n82\t## Per-language layout\n83\t\n84\tSpecs live under `langs/<name>/`:\n85\t\n86\t```\n87\tlangs/lua/\n88\t    spec.c              ← implements lang_spec_t (handles → lua_State)\n89\t    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n90\t    spec.so             ← built artifact\n91\t\n92\tlangs/bash/\n93\t    spec.c              ← bridges to bash-server.sh via Unix domain socket\n94\t    bash-server.sh      ← persistent subprocess started by spec.init\n95\t    Makefile\n96\t\n97\tlangs/c/\n98\t    spec.c              ← uses dlopen/dlsym; compile = gcc -shared -fPIC\n99\t    Makefile\n100\t\n101\tlangs/python/           ← user-added; not shipped\n102\t    spec.c\n103\t    Makefile\n104\t```\n105\t\n106\tThe pool runner has no compiled-in knowledge of any specific language.\n107\tEven Lua is loaded as a `.so` at startup. This keeps the boundary honest\n108\t— there is no temptation to special-case the \"shipped\" languages.\n109\t\n110\t## Built-in specs (shipped, not privileged)\n111\t\n112\tSoraMech ships specs for:\n113\t- **Lua** — handle is a `lua_State`. `invoke` calls `luaL_loadfile` (cached)\n114\t  + `lua_pcall`. Args pushed as Lua strings; return read as Lua string.\n115\t- **C** — handle is a small `dlopen` handle cache. `compile` runs\n116\t  `gcc -shared -fPIC -o <out_path> <src_path>`. `invoke` does\n117\t  `dlsym` + direct call.\n118\t- **Bash** — handle is a Unix domain socket connected to a persistent\n119\t  bash subprocess (`bash-server.sh`). `invoke` sends a framed request,\n120\t  reads a framed response.\n121\t\n122\tThese are the reference implementations. They demonstrate the spec\n123\tinterface for in-process FFI (Lua, C) and for out-of-process socket\n124\tservers (Bash, and any future language whose runtime cannot be embedded).\n125\t\n126\t## Compilation\n127\t\n128\tThe optional `compile` hook runs at map load (or at editor compile-button\n129\ttime, issue 219). For C, it produces a `.so` next to the source. For\n130\tLua and Bash, no compilation step is needed; `compile` is `NULL`.\n131\t\n132\tCompilation outputs go in the map's `compiled/bin/` directory (issue\n133\t222). The dispatch layer passes the compiled artifact path to `invoke`,\n134\tnot the original source path, when a compiled artifact exists.\n135\t\n136\t## Iterator counter prepending\n137\t\n138\tThe iterator counter (issue 221) is prepended to the input array by the\n139\tdispatch layer, not by the spec. From the spec's perspective, an\n140\titerator box just has one extra input. The spec doesn't know which\n141\tinput is the counter — that's a graph-level concept.\n142\t\n143\t## Errors crash the program\n144\t\n145\tA nonzero return from `invoke` is a fatal error. The dispatch layer\n146\tprints the error context (box id, function name, language) to stderr\n147\tand aborts the process. There is no recovery, no retry, no per-task\n148\t\"failed\" state, no fallback. There are no timeouts on stalled tasks,\n149\tno wait-list garbage collection, no failure propagation through the\n150\tgraph.\n151\t\n152\tThe reasoning: a task that cannot produce a correct return value is a\n153\tbug. Bugs do not belong in production. Building in detection and\n154\trecovery for bug states adds runtime cost and complexity to handle a\n155\tcase that should not exist. If a bug surfaces in production, the\n156\tprogram crashes loudly; the developer fixes the bug and redeploys.\n157\t\n158\tThe spec is still responsible for catching language-level errors (Lua\n159\t`error()`, C signals it can intercept, Bash nonzero exit) and\n160\ttranslating them into a nonzero return — so that the dispatch layer\n161\tsees a clean signal instead of an undefined post-error state. Once\n162\treturned, the program ends.\n163\t\n164\t## User-facing documentation\n165\t\n166\tThe interface is published in `langs/lang-spec.h`, which every spec\n167\timplementation includes. That header is the source of truth for the\n168\tcontract.\n169\t\n170\tUser-facing docs that mention the language spec system:\n171\t- `README.md` — short paragraph in the features list pointing out that\n172\t  any language can be added by writing a spec, with a one-line example\n173\t  of what that means\n174\t- `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) — the long-form guide\n175\t  on writing a spec: walk through the Lua spec as a small reference,\n176\t  show what `init` / `invoke` / `teardown` do, point at the C spec for\n177\t  the `compile`-using case and the Bash spec for the\n178\t  socket-server case\n179\t- `docs/000-table-of-contents.md` — index entry for the new doc\n180\t\n181\tWithout these the spec system is invisible — users would never know it\n182\texists or how to extend it.\n183\t\n184\t## Open questions\n185\t\n186\t(none currently)\n187\t\n188\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n189\t\n190\t1. Write `langs/lang-spec.h` — the public interface header.\n191\t2. Write `langs/lua/spec.c` first. Lua is the easiest because it's already\n192\t   our default language and the existing driver gives a reference behavior.\n193\t3. Write `langs/c/spec.c` — adds `compile` callback, exercises the dlopen\n194\t   path.\n195\t4. Write `langs/bash/spec.c` + `langs/bash/bash-server.sh` — exercises\n196\t   the out-of-process socket model. This is the proof that languages\n197\t   without an embeddable runtime fit the same interface.\n198\t5. Pool runner registry: `dlopen` every `langs/*/spec.so` at startup,\n199\t   register by `name`. Box files are routed to specs by `file_ext`.\n200\t6. Smoke test: a map with one Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all\n201\t   running in the pool, all going through the spec interface. No\n202\t   special-cased code paths.\n203\t\n204\t## Relevant files\n205\t\n206\t- `drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`, `drivers/c.sh` — current ad-hoc\n207\t  drivers, replaced by `langs/<name>/spec.c`\n208\t- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool startup invokes\n209\t  spec `init` per worker per language\n210\t- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — dispatch layer reads slots and\n211\t  passes raw bytes to specs (specs do not touch slots)\n212\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — calls `invoke` per task\n213\t- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — compile button\n214\t  runs spec `compile` for every box\n215\t- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — Option 1 (FFI) and Option 3 (Unix\n216\t  socket) describe the two execution models specs implement\n217\t\n218\t## Implementation log\n219\t\n220\t### Registry — 2026-05-12\n221\t\n222\t`src/011-spec-registry.{c,h}` scans a `langs/` directory, dlopens\n223\tevery `<name>/spec.so` it finds with `RTLD_NOW | RTLD_LOCAL`, and\n224\texposes name + extension lookup plus enumeration. The three\n225\tshipped stubs (lua/c/bash) load cleanly and round-trip through\n226\t`spec_registry_get` and `spec_registry_for_ext`. Four unit tests\n227\tin `tests/011-spec-registry-test.c` cover the load, missing dir,\n228\tnull inputs, and accessor safety.\n229\t\n230\tDeferred: hooking `spec->init(worker_idx)` into the pool's\n231\t`worker_main` between TLS setup and the init barrier. That's the\n232\tfinal piece that makes 303 fully wired; lands in a follow-on once\n233\ta spec has a real `init` body to call (issue 306 onward).\n234\t\n235\t### Per-worker init / teardown helper — 2026-05-12\n236\t\n237\t`spec_registry_init_worker(r, worker_idx, handles, cap)` and the\n238\tmatching `_teardown_worker` walk the registry, call each spec's\n239\tinit/teardown, and stash handles in a caller-provided array.\n240\tIndex in the array matches index in the registry. Specs with NULL\n241\tinit contribute NULL handles; teardown skips NULL slots. A new\n242\tunit test runs against the three shipped specs and now confirms\n243\tthat the Lua spec's init returns a non-NULL `lua_State` while the\n244\tstill-stub C and Bash specs leave their slots NULL.\n245\t\n246\tWhat's still ahead inside 303: actually calling the helper from\n247\tthe pool's `worker_main` so each worker thread populates its\n248\t`worker_ctx_t.handles[]` before crossing the init barrier. Small\n249\tchange; lives in `libs/task-pool/pool.c` and needs the runner to\n250\tpass a `spec_registry_t *` into `pool_create` (or to a new\n251\t`pool_init_specs` API). Lands in the next pass.\n252\t\n253\t### Pool worker hook — 2026-05-12\n254\t\n255\t`libs/task-pool/pool.{c,h}` grew a per-worker init callback:\n256\t`pool_set_worker_init(p, cb, user)` and `pool_init_barrier` now\n257\treturns an int (0 ok, -1 if any worker's callback failed). The\n258\tinit barrier became a three-stage handshake so callbacks\n259\tregistered between `pool_create` and `pool_init_barrier` can't\n260\trace the workers — stage 1 parks workers until the barrier\n261\tauthorises them, stage 2 runs each worker's callback, stage 3\n262\treleases everyone into the task loop.\n263\t\n264\t`tests/303-pool-spec-init-test.c` wires `spec_registry_init_worker`\n265\tinto the pool callback (a two-line trampoline) and asserts that\n266\tspawned tasks see a non-NULL `lua_State` in\n267\t`pool_current_worker->handles[lua_idx]`, with each worker getting\n268\tits own distinct state. The pool-internal callback test in\n269\t`tests/301-pool-test.c` covers the success and failure paths\n270\twithout the registry. 303 is now functionally complete end to\n271\tend — the registry loads specs, the helper inits them per\n272\tworker, and the pool's worker_main calls them through the hook.\n273\t"

```json
{
  "userType":"external",

      "content":"# 301 — Thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe executor (`src/004-executor.lua`) runs boxes synchronously in a\nsingle Lua coroutine. There is no thread pool, no pthreads, and no\nper-thread language runtime state.\n\n## Phase model\n\nPhase 2 is the synchronous interpreter path. It is the development\ntarget while editor work is in progress.\n\nPhase 3 is the thread pool path. It is the only execution path going\nforward. The synchronous interpreter does not stay around as an\nalternative entry point — once phase 3 lands, the pool runner\nreplaces it. There is no \"fallback to synchronous\" mode.\n\n### Phase 2 → 3 refactor surface\n\nThe following components are replaced (not extended) in phase 3:\n\n| Phase 2 file                  | Phase 3 replacement                  |\n|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------|\n| `src/003-loader.lua`          | C loader inside `src/008-pool-runner.c` |\n| `src/004-executor.lua`        | C task dispatch layer (issue 304)    |\n| `src/007-runner-main.lua`     | `src/008-pool-runner.c`              |\n| `drivers/*.sh`                | Language runtime spec (issue 303)    |\n\nAll threading-pool-adjacent functionality is C code that lives next to\nthe pool. There is no embedded Lua runtime for graph loading or\ndispatch — Lua appears only as a language runtime that boxes can use,\non equal footing with C, Bash, and any future language.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### Pool source\nThe thread pool is **SoraMech-owned**, written from scratch under\n`libs/task-pool/`. The 3d-rts pool at\n`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\nis the **design reference**, not a dependency. We need full control\nover the spawn primitive, the worker context, the init barrier\n(below), and iterator-pinning extensions — all reasons not to inherit\nan external implementation.\n\nThe pool exposes (at minimum):\n\n```c\npool_t *pool_create(int n_workers);\nvoid    pool_destroy(pool_t *p);\nvoid    pool_spawn(pool_t *p, action_fn_t fn, void *arg);\nvoid    pool_wait_quiescent(pool_t *p);   // blocks until active count hits zero\nvoid    pool_init_barrier(pool_t *p);     // see \"Init barrier\" below\n```\n\n3d-rts's frame-ring + park-on-slot machinery is referenced for\npatterns; we don't reimplement features we don't need.\n\n### Where the pool lives in the process\nThe pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map\nrun. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and\ndestroyed after the run completes.\n\nThe C entry point (`src/008-pool-runner.c`):\n\n```c\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n    // 1. parse map path from argv\n    // 2. load and validate graph (C loader, no Lua involved)\n    // 3. determine which language runtimes the map uses\n    // 4. allocate per-input-port slots for every box (issue 302)\n    // 5. pool = pool_create(n_workers)\n    // 6. init per-worker language runtime handles for each language present\n    // 7. pool_init_barrier(pool)  ← block until every worker is fully initialized\n    // 8. push every input port's literal value into its slot\n    // 9. spawn tasks for boxes whose input set is now satisfied\n    // 10. pool_wait_quiescent(pool)\n    // 11. write last-run.jsonl\n    // 12. pool_destroy(pool)\n}\n```\n\n### Init barrier\n\nWorkers are not safe to dispatch tasks to until **every worker has\nfully completed init for every language spec the map uses**. If the\nmain thread spawns a task before a worker's `lua_State` is up, the\ntask lands on a null handle.\n\n`pool_init_barrier` is the join point:\n\n1. Each worker's startup runs all `lang->init(worker_idx)` calls in\n   a defined order, populating its `worker_ctx_t.handles[]`.\n2. After completing its inits, each worker increments a shared\n   atomic `workers_ready` counter and blocks on a condition\n   variable.\n3. The main thread waits until `workers_ready == n_workers`.\n4. Main thread broadcasts the condition variable; all workers\n   release simultaneously and begin pulling tasks.\n\nThis is a one-shot barrier — it runs once at pool startup. After\nquiescence it doesn't re-engage; teardown takes a different path.\n\nThe barrier also protects against partial init failures: if any\nworker's `init` returns an error, the barrier never completes and\nthe main thread can detect it via a timeout or per-worker status\nflag.\n\n### Graph loading: ported to C\nThe graph loader is ported from `src/003-loader.lua` to C and lives\ninside (or alongside) `008-pool-runner.c`. The pool runner has no\nembedded Lua state for loader purposes. JSON parsing uses a small\nvendored C JSON library (cJSON or similar; decision deferred to\nimplementation).\n\nLua appears in the runner only when a box's language is Lua — and even\nthen, only inside that worker's language runtime handle. The pool\nrunner itself does not link to liblua at the top level.\n\n### Per-worker language runtimes\nNo language is treated as the \"native\" or preferred language at the\nthread level. Every box — regardless of language — goes through the\nsame task dispatch path. The per-box cost is determined by that box's\ninvocation wrapper, not by any map-level language setting.\n\nEach worker thread holds a set of language runtime handles, one per\nlanguage it may be asked to run. These are initialized once at pool\nstartup, before any tasks are submitted, and torn down at shutdown:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void   *handles[N_LANGS];   // opaque per-language runtime state\n    int     thread_idx;\n} worker_ctx_t;\n```\n\nOnly the language handles actually needed by the map are initialized.\nIf the map contains no Bash boxes, no Bash handle is started for any\nworker. The graph loader determines which languages are present and\npasses that set to the pool runner at startup.\n\nThe per-language initialization protocol is defined by the language\nruntime spec (issue 303). The pool runner calls each spec's `init`\nfunction at startup and its `teardown` function at shutdown.\n\n### Worker context access\nWorker context is stored in thread-local storage (`__thread\nworker_ctx_t *current_worker`), set by each worker immediately after\nthe thread is started. This avoids per-task `pthread_self()` lookups.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Slots are owned by input ports (issue 302)\nEach box has one ring-buffer slot per input port, allocated at\ngraph load time and durable for the run. The pool runner walks\nevery box during the load step and populates a per-box slot table.\nSlots are not allocated per-task; tasks pop and push but never\nallocate. See issue 302 for the slot lifecycle and lifetime model.\n\n### Quiescence\nThe runner tracks an active-task counter, incremented on `pool_spawn`\nand decremented when a task reaches `ACT_DONE`. The main thread waits\non a condition variable that signals when the counter reaches zero.\n\nThis naturally handles iterators that re-queue themselves: each\nre-queue increments the counter, each completion decrements. When the\ncounter reaches zero, the run is over.\n\nDeadlock is not a concern at runtime. The graph validator (running at\nload) rejects non-iterator cycles and inputs without producers. Errors\ninside a task crash the program (issue 303), so there is no\nhalf-completed-producer case to worry about. An iterator parking\nbecause its upstream queue is empty is not deadlock — it is the\nnatural end-of-stream condition; once the active-task counter reaches\nzero with the iterator parked, the run ends cleanly.\n\n## Open questions\n- Vendored JSON library: cJSON, jsmn, or hand-rolled. cJSON is heavier\n  but easiest. Decision deferred.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Vendor `900-task-pool.h` + `.c` into `libs/task-pool/`.\n2. Vendor a JSON parser into `libs/json/`.\n3. Port `003-loader.lua` to C inside `src/008-pool-runner.c`.\n4. Write the pool lifecycle skeleton: pool_create, worker context TLS,\n   active-task counter, quiescence wait.\n5. Add `Makefile` target `soramech-pool` that compiles the C runner and\n   links against the vendored pool and JSON parser.\n6. Smoke test: single-box Lua map, pool with 2 workers, box runs, result\n   written. No task graph complexity yet.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `libs/task-pool/` — SoraMech-built pool (to be created)\n- `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` — design reference only\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — current Lua loader, to be ported to C\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — current synchronous executor, to be replaced\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — current Lua runner, to be replaced\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — per-port slot model\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — per-language init/call/teardown\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — replaces 004-executor.lua\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — threading roadmap and IPC options\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Pool skeleton — 2026-05-12\n\nWhat shipped:\n- `libs/task-pool/pool.h` + `pool.c` — SoraMech-owned pool with N\n  pthread workers, a singly-linked FIFO queue under one mutex,\n  atomic active-task counter with its own cv for quiescence wait,\n  one-shot init barrier with workers_ready / init_released\n  predicates under a third mutex. Worker count defaults to logical\n  CPUs (capped at `POOL_MAX_WORKERS=16`), overridable via\n  `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`. Recursive `pool_spawn` from inside an\n  action works — the queue mutex is re-entered cleanly.\n- TLS `pool_current_worker` for actions that need their worker\n  index or the back-pointer to the pool.\n- `tests/301-pool-test.c` — 8 unit tests: create/destroy with no\n  tasks, default worker count, cap-at-max, single spawn, 1000-task\n  spawn-and-quiesce, TLS context observable from inside actions,\n  recursive spawn (depth 10 → 11 invocations), and 8 concurrent\n  producer threads each pushing 500 tasks while 4 workers drain\n  (4000 total). All pass under STRICT.\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` now loads the graph via 305 and stands up\n  the pool: `./soramech-pool tests/maps/hello` prints the box count,\n  entry box, and worker count, then quiesces cleanly with no tasks.\n\nWhat's deferred to follow-ons within 301:\n- **Per-worker spec init** between `pool_create` and\n  `pool_init_barrier`. The hook is documented in `worker_main`;\n  lands with issue 303 once specs can be `dlopen`ed and\n  per-worker handles allocated.\n- **Priority queue.** Issue 310 covers the \"wired in, no-op\n  behaviorally\" upgrade. Current queue is plain FIFO.\n\nNeither blocks 304 (dispatch) from starting.\n\n### Per-worker teardown hook — 2026-05-12\n\nSymmetric counterpart to `pool_set_worker_init`. Registered via\n`pool_set_worker_teardown(p, cb, user)`; the worker thread runs\nthe callback right before exiting, after the task loop drains.\nThe runner uses it to call `spec_registry_teardown_worker`,\nwhich sends bash subprocesses `QUIT`, closes their socket fds,\nand waitpids them. Without this, soramech-pool was leaking\norphan bash processes (16 per run) that piled up across runs\nand slowed startup. Verified: zero orphans after a fresh run.\n",

{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"faa511a4-8e3b-4b38-9bfc-db32ffcb4882",

      "content":"# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\nhave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\naccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n\n## Concept\n\n### Slots belong to input ports, not tasks\n\nEach box has **one slot per input port**, allocated when the graph\nloads and persisting for the life of the run. A wire is a routing\ndeclaration: \"the producer's output port pushes a copy of its value\ninto this consumer's named input slot.\" The producer never owns a\nslot — its output is a routing event, not a stored value.\n\nWhen a producer fires, the dispatch layer copies the value into\nevery downstream input slot wired to that output. Fan-out is N\npushes (one per consumer); fan-in is N producers all pushing into\nthe same consumer's slot. Both behaviors fall out of the same\npush-into-input-slot mechanic.\n\nSlots live in process heap memory, accessible to every worker\nthread. Cross-process visibility is not required: language specs\n(issue 303) only ever receive byte pointers — never raw slot\naddresses — so out-of-process specs (Bash) work via sockets, not\nshared memory.\n\n### Tasks are ephemeral; box state is durable\n\nA **task** is one invocation: pop one value from each of the box's\ninput slots, run the box's logic, push the output to every\ndownstream input slot. Tasks have no persistent identity — they're\njust stack frames on workers. Tasks are spawned dynamically by the\ndispatch layer when a box's input set is ready (every input slot\nholds at least one value).\n\nThe **box** is the durable thing: it owns its input port slots, any\ncounter state (for iterators), its language spec handle, and so\non. The box exists from graph load until run end. Tasks come and\ngo.\n\nThis is uniform across iterator and non-iterator boxes. Both run N\ntimes where N depends on how many invocations their inputs supply\n(possibly 1, possibly thousands). The difference is just what the\ntask does:\n- **Plain call task**: invoke spec on the popped values, push the\n  return to outputs.\n- **Iterator task**: read box's counter, route the popped value to\n  output port `iterator_outputs[counter]`, increment counter mod N.\n  No spec invocation.\n- **Comparator task**: invoke spec on the popped values, compare\n  the return against `comparand`, route to the matching `lt` /\n  `eq` / `gt` branch.\n\n### All slots are ring buffers; read mode varies\n\nThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells,\neach of `cell_capacity` bytes. The number of cells (`n_cells`) and\nthe read mode are both compile-time properties of the input port:\n\n- **1-cell + peek mode**: the value the producer wrote stays in the\n  cell. Tasks read via `slot_peek` — read without draining — and\n  every subsequent task on this consumer reads the same value\n  unless the producer overwrites it. Used for **single-push wires**\n  (a literal, or a wire from a producer box whose invocation count\n  is exactly 1). Multiple consumer tasks read the value as many\n  times as needed; the cell is never empty.\n- **N-cell + pop mode**: a queue. Producers push; consumers\n  `slot_pop` — drain one cell per task. Used for **multi-push wires**:\n  any wire whose producer has more than one task invocation\n  during the run. The producer's pushes accumulate, the consumer\n  drains in pop order.\n\nCompile-time analysis classifies each wire. A producer is\n\"runs-once\" if no transitive ancestor is an iterator; otherwise\nit's \"runs-N-times.\" Wires from runs-once producers get 1-cell\npeek slots; wires from runs-N-times producers get N-cell pop slots.\n\n`n_cells` for pop slots is sized for worst-case backlog (or a\ndefault like 64 with growth on demand). Lists grow if the producer\noutruns the consumer past the pre-allocation.\n\nFan-in: multiple producers pushing into the same N-cell pop slot\nland in arrival order. The consumer pops FIFO unless the cell\ncarries an ordering tag (see \"Cell tagging\" below).\n\n### Atomic-counter slot mode\n\nA slot allocated with `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` carries a single\n4-byte unsigned integer cell, read via a special op:\n\n```c\nuint32_t slot_read_inc(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);\n// Returns the current value mod `mod`, then atomically increments\n// the underlying counter. Concurrent readers each get a distinct\n// value. Counter wraps at 2^32; mod handles N-branch routing.\n```\n\nUsed for iterator counters (issue 304): the iterator box has an\nauto-allocated `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot at load time; the\ndispatch action calls `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_branches)`\nto pick its output branch. Multiple iterator tasks can read\nconcurrently from the same counter slot in parallel — each gets a\nunique routing index — without any per-box mutable state and\nwithout the serial dependency of a self-push counter.\n\nThe slot's \"cell\" is just an `atomic_uint32_t`. No push is ever\nperformed; reads do the work. From the dispatch action's\nperspective it's just another slot; from the slot store's\nperspective the read op is special-cased.\n\n### Cell tagging (for parallel-iterator ordering)\n\nA cell can optionally carry a 4-byte ordering tag alongside its\nsize and data:\n\n```\nCell layout (N-cell pop slot)\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     filled_size\n4       4     tag      (0 if untagged; iterator counter snapshot otherwise)\n8       …     data\n```\n\nSlots created for wires from parallel iterators (issue 304) are\ntagged. Pop on a tagged slot returns the cell with the lowest tag,\nnot the head cell — preserving iterator-counter order across pushes\nthat arrived out of order from parallel iterator workers.\n\nUntagged slots default tag to 0 and pop FIFO at no extra cost. The\ntag-aware pop is a per-slot mode flag set at allocation time.\n\n### Asynchrony\nThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\nfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\nis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n\n## Slot layout\n\nEach slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`\nbytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:\n\n```\nSlot header\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)\n4       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation)\n8       4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)\n12      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)\n16      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)\n17      3     _pad\n20      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))\n```\n\nEach cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`\nbytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across\nslots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing\nsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\nhow big it needs the cells.\n\n`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\nspins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —\nif contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without\nchanging the API.\n\nWrites to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is\nadvanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to\nsee the complete value at the head cell.\n\n## Lifetime\n\nA slot — the named input port on a box — is owned by its box and\nlives from graph load until run end. That hasn't changed. What\nhas changed is the values that pass through slots: they are\nreference-counted memory chunks served by a single unified\nallocator (see \"Allocation strategy\" below), not malloc'd memory\nthat lives the whole run.\n\nEvery value handed to a consumer carries a reference. When a\nconsumer is done with a value, it drops its reference. When the\nlast reference drops, the chunk holding the value goes back to\nthe allocator's free-lists, available for the next request. Two\nneighbor-merge steps and an on-demand sweep keep fragmentation\nunder control (described in the allocator section).\n\nThe earlier note in this document — \"no per-slot reference\ncounting\" — referred to the box's own slot record, not to the\nvalues flowing through it. The slot record itself is still\nallocated once at graph load and not freed until run end. The\nvalues inside the slot are the things that get refcounted, freed,\nand recycled. The distinction matters: there's one slot per\ninput port, and many values flow through that slot over the life\nof a run.\n\nRun termination is still governed by the pool's active-task\ncounter (issue 301): when no task is running and no further\nspawns are pending, the run is over. The allocator and refcount\nmachinery don't influence termination — they just ensure memory\ngets returned to the free-lists as values become unreferenced\nduring the run.\n\n### No wait lists\n\nTasks never park on slots. Tasks are spawned by the dispatch\nlayer's spawn-on-input-arrival rule and run to completion; they\nnever block. A slot that has no value yet simply means the\nspawn rule hasn't fired for that consumer yet. No wait list,\nno per-slot wake-up traversal — just a check after each push.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots are allocated from process heap memory. The slot store owns a\nper-run allocator (described under \"Allocation strategy\" below) that\nhands out memory chunks to slots. Plain `malloc`-class memory is\nsufficient — every worker thread in the process can read and write\nit, and no spec ever needs to access it from a child process.\n\nSynchronization within a slot uses the per-slot `touched` flag for\nheader mutations. There is no allocator-wide mutex on the\nread/write path; only the per-size-class free lists in the\nallocator have their own locks.\n\n## Slot creation\n\nSlot creation happens at **graph load**, not per task. The graph\nloader walks every box, allocates one ring buffer per input port,\nand parks the slot on the box's per-port slot table. The dispatch\nlayer never allocates new slots at runtime in the steady state —\nall slots that will ever exist are created up front.\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n```\n\n`cell_capacity` and `n_cells` come from compile-time analysis of\nthe graph. Boxes downstream of iterators get larger `n_cells` to\nabsorb the iterator's worst-case backlog.\n\nIf a slot's pre-allocated `n_cells` proves too small at runtime\n(producer outpaces consumer beyond the pre-allocation), the slot's\nring grows — see \"Allocation strategy\" below.\n\n## C API surface\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc       (slot_store_t *s, int cell_capacity, int n_cells, int flags);\nvoid      slot_push        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size, uint32_t tag);\nint       slot_peek        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // 1-cell: read without draining\nint       slot_pop         (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // N-cell: drain head (or lowest-tag)\nuint32_t  slot_read_inc    (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);            // SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER only\nint       slot_has_value   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);                          // for spawn-rule check\n```\n\nFlags include:\n- `SLOT_TAGGED`: cells carry ordering tags; `slot_pop` returns the\n  lowest-tag cell.\n- `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER`: slot holds a single atomic uint32; reads\n  via `slot_read_inc` only. `slot_push` / `slot_peek` / `slot_pop`\n  are not valid on atomic-counter slots.\n\nPush always takes a `tag` argument; untagged slots ignore it (or\ntreat 0 as \"no order\").\n\n1-cell peek slot use: producer `push` once at startup (literal) or\nwhen its single invocation completes (single-push wire). All\nconsumer tasks `peek` to read the value as many times as their box\nruns. The cell is never empty after the initial push.\n\nN-cell pop slot use: producers `push` repeatedly. Consumer tasks\n`pop` one cell each. For tagged slots, `pop` returns the\nlowest-tag cell; for untagged, FIFO. Pop on an empty slot is a\nbug — the spawn rule guarantees the slot is non-empty before a\ntask spawns.\n\nThere is no `slot_ref` / `slot_unref` — slot lifetime is the run.\n\n## Submission timing\n\nTasks are spawned dynamically in response to slot pushes. Each box\nhas small per-box state used by the dispatch layer:\n\n```\nbox_runtime_state {\n    slot_id_t  *input_slots;     // one per input port (set at load)\n    int        *port_modes;      // PEEK or POP, per input port\n    int         n_inputs;\n    slot_id_t   counter_slot;    // iterator only: SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER slot;\n                                 // 0 / unused otherwise\n};\n```\n\nThe spawning rule:\n- When a producer pushes to one of a box's input slots, the\n  dispatch layer checks **does every input slot have a value\n  available?** \"Available\" means:\n  - For peek-mode (1-cell) slots: cell has been written at least\n    once. Once a peek slot is filled, it stays available — every\n    subsequent spawn-check on this box passes the peek-port check.\n  - For pop-mode (N-cell) slots: queue is non-empty.\n- If yes, spawn a `dispatch_task_t` and submit to the pool. The\n  task pops (or peeks) one value from each input slot when it\n  runs.\n- Each push that completes the input set triggers exactly one\n  spawn. Multiple pushes accumulate in pop slots; each pop\n  consumes one, and if more remain, the next push (or check)\n  re-fires the spawn rule.\n\nThis makes the pool's queue the rate buffer: pushes accumulate\nin pop slots (possibly multiple per slot), and one task per\naccumulated value gets spawned.\n\nTasks never block on slots. They're spawned after inputs are\nready, run to completion, and disappear. Blocking-and-waking\nmachinery is unnecessary — the spawn-on-arrival rule is the\nsynchronization primitive.\n\nThe pool's queue is the only queue. There is no separate \"blocked\ntasks\" structure.\n\n## Allocation strategy: one unified allocator for every value\n\nThere is one allocator. It serves both values whose size is known\nfrom the graph at compile time and values whose size only becomes\nknown when they're produced (LLM responses, dynamic arrays, anything\nwhere the upper bound isn't a useful number). The earlier draft of\nthis document split these into two stores — a size-class slot\nallocator for the known case, a separate \"large-value heap\" for the\nunknown case. That split was a mistake. They are the same problem\nand they reuse the same machinery; treating them as two stores led\nto the unknown-size path being a monotonically-growing pool that\nnever reclaims, which is a memory leak by design.\n\n### How the allocator learns sizes ahead of time\n\nBefore the run starts, the loader walks every box in the graph and\nreads the size that box declares for its output. A box that always\nproduces a 32-byte number declares 32. A box that always produces a\n4-megabyte image declares 4 megabytes. The loader collects every\ndistinct declared size, deduplicates them, and creates one free-list\nper distinct size. Each list is pre-populated with enough chunks to\ncover the static demand for that size.\n\nBoxes whose output size depends on runtime — the LLM case — declare\n\"size unknown.\" The loader doesn't create a pre-warmed list for those\nboxes; it knows their values will be allocated on demand.\n\nBoth kinds share the same underlying memory region. The difference is\nonly whether the loader had a list pre-warmed for the value's size.\n\n### Two doors, one allocator\n\n**Door 1 — declared-size allocation.** Given a request for size N,\nwhere N matches a declared size class: pop the head of that class's\nfree-list. One step. This is the common path for the vast majority\nof values; nearly every box in a typical graph has a declared output\nsize.\n\n**Door 2 — runtime-size allocation.** Given a request for an unknown\nsize at runtime: find the smallest size class whose chunks are large\nenough. If that class is exhausted, try the next-larger. If the\nchunk handed out is oversized for the request, slice the unused tail\ninto a residual chunk and push that residual onto the appropriate\nsmaller free-list. The residual is only kept if it's at least as large\nas the smallest declared size class — anything smaller is left as\ninternal waste rather than fragmenting the lists with stubs.\n\nBoth doors fall through to the same fragmentation-recovery and growth\nmachinery below when their free-lists can't satisfy a request.\n\n### Reference counting drives deallocation\n\nEvery value the allocator hands out is reference-counted. The dispatch\nlayer increments the count when handing a value to a consumer and\ndecrements it when the consumer is done. When the count reaches zero,\nthe chunk is returned to the allocator.\n\nThe return-to-allocator step does two things atomically: pushes the\nchunk onto the appropriate free-list AND checks the chunk's two\nphysical neighbors. If either neighbor is also free, the deallocator\nmerges them into a larger chunk and pushes the merged chunk onto the\nfree-list for the merged size. This eager neighbor-merge is O(1) and\nkeeps small-scale fragmentation from accumulating on the hot path.\n\nReference counting requires touching every place that hands out a\npointer to an allocator-managed value. That cost is paid once. After\nthe wiring exists, both doors above benefit from the same recycling.\n\n### When does the bigger sweep run\n\nThe eager neighbor-merge above catches the common case. It misses\npatterns where free chunks are scattered with allocated chunks between\nthem — the cheap merge can't see past its immediate neighbors.\n\nA deeper sweep that walks the whole address-ordered chunk list\nlooking for runs of contiguous free chunks runs on two deterministic\ntriggers, both decoupled from wall-clock time:\n\n1. **At the moment an allocation would otherwise fail.** When a\n   request can't be satisfied from any free-list — including after\n   trying larger classes and slicing — the system runs the deep sweep\n   before falling back to asking the operating system for more memory.\n   If the sweep produces a chunk large enough to satisfy the request,\n   the allocation succeeds and no growth happens. This is the\n   mandatory trigger: the sweep is the immediate alternative to\n   monotonic growth, and it fires exactly when its work has value.\n\n2. **At quiescence — moments when no task is running.** The dispatch\n   layer already recognizes these moments because it uses them to\n   decide a run is complete. Between batches is a natural opportunity\n   because no tasks are reading or writing chunks at that instant.\n   This is the opportunistic trigger.\n\nThe mandatory trigger is enough on its own. The opportunistic trigger\nis a tunable knob that can be enabled later if profiling shows\nfragmentation surviving the cheap merge faster than the mandatory\ntrigger catches up.\n\nA third option was considered — trigger when the count of small free\nfragments crosses a threshold — but rejected for now. It works, but\nit needs the threshold tuned, and the two triggers above cover the\nsame ground without that tuning step.\n\n### Physical-order chunk list (for the merge steps)\n\nBoth the eager neighbor-merge and the deeper sweep need to know\nwhich chunks are physically adjacent in memory. The size-class\nfree-lists don't carry that information — they're indexed by size,\nnot address.\n\nThe supporting structure is a doubly-linked list of all chunks (free\nand allocated) in address order. Splits and merges are O(1) given a\nchunk pointer. Neighbor lookup is O(1). The cost is pointer-chasing\nduring the deeper sweep, but the sweep only runs at the two triggers\nabove, not on the hot path.\n\nIf profiling later shows traversal cost hurting at sweep time, the\nlist can be swapped for a sorted-by-address array of `(start, end)`\npairs with an auxiliary index — the allocator's external API doesn't\nchange.\n\n### Why one allocator instead of two\n\nThe split design existed because the original two-tier scheme had a\n\"large-value heap\" carved out for variable-size payloads, on the\ntheory that mixing variable and fixed sizes in the same pool would\ncomplicate the fixed-size path. That reasoning doesn't survive\ncontact with reference counting and free-list recycling: with\nrefcount-driven free, the fixed-size path stays fast because most\nrequests match a declared class and pop in one step regardless of\nwhat else is in the region.\n\nSplitting them also meant the variable-size pool had to grow\nforever, because writing the same allocator twice — once with\nreclamation, once without — was more work than was budgeted in early\nphase 3. That's the position the current code is in. Unified gets us\nthe reclamation everywhere, with no extra design work.\n\n### Growth (last resort)\n\nWhen both doors fail and the deep sweep can't produce a fitting\nchunk, the allocator grows by asking the operating system for a new\nregion, dividing it into chunks per the declared size classes (or\ninto a single large chunk if the request was for an unknown size\nbeyond all declared classes), and threading the new chunks into the\nfree-lists and the address-ordered list.\n\nGrowth is the rare case. With pre-warmed free-lists sized to static\ndemand and refcount-driven recycling, a well-behaved graph never\nreaches growth — every allocation either pops a pre-warmed chunk or\nrecycles one whose last reference just dropped.\n\n## No type tags\n\nSlots store opaque bytes. The producer wrote N bytes; the consumer\nreads N bytes. What those bytes mean is the language spec's business\non each side, and the wire's metadata in the graph (issue 219's\ncompiler can check producer-output type vs consumer-input type at\nbuild time). The slot store does not interpret values — it does not\nneed to know if they are strings, numbers, JSON, images, or anything\nelse. Removed the type-tag field from the header for that reason.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n  ring-buffer slots implement\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Core milestone — 2026-05-12\n\nWhat shipped:\n- `src/009-slot-store.h` — the public API exactly as the design\n  describes: `slot_alloc` / `slot_push` / `slot_peek` / `slot_pop` /\n  `slot_read_inc` / `slot_has_value` / `slot_fill_count`. Plus the\n  store lifecycle pair and a small inspection helper for tests.\n- `src/009-slot-store.c` — implementation. Plain-malloc per slot\n  (size-class free lists deferred); ring slots and atomic-counter\n  slots both supported; the SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED variant of pop scans\n  for the lowest-tag filled cell. Per-slot spinlock via\n  `atomic_flag`. Atomic counter via `atomic_fetch_add_explicit`,\n  no lock.\n- `tests/009-slot-store-test.c` — 12 unit tests covering peek\n  semantics, FIFO pop, tagged pop ordering (in-order and\n  interleaved), atomic counter (sequential + 8-thread concurrent),\n  bad-argument paths, ring-full / empty edge cases, and a\n  multi-thread producer/consumer race over 5000 values.\n- Makefile additions: `test` target builds test binaries via a\n  pattern rule and runs them. Per-test prerequisites listed\n  explicitly so each binary links the minimal set of source `.o`s.\n- File index counter advanced to `009`.\n\nVerified clean build and 12/12 tests pass in `make STRICT=1`\n(`-Werror -Wextra -Wpedantic`).\n\nWhat's deferred to a follow-on within 302:\n- **Size-class free lists with coalescing.** The current\n  implementation `malloc`s each slot independently. That's correct\n  but unoptimized. Slots are allocated once at graph load and never\n  freed until run end, so under the current usage pattern free-list\n  reuse buys nothing. Lands once profiling justifies it (or once\n  long-running maps surface allocation pressure).\n- **Large-value heap for variable-size payloads.** Slots currently\n  store fixed-size cells; very large outputs (multi-MB LLM\n  responses, dynamically-sized arrays) will need the two-tier\n  scheme described under \"Large-value heap\" above. Blocks no\n  in-flight phase 3 work until a graph wants variable-size outputs.\n\nNeither deferred item blocks 301 / 304 / 305 / 306 / 307 / 308.\n\n### Large-value heap milestone — 2026-05-19\n\nThe variable-size payload follow-on landed in two layers:\n\n1. **`src/015-large-value-heap.{c,h}`** — chunked arena allocator.\n   Default 64 KB chunks; oversized allocations (larger than the\n   default chunk) get their own exact-fit chunk so one large value\n   doesn't bloat the regular bump chunks. Pointer stability is the\n   load-bearing property: chunks never move once allocated, so a\n   consumer's pointer survives any number of subsequent producer\n   allocations. Eight unit tests in\n   `tests/015-large-value-heap-test.c` cover the create/destroy\n   round-trip, single + multi alloc within a chunk, oversized\n   allocations getting their own chunks, pointer stability across\n   forced growth, zero-size allocations returning non-NULL, the\n   stats accessors, and an eight-thread / eight-thousand-alloc\n   concurrency stress test that asserts every returned pointer is\n   unique and writable.\n\n2. **Slot-store integration.** Added `SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE` to\n   `slot_alloc`. Cell layout for LARGE_VALUE slots is\n   `filled_size (4 bytes) + pad/tag (4 bytes) + stable pointer\n   (8 bytes)` — the 8-byte payload offset keeps the pointer\n   naturally aligned regardless of whether SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED is\n   also set. The slot store lazy-creates one shared lvh heap on\n   the first LARGE_VALUE allocation; the heap is destroyed\n   alongside the store. Push allocates from the heap *outside*\n   the slot spinlock (the heap has its own mutex; nesting is\n   fine, but reducing time-under-spinlock keeps the lock fast for\n   other producers). Peek and pop follow the cell's pointer and\n   memcpy the requested bytes back into the caller's buffer.\n\nFour new slot-store tests cover the new path:\n`large_value_push_pop` (100 KB payload, double-peek, then pop);\n`large_value_buf_too_small` (oversized payload + small dest →\n-1, cell preserved); `large_value_multi_push_fifo` (three\ndifferent-size values pushed and popped in order); and\n`large_value_tagged_ordering` (LARGE_VALUE + TAGGED → pops\nreturn lowest-tag-first with bytes intact).\n\nWhat this unblocks: any box that wants to emit a variable-size\noutput can now declare its downstream consumer slots with\nSLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE and produce payloads whose size isn't\nknown at graph-load time. The wiring from declared box output\ntype to the LARGE_VALUE flag in `graph_attach_runtime` lands as\na follow-on once a fixture or real graph requires it; the\nfoundation is in place.\n\n### Producer-driven LARGE_VALUE wiring — 2026-05-19\n\nThe \"wiring from declared box output type\" deferred above is\nnow in place. During `graph_attach_runtime`, each consumer\ninput slot's flags get OR'd with `SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE` if any\nproducer feeding that port declares `output_capacity == 0`. The\nrule covers both data boxes (which default to 0 because the\nfield isn't in their JSON schema) and call boxes that opt into\nvariable-size output by setting `\"output_capacity\": 0`. A\nmixed-language fan-in where any producer is variable-size\nupgrades the whole slot to LARGE_VALUE — the conservative call,\nsince the slot can only carry one format and the LVH path\nhandles small payloads correctly too.\n\nA new test in `tests/010-graph-loader-test.c`\n(`variable_size_producer_lvh_wiring`) attaches the hello fixture\nwith a deliberately tight default_cell_bytes of 512, then\nasserts a 2 KB push succeeds on greet's `name` port (fed by\ndata box `who`) and fails on greet's `salutation` port (literal\nonly, no producer). The discriminator is the slot's capacity:\nwithout LARGE_VALUE the 2 KB push exceeds 512 and is rejected;\nwith it the heap absorbs the bytes and the push lands.\n\nThe remaining phase-3 checklist item \"Variable-size outputs\nwork via the large-value heap\" is now satisfied end-to-end at\nthe slot-store boundary. A graph fixture that exercises the\npath on the dispatch side — a Lua box returning a multi-KB\nstring and a downstream box reading it — is a one-line fixture\naddition and lands with the 6-more-integration-fixtures task.\n\nWhat's still deferred within 302:\n- **Size-class free lists with coalescing.** Still no need.\n- **Per-allocation free in the large-value heap.** The heap\n  grows monotonically for the life of a run. Long-running\n  iterator loops that emit large values will pin memory until\n  run end. Acceptable for current fixtures; a size-class\n  allocator with eager-coalesce is the upgrade path if profiling\n  flags it.\n\n### Retraction of the monotonic-growth deferral — 2026-05-19\n\nThe two deferrals listed immediately above this entry no longer\nreflect the design. Monotonic growth was being described as\n\"acceptable for current fixtures.\" It isn't acceptable — it's a\nmemory leak by design, and any long-running workload (multi-day\nruns, anything driven by an LLM in a loop, anything that\naccumulates) will reproduce it as a real problem. Calling it\ndeferred made it easier to skip; calling it a leak makes it clear\nwhy the skip isn't safe.\n\nThe design above this implementation log has been rewritten\naccordingly. There are no longer two stores. There is one\nallocator that serves both compile-time-known sizes and\nruntime-only-known sizes from a shared pool, with reference\ncounting driving deallocation, an O(1) eager neighbor-merge on\nreturn, and a deeper sweep on the two triggers described in the\nallocator section (\"at the moment an allocation would otherwise\nfail\" and \"at quiescence between task batches\"). Both triggers\nare deterministic — they react to the program's own behavior\nrather than to wall-clock time.\n\nWhat this means in terms of work remaining:\n\n- The chained-block region currently serving variable-size values\n  gets replaced by the unified allocator above. The slot-store\n  cells that hold large-value pointers stay; what they point into\n  changes from the bump-allocated chain to the size-class\n  allocator's chunks.\n- The slot store's small-fixed-size path adopts the same\n  allocator. Today that path malloc's each slot's cell-array\n  separately; under the new design every cell-array is a chunk\n  from the unified allocator.\n- The dispatch layer learns to increment and decrement reference\n  counts when it hands values from producer to consumer. This is\n  the widest change in scope — many places — but each individual\n  change is one line. The new allocator depends on these calls\n  being correct: a missed decrement leaks; a missed increment\n  frees a value that's still in use.\n- The address-ordered chunk list (described in the allocator\n  section) is added alongside the size-class lists.\n- The deeper sweep is implemented and wired into the two trigger\n  points.\n\nThe implementation has not been started; this entry is the\ndesign commitment, not a completion notice. The earlier\n\"acceptable for current fixtures\" framing is withdrawn.\n",
