    "file":{
      "content":"# 305 — C graph loader (replaces 003-loader.lua)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe phase 2 loader at `src/003-loader.lua` reads a map directory's\n`boxes/*.json`, `data/*.json`, and metadata, decodes JSON via dkjson,\nruns schema validation, builds the in-memory graph table, and detects\nentry boxes. It is Lua. The synchronous executor consumes its output.\n\nThe phase 3 pool runner (issue 301) cannot embed a Lua state for\nloading — Lua appears in the runner only as a per-box language runtime,\nnever as the runner's own scripting layer. The loader is therefore\nported to C and lives inside (or alongside) `src/008-pool-runner.c`.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe C graph loader is the first phase of the pool runner's startup. It:\n1. Walks the map directory.\n2. Parses every JSON file.\n3. Validates schema and connection topology.\n4. Builds a single `graph_t` struct that the pool runner and dispatch\n   layer consume.\n\nThe loader is a one-shot at startup. It crashes the program on any\nvalidation failure (per the hard-crash policy in issue 303). There is\nno recovery, no skip-bad-boxes mode.\n\n## Inputs\n\nThe map directory layout (unchanged from phase 2):\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/\n    meta.json          ← entry box, src_dirs, run-level metadata\n    boxes/*.json       ← one file per box\n    data/*.json        ← static data values (literal inputs)\n    src/*              ← box function source files (resolved via meta.src_dirs)\n```\n\nThe loader is given the map directory path as a C string.\n\n## Output: `graph_t`\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int           n_boxes;\n    box_t        *boxes;            // array of box descriptors\n    int           n_connections;\n    connection_t *connections;\n    int           n_size_classes;\n    int          *size_classes;     // distinct slot sizes the graph uses\n    int           n_entry_boxes;\n    int          *entry_box_ids;    // indices into boxes[]\n    int           n_languages;\n    const char  **languages;        // distinct language names used\n} graph_t;\n\ntypedef struct {\n    char         *id;               // user-defined box id (\"classifier\", \"stamp\", …)\n    char         *kind;             // \"call\" | \"data\"\n    char         *lang;             // \"lua\" | \"c\" | \"bash\" | ...; NULL for data and iterator/comparator\n    char         *ref;               // file path; NULL for data/iterator/comparator\n    char         *fn;                // function name; NULL for data/iterator/comparator\n    int           n_inputs;\n    input_decl_t *inputs;\n    int           output_capacity;  // bytes; 0 if variable-size (uses large-value heap)\n    int           is_comparator;\n    int           is_iterator;\n    int           n_iter_outputs;\n    char        **iter_output_names;\n    // …\n} box_t;\n\ntypedef struct {\n    int   from_box_id;\n    char *from_branch;              // NULL for plain call; \"lt\"/\"eq\"/\"gt\" for comparator;\n                                    // iterator output name otherwise\n    int   to_box_id;\n    char *to_input_name;\n    int   to_input_index;\n} connection_t;\n```\n\nStrings are owned by the graph (allocated from a single arena attached\nto the graph; freed when the graph is destroyed at the end of the run).\n\n## Loading phases\n\n### 1. Directory walk\nOpen the map directory, enumerate `boxes/`, `data/`, and the optional\n`meta.json`. Each entry is queued for parsing.\n\n### 2. JSON parse\nUse the vendored JSON parser (issue 301 lists cJSON / jsmn / hand-rolled\nas candidates). Each file becomes a parsed JSON tree. Parse errors are\nfatal — print the file path and the parser's error message, abort.\n\n### 3. Schema validation\nBox kinds and what they mean at runtime:\n\n- **`call`** is a verb — a box that runs a function (or, for iterator\n  and comparator variants, a dispatch-layer routing primitive). Each\n  call box becomes a `dispatch_task_t` in the pool when its inputs\n  are ready.\n- **`data`** is a noun — a literal value embedded in the map. It has\n  no function and produces no task in the pool. Its output slot is\n  allocated and filled at startup by the loader and remains filled\n  for the duration of the run; downstream consumers read it like any\n  other slot.\n\nRequired fields per kind:\n- `id`, `kind` always required.\n- For `kind == \"call\"`: either (a) `lang`, `ref`, `fn` (plain call\n  box), or (b) `iterator_outputs` (iterator box, no `ref`/`fn`), or\n  (c) `comparator` field set (comparator box, no `ref`/`fn`).\n- For `kind == \"data\"`: a `value` field; no `inputs` or `connections`\n  (other than outgoing wires from this box's output slot).\n\nBox ids must be unique across the map. Connection endpoints must\nreference valid box ids and valid input names.\n\nSchema rules mirror `src/001-schema.lua`. The C validator is a port of\nthat file's logic, simplified by the absence of port-named branching\n(removed in issue 108 cleanup).\n\n### 4. Topology validation\n- Every connection's `from_box` and `to_box` exist.\n- Every connection's `to_input_name` matches a declared input on the\n  destination box.\n- No non-iterator cycles. The validator runs DFS; any cycle that does\n  not pass through an iterator box is rejected.\n- Every required input has at least one connection feeding it (or is\n  fed by a `data` box).\n\nValidation failure aborts the program with a precise error message —\nwhich box, which connection, what was wrong.\n\n### 5. Slot size class enumeration\nWalk every box and queued-input declaration to enumerate the distinct\nslot sizes the graph will need. Each unique size becomes a size class\nin the slot allocator (issue 302). Output:\n\n```c\ngraph->size_classes      = { 64, 256, 1024, 65536 };  // example\ngraph->n_size_classes    = 4;\n```\n\nThe slot allocator pre-populates each class's free list with\n`n_workers × (count of boxes whose output is this size)` slots. This\ncovers the worst case — every worker concurrently producing an output\nat this size class — without overshooting. Demand beyond this triggers\ngrowth (issue 302); the per-thread multiplier is the right ceiling for\nthe static count, while leaving headroom for iterators that allocate\nper-invocation slots.\n\n### 6. Entry-box detection\nA box is an entry box if either:\n- It has zero inputs, or\n- All of its inputs are connected only to `data` boxes (literal values\n  with no upstream computation).\n\nEntry boxes are submitted to the pool first; everything else fires from\npost-action routing in the dispatch layer.\n\nA map can have any number of entry boxes. The user lays out the\ninitial program state via `data` boxes and entry-point call boxes; the\nrunner submits all entries at once, and the graph propagates from\nthere. There is no singular `main`.\n\n### 7. Language enumeration\nCollect the distinct `lang` values across all plain call boxes. The\npool runner uses this set to decide which language specs (issue 303)\nto load and which per-worker handles to initialize.\n\nIterator and comparator boxes have no `lang` and contribute nothing\nhere.\n\n### Note on built-in primitives vs shipped libraries\n\nThere are two distinct categories of \"things the user gets out of the\nbox,\" and they live in different places:\n\n- **Dispatch-layer primitives** are graph-topology operations whose\n  semantics are routing, not data transformation. Iterator and\n  comparator are the two so far. They have no `lang` / `ref` / `fn` —\n  the dispatch layer implements their behavior directly. Splitter\n  / fan-out is already free via wire fan-out and does not need its\n  own box kind. Possible future primitives: a \"gate\" (forward only\n  when a control input is truthy), a \"merge\" (forward whichever\n  input arrives first). These are not on the roadmap; flagged here\n  so the door stays open.\n- **Shipped libraries** are data-transformation utilities — JSON\n  parse/serialize, file read/write, string concat/split, regex,\n  shell-out. These are language-specific (string semantics differ\n  between Lua, C, and Bash) and ship as `libs/<name>.<ext>` per\n  language. They are not built into the dispatch layer; they are\n  ordinary call-box source files that users wire into their maps.\n  `libs/ollama.lua` is an existing example.\n\nThe distinction matters: dispatch-layer primitives change the graph\nmodel; shipped libraries don't. A dispatch primitive can do things a\nfunction call cannot (like routing on a counter); a library is just\ncode that happens to be vendored.\n\n## Error policy\n\nAny failure in any phase aborts the program. The loader prints:\n- The map path\n- The phase that failed (parse / schema / topology / etc.)\n- The specific file or box that caused the failure\n- The parser's or validator's diagnostic message\n\nThen `exit(1)`. There is no partial-load mode.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- JSON library choice: cJSON (heaviest, easiest, well-maintained),\n  jsmn (tiny, no allocations, manual tree walking), or hand-rolled\n  (smallest dependency footprint, more code). Decision deferred to\n  implementation time.\n### String storage\n\nA \"string arena\" is a single `malloc`-backed buffer the graph loader\nuses to store every string it owns (box ids, file paths, function\nnames, branch tags) packed end-to-end. Each string is a `char *`\npointing into the arena. Allocating a string is just bumping the\narena's offset; freeing happens once when the arena is destroyed at\nthe end of the run, in a single `free(arena_buffer)`.\n\nThis is faster and simpler than calling `malloc` per string: one\n`free` for thousands of strings, no fragmentation, and lookup is\njust a pointer.\n\nThe arena starts small and grows on demand by `realloc`-ing to a\nlarger size when the current buffer fills up. Because every stored\nstring is referenced by a `char *` into the arena, a `realloc` that\nmoves the buffer would invalidate all the pointers — so the loader\neither uses a series of fixed-size chunks (a chunk list rather than a\nsingle growable buffer) or pre-sizes the arena from the file count\nto avoid mid-load realloc. Chunk-list is the standard answer.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Vendor the chosen JSON parser into `libs/json/`.\n2. Define `graph_t`, `box_t`, `connection_t`, `input_decl_t` in\n   `src/008-pool-runner.c` (or a sibling header).\n3. Implement phase 1 (directory walk) and phase 2 (parse). Smoke test:\n   load `maps/hello`, print the parsed tree.\n4. Implement phase 3 (schema validation) one rule at a time. Each\n   rule has a unit test against a malformed map fixture.\n5. Implement phase 4 (topology validation), including the cycle\n   detector. Test against `maps/branch-test` (valid) and a fixture\n   with a non-iterator cycle (invalid).\n6. Implement phase 5 (size class enumeration). Output should match\n   the box outputs declared in `maps/hello` and `maps/classify-demo`.\n7. Implement phases 6 (entry boxes) and 7 (languages). Verify against\n   known maps.\n8. Wire the loader into `src/008-pool-runner.c`'s `main` so the pool\n   runner starts by loading and validating before doing anything\n   else.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — phase 2 loader, ported by this issue\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — phase 2 schema validator, also ported\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool runner that owns and uses the loader\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle that\n  consumes the graph\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot allocator that consumes\n  the size class list\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec registry that consumes\n  the language list\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that consumes\n  the box and connection arrays\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — the compiler is the other consumer of\n  the same validation logic; the C loader and the compiler should\n  share validation code if possible\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Phase 1 + 2 + early phase 3 — 2026-05-12\n\nWhat shipped:\n- `src/010-graph-loader.h` — public types and API. `graph_t` is\n  opaque; the box / connection / input declaration shapes are\n  public so the dispatch layer (issue 304) can walk them directly.\n  Routing kinds align with issue 233 — `routing_t` with `kind`\n  plus per-kind parameters, no legacy `comparand` /\n  `iterator_outputs` top-level fields.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.c` — implementation. Pipeline: open the\n  map dir, parse `meta.json` via the project JSON parser\n  (issue 314), walk every `.json` under `boxes/`, parse each into\n  a `box_t`, enforce kind-specific required fields (ref/routing\n  for call; path for data; inputs only for file_write), validate\n  id uniqueness across boxes. Errors return a malloc'd\n  `<file>:<line>: <message>` diagnostic via the `**err`\n  out-parameter; the pool runner's main is expected to print and\n  abort.\n- `tests/maps/hello/` and `tests/maps/branching/` — fixture maps\n  exercising the call/data combo, comparator routing (lt/eq/gt\n  branches all present), and iterator routing (n_outputs=3).\n- `tests/010-graph-loader-test.c` — 7 unit tests covering\n  successful loads of both fixtures, missing map directory,\n  NULL argument, unknown box kind, missing routing, and\n  duplicate box id. Malformed-shape tests use mkdtemp scratch\n  dirs so the tracked fixtures stay valid.\n- Memory model: one `json_arena_t` per loaded graph holds every\n  string and every parsed tree from every file; the box,\n  connection, and input declaration arrays are plain malloc.\n  `graph_destroy` releases all of it.\n- `.gitignore` anchored to `/maps/` so `tests/maps/` is tracked.\n- Makefile per-test dependency line for `010-graph-loader-test`\n  linking the loader and the JSON parser.\n\nVerified `make STRICT=1` builds cleanly; 33 tests across three\nsuites (slot store 12, graph loader 7, JSON 14) all pass.\n\nWhat's deferred to follow-on iterations within 305:\n- **Phase 4 — topology validation.** Connection endpoints store\n  string refs only. The next pass resolves `to_box` to integer\n  indices, verifies endpoints exist, and detects non-iterator\n  cycles via DFS.\n- **Phase 5 — slot size class enumeration.** The loader needs to\n  walk every box output and produce the distinct `cell_capacity`\n  values the slot store's allocator pre-populates.\n- **Phase 6 — entry-box detection.** A box with zero inputs or\n  with all inputs fed only by `data` boxes is an entry. The pool\n  runner spawns initial tasks for these.\n- **Phase 7 — language enumeration.** Distinct `lang` values\n  across call boxes, handed to the spec registry (issue 303).\n- The remaining routing kinds from issue 233 (randomizer,\n  weighted, distributor) — the parser currently rejects them with\n  a precise message.\n\nNone of those block 301 / 303 / 306. Topology and language\nenumeration land before 304 (the dispatch layer) since the\ndispatch action needs both.\n\n### Topology endpoint resolution — 2026-05-12\n\nAfter `load_boxes` succeeds, a `resolve_topology` pass walks every\noutgoing connection on every box and resolves the `to_box` string\nto its index in `graph->boxes`, and `to_input` to its index in\nthe target box's `inputs[]`. Both string refs are preserved on\n`connection_t` for diagnostics. Misses surface as\n`box 'X' has a connection to nonexistent box 'Y'` or\n`... nonexistent input 'Z'`. Two new fixture-based failure tests\nplus an assertion on the resolved indices in the happy-path\n`load_hello` test. The `branching` fixture grew three more box\nfiles (`small`, `exact`, `big`) so its three comparator branches\nhave real targets now.\n\nStill deferred within 305: slot size class enumeration, entry-box\ndetection, language enumeration.\n\n### Non-iterator cycle detection — 2026-05-12\n\nStandard DFS with white/gray/black coloring; the only twist is\nthat we skip outgoing edges from iterator-routing boxes, since\ncycles passing through an iterator are legitimate (the iterator's\ninput queue eventually empties and the loop terminates). Two new\nfixture-based tests cover the reject case (`a → b → a`, no\niterator) and the allowed case (`a → iter → b → a`).\n\n### Runtime attach (slot allocation + spec resolution) — 2026-05-12\n\n`graph_attach_runtime(g, slots, specs, default_cell_bytes, err)`\nwalks every box and:\n- allocates one 1-cell peek slot per declared input port via\n  `slot_alloc`, storing the slot id in `box->input_slot_ids[i]`;\n- resolves the spec for each call box by looking up `box->lang`\n  in the registry (or, as a fallback, by matching the file\n  extension of `box->ref`), storing the result on\n  `box->spec_idx`.\n\nThe graph also remembers its `map_dir` so the dispatch layer can\nresolve relative paths for data boxes and file_write boxes.\n\nWhat's still deferred:\n- **Language enumeration on the graph.** We resolve per-box but\n  don't expose the distinct set of languages a map uses, so\n  workers init every spec rather than only the ones in use.\n\n### Per-input slot modes + multi-spawn propagation — 2026-05-12\n\n`graph_attach_runtime` now picks the slot mode per input port:\n- A new BFS pass (`propagate_multi_spawn`) seeds every iterator-\n  routing call box as `multi_spawn = 1` and propagates the flag\n  forward through the connection graph. Every box reachable from\n  an iterator is now flagged.\n- For multi-spawn boxes, each input slot is allocated as a\n  16-cell pop ring. For single-spawn boxes, the legacy 1-cell\n  peek slot is used.\n- `box->input_slot_modes[]` carries the per-port mode\n  (`SLOT_MODE_PEEK` / `SLOT_MODE_POP`) so the dispatch action\n  picks the right read op.\n\nThis is the compile-time wire classification the architecture\ndoc described, with a single-step forward propagation rule. A\nproper per-wire classification (an iterator-rooted wire is\nmulti-push regardless of the immediate consumer's status) would\nallow finer-grained mode picks; the current rule is conservative\nin the right direction (slots that *could* be POP are POP).\n",

It is Lua. The synchronous executor consumes its output.\n11\t\n12\tThe phase 3 pool runner (issue 301) cannot embed a Lua state for\n13\tloading — Lua appears in the runner only as a per-box language runtime,\n14\tnever as the runner's own scripting layer. The loader is therefore\n15\tported to C and lives inside (or alongside) `src/008-pool-runner.c`.\n16\t\n17\t## Concept\n18\t\n19\tThe C graph loader is the first phase of the pool runner's startup. It:\n20\t1. Walks the map directory.\n21\t2. Parses every JSON file.\n22\t3. Validates schema and connection topology.\n23\t4. Builds a single `graph_t` struct that the pool runner and dispatch\n24\t   layer consume.\n25\t\n26\tThe loader is a one-shot at startup. It crashes the program on any\n27\tvalidation failure (per the hard-crash policy in issue 303). There is\n28\tno recovery, no skip-bad-boxes mode.\n29\t\n30\t## Inputs\n31\t\n32\tThe map directory layout (unchanged from phase 2):\n33\t\n34\t```\n35\tmaps/<name>/\n36\t    meta.json          ← entry box, src_dirs, run-level metadata\n37\t    boxes/*.json       ← one file per box\n38\t    data/*.json        ← static data values (literal inputs)\n39\t    src/*              ← box function source files (resolved via meta.src_dirs)\n40\t```\n41\t\n42\tThe loader is given the map directory path as a C string.\n43\t\n44\t## Output: `graph_t`\n45\t\n46\t```c\n47\ttypedef struct {\n48\t    int           n_boxes;\n49\t    box_t        *boxes;            // array of box descriptors\n50\t    int           n_connections;\n51\t    connection_t *connections;\n52\t    int           n_size_classes;\n53\t    int          *size_classes;     // distinct slot sizes the graph uses\n54\t    int           n_entry_boxes;\n55\t    int          *entry_box_ids;    // indices into boxes[]\n56\t    int           n_languages;\n57\t    const char  **languages;        // distinct language names used\n58\t} graph_t;\n59\t\n60\ttypedef struct {\n61\t    char         *id;               // user-defined box id (\"classifier\", \"stamp\", …)\n62\t    char         *kind;             // \"call\" | \"data\"\n63\t    char         *lang;             // \"lua\" | \"c\" | \"bash\" | ...; NULL for data and iterator/comparator\n64\t    char         *ref;               // file path; NULL for data/iterator/comparator\n65\t    char         *fn;                // function name; NULL for data/iterator/comparator\n66\t    int           n_inputs;\n67\t    input_decl_t *inputs;\n68\t    int           output_capacity;  // bytes; 0 if variable-size (uses large-value heap)\n69\t    int           is_comparator;\n70\t    int           is_iterator;\n71\t    int           n_iter_outputs;\n72\t    char        **iter_output_names;\n73\t    // …\n74\t} box_t;\n75\t\n76\ttypedef struct {\n77\t    int   from_box_id;\n78\t    char *from_branch;              // NULL for plain call; \"lt\"/\"eq\"/\"gt\" for comparator;\n79\t                                    // iterator output name otherwise\n80\t    int   to_box_id;\n81\t    char *to_input_name;\n82\t    int   to_input_index;\n83\t} connection_t;\n84\t```\n85\t\n86\tStrings are owned by the graph (allocated from a single arena attached\n87\tto the graph; freed when the graph is destroyed at the end of the run).\n88\t\n89\t## Loading phases\n90\t\n91\t### 1. Directory walk\n92\tOpen the map directory, enumerate `boxes/`, `data/`, and the optional\n93\t`meta.json`. Each entry is queued for parsing.\n94\t\n95\t### 2. JSON parse\n96\tUse the vendored JSON parser (issue 301 lists cJSON / jsmn / hand-rolled\n97\tas candidates). Each file becomes a parsed JSON tree. Parse errors are\n98\tfatal — print the file path and the parser's error message, abort.\n99\t\n100\t### 3. Schema validation\n101\tBox kinds and what they mean at runtime:\n102\t\n103\t- **`call`** is a verb — a box that runs a function (or, for iterator\n104\t  and comparator variants, a dispatch-layer routing primitive). Each\n105\t  call box becomes a `dispatch_task_t` in the pool when its inputs\n106\t  are ready.\n107\t- **`data`** is a noun — a literal value embedded in the map. It has\n108\t  no function and produces no task in the pool. Its output slot is\n109\t  allocated and filled at startup by the loader and remains filled\n110\t  for the duration of the run; downstream consumers read it like any\n111\t  other slot.\n112\t\n113\tRequired fields per kind:\n114\t- `id`, `kind` always required.\n115\t- For `kind == \"call\"`: either (a) `lang`, `ref`, `fn` (plain call\n116\t  box), or (b) `iterator_outputs` (iterator box, no `ref`/`fn`), or\n117\t  (c) `comparator` field set (comparator box, no `ref`/`fn`).\n118\t- For `kind == \"data\"`: a `value` field; no `inputs` or `connections`\n119\t  (other than outgoing wires from this box's output slot).\n120\t\n121\tBox ids must be unique across the map. Connection endpoints must\n122\treference valid box ids and valid input names.\n123\t\n124\tSchema rules mirror `src/001-schema.lua`. The C validator is a port of\n125\tthat file's logic, simplified by the absence of port-named branching\n126\t(removed in issue 108 cleanup).\n127\t\n128\t### 4. Topology validation\n129\t- Every connection's `from_box` and `to_box` exist.\n130\t- Every connection's `to_input_name` matches a declared input on the\n131\t  destination box.\n132\t- No non-iterator cycles. The validator runs DFS; any cycle that does\n133\t  not pass through an iterator box is rejected.\n134\t- Every required input has at least one connection feeding it (or is\n135\t  fed by a `data` box).\n136\t\n137\tValidation failure aborts the program with a precise error message —\n138\twhich box, which connection, what was wrong.\n139\t\n140\t### 5. Slot size class enumeration\n141\tWalk every box and queued-input declaration to enumerate the distinct\n142\tslot sizes the graph will need. Each unique size becomes a size class\n143\tin the slot allocator (issue 302). Output:\n144\t\n145\t```c\n146\tgraph->size_classes      = { 64, 256, 1024, 65536 };  // example\n147\tgraph->n_size_classes    = 4;\n148\t```\n149\t\n150\tThe slot allocator pre-populates each class's free list with\n151\t`n_workers × (count of boxes whose output is this size)` slots. This\n152\tcovers the worst case — every worker concurrently producing an output\n153\tat this size class — without overshooting. Demand beyond this triggers\n154\tgrowth (issue 302); the per-thread multiplier is the right ceiling for\n155\tthe static count, while leaving headroom for iterators that allocate\n156\tper-invocation slots.\n157\t\n158\t### 6. Entry-box detection\n159\tA box is an entry box if either:\n160\t- It has zero inputs, or\n161\t- All of its inputs are connected only to `data` boxes (literal values\n162\t  with no upstream computation).\n163\t\n164\tEntry boxes are submitted to the pool first; everything else fires from\n165\tpost-action routing in the dispatch layer.\n166\t\n167\tA map can have any number of entry boxes. The user lays out the\n168\tinitial program state via `data` boxes and entry-point call boxes; the\n169\trunner submits all entries at once, and the graph propagates from\n170\tthere. There is no singular `main`.\n171\t\n172\t### 7. Language enumeration\n173\tCollect the distinct `lang` values across all plain call boxes. The\n174\tpool runner uses this set to decide which language specs (issue 303)\n175\tto load and which per-worker handles to initialize.\n176\t\n177\tIterator and comparator boxes have no `lang` and contribute nothing\n178\there.\n179\t\n180\t### Note on built-in primitives vs shipped libraries\n181\t\n182\tThere are two distinct categories of \"things the user gets out of the\n183\tbox,\" and they live in different places:\n184\t\n185\t- **Dispatch-layer primitives** are graph-topology operations whose\n186\t  semantics are routing, not data transformation. Iterator and\n187\t  comparator are the two so far. They have no `lang` / `ref` / `fn` —\n188\t  the dispatch layer implements their behavior directly. Splitter\n189\t  / fan-out is already free via wire fan-out and does not need its\n190\t  own box kind. Possible future primitives: a \"gate\" (forward only\n191\t  when a control input is truthy), a \"merge\" (forward whichever\n192\t  input arrives first). These are not on the roadmap; flagged here\n193\t  so the door stays open.\n194\t- **Shipped libraries** are data-transformation utilities — JSON\n195\t  parse/serialize, file read/write, string concat/split, regex,\n196\t  shell-out. These are language-specific (string semantics differ\n197\t  between Lua, C, and Bash) and ship as `libs/<name>.<ext>` per\n198\t  language. They are not built into the dispatch layer; they are\n199\t  ordinary call-box source files that users wire into their maps.\n200\t  `libs/ollama.lua` is an existing example.\n201\t\n202\tThe distinction matters: dispatch-layer primitives change the graph\n203\tmodel; shipped libraries don't. A dispatch primitive can do things a\n204\tfunction call cannot (like routing on a counter); a library is just\n205\tcode that happens to be vendored.\n206\t\n207\t## Error policy\n208\t\n209\tAny failure in any phase aborts the program. Two new fixture-based failure tests\n350\tplus an assertion on the resolved indices in the happy-path\n351\t`load_hello` test.       "content":"# 306 — Lua language spec implementation (reference spec)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nLua boxes today run via `drivers/lua.sh`, which spawns a fresh `luajit`\nprocess per box invocation, feeds it stdin, and reads stdout. Process\nspawn cost dominates; each call is its own fresh interpreter. There is\nno persistent Lua state between calls.\n\n## Concept\nThe Lua language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for Lua. It\nis the first reference implementation of the spec interface and the\nproof that the in-process FFI model works. It is also the simplest\ncase — no compile step, no out-of-process server.\n\nEach worker thread gets its own `lua_State`. States are not shared.\nPer-thread states need no locking on the call path; the state's\ninternals are only ever touched by the worker that owns it.\n\n`langs/lua/spec.c` is built into `langs/lua/spec.so` and loaded by\nthe pool runner via `dlopen` at startup, like any other spec.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\nInit creates a fresh `lua_State` and configures it:\n\n```c\nvoid *lua_init(int worker_idx) {\n    lua_State *L = luaL_newstate();\n    luaL_openlibs(L);\n    set_package_path(L);   // libs/, map src/, meta.json src_dirs\n    return L;\n}\n\nvoid lua_teardown(void *handle) {\n    lua_close((lua_State *)handle);\n}\n```\n\n`set_package_path` writes `package.path` and `package.cpath` to\ninclude exactly one directory: the map's own `src/`. Everything the\nmap needs — vendored libs, helper modules, anything — is copied into\n`src/` by the compile step (issue 222). The compiled map is then a\nself-contained directory: ship the directory to someone else and it\nruns without further setup.\n\nThis is a tightening of the phase 2 path, which also included\nSoraMech's central `libs/` and any `meta.json src_dirs`. The new rule\nis: one place to look for functions, the map's own `src/`, full stop.\nCompile is the step that resolves dependencies into that location.\n\n## File-and-function caching\n\nA naive `invoke` would `luaL_loadfile` and look up the function on\nevery call. Both are unnecessary work — the file's chunk does not\nchange during a run, and the function reference is stable.\n\nThe Lua spec keeps a per-handle cache: for each box source file\nloaded, store the table returned by the file's chunk as a Lua\nregistry key (`LUA_REGISTRYINDEX`). On first invocation:\n1. `luaL_loadfile(L, file_path)` — loads the chunk.\n2. `lua_pcall(L, 0, 1, 0)` — runs the chunk, expecting a returned\n   table.\n3. Store the table in the registry under a key derived from `file_path`.\n\nOn subsequent invocations:\n1. Look up the registry entry by `file_path`.\n2. Index it by `fn_name` to get the function reference.\n3. Skip `luaL_loadfile` entirely.\n\nThe cache is per-`lua_State` and therefore per-worker; no\nsynchronization is needed.\n\n## Box file convention\n\nA Lua box file returns a table whose keys are the box's exported\nfunction names:\n\n```lua\n-- maps/<name>/src/classify.lua\nlocal M = {}\n\nfunction M.classify(text)\n    if text:match(\"^%d+$\") then return \"numeric\"\n    elseif text:match(\"[a-z]\") then return \"alpha\"\n    else return \"other\"\n    end\nend\n\nreturn M\n```\n\nThe box JSON references it by `ref = \"classify.lua\"`, `fn = \"classify\"`.\nThe spec loads `classify.lua`, stores its returned table, and indexes\ninto it with `\"classify\"` to get the function.\n\nThis is the existing phase 2 convention — kept as-is.\n\n## Input marshalling\n\nInputs arrive at `invoke` as `(void *bytes, int size)` pairs. The\nspec is responsible for converting each input's bytes into the Lua\nvalue type the user's function expects. The user's function sees\narguments as native Lua values — never a raw byte buffer that the\nfunction has to parse itself.\n\nEach input has a declared type in the box JSON\n(`{\"name\": \"count\", \"type\": \"number\"}`). The graph loader (issue 305)\nrecords this type on the `input_decl_t` and passes the type alongside\nthe bytes when calling `invoke`. The Lua spec dispatches on type:\n\n| Declared type | Lua spec action                                             |\n|---------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `string`      | `lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`                           |\n| `number`      | parse with `strtod`, `lua_pushnumber`                       |\n| `integer`     | parse with `strtoll`, `lua_pushinteger`                     |\n| `boolean`     | strcmp against `\"true\"` / `\"false\"`, `lua_pushboolean`      |\n| `json`        | call `dkjson.decode` on the bytes, push the resulting table |\n| `bytes`       | `lua_pushlstring` (raw, may contain nulls)                  |\n| `any`         | treat as `string` for now                                   |\n\nThe Lua function then takes typed arguments:\n\n```lua\nfunction M.add(a, b)            -- both already numbers\n    return a + b\nend\n\nfunction M.classify(payload)    -- payload is already a table\n    return payload.kind\nend\n```\n\nThe user does not write `tonumber` or `dkjson.decode` calls inside\ntheir box function. The spec did that work before the function was\ncalled.\n\nIf a parse fails (`json` input that isn't valid JSON, `number` input\nthat isn't a number), the spec returns nonzero and the dispatch layer\naborts (per issue 303).\n\n## Return marshalling\n\nThe Lua function returns one or more values. The spec converts the\nreturn into bytes for the output slot:\n\n| Return shape           | Spec action                                                   |\n|------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|\n| Single string          | `lua_tolstring` → copy into `out_buf`                         |\n| Single number          | `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ...)` into `out_buf`                       |\n| Single boolean         | write `\"true\"` or `\"false\"`                                   |\n| Single table           | `dkjson.encode` into `out_buf`                                |\n| Single nil             | `*out_size = 0` (zero-byte output)                            |\n| Multiple values        | wrap into a table `{v1, v2, ...}` and `dkjson.encode`         |\n\n`nil` is a valid return. The spec writes zero bytes and sets\n`*out_size = 0`. Downstream consumers receive a zero-byte slot value;\nhow they interpret it depends on their declared input type (typed\n`number` consumer fails to parse; typed `string` consumer gets an\nempty string; typed `json` consumer parses zero bytes as `null` via\ndkjson). We cannot demand that user functions never return nil, so we\nhandle it.\n\nMultiple return values are wrapped into a table and JSON-encoded.\nPhase 2 silently dropped extra returns; phase 3 keeps them — the\nserialized form is `[v1, v2, ...]`.\n\nOutput buffer is sized to the box's declared `output_capacity`\n(issue 305's `box_t`). If the serialized value exceeds that, abort\n(per the hard-crash policy in issue 303). For variable-size outputs\nthe box declares `output_capacity = 0` and uses the large-value heap\n(issue 302); the spec writes into that heap and stores the handle in\n`out_buf`.\n\ndkjson is the table serializer in both directions (input parsing\nabove and output serialization here). It is already vendored.\n\n## Error handling\n\nEvery `lua_pcall` is wrapped:\n```c\nint rc = lua_pcall(L, n_args, 1, 0);\nif (rc != LUA_OK) {\n    fprintf(stderr, \"[lua spec] %s:%s — %s\\n\",\n            file_path, fn_name, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n    lua_pop(L, 1);\n    return 1;  // dispatch layer aborts the program\n}\n```\n\nLua errors (`error(...)`, runtime errors, syntax errors during file\nload) all surface here as nonzero `pcall` returns. The spec prints\nthe box context and the Lua error message to stderr, then returns\nnonzero. The dispatch layer aborts.\n\nThere is no try-and-recover. Per issue 303, errors crash the program.\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/lua/\n    spec.c          ← lang_spec_t implementation\n    Makefile        ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so         ← built artifact (gitignored)\n```\n\nThe Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall \\\n\t    -I$(LUA_INCLUDE) \\\n\t    -o $@ $< \\\n\t    -L$(LUA_LIB) -lluajit-5.1\n```\n\nLuaJIT is the assumed runtime — it matches the phase 2 driver and the\nproject preference (LuaJIT-compatible Lua, no 5.4 syntax). The build\nlinks against the system LuaJIT shared library.\n\n## Open questions\n\n(none currently — earlier questions resolved as follows:)\n\n- nil return: valid. Zero-byte output, downstream consumers\n  interpret per their declared input type.\n- Multiple return values: wrapped into a table and JSON-encoded via\n  dkjson. No values dropped.\n- Table serializer: dkjson, already vendored. Used in both\n  directions (input parsing and output serialization).\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/lua/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Implement `init` and `teardown`. Verify the pool runner can\n   `dlopen` the spec and call `init` per worker without errors.\n3. Implement file-and-function caching — load a file, store its\n   returned table in the registry, look it up later.\n4. Implement input marshalling: push bytes as strings, count args.\n5. Implement `lua_pcall` invocation with error wrapping.\n6. Implement string return marshalling. Smoke test: `maps/hello`\n   end-to-end through the pool.\n7. Implement number return marshalling.\n8. Implement table-via-JSON return marshalling.\n9. Add `package.path` resolution for libs/, src/, and `meta.src_dirs`.\n10. Test against `maps/classify-demo` and `maps/driver-test` (Lua\n    portions).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh` — phase 2 Lua driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap for\n  variable-size returns\n- `libs/dkjson` (vendored) — table-to-JSON serialization\n- `maps/hello`, `maps/classify-demo` — Lua-only smoke test maps\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Init + invoke + teardown — 2026-05-12\n\n`langs/lua/spec.c` now exports a real `lang_spec_t`:\n\n- `init(worker_idx)` creates a `lua_State` and opens the standard\n  libraries via `luaL_openlibs`. Returns the state as the per-\n  worker handle.\n- `teardown(handle)` calls `lua_close`.\n- `invoke(handle, file_path, fn_name, inputs, sizes, n, out_buf,\n  out_cap, out_size)` loads the file with `luaL_loadfile`,\n  executes the chunk (which is expected to return a module\n  table), pulls the named function out of that table, pushes each\n  input as a Lua string, calls via `lua_pcall`, and copies the\n  return as a string into the caller's buffer. The state's stack\n  is rewound to its baseline depth at every entry/exit so\n  cross-call leaks don't accumulate. Errors at every step\n  surface as nonzero return and a stderr message.\n\nFive end-to-end tests in `tests/306-lua-spec-test.c` exercise the\ninit/teardown round-trip, a `greet(name, salutation)` call with\nboth args, the same call with one arg (the Lua side defaults\nsalutation to \"Hello\"), and the two failure modes (missing\nfunction, missing file). The test loads the spec through the\nreal spec registry via dlopen, so this is the actual artifact\nthe pool runner will consume.\n\nDeferred:\n- **Rich return types.** The current invoke serializes the return\n  with `lua_tolstring`, which handles strings/numbers/booleans/\n  nil via tostring semantics. Tables, closures, and other\n  structured values land with the fast-path work in issue 312.\n\n### Per-worker module cache — 2026-05-12\n\n`lua_init` now seeds an empty Lua table at\n`LUA_REGISTRYINDEX[LUA_CACHE_KEY]`. `lua_invoke` looks up the\nbox's `file_path` in that table; on a hit it skips the\n`luaL_loadfile + lua_pcall` round-trip and uses the cached\nmodule table directly; on a miss it loads, runs the chunk,\nverifies the module table shape, and stashes the result in the\ncache before proceeding.\n\nThe cache is per-worker (each worker has its own `lua_State`),\nwhich means no locking. It's also per-file-path string, so two\nboxes that share a source file share a module table on each\nworker — calling `M.greet` from one box doesn't reload the\nchunk when another box later calls `M.farewell` on the same\nfile.\n\nCache invalidation is intentionally absent for now: once a file\nis loaded, its module table sticks for the run. If the box\nsource changes mid-run, the worker won't notice. Fine for the\nread-once-then-execute usage; revisit when there's a use case\nfor hot-reload.\n",

Skip `luaL_loadfile` entirely.\n72\t\n73\tThe cache is per-`lua_State` and therefore per-worker; no\n74\tsynchronization is needed.\n75\t\n76\t## Box file convention\n77\t\n78\tA Lua box file returns a table whose keys are the box's exported\n79\tfunction names:\n80\t\n81\t```lua\n82\t-- maps/<name>/src/classify.lua\n83\tlocal M = {}\n84\t\n85\tfunction M.classify(text)\n86\t    if text:match(\"^%d+$\") then return \"numeric\"\n87\t    elseif text:match(\"[a-z]\") then return \"alpha\"\n88\t    else return \"other\"\n89\t    end\n90\tend\n91\t\n92\treturn M\n93\t```\n94\t\n95\tThe box JSON references it by `ref = \"classify.lua\"`, `fn = \"classify\"`.\n96\tThe spec loads `classify.lua`, stores its returned table, and indexes\n97\tinto it with `\"classify\"` to get the function.\n98\t\n99\tThis is the existing phase 2 convention — kept as-is.\n100\t\n101\t## Input marshalling\n102\t\n103\tInputs arrive at `invoke` as `(void *bytes, int size)` pairs. The\n104\tspec is responsible for converting each input's bytes into the Lua\n105\tvalue type the user's function expects. The user's function sees\n106\targuments as native Lua values — never a raw byte buffer that the\n107\tfunction has to parse itself.\n108\t\n109\tEach input has a declared type in the box JSON\n110\t(`{\"name\": \"count\", \"type\": \"number\"}`). The graph loader (issue 305)\n111\trecords this type on the `input_decl_t` and passes the type alongside\n112\tthe bytes when calling `invoke`. The Lua spec dispatches on type:\n113\t\n114\t| Declared type | Lua spec action                                             |\n115\t|---------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|\n116\t| `string`      | `lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`                           |\n117\t| `number`      | parse with `strtod`, `lua_pushnumber`                       |\n118\t| `integer`     | parse with `strtoll`, `lua_pushinteger`                     |\n119\t| `boolean`     | strcmp against `\"true\"` / `\"false\"`, `lua_pushboolean`      |\n120\t| `json`        | call `dkjson.decode` on the bytes, push the resulting table |\n121\t| `bytes`       | `lua_pushlstring` (raw, may contain nulls)                  |\n122\t| `any`         | treat as `string` for now                                   |\n123\t\n124\tThe Lua function then takes typed arguments:\n125\t\n126\t```lua\n127\tfunction M.add(a, b)            -- both already numbers\n128\t    return a + b\n129\tend\n130\t\n131\tfunction M.classify(payload)    -- payload is already a table\n132\t    return payload.kind\n133\tend\n134\t```\n135\t\n136\tThe user does not write `tonumber` or `dkjson.decode` calls inside\n137\ttheir box function. The spec did that work before the function was\n138\tcalled.\n139\t\n140\tIf a parse fails (`json` input that isn't valid JSON, `number` input\n141\tthat isn't a number), the spec returns nonzero and the dispatch layer\n142\taborts (per issue 303).\n143\t\n144\t## Return marshalling\n145\t\n146\tThe Lua function returns one or more values. The spec converts the\n147\treturn into bytes for the output slot:\n148\t\n149\t| Return shape           | Spec action                                                   |\n150\t|------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|\n151\t| Single string          | `lua_tolstring` → copy into `out_buf`                         |\n152\t| Single number          | `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ...)` into `out_buf`                       |\n153\t| Single boolean         | write `\"true\"` or `\"false\"`                                   |\n154\t| Single table           | `dkjson.encode` into `out_buf`                                |\n155\t| Single nil             | `*out_size = 0` (zero-byte output)                            |\n156\t| Multiple values        | wrap into a table `{v1, v2, ...}` and `dkjson.encode`         |\n157\t\n158\t`nil` is a valid return. The spec writes zero bytes and sets\n159\t`*out_size = 0`. Downstream consumers receive a zero-byte slot value;\n160\thow they interpret it depends on their declared input type (typed\n161\t`number` consumer fails to parse; typed `string` consumer gets an\n162\tempty string; typed `json` consumer parses zero bytes as `null` via\n163\tdkjson). We cannot demand that user functions never return nil, so we\n164\thandle it.\n165\t\n166\tMultiple return values are wrapped into a table and JSON-encoded.\n167\tPhase 2 silently dropped extra returns; phase 3 keeps them — the\n168\tserialized form is `[v1, v2, ...]`.\n169\t\n170\tOutput buffer is sized to the box's declared `output_capacity`\n171\t(issue 305's `box_t`). If the serialized value exceeds that, abort\n172\t(per the hard-crash policy in issue 303). For variable-size outputs\n173\tthe box declares `output_capacity = 0` and uses the large-value heap\n174\t(issue 302); the spec writes into that heap and stores the handle in\n175\t`out_buf`.\n176\t\n177\tdkjson is the table serializer in both directions (input parsing\n178\tabove and output serialization here). It is already vendored.\n179\t\n180\t## Error handling\n181\t\n182\tEvery `lua_pcall` is wrapped:\n183\t```c\n184\tint rc = lua_pcall(L, n_args, 1, 0);\n185\tif (rc != LUA_OK) {\n186\t    fprintf(stderr, \"[lua spec] %s:%s — %s\\n\",\n187\t            file_path, fn_name, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n188\t    lua_pop(L, 1);\n189\t    return 1;  // dispatch layer aborts the program\n190\t}\n191\t```\n192\t\n193\tLua errors (`error(...)`, runtime errors, syntax errors during file\n194\tload) all surface here as nonzero `pcall` returns. The spec prints\n195\tthe box context and the Lua error message to stderr, then returns\n196\tnonzero. The dispatch layer aborts.\n197\t\n198\tThere is no try-and-recover. Per issue 303, errors crash the program.\n199\t\n200\t## Build\n201\t\n202\t```\n203\tlangs/lua/\n204\t    spec.c          ← lang_spec_t implementation\n205\t    Makefile        ← builds spec.so\n206\t    spec.so         ← built artifact (gitignored)\n207\t```\n208\t\n209\tThe Makefile target:\n210\t```make\n211\tspec.so: spec.c\n212\t\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall \\\n213\t\t    -I$(LUA_INCLUDE) \\\n214\t\t    -o $@ $< \\\n215\t\t    -L$(LUA_LIB) -lluajit-5.1\n216\t```\n217\t\n218\tLuaJIT is the assumed runtime — it matches the phase 2 driver and the\n219\tproject preference (LuaJIT-compatible Lua, no 5.4 syntax). The build\n220\tlinks against the system LuaJIT shared library.\n221\t\n222\t## Open questions\n223\t\n224\t(none currently — earlier questions resolved as follows:)\n225\t\n226\t- nil return: valid. Zero-byte output, downstream consumers\n227\t  interpret per their declared input type.\n228\t- Multiple return values: wrapped into a table and JSON-encoded via\n229\t  dkjson. No values dropped.\n230\t- Table serializer: dkjson, already vendored. Used in both\n231\t  directions (input parsing and output serialization).\n232\t\n233\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n234\t\n235\t1. Set up `langs/lua/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n236\t   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n237\t2. Implement `init` and `teardown`. Verify the pool runner can\n238\t   `dlopen` the spec and call `init` per worker without errors.\n239\t3. Implement file-and-function caching — load a file, store its\n240\t   returned table in the registry, look it up later.\n241\t4. Implement input marshalling: push bytes as strings, count args.\n242\t5. Implement `lua_pcall` invocation with error wrapping.\n243\t6. Implement string return marshalling. Smoke test: `maps/hello`\n244\t   end-to-end through the pool.\n245\t7. Implement number return marshalling.\n246\t8. Implement table-via-JSON return marshalling.\n247\t9. Add `package.path` resolution for libs/, src/, and `meta.src_dirs`.\n248\t10. Test against `maps/classify-demo` and `maps/driver-test` (Lua\n249\t    portions).\n250\t\n251\t## Relevant files\n252\t\n253\t- `drivers/lua.sh` — phase 2 Lua driver, retired by this spec\n254\t- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n255\t- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n256\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n257\t  `invoke`\n258\t- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap for\n259\t  variable-size returns\n260\t- `libs/dkjson` (vendored) — table-to-JSON serialization\n261\t- `maps/hello`, `maps/classify-demo` — Lua-only smoke test maps\n262\t\n263\t## Implementation log\n264\t\n265\t### Init + invoke + teardown — 2026-05-12\n266\t\n267\t`langs/lua/spec.c` now exports a real `lang_spec_t`:\n268\t\n269\t- `init(worker_idx)` creates a `lua_State` and opens the standard\n270\t  libraries via `luaL_openlibs`. Returns the state as the per-\n271\t  worker handle.\n272\t- `teardown(handle)` calls `lua_close`.\n273\t- `invoke(handle, file_path, fn_name, inputs, sizes, n, out_buf,\n274\t  out_cap, out_size)` loads the file with `luaL_loadfile`,\n275\t  executes the chunk (which is expected to return a module\n276\t  table), pulls the named function out of that table, pushes each\n277\t  input as a Lua string, calls via `lua_pcall`, and copies the\n278\t  return as a string into the caller's buffer. The state's stack\n279\t  is rewound to its baseline depth at every entry/exit so\n280\t  cross-call leaks don't accumulate. Errors at every step\n281\t  surface as nonzero return and a stderr message.\n282\t\n283\tFive end-to-end tests in `tests/306-lua-spec-test.c` exercise the\n284\tinit/teardown round-trip, a `greet(name, salutation)` call with\n285\tboth args, the same call with one arg (the Lua side defaults\n286\tsalutation to \"Hello\"), and the two failure modes (missing\n287\tfunction, missing file). The test loads the spec through the\n288\treal spec registry via dlopen, so this is the actual artifact\n289\tthe pool runner will consume.\n290\t\n291\tDeferred:\n292\t- **Rich return types.** The current invoke serializes the return\n293\t  with `lua_tolstring`, which handles strings/numbers/booleans/\n294\t  nil via tostring semantics. Tables, closures, and other\n295\t  structured values land with the fast-path work in issue 312.\n296\t\n297\t### Per-worker module cache — 2026-05-12\n298\t\n299\t`lua_init` now seeds an empty Lua table at\n300\t`LUA_REGISTRYINDEX[LUA_CACHE_KEY]`. `lua_invoke` looks up the\n301\tbox's `file_path` in that table; on a hit it skips the\n302\t`luaL_loadfile + lua_pcall` round-trip and uses the cached\n303\tmodule table directly; on a miss it loads, runs the chunk,\n304\tverifies the module table shape, and stashes the result in the\n305\tcache before proceeding.\n306\t\n307\tThe cache is per-worker (each worker has its own `lua_State`),\n308\twhich means no locking. It's also per-file-path string, so two\n309\tboxes that share a source file share a module table on each\n310\tworker — calling `M.greet` from one box doesn't reload the\n311\tchunk when another box later calls `M.farewell` on the same\n312\tfile.\n313\t\n314\tCache invalidation is intentionally absent for now: once a file\n315\tis loaded, its module table sticks for the run. If the box\n316\tsource changes mid-run, the worker won't notice. Fine for the\n317\tread-once-then-execute usage; revisit when there's a use case\n318\tfor hot-reload.\n319\t"

```json
{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"ffe35111-3809-438e-8393-38e9d4512420",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-20T19:07:56.672Z",

  "toolUseResult":{
    "type":"text",
    "file":{
      "content":"# 307 — C language spec implementation\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nC boxes today run via `drivers/c.sh`, which compiles the source on\ndemand (mtime-based recompile to a binary), then spawns the binary as\na subprocess and reads stdout. Process spawn cost dominates; each call\nis its own freshly-launched executable. The phase 2 driver compiles\nto a standalone binary, not a `.so`.\n\n## Concept\nThe C language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for C. It is\nthe second reference implementation, and the first one that exercises\nthe `compile` callback. After compile, invocation is in-process via\n`dlopen` / `dlsym` — the user's compiled function is called directly\nthrough a function pointer, with no subprocess and no IPC.\n\nThis is the \"Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI\" model from\n`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`, applied to C: same-process call,\nnanosecond-overhead invocation, native-typed access. The only thing\nthe C spec adds over the Lua spec is the compile step.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\n`init` returns a small struct holding the dlopen-handle cache:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void  *so_handles[MAX_BOXES];   // per-file .so handle, indexed by file id\n    void  *fn_ptrs   [MAX_BOXES];   // per-(file, fn) cached function pointer\n    int    n_cached;\n    // (a hash table could replace these arrays if MAX_BOXES grows large)\n} c_handle_t;\n\nvoid *c_init(int worker_idx);\nvoid  c_teardown(void *handle);    // dlclose every cached handle\n```\n\nEach worker thread has its own cache. The same `.so` will end up\nloaded once per worker, since `dlopen` with the same path on the same\nprocess returns a refcounted handle (the underlying code segment is\nshared across all callers — the per-worker `dlopen` is just a\nrefcount bump after the first).\n\n## Compile callback\n\nThe C spec's `compile` callback receives the box's metadata in\naddition to the source and output paths, so it knows the function's\nsignature and can generate the wrapper:\n\n```c\nint c_compile(const char *src_path, const char *out_path, const box_t *box);\n```\n\n(This is a small extension to `lang_spec_t` in issue 303 — `compile`\ngains a `box_t` pointer. Lua's compile is NULL, so unaffected.)\n\nThe callback:\n1. Reads `box->inputs`, `box->returns`, `box->headers`, `box->link_libs`,\n   `box->cflags` from the box metadata.\n2. Generates a wrapper `.c` file (see \"Wrapper generation\" below) in\n   the map's `compiled/bin/` directory next to where the `.so` will\n   land.\n3. Forks and execs the system `cc` with:\n   - `-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall` (defaults)\n   - The user's `cflags`, if any\n   - The wrapper `.c` and the user's `src_path` (if `ref` is set)\n   - `-o out_path`\n   - `-l<lib>` for each entry in `box->link_libs`\n4. Waits for the compiler, returns 0 on success, 1 on failure.\n\nIf the resulting `.so` is newer than the user's source and the\nwrapper, compile is skipped (mtime check, same as phase 2).\n\nThe compiler is `cc` — the system default. `gcc` on most Linux,\n`clang` on macOS. No SoraMech-specific compiler dependency.\n\n### cflags in box JSON\nThe `cflags` field on the box JSON is a string of additional compiler\nflags (`-O0 -g`, `-mavx2`, etc.). It is set by the user in the\ninspector — a \"Compile flags\" text input shown when a C-language box\nis selected. The editor saves it as part of the box's JSON; reads\npreserve the field; saves write it back. Nothing overwrites it.\n\n## Box file convention: any C function, no boilerplate\n\n**The rule, stated as a rule:** a box author writes code as if\nSoraMech does not exist. The function they write must be a\nfunction their non-SoraMech compiler can compile, their\nnon-SoraMech editor can lint, their non-SoraMech test harness\ncan call. No SoraMech-prefixed macros. No SoraMech-shaped\nreturn types. No `#include \"soramech.h\"`. Nothing in the\nauthor's source betrays that the function will ever cross\nSoraMech's wire.\n\nSoraMech bends to the language. The language never bends to\nSoraMech. This is non-negotiable across every spec; it's the\nreason for the spec interface in the first place.\n\nUsers do not write a SoraMech-specific C signature. They reference\nany C function — whether one they wrote themselves, or one from a\nlibrary (zlib, OpenCV, libcurl, anything they have headers for) —\nand the C spec generates a thin wrapper that bridges SoraMech's\nbytes-in / bytes-out ABI to the function's natural typed C\nsignature.\n\n### What the user provides\nEither:\n- A `.c` file containing the function, referenced by `ref` in the\n  box JSON; or\n- A library function from a header, no `.c` file of their own — the\n  `ref` field is omitted, the function name and headers are\n  declared in the box JSON, and the library is named in\n  `link_libs`.\n\n### Box JSON for a user-written function\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"classify\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"c\",\n  \"ref\": \"classify.c\",\n  \"fn\": \"classify\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    {\"name\": \"text\",   \"type\": \"string\"},\n    {\"name\": \"weight\", \"type\": \"int\"}\n  ],\n  \"returns\": \"int\"\n}\n```\n\nThe user's `.c` file is naturally written:\n\n```c\n// maps/<name>/src/classify.c\nint classify(const char *text, int weight) {\n    if (text[0] >= '0' && text[0] <= '9') return weight * 1;\n    return weight * 2;\n}\n```\n\nNo header to include, no macro, no `int classify(SM_BOX_ARGS)`.\nJust a function with a typed signature.\n\n### Box JSON for a library function (no user source)\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"compress\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"c\",\n  \"fn\": \"compress2\",\n  \"headers\": [\"<zlib.h>\"],\n  \"link_libs\": [\"z\"],\n  \"inputs\": [\n    {\"name\": \"src\",   \"type\": \"bytes\"},\n    {\"name\": \"level\", \"type\": \"int\"}\n  ],\n  \"returns\": \"bytes\"\n}\n```\n\nThe wrapper includes `<zlib.h>`, calls `compress2`, and the linker\npulls in `libz` via `-lz`. No user-written `.c` file.\n\n### Wrapper generation\n\nThe compile callback emits a wrapper `.c` for each C box. The\nwrapper has a fixed entry-point name (`sm_box_entry`) that the spec\nalways `dlsym`s. It declares the user's function (extern), unpacks\nSoraMech's input bytes into typed C arguments per the box's `inputs`\ndeclaration, calls the user's function, and writes the return value\ninto `sm_out_buf` per the box's `returns` declaration.\n\nFor `classify` above, the generated wrapper is roughly:\n\n```c\n// generated: classify_wrap.c\nextern int classify(const char *, int);\n\nint sm_box_entry(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n                 void *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size) {\n    const char *text   = (const char *)inputs[0];\n    int         weight = atoi((const char *)inputs[1]);\n    int         result = classify(text, weight);\n    *out_size = snprintf(out_buf, out_cap, \"%d\", result);\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\nThe wrapper is mechanical — same template for every box, varying\nonly in the input-marshalling lines and the return-encoding line.\nThe compile step writes it to `compiled/bin/<box-id>_wrap.c` and\ncompiles `<box-id>_wrap.c` plus the user's source (if any) into a\nsingle `.so`.\n\nThis means the C spec implements typed function calls without\nlibffi (which would do the marshalling at runtime via the C ABI\nmetadata). The same effect is achieved at compile time with\nstraightforward generated code, no runtime dependency.\n\n## Input marshalling (in the generated wrapper)\n\nThe wrapper converts SoraMech's `(bytes, size)` input pairs into the\ntyped C arguments the user's function expects, based on the\ndeclared input types in the box JSON:\n\n| Declared type | Wrapper action                                                  |\n|---------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `string`      | `(const char *)inputs[i]`                                       |\n| `int`         | `atoi((const char *)inputs[i])`                                 |\n| `long`        | `strtoll(...)`                                                  |\n| `double`      | `strtod(...)`                                                   |\n| `bool`        | `strcmp(\"true\", inputs[i]) == 0`                                |\n| `bytes`       | `(const void *)inputs[i]`, paired with `sizes[i]` for the size  |\n| `json`        | `cJSON_ParseWithLength(inputs[i], sizes[i])` → `cJSON *`        |\n\nThe `json` case uses the same vendored cJSON the graph loader uses\n(issue 305) — one JSON library shared across the runner. When a box\ninput is declared `\"type\": \"json\"`, the wrapper passes a `cJSON *`\nto the user's function. The user navigates the tree with cJSON's\nAPI (`cJSON_GetObjectItem`, `cJSON_GetArrayItem`, etc.) and the\nwrapper frees the parsed tree after the function returns.\n\nIf a parse fails (a `json` input that is not valid JSON, an `int`\ninput that does not parse as an integer), the wrapper aborts the\nprogram with the box id and the input position (per issue 303).\n\n## Output encoding (in the generated wrapper)\n\nThe wrapper takes the user function's return value and serializes\nit into `sm_out_buf`, based on the declared `returns` type:\n\n| Declared `returns` | Wrapper action                                              |\n|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `string`           | the user returns `const char *`; `strcpy` + set `out_size` |\n| `int`              | `snprintf(\"%d\", ret)`                                       |\n| `long`             | `snprintf(\"%lld\", ret)`                                     |\n| `double`           | `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ret)`                                    |\n| `bool`             | write `\"true\"` or `\"false\"`                                 |\n| `bytes`            | the user returns `(void *, int)` via an out-parameter pair (see below) |\n| `json`             | the user returns `cJSON *`; `cJSON_PrintUnformatted` → bytes |\n| `void`             | `*out_size = 0` (zero-byte output)                          |\n\nFor `bytes` returns, the user function's signature has the form\n`int my_fn(... const char *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size)` —\nextra parameters that the wrapper passes through from\n`sm_out_buf` / `sm_out_capacity` / `sm_out_size`. This handles\nlibrary functions like `compress` that write their output via an\nout-pointer rather than a return value. The box JSON declares\n`\"returns\": \"bytes\"` and the wrapper threads the buffer through.\n\nIf the encoded value exceeds `sm_out_capacity`, the wrapper aborts\n(per issue 303). For boxes whose output capacity is not known at\ncompile time, see \"Variable-size outputs\" below — the wrapper\nroutes through the large-value heap.\n\n## Variable-size outputs\n\nFor boxes whose output capacity is not known at compile time (issue\n302's large-value heap): the box JSON declares `output_capacity = 0`\nand the wrapper allocates from the large-value heap on each call.\nFor `bytes` and `json` returns, the wrapper transparently picks the\nheap path when the box is variable-size — the user's function is\nunchanged either way. The handle (pointer + size into the\nlarge-value heap) is what ends up in `sm_out_buf`.\n\nFor string returns, similarly: if the returned string exceeds the\ndeclared fixed `output_capacity`, the wrapper falls back to the\nlarge-value heap. This decision is made at compile time based on the\nbox JSON, not at runtime.\n\n## Thread safety of user code\n\nThe same `.so` is loaded by every worker thread that may call into\nit. **Static variables and globals declared in the user's C source\nare shared mutable state across all workers** unless explicitly\nmade `const`.\n\nA note on `static` in C: it does not mean immutable. `static` at\nfile scope means \"this symbol has internal linkage, only visible\ninside this `.c` file.\" `static` inside a function means \"this\nvariable persists across calls.\" Either way, the variable itself is\nmutable — `static int counter = 0; counter++;` is perfectly legal\nand does what it says, just with internal linkage. Immutable in C\nis `const`.\n\nSo:\n- `static int counter = 0;` at file scope — racy, shared across workers.\n- `static int x = 0;` inside a function body — racy, shared across workers calling that function.\n- `const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n- `static const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n\nBox functions must be reentrant — no mutable shared state without\nexplicit locking. The C spec does not enforce this; the rule lives\nin `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) for box authors to\nread.\n\n### Library functions that need global init\n\nMany real C libraries require a one-time setup call before any of\ntheir functions work — `curl_global_init` for libcurl,\n`OPENSSL_init_crypto` for OpenSSL, etc. A SoraMech box that calls\ninto such a library cannot just be wired in cold; the library's\nstate has to exist before the call.\n\nTwo patterns handle this without changing the spec interface:\n\n1. **Init box wired as an entry point.** The user creates a small C\n   box whose function is the library's init call (e.g.\n   `curl_global_init`). They mark it as an entry box and wire it\n   such that any box using libcurl is downstream of it. The init\n   runs once at startup before any consumer fires. Process-global\n   library state — which is what most C libraries actually use — is\n   set up by the time anyone needs it. Pairs with a teardown box\n   wired as a terminal node if needed.\n\n2. **Per-worker init via spec extension** (future). For libraries\n   that need per-worker setup (each thread gets its own handle),\n   the C spec gains an optional per-box `worker_init_fn` field in\n   the box JSON. The spec calls that function once per worker\n   thread during pool startup, before any box invoke. Not in scope\n   yet — pattern (1) covers the common case.\n\nThe init-box approach is the recommended starting point. The\nspec-extension path is the escape hatch when (1) does not fit.\n\nA future fallback exists: `dlmopen`, a Linux variant of `dlopen`\nthat loads each library into its own isolated \"namespace,\" giving\neach worker its own copy of the library's symbols (statics\nincluded). Two threads using two different namespaces would not\nshare static state. Less portable than `dlopen` (Linux-only), so\nnot the default — flagged here as the escape hatch if static-\nvariable races become a real problem.\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/c/\n    spec.c              ← lang_spec_t implementation\n    soramech-c.h        ← user-facing header (shipped to maps via compile step)\n    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so             ← built artifact (gitignored)\n```\n\nSpec Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -o $@ $< -ldl\n```\n\nLinking against `libdl` for `dlopen` / `dlsym` is the only\ndependency. No interpreter, no helper library beyond libc.\n\n### What `dlopen` and `dlsym` do\n- `dlopen(\"path/to/file.so\", flags)` loads a shared library at\n  runtime. The OS loader maps the library's code into the process's\n  memory and returns a handle. Same idea as Windows'\n  `LoadLibrary`.\n- `dlsym(handle, \"name\")` looks up a symbol — a function or a\n  variable — by name inside an already-loaded library, and returns\n  a pointer to it. Same idea as Windows' `GetProcAddress`.\n\nTogether they are how a program loads and calls code that wasn't\nlinked at compile time. Plugin systems are the classic use case.\nHere, every C box compiles to its own `.so`; the spec `dlopen`s the\n`.so` once per worker, `dlsym`s `sm_box_entry` once per file, and\ncalls the resulting function pointer per invocation.\n\nThe user's C box files are compiled by the `compile` callback at map\nload time, not by this Makefile. The Makefile here builds only the\nspec itself.\n\n## Error handling\n\n- `dlopen` failure (missing `.so`, link errors): print path + `dlerror()`\n  to stderr, return 1, dispatch layer aborts.\n- `dlsym` failure (missing function): print file/fn + `dlerror()`,\n  return 1, abort.\n- Compile failure: `cc` exit nonzero, print compiler stderr (already\n  routed there by `cc`), return 1, abort.\n- User function returns nonzero: propagate that as the spec's return,\n  abort.\n\nNo retry, no fallback. Per issue 303.\n\n## Open questions\n\n(none currently — earlier questions resolved as follows:)\n\n- Per-box `cflags`: yes, add the field to the box JSON. The\n  inspector shows a \"Compile flags\" text input when a C-language\n  box is selected (phase 2 inspector work).\n- Typed signatures: handled via compile-time wrapper generation\n  (see \"Box file convention\" above). No libffi runtime dependency.\n- Static-variable isolation via `dlmopen`: deferred. Current rule\n  is \"C box authors write reentrant code\"; if that breaks down in\n  practice, fall back to per-worker `dlmopen` namespaces (Linux-only).\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/c/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Implement `init` and `teardown` with the dlopen-handle cache.\n3. Implement `compile` — fork/exec `cc` with the standard flags.\n   Smoke test: compile a single hello-world `.c` file.\n4. Implement `invoke` — dlsym, direct call, propagate return.\n5. Write `soramech-c.h` with the `SM_BOX_ARGS` macro and the basic\n   input/output helpers.\n6. Smoke test: a C box that takes one string input, writes a string\n   output, runs end-to-end through the pool.\n7. Add the typed input helpers (`sm_in_int`, `sm_in_double`, etc.).\n8. Add the typed output helpers.\n9. Test against `maps/driver-test` (C portions).\n10. Add variable-size output support (`sm_out_alloc`, `sm_out_handle`).\n11. Document in `docs/005-language-specs.md` once it exists, with a\n    note on thread safety.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/c.sh` — phase 2 C driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap\n- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — where compiled\n  `.so`s live (`compiled/bin/`)\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — sister spec; same shape, no\n  compile step\n- `maps/driver-test` — multi-language test map including C boxes\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Compile + invoke — 2026-05-12\n\n`langs/c/spec.c`:\n- `compile(src, out)` forks gcc with `-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall`.\n- `init` allocates a 32-entry dlopen cache; `teardown` walks it.\n- `invoke` looks up the .so in the cache or dlopens it, dlsyms\n  the named function, and calls it through a fixed signature:\n  `int fn(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n  void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)`.\n\nConvention: C box functions all match that signature. The\noptional typed-wrapper mode (per-box signature parsing +\ngenerated marshaller) is deferred until a box wants types that\ndiverge from the byte-array shape.\n\n`tests/maps/hello/src/echo.c` ships two fixture functions; five\ntests in `tests/307-c-spec-test.c` compile and invoke them, plus\nthe missing-symbol and bad-source failure modes.\n",
