```json
        "content":"1\t# 307 — C language spec implementation\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tC boxes today run via `drivers/c.sh`, which compiles the source on\n8\tdemand (mtime-based recompile to a binary), then spawns the binary as\n9\ta subprocess and reads stdout. Process spawn cost dominates; each call\n10\tis its own freshly-launched executable. The phase 2 driver compiles\n11\tto a standalone binary, not a `.so`.\n12\t\n13\t## Concept\n14\tThe C language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for C. It is\n15\tthe second reference implementation, and the first one that exercises\n16\tthe `compile` callback. After compile, invocation is in-process via\n17\t`dlopen` / `dlsym` — the user's compiled function is called directly\n18\tthrough a function pointer, with no subprocess and no IPC.\n19\t\n20\tThis is the \"Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI\" model from\n21\t`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`, applied to C: same-process call,\n22\tnanosecond-overhead invocation, native-typed access. The only thing\n23\tthe C spec adds over the Lua spec is the compile step.\n24\t\n25\t## Per-worker state\n26\t\n27\t`init` returns a small struct holding the dlopen-handle cache:\n28\t\n29\t```c\n30\ttypedef struct {\n31\t    void  *so_handles[MAX_BOXES];   // per-file .so handle, indexed by file id\n32\t    void  *fn_ptrs   [MAX_BOXES];   // per-(file, fn) cached function pointer\n33\t    int    n_cached;\n34\t    // (a hash table could replace these arrays if MAX_BOXES grows large)\n35\t} c_handle_t;\n36\t\n37\tvoid *c_init(int worker_idx);\n38\tvoid  c_teardown(void *handle);    // dlclose every cached handle\n39\t```\n40\t\n41\tEach worker thread has its own cache. The same `.so` will end up\n42\tloaded once per worker, since `dlopen` with the same path on the same\n43\tprocess returns a refcounted handle (the underlying code segment is\n44\tshared across all callers — the per-worker `dlopen` is just a\n45\trefcount bump after the first).\n46\t\n47\t## Compile callback\n48\t\n49\tThe C spec's `compile` callback receives the box's metadata in\n50\taddition to the source and output paths, so it knows the function's\n51\tsignature and can generate the wrapper:\n52\t\n53\t```c\n54\tint c_compile(const char *src_path, const char *out_path, const box_t *box);\n55\t```\n56\t\n57\t(This is a small extension to `lang_spec_t` in issue 303 — `compile`\n58\tgains a `box_t` pointer. Lua's compile is NULL, so unaffected.)\n59\t\n60\tThe callback:\n61\t1. Reads `box->inputs`, `box->returns`, `box->headers`, `box->link_libs`,\n62\t   `box->cflags` from the box metadata.\n63\t2. Generates a wrapper `.c` file (see \"Wrapper generation\" below) in\n64\t   the map's `compiled/bin/` directory next to where the `.so` will\n65\t   land.\n66\t3. Forks and execs the system `cc` with:\n67\t   - `-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall` (defaults)\n68\t   - The user's `cflags`, if any\n69\t   - The wrapper `.c` and the user's `src_path` (if `ref` is set)\n70\t   - `-o out_path`\n71\t   - `-l<lib>` for each entry in `box->link_libs`\n72\t4. Waits for the compiler, returns 0 on success, 1 on failure.\n73\t\n74\tIf the resulting `.so` is newer than the user's source and the\n75\twrapper, compile is skipped (mtime check, same as phase 2).\n76\t\n77\tThe compiler is `cc` — the system default. `gcc` on most Linux,\n78\t`clang` on macOS. No SoraMech-specific compiler dependency.\n79\t\n80\t### cflags in box JSON\n81\tThe `cflags` field on the box JSON is a string of additional compiler\n82\tflags (`-O0 -g`, `-mavx2`, etc.). It is set by the user in the\n83\tinspector — a \"Compile flags\" text input shown when a C-language box\n84\tis selected. The editor saves it as part of the box's JSON; reads\n85\tpreserve the field; saves write it back. Nothing overwrites it.\n86\t\n87\t## Box file convention: any C function, no boilerplate\n88\t\n89\t**The rule, stated as a rule:** a box author writes code as if\n90\tSoraMech does not exist. The function they write must be a\n91\tfunction their non-SoraMech compiler can compile, their\n92\tnon-SoraMech editor can lint, their non-SoraMech test harness\n93\tcan call. No SoraMech-prefixed macros. No SoraMech-shaped\n94\treturn types. No `#include \"soramech.h\"`. Nothing in the\n95\tauthor's source betrays that the function will ever cross\n96\tSoraMech's wire.\n97\t\n98\tSoraMech bends to the language. The language never bends to\n99\tSoraMech. This is non-negotiable across every spec; it's the\n100\treason for the spec interface in the first place.\n101\t\n102\tUsers do not write a SoraMech-specific C signature. They reference\n103\tany C function — whether one they wrote themselves, or one from a\n104\tlibrary (zlib, OpenCV, libcurl, anything they have headers for) —\n105\tand the C spec generates a thin wrapper that bridges SoraMech's\n106\tbytes-in / bytes-out ABI to the function's natural typed C\n107\tsignature.\n108\t\n109\t### What the user provides\n110\tEither:\n111\t- A `.c` file containing the function, referenced by `ref` in the\n112\t  box JSON; or\n113\t- A library function from a header, no `.c` file of their own — the\n114\t  `ref` field is omitted, the function name and headers are\n115\t  declared in the box JSON, and the library is named in\n116\t  `link_libs`.\n117\t\n118\t### Box JSON for a user-written function\n119\t\n120\t```json\n121\t{\n122\t  \"id\": \"classify\",\n123\t  \"kind\": \"call\",\n124\t  \"lang\": \"c\",\n125\t  \"ref\": \"classify.c\",\n126\t  \"fn\": \"classify\",\n127\t  \"inputs\": [\n128\t    {\"name\": \"text\",   \"type\": \"string\"},\n129\t    {\"name\": \"weight\", \"type\": \"int\"}\n130\t  ],\n131\t  \"returns\": \"int\"\n132\t}\n133\t```\n134\t\n135\tThe user's `.c` file is naturally written:\n136\t\n137\t```c\n138\t// maps/<name>/src/classify.c\n139\tint classify(const char *text, int weight) {\n140\t    if (text[0] >= '0' && text[0] <= '9') return weight * 1;\n141\t    return weight * 2;\n142\t}\n143\t```\n144\t\n145\tNo header to include, no macro, no `int classify(SM_BOX_ARGS)`.\n146\tJust a function with a typed signature.\n147\t\n148\t### Box JSON for a library function (no user source)\n149\t\n150\t```json\n151\t{\n152\t  \"id\": \"compress\",\n153\t  \"kind\": \"call\",\n154\t  \"lang\": \"c\",\n155\t  \"fn\": \"compress2\",\n156\t  \"headers\": [\"<zlib.h>\"],\n157\t  \"link_libs\": [\"z\"],\n158\t  \"inputs\": [\n159\t    {\"name\": \"src\",   \"type\": \"bytes\"},\n160\t    {\"name\": \"level\", \"type\": \"int\"}\n161\t  ],\n162\t  \"returns\": \"bytes\"\n163\t}\n164\t```\n165\t\n166\tThe wrapper includes `<zlib.h>`, calls `compress2`, and the linker\n167\tpulls in `libz` via `-lz`. No user-written `.c` file.\n168\t\n169\t### Wrapper generation\n170\t\n171\tThe compile callback emits a wrapper `.c` for each C box. The\n172\twrapper has a fixed entry-point name (`sm_box_entry`) that the spec\n173\talways `dlsym`s. It declares the user's function (extern), unpacks\n174\tSoraMech's input bytes into typed C arguments per the box's `inputs`\n175\tdeclaration, calls the user's function, and writes the return value\n176\tinto `sm_out_buf` per the box's `returns` declaration.\n177\t\n178\tFor `classify` above, the generated wrapper is roughly:\n179\t\n180\t```c\n181\t// generated: classify_wrap.c\n182\textern int classify(const char *, int);\n183\t\n184\tint sm_box_entry(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n185\t                 void *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size) {\n186\t    const char *text   = (const char *)inputs[0];\n187\t    int         weight = atoi((const char *)inputs[1]);\n188\t    int         result = classify(text, weight);\n189\t    *out_size = snprintf(out_buf, out_cap, \"%d\", result);\n190\t    return 0;\n191\t}\n192\t```\n193\t\n194\tThe wrapper is mechanical — same template for every box, varying\n195\tonly in the input-marshalling lines and the return-encoding line.\n196\tThe compile step writes it to `compiled/bin/<box-id>_wrap.c` and\n197\tcompiles `<box-id>_wrap.c` plus the user's source (if any) into a\n198\tsingle `.so`.\n199\t\n200\tThis means the C spec implements typed function calls without\n201\tlibffi (which would do the marshalling at runtime via the C ABI\n202\tmetadata). The same effect is achieved at compile time with\n203\tstraightforward generated code, no runtime dependency.\n204\t\n205\t## Input marshalling (in the generated wrapper)\n206\t\n207\tThe wrapper converts SoraMech's `(bytes, size)` input pairs into the\n208\ttyped C arguments the user's function expects, based on the\n209\tdeclared input types in the box JSON:\n210\t\n211\t| Declared type | Wrapper action                                                  |\n212\t|---------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|\n213\t| `string`      | `(const char *)inputs[i]`                                       |\n214\t| `int`         | `atoi((const char *)inputs[i])`                                 |\n215\t| `long`        | `strtoll(...)`                                                  |\n216\t| `double`      | `strtod(...)`                                                   |\n217\t| `bool`        | `strcmp(\"true\", inputs[i]) == 0`                                |\n218\t| `bytes`       | `(const void *)inputs[i]`, paired with `sizes[i]` for the size  |\n219\t| `json`        | `cJSON_ParseWithLength(inputs[i], sizes[i])` → `cJSON *`        |\n220\t\n221\tThe `json` case uses the same vendored cJSON the graph loader uses\n222\t(issue 305) — one JSON library shared across the runner. This decision is made at compile time based on the\n274\tbox JSON, not at runtime.\n275\t\n276\t## Thread safety of user code\n277\t\n278\tThe same `.so` is loaded by every worker thread that may call into\n279\tit. **Static variables and globals declared in the user's C source\n280\tare shared mutable state across all workers** unless explicitly\n281\tmade `const`.\n282\t\n283\tA note on `static` in C: it does not mean immutable. `static` at\n284\tfile scope means \"this symbol has internal linkage, only visible\n285\tinside this `.c` file.\" `static` inside a function means \"this\n286\tvariable persists across calls.\" Either way, the variable itself is\n287\tmutable — `static int counter = 0; counter++;` is perfectly legal\n288\tand does what it says, just with internal linkage. Immutable in C\n289\tis `const`.\n290\t\n291\tSo:\n292\t- `static int counter = 0;` at file scope — racy, shared across workers.\n293\t- `static int x = 0;` inside a function body — racy, shared across workers calling that function.\n294\t- `const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n295\t- `static const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n296\t\n297\tBox functions must be reentrant — no mutable shared state without\n298\texplicit locking. The C spec does not enforce this; the rule lives\n299\tin `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) for box authors to\n300\tread.\n301\t\n302\t### Library functions that need global init\n303\t\n304\tMany real C libraries require a one-time setup call before any of\n305\ttheir functions work — `curl_global_init` for libcurl,\n306\t`OPENSSL_init_crypto` for OpenSSL, etc. A SoraMech box that calls\n307\tinto such a library cannot just be wired in cold; the library's\n308\tstate has to exist before the call.\n309\t\n310\tTwo patterns handle this without changing the spec interface:\n311\t\n312\t1. **Init box wired as an entry point.** The user creates a small C\n313\t   box whose function is the library's init call (e.g.\n314\t   `curl_global_init`). They mark it as an entry box and wire it\n315\t   such that any box using libcurl is downstream of it. The init\n316\t   runs once at startup before any consumer fires. Process-global\n317\t   library state — which is what most C libraries actually use — is\n318\t   set up by the time anyone needs it. Pairs with a teardown box\n319\t   wired as a terminal node if needed.\n320\t\n321\t2. **Per-worker init via spec extension** (future). For libraries\n322\t   that need per-worker setup (each thread gets its own handle),\n323\t   the C spec gains an optional per-box `worker_init_fn` field in\n324\t   the box JSON. The spec calls that function once per worker\n325\t   thread during pool startup, before any box invoke. Not in scope\n326\t   yet — pattern (1) covers the common case.\n327\t\n328\tThe init-box approach is the recommended starting point. The\n329\tspec-extension path is the escape hatch when (1) does not fit.\n330\t\n331\tA future fallback exists: `dlmopen`, a Linux variant of `dlopen`\n332\tthat loads each library into its own isolated \"namespace,\" giving\n333\teach worker its own copy of the library's symbols (statics\n334\tincluded). Two threads using two different namespaces would not\n335\tshare static state. Less portable than `dlopen` (Linux-only), so\n336\tnot the default — flagged here as the escape hatch if static-\n337\tvariable races become a real problem.\n338\t\n339\t## Build\n340\t\n341\t```\n342\tlangs/c/\n343\t    spec.c              ← lang_spec_t implementation\n344\t    soramech-c.h        ← user-facing header (shipped to maps via compile step)\n345\t    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n346\t    spec.so             ← built artifact (gitignored)\n347\t```\n348\t\n349\tSpec Makefile target:\n350\t```make\n351\tspec.so: spec.c\n352\t\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -o $@ $< -ldl\n353\t```\n354\t\n355\tLinking against `libdl` for `dlopen` / `dlsym` is the only\n356\tdependency. No interpreter, no helper library beyond libc.\n357\t\n358\t### What `dlopen` and `dlsym` do\n359\t- `dlopen(\"path/to/file.so\", flags)` loads a shared library at\n360\t  runtime. The OS loader maps the library's code into the process's\n361\t  memory and returns a handle. Same idea as Windows'\n362\t  `LoadLibrary`.\n363\t- `dlsym(handle, \"name\")` looks up a symbol — a function or a\n364\t  variable — by name inside an already-loaded library, and returns\n365\t  a pointer to it. Same idea as Windows' `GetProcAddress`.\n366\t\n367\tTogether they are how a program loads and calls code that wasn't\n368\tlinked at compile time. Plugin systems are the classic use case.\n369\tHere, every C box compiles to its own `.so`; the spec `dlopen`s the\n370\t`.so` once per worker, `dlsym`s `sm_box_entry` once per file, and\n371\tcalls the resulting function pointer per invocation.\n372\t\n373\tThe user's C box files are compiled by the `compile` callback at map\n374\tload time, not by this Makefile. The Makefile here builds only the\n375\tspec itself.\n376\t\n377\t## Error handling\n378\t\n379\t- `dlopen` failure (missing `.so`, link errors): print path + `dlerror()`\n380\t  to stderr, return 1, dispatch layer aborts.\n381\t- `dlsym` failure (missing function): print file/fn + `dlerror()`,\n382\t  return 1, abort.\n383\t- Compile failure: `cc` exit nonzero, print compiler stderr (already\n384\t  routed there by `cc`), return 1, abort.\n385\t- User function returns nonzero: propagate that as the spec's return,\n386\t  abort.\n387\t\n388\tNo retry, no fallback. Per issue 303.\n389\t\n390\t## Open questions\n391\t\n392\t(none currently — earlier questions resolved as follows:)\n393\t\n394\t- Per-box `cflags`: yes, add the field to the box JSON. The\n395\t  inspector shows a \"Compile flags\" text input when a C-language\n396\t  box is selected (phase 2 inspector work).\n397\t- Typed signatures: handled via compile-time wrapper generation\n398\t  (see \"Box file convention\" above). No libffi runtime dependency.\n399\t- Static-variable isolation via `dlmopen`: deferred. Current rule\n400\t  is \"C box authors write reentrant code\"; if that breaks down in\n401\t  practice, fall back to per-worker `dlmopen` namespaces (Linux-only).\n402\t\n403\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n404\t\n405\t1. Set up `langs/c/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n406\t   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n407\t2. Implement `init` and `teardown` with the dlopen-handle cache.\n408\t3. Implement `compile` — fork/exec `cc` with the standard flags.\n409\t   Smoke test: compile a single hello-world `.c` file.\n410\t4. Implement `invoke` — dlsym, direct call, propagate return.\n411\t5. Write `soramech-c.h` with the `SM_BOX_ARGS` macro and the basic\n412\t   input/output helpers.\n413\t6. Smoke test: a C box that takes one string input, writes a string\n414\t   output, runs end-to-end through the pool.\n415\t7. Add the typed input helpers (`sm_in_int`, `sm_in_double`, etc.).\n416\t8. Add the typed output helpers.\n417\t9. Test against `maps/driver-test` (C portions).\n418\t10. Add variable-size output support (`sm_out_alloc`, `sm_out_handle`).\n419\t11. Document in `docs/005-language-specs.md` once it exists, with a\n420\t    note on thread safety.\n421\t\n422\t## Relevant files\n423\t\n424\t- `drivers/c.sh` — phase 2 C driver, retired by this spec\n425\t- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n426\t- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n427\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n428\t  `invoke`\n429\t- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap\n430\t- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — where compiled\n431\t  `.so`s live (`compiled/bin/`)\n432\t- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — sister spec; same shape, no\n433\t  compile step\n434\t- `maps/driver-test` — multi-language test map including C boxes\n435\t\n436\t## Implementation log\n437\t\n438\t### Compile + invoke — 2026-05-12\n439\t\n440\t`langs/c/spec.c`:\n441\t- `compile(src, out)` forks gcc with `-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall`.\n442\t- `init` allocates a 32-entry dlopen cache; `teardown` walks it.\n443\t- `invoke` looks up the .so in the cache or dlopens it, dlsyms\n444\t  the named function, and calls it through a fixed signature:\n445\t  `int fn(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n446\t  void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)`.\n447\t\n448\tConvention: C box functions all match that signature. The\n449\toptional typed-wrapper mode (per-box signature parsing +\n450\tgenerated marshaller) is deferred until a box wants types that\n451\tdiverge from the byte-array shape.\n452\t\n453\t`tests/maps/hello/src/echo.c` ships two fixture functions; five\n454\ttests in `tests/307-c-spec-test.c` compile and invoke them, plus\n455\tthe missing-symbol and bad-source failure modes.\n456\t"
      }],
```

```json
{
```

```json
  "toolUseResult":{

    "file":{
      "content":"# 308 — Bash language spec implementation\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nBash boxes today run via `drivers/bash.sh`, which `source`s the box\nfile and invokes the function in a fresh subshell per call. Like the\nphase 2 Lua and C drivers, every invocation is a new process; spawn\ncost dominates. There is no persistent Bash interpreter between\ncalls.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe Bash language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for Bash.\nUnlike the Lua and C specs, Bash cannot be embedded in the runner\nprocess — there is no \"libbash.so\" to link against, and no in-process\nAPI for executing Bash code. The Bash spec uses **Option 3 — Unix\ndomain socket servers** from `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`: each\nworker thread starts and talks to its own persistent Bash subprocess\nover a Unix domain socket. The subprocess stays alive for the whole\nrun, accepting one box invocation at a time.\n\nThis makes Bash the proof case that the spec interface accommodates\nlanguages that cannot be embedded. The spec contract from the\ndispatch layer's perspective is the same: byte buffers in, byte\nbuffers out, abort on nonzero return. Where those bytes go (a\n`lua_State`, a function pointer, or a socket) is the spec's\nbusiness.\n\n## Architecture\n\n```\nWorker thread N                  Bash subprocess N\n─────────────────                 ─────────────────\nspec.invoke(...)                  /tmp/soramech-<run-id>-bash-N.sock\n   |                                       |\n   send framed request    ──────────►      receive\n   recv framed response   ◄──────────      execute box function\n                                           send framed response\n```\n\nOne Bash subprocess per worker thread, addressed by a per-worker\nsocket path. The subprocess runs `bash-server.sh` (shipped alongside\n`spec.c`), which `source`s box files on demand, calls the named\nfunction, and writes back the result.\n\nThe subprocess is single-threaded by Bash's nature, but that is\nfine: one worker thread sends one request at a time. A 16-worker\npool means 16 Bash subprocesses, each handling its own thread's\nrequests serially. The pool's parallelism comes from running 16\nworker threads (and 16 subprocesses) concurrently — not from any\none Bash subprocess.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\n`init` for the Bash spec:\n1. Picks a socket path: `/tmp/soramech-<run-id>-bash-<worker_idx>.sock`.\n2. Forks a child process.\n3. Child execs `bash-server.sh <socket-path>`.\n4. Parent waits briefly for the socket to exist, then connects via\n   `connect(AF_UNIX, ...)`.\n5. Returns a handle holding the connected socket fd.\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int   sock_fd;\n    pid_t server_pid;\n    char  socket_path[256];\n} bash_handle_t;\n```\n\n`teardown`:\n1. Sends a `{ \"op\": \"shutdown\" }` framed message.\n2. `close(sock_fd)`.\n3. `waitpid(server_pid)` to reap the subprocess.\n4. `unlink(socket_path)`.\n\n## Wire protocol\n\nLength-prefix framing, identical in both directions:\n- 4 bytes: big-endian message length, in bytes.\n- N bytes: message body, JSON-encoded.\n\nThis handles bytes containing newlines, nulls, or any other character\nwithout ambiguity.\n\n### Request\n\n```json\n{\n  \"op\": \"invoke\",\n  \"file\": \"/abs/path/to/box.sh\",\n  \"fn\": \"process\",\n  \"args\": [\"arg0_bytes\", \"arg1_bytes\", ...]\n}\n```\n\n### Response (success)\n\n```json\n{\n  \"ok\": true,\n  \"out\": \"result_bytes\"\n}\n```\n\n### Response (error)\n\n```json\n{\n  \"ok\": false,\n  \"err\": \"bash error message\",\n  \"stderr\": \"any captured stderr\"\n}\n```\n\nA nonzero exit from the box function, a syntax error during `source`,\nor a Bash signal all surface as `\"ok\": false`. The spec returns\nnonzero from `invoke`, the dispatch layer aborts (issue 303).\n\n## bash-server.sh\n\nThe subprocess script is small. Roughly:\n\n```bash\n#!/usr/bin/env bash\n# bash-server.sh <socket-path>\nSOCKET=\"$1\"\n\n# Set up a listening socket using socat (or python -c 'socket...' fallback).\n# Read length-prefix framed messages, dispatch.\nwhile read_request; do\n    case \"${OP}\" in\n        invoke)\n            if ! declare -F \"${FN}\" > /dev/null; then\n                source \"${FILE}\"\n            fi\n            OUTPUT=\"$( \"${FN}\" \"${ARGS[@]}\" 2>/tmp/bash-stderr )\"\n            RC=$?\n            if [ \"${RC}\" -eq 0 ]; then\n                send_response_ok \"${OUTPUT}\"\n            else\n                send_response_err \"$(< /tmp/bash-stderr)\"\n            fi\n            ;;\n        shutdown)\n            exit 0\n            ;;\n    esac\ndone\n```\n\nThe actual implementation has more error checking and uses `socat`\nor a small inline tool to handle framed socket I/O (Bash has no\nnative length-prefix socket reader). `socat` is broadly available;\nfor systems without it, a 30-line C tool can ship alongside.\n\nThe `source`-once-per-file caching is automatic from Bash's\nperspective: once a file is sourced, its functions are defined in\nthe shell's environment. Subsequent calls reuse them.\n\n## Box file convention\n\nA Bash box file defines functions by name:\n\n```bash\n# maps/<name>/src/process.sh\nprocess() {\n    local input=\"$1\"\n    local count=\"$2\"\n    echo \"${input}-${count}\"\n}\n```\n\nThe box JSON references it as `ref = \"process.sh\"`, `fn = \"process\"`.\nInputs become positional args (`$1`, `$2`, …). The function's stdout\nis captured and returned as the output value.\n\nThis is the existing phase 2 convention — kept as-is.\n\n## Input marshalling\n\nInputs are passed as positional arguments to the Bash function. Each\ninput is bytes; Bash treats them as strings (with the usual caveat\nthat null bytes are not survivable in Bash variables). Type-aware\nmarshalling like the Lua and C specs do is not applicable — Bash has\none type, \"string.\" Numeric and boolean inputs arrive as their\ntext form (`\"42\"`, `\"true\"`); the function uses arithmetic expansion\nor `[[ ]]` tests as needed.\n\n## Output marshalling\n\nThe function's stdout is captured by `$(...)` and sent back as the\noutput bytes. A `nil` / empty equivalent is just an empty string.\nThe output type declared in the box JSON is advisory for downstream\nconsumers — the bytes themselves are whatever the function `echo`ed.\n\n## Variable-size outputs\n\nFor variable-size outputs (issue 302's large-value heap), the\nspec.c side allocates from the large-value heap on receiving the\nresponse, copies the response bytes there, stores the handle in\n`out_buf`. The Bash subprocess does not interact with the heap —\nit just sends back its full output, and the spec.c places it.\n\n## Idle cost\n\nEach Bash subprocess at rest is blocked on `read` from its socket.\nZero CPU. Roughly 3–5 MB RSS per process. For a 16-worker pool that\nis 50–80 MB total. Acceptable.\n\nThe subprocesses start at pool init and stay alive until pool\nshutdown. There is no per-call subprocess churn.\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/bash/\n    spec.c            ← lang_spec_t implementation (socket client)\n    bash-server.sh    ← persistent subprocess\n    Makefile          ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so           ← built artifact\n```\n\nSpec Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -o $@ $<\n```\n\nNo external dependencies beyond libc. The spec uses the standard\nPOSIX socket API. `bash-server.sh` requires `bash` and `socat`\n(or the bundled framing helper) at runtime.\n\n## Error handling\n\n- Subprocess fails to start (missing `bash` or `bash-server.sh`):\n  `init` returns NULL. Pool runner aborts.\n- Subprocess dies mid-run (segfault, killed): `read` returns 0 or\n  short; `invoke` returns nonzero, dispatch layer aborts.\n- Box function nonzero exit: `\"ok\": false` in response, spec\n  returns nonzero, abort.\n- Wire protocol corruption (bad length prefix, malformed JSON):\n  `invoke` returns nonzero, abort.\n\nNo retry, no respawn. Per issue 303, errors crash the program.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- `socat` vs a bundled C framing helper: `socat` is broadly\n  available but is not always installed by default (Alpine, minimal\n  containers). A small bundled tool removes the external dependency.\n  Decide based on what's convenient when implementing.\n- Per-worker stderr capture: the example uses a shared\n  `/tmp/bash-stderr` which would race between workers. Real\n  implementation needs per-worker stderr (e.g., a pipe back to the\n  subprocess that reads in a separate Bash background job, or just\n  per-worker stderr files).\n- Bundled framing helper: if we ship one, it lives in\n  `langs/bash/bash-frame` and is built by the Makefile. Decision\n  deferred.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/bash/` directory with a Makefile that builds an\n   empty `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Write `bash-server.sh` standalone — accepts framed requests on\n   a socket, sources files, calls functions, writes framed\n   responses. Test by hand with `socat` from the command line.\n3. Implement `init` in `spec.c`: fork, exec `bash-server.sh`, wait\n   for socket, connect, return handle.\n4. Implement `teardown`: send shutdown, close socket, reap, unlink.\n5. Implement `invoke`: build request JSON, send framed, read framed\n   response, parse, copy output bytes, return.\n6. Smoke test: a Bash box with one input, one output, runs end-to-end\n   through the pool.\n7. Add error-path handling: bad responses, dead subprocess, nonzero\n   exit codes.\n8. Test against `maps/driver-test` (Bash portions).\n9. Add variable-size output support: route large responses through\n   the large-value heap.\n10. Decide socat-vs-bundled-framer based on implementation experience.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/bash.sh` — phase 2 Bash driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap for\n  variable-size returns\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — Option 3 (Unix domain sockets),\n  the model this spec uses\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — sister spec, in-process Lua\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — sister spec, in-process C with\n  compile step\n- `maps/driver-test` — multi-language test map including Bash boxes\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### fork+exec invoke — 2026-05-12\n\nFirst-pass implementation: every invoke forks bash with an inline\n`-c` script that sources the box file and calls the named\nfunction with the inputs as positional args. Child's stdout is\nread through a pipe — that becomes the output bytes. Slow (~1 ms\nper call), but it gets bash boxes running end-to-end. The\npersistent Unix-domain-socket model lands as a follow-on.\n\n### Persistent socketpair + line-protocol — 2026-05-12\n\nReplaced the fork+exec path with a persistent bash subprocess per\nworker thread. Each worker's `bash_init` does\n`socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM | SOCK_CLOEXEC)`, forks bash,\nand execs `langs/bash/bash-server.sh` with the child-side socket\nfd dup'd to stdin and stdout. The `SOCK_CLOEXEC` flag is load-\nbearing: without it, concurrent worker forks would inherit each\nother's parent-side fds, the bash subprocesses would never see\nEOF, and orphan processes would pile up.\n\nThe on-the-wire protocol is line-oriented:\n\n```\nRequest:                          Response:\n  <n_args>\\n        (or QUIT)       <exit_status>\\n\n  <file_path>\\n                     <output_length>\\n\n  <fn_name>\\n                       <output_bytes>\n  <arg1>\\n\n  <arg2>\\n\n  ...\n```\n\n`bash-server.sh` keeps an associative array of sourced files so a\nbox source is sourced exactly once per worker — analogous to the\nLua spec's per-worker module cache (issue 306).\n\nPer-worker teardown plumbed through the pool (issue 301's new\n`pool_set_worker_teardown` callback) sends `QUIT\\n`, closes the\nparent fd, and `waitpid`s the subprocess with a 1-second\nshort-poll fallback to `SIGTERM`. Verified: zero orphan bash\nprocesses after a `soramech-pool` run.\n\nLimitations of the current protocol:\n- Arguments containing literal newlines are not supported\n  (line-oriented framing). Box authors who need them base64-encode.\n- Single-request/single-response; long-running bash boxes\n  serialize behind themselves on the same worker. Multi-worker\n  pools dispatch in parallel, so this is rarely the bottleneck.\n\n`tests/maps/hello/src/echo.sh` ships three fixture functions.\nFive tests in `tests/308-bash-spec-test.c` cover happy paths\nplus the missing-function failure mode; all pass against the\npersistent-subprocess implementation.\n\n### Self-locating `bash-server.sh` — 2026-05-19\n\nOriginal implementation hard-coded the server path as\ncwd-relative (`langs/bash/bash-server.sh`), which defeated the\ncompile-pipeline portability goal in issue 309. Replaced with a\n`dladdr()`-based lookup that takes the dirname of *this*\n`spec.so` and joins `bash-server.sh` to it. So when a compiled\nartifact ships `compiled/langs/bash/{spec.so,bash-server.sh}`\nside-by-side, the spec finds the script no matter what cwd the\nrunner was invoked from.\n\n`SORAMECH_BASH_SERVER` still overrides the lookup, and there's\nstill a cwd-relative fallback — but the fallback emits a stderr\nwarning so it can't silently mask a packaging bug. `-ldl` added\nto `langs/bash/Makefile` for the new `dladdr` dependency.\n",
      "numLines":372,

        "tool_use_id":"toolu_01MpJ7nmuihyz1Mn5dTxswQv",
        "content":"1\t# 308 — Bash language spec implementation\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tBash boxes today run via `drivers/bash.sh`, which `source`s the box\n8\tfile and invokes the function in a fresh subshell per call. Like the\n9\tphase 2 Lua and C drivers, every invocation is a new process; spawn\n10\tcost dominates. There is no persistent Bash interpreter between\n11\tcalls.\n12\t\n13\t## Concept\n14\t\n15\tThe Bash language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for Bash.\n16\tUnlike the Lua and C specs, Bash cannot be embedded in the runner\n17\tprocess — there is no \"libbash.so\" to link against, and no in-process\n18\tAPI for executing Bash code. The Bash spec uses **Option 3 — Unix\n19\tdomain socket servers** from `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`: each\n20\tworker thread starts and talks to its own persistent Bash subprocess\n21\tover a Unix domain socket. The subprocess stays alive for the whole\n22\trun, accepting one box invocation at a time.\n23\t\n24\tThis makes Bash the proof case that the spec interface accommodates\n25\tlanguages that cannot be embedded. The spec contract from the\n26\tdispatch layer's perspective is the same: byte buffers in, byte\n27\tbuffers out, abort on nonzero return. Where those bytes go (a\n28\t`lua_State`, a function pointer, or a socket) is the spec's\n29\tbusiness.\n30\t\n31\t## Architecture\n32\t\n33\t```\n34\tWorker thread N                  Bash subprocess N\n35\t─────────────────                 ─────────────────\n36\tspec.invoke(...)                  /tmp/soramech-<run-id>-bash-N.sock\n37\t   |                                       |\n38\t   send framed request    ──────────►      receive\n39\t   recv framed response   ◄──────────      execute box function\n40\t                                           send framed response\n41\t```\n42\t\n43\tOne Bash subprocess per worker thread, addressed by a per-worker\n44\tsocket path. The subprocess runs `bash-server.sh` (shipped alongside\n45\t`spec.c`), which `source`s box files on demand, calls the named\n46\tfunction, and writes back the result.\n47\t\n48\tThe subprocess is single-threaded by Bash's nature, but that is\n49\tfine: one worker thread sends one request at a time. A 16-worker\n50\tpool means 16 Bash subprocesses, each handling its own thread's\n51\trequests serially. The pool's parallelism comes from running 16\n52\tworker threads (and 16 subprocesses) concurrently — not from any\n53\tone Bash subprocess.\n54\t\n55\t## Per-worker state\n56\t\n57\t`init` for the Bash spec:\n58\t1. Picks a socket path: `/tmp/soramech-<run-id>-bash-<worker_idx>.sock`.\n59\t2. Forks a child process.\n60\t3. Child execs `bash-server.sh <socket-path>`.\n61\t4. Parent waits briefly for the socket to exist, then connects via\n62\t   `connect(AF_UNIX, ...)`.\n63\t5. Returns a handle holding the connected socket fd.\n64\t\n65\t```c\n66\ttypedef struct {\n67\t    int   sock_fd;\n68\t    pid_t server_pid;\n69\t    char  socket_path[256];\n70\t} bash_handle_t;\n71\t```\n72\t\n73\t`teardown`:\n74\t1. Sends a `{ \"op\": \"shutdown\" }` framed message.\n75\t2. `close(sock_fd)`.\n76\t3. `waitpid(server_pid)` to reap the subprocess.\n77\t4. `unlink(socket_path)`.\n78\t\n79\t## Wire protocol\n80\t\n81\tLength-prefix framing, identical in both directions:\n82\t- 4 bytes: big-endian message length, in bytes.\n83\t- N bytes: message body, JSON-encoded.\n84\t\n85\tThis handles bytes containing newlines, nulls, or any other character\n86\twithout ambiguity.\n87\t\n88\t### Request\n89\t\n90\t```json\n91\t{\n92\t  \"op\": \"invoke\",\n93\t  \"file\": \"/abs/path/to/box.sh\",\n94\t  \"fn\": \"process\",\n95\t  \"args\": [\"arg0_bytes\", \"arg1_bytes\", ...]\n96\t}\n97\t```\n98\t\n99\t### Response (success)\n100\t\n101\t```json\n102\t{\n103\t  \"ok\": true,\n104\t  \"out\": \"result_bytes\"\n105\t}\n106\t```\n107\t\n108\t### Response (error)\n109\t\n110\t```json\n111\t{\n112\t  \"ok\": false,\n113\t  \"err\": \"bash error message\",\n114\t  \"stderr\": \"any captured stderr\"\n115\t}\n116\t```\n117\t\n118\tA nonzero exit from the box function, a syntax error during `source`,\n119\tor a Bash signal all surface as `\"ok\": false`. The spec returns\n120\tnonzero from `invoke`, the dispatch layer aborts (issue 303).\n121\t\n122\t## bash-server.sh\n123\t\n124\tThe subprocess script is small. Roughly:\n125\t\n126\t```bash\n127\t#!/usr/bin/env bash\n128\t# bash-server.sh <socket-path>\n129\tSOCKET=\"$1\"\n130\t\n131\t# Set up a listening socket using socat (or python -c 'socket...' fallback).\n132\t# Read length-prefix framed messages, dispatch.\n133\twhile read_request; do\n134\t    case \"${OP}\" in\n135\t        invoke)\n136\t            if ! declare -F \"${FN}\" > /dev/null; then\n137\t                source \"${FILE}\"\n138\t            fi\n139\t            OUTPUT=\"$( \"${FN}\" \"${ARGS[@]}\" 2>/tmp/bash-stderr )\"\n140\t            RC=$?\n141\t            if [ \"${RC}\" -eq 0 ]; then\n142\t                send_response_ok \"${OUTPUT}\"\n143\t            else\n144\t                send_response_err \"$(< /tmp/bash-stderr)\"\n145\t            fi\n146\t            ;;\n147\t        shutdown)\n148\t            exit 0\n149\t            ;;\n150\t    esac\n151\tdone\n152\t```\n153\t\n154\tThe actual implementation has more error checking and uses `socat`\n155\tor a small inline tool to handle framed socket I/O (Bash has no\n156\tnative length-prefix socket reader). `socat` is broadly available;\n157\tfor systems without it, a 30-line C tool can ship alongside.\n158\t\n159\tThe `source`-once-per-file caching is automatic from Bash's\n160\tperspective: once a file is sourced, its functions are defined in\n161\tthe shell's environment. Subsequent calls reuse them.\n162\t\n163\t## Box file convention\n164\t\n165\tA Bash box file defines functions by name:\n166\t\n167\t```bash\n168\t# maps/<name>/src/process.sh\n169\tprocess() {\n170\t    local input=\"$1\"\n171\t    local count=\"$2\"\n172\t    echo \"${input}-${count}\"\n173\t}\n174\t```\n175\t\n176\tThe box JSON references it as `ref = \"process.sh\"`, `fn = \"process\"`.\n177\tInputs become positional args (`$1`, `$2`, …). The function's stdout\n178\tis captured and returned as the output value.\n179\t\n180\tThis is the existing phase 2 convention — kept as-is.\n181\t\n182\t## Input marshalling\n183\t\n184\tInputs are passed as positional arguments to the Bash function. Each\n185\tinput is bytes; Bash treats them as strings (with the usual caveat\n186\tthat null bytes are not survivable in Bash variables). Type-aware\n187\tmarshalling like the Lua and C specs do is not applicable — Bash has\n188\tone type, \"string.\" Numeric and boolean inputs arrive as their\n189\ttext form (`\"42\"`, `\"true\"`); the function uses arithmetic expansion\n190\tor `[[ ]]` tests as needed.\n191\t\n192\t## Output marshalling\n193\t\n194\tThe function's stdout is captured by `$(...)` and sent back as the\n195\toutput bytes. A `nil` / empty equivalent is just an empty string.\n196\tThe output type declared in the box JSON is advisory for downstream\n197\tconsumers — the bytes themselves are whatever the function `echo`ed.\n198\t\n199\t## Variable-size outputs\n200\t\n201\tFor variable-size outputs (issue 302's large-value heap), the\n202\tspec.c side allocates from the large-value heap on receiving the\n203\tresponse, copies the response bytes there, stores the handle in\n204\t`out_buf`. The Bash subprocess does not interact with the heap —\n205\tit just sends back its full output, and the spec.c places it.\n206\t\n207\t## Idle cost\n208\t\n209\tEach Bash subprocess at rest is blocked on `read` from its socket.\n210\tZero CPU. Roughly 3–5 MB RSS per process. For a 16-worker pool that\n211\tis 50–80 MB total. Acceptable.\n212\t\n213\tThe subprocesses start at pool init and stay alive until pool\n214\tshutdown. There is no per-call subprocess churn.\n215\t\n216\t## Build\n217\t\n218\t```\n219\tlangs/bash/\n220\t    spec.c            ← lang_spec_t implementation (socket client)\n221\t    bash-server.sh    ← persistent subprocess\n222\t    Makefile          ← builds spec.so\n223\t    spec.so           ← built artifact\n224\t```\n225\t\n226\tSpec Makefile target:\n227\t```make\n228\tspec.so: spec.c\n229\t\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -o $@ $<\n230\t```\n231\t\n232\tNo external dependencies beyond libc. The spec uses the standard\n233\tPOSIX socket API. `bash-server.sh` requires `bash` and `socat`\n234\t(or the bundled framing helper) at runtime.\n235\t\n236\t## Error handling\n237\t\n238\t- Subprocess fails to start (missing `bash` or `bash-server.sh`):\n239\t  `init` returns NULL. Pool runner aborts.\n240\t- Subprocess dies mid-run (segfault, killed): `read` returns 0 or\n241\t  short; `invoke` returns nonzero, dispatch layer aborts.\n242\t- Box function nonzero exit: `\"ok\": false` in response, spec\n243\t  returns nonzero, abort.\n244\t- Wire protocol corruption (bad length prefix, malformed JSON):\n245\t  `invoke` returns nonzero, abort.\n246\t\n247\tNo retry, no respawn. Per issue 303, errors crash the program.\n248\t\n249\t## Open questions\n250\t\n251\t- `socat` vs a bundled C framing helper: `socat` is broadly\n252\t  available but is not always installed by default (Alpine, minimal\n253\t  containers). A small bundled tool removes the external dependency.\n254\t  Decide based on what's convenient when implementing.\n255\t- Per-worker stderr capture: the example uses a shared\n256\t  `/tmp/bash-stderr` which would race between workers. Real\n257\t  implementation needs per-worker stderr (e.g., a pipe back to the\n258\t  subprocess that reads in a separate Bash background job, or just\n259\t  per-worker stderr files).\n260\t- Bundled framing helper: if we ship one, it lives in\n261\t  `langs/bash/bash-frame` and is built by the Makefile. Decision\n262\t  deferred.\n263\t\n264\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n265\t\n266\t1. Set up `langs/bash/` directory with a Makefile that builds an\n267\t   empty `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n268\t2. Write `bash-server.sh` standalone — accepts framed requests on\n269\t   a socket, sources files, calls functions, writes framed\n270\t   responses. Test by hand with `socat` from the command line.\n271\t3. Implement `init` in `spec.c`: fork, exec `bash-server.sh`, wait\n272\t   for socket, connect, return handle.\n273\t4. Implement `teardown`: send shutdown, close socket, reap, unlink.\n274\t5. Implement `invoke`: build request JSON, send framed, read framed\n275\t   response, parse, copy output bytes, return.\n276\t6. Smoke test: a Bash box with one input, one output, runs end-to-end\n277\t   through the pool.\n278\t7. Add error-path handling: bad responses, dead subprocess, nonzero\n279\t   exit codes.\n280\t8. Test against `maps/driver-test` (Bash portions).\n281\t9. Add variable-size output support: route large responses through\n282\t   the large-value heap.\n283\t10. Decide socat-vs-bundled-framer based on implementation experience.\n284\t\n285\t## Relevant files\n286\t\n287\t- `drivers/bash.sh` — phase 2 Bash driver, retired by this spec\n288\t- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n289\t- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n290\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n291\t  `invoke`\n292\t- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap for\n293\t  variable-size returns\n294\t- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — Option 3 (Unix domain sockets),\n295\t  the model this spec uses\n296\t- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — sister spec, in-process Lua\n297\t- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — sister spec, in-process C with\n298\t  compile step\n299\t- `maps/driver-test` — multi-language test map including Bash boxes\n300\t\n301\t## Implementation log\n302\t\n303\t### fork+exec invoke — 2026-05-12\n304\t\n305\tFirst-pass implementation: every invoke forks bash with an inline\n306\t`-c` script that sources the box file and calls the named\n307\tfunction with the inputs as positional args. Child's stdout is\n308\tread through a pipe — that becomes the output bytes. Slow (~1 ms\n309\tper call), but it gets bash boxes running end-to-end. The\n310\tpersistent Unix-domain-socket model lands as a follow-on.\n311\t\n312\t### Persistent socketpair + line-protocol — 2026-05-12\n313\t\n314\tReplaced the fork+exec path with a persistent bash subprocess per\n315\tworker thread. Each worker's `bash_init` does\n316\t`socketpair(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM | SOCK_CLOEXEC)`, forks bash,\n317\tand execs `langs/bash/bash-server.sh` with the child-side socket\n318\tfd dup'd to stdin and stdout. The `SOCK_CLOEXEC` flag is load-\n319\tbearing: without it, concurrent worker forks would inherit each\n320\tother's parent-side fds, the bash subprocesses would never see\n321\tEOF, and orphan processes would pile up.\n322\t\n323\tThe on-the-wire protocol is line-oriented:\n324\t\n325\t```\n326\tRequest:                          Response:\n327\t  <n_args>\\n        (or QUIT)       <exit_status>\\n\n328\t  <file_path>\\n                     <output_length>\\n\n329\t  <fn_name>\\n                       <output_bytes>\n330\t  <arg1>\\n\n331\t  <arg2>\\n\n332\t  ...\n333\t```\n334\t\n335\t`bash-server.sh` keeps an associative array of sourced files so a\n336\tbox source is sourced exactly once per worker — analogous to the\n337\tLua spec's per-worker module cache (issue 306).\n338\t\n339\tPer-worker teardown plumbed through the pool (issue 301's new\n340\t`pool_set_worker_teardown` callback) sends `QUIT\\n`, closes the\n341\tparent fd, and `waitpid`s the subprocess with a 1-second\n342\tshort-poll fallback to `SIGTERM`. Verified: zero orphan bash\n343\tprocesses after a `soramech-pool` run.\n344\t\n345\tLimitations of the current protocol:\n346\t- Arguments containing literal newlines are not supported\n347\t  (line-oriented framing). Box authors who need them base64-encode.\n348\t- Single-request/single-response; long-running bash boxes\n349\t  serialize behind themselves on the same worker. Multi-worker\n350\t  pools dispatch in parallel, so this is rarely the bottleneck.\n351\t\n352\t`tests/maps/hello/src/echo.sh` ships three fixture functions.\n353\tFive tests in `tests/308-bash-spec-test.c` cover happy paths\n354\tplus the missing-function failure mode; all pass against the\n355\tpersistent-subprocess implementation.\n356\t\n357\t### Self-locating `bash-server.sh` — 2026-05-19\n358\t\n359\tOriginal implementation hard-coded the server path as\n360\tcwd-relative (`langs/bash/bash-server.sh`), which defeated the\n361\tcompile-pipeline portability goal in issue 309. Replaced with a\n362\t`dladdr()`-based lookup that takes the dirname of *this*\n363\t`spec.so` and joins `bash-server.sh` to it. So when a compiled\n364\tartifact ships `compiled/langs/bash/{spec.so,bash-server.sh}`\n365\tside-by-side, the spec finds the script no matter what cwd the\n366\trunner was invoked from.\n367\t\n368\t`SORAMECH_BASH_SERVER` still overrides the lookup, and there's\n369\tstill a cwd-relative fallback — but the fallback emits a stderr\n370\twarning so it can't silently mask a packaging bug. `-ldl` added\n371\tto `langs/bash/Makefile` for the new `dladdr` dependency.\n372\t"
      }],
```

```json
{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"dc31dc1f-9a03-4ecc-b0d5-79be1121a259",

      "content":"# 309 — Build system & Makefile orchestration\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nPhase 2 has no compiled binary. The runner is a Lua script\n(`src/007-runner-main.lua`) invoked via `luajit`. Drivers are shell\nscripts that compile per-box C source on demand. There is no\ntop-level Makefile, no vendoring of C dependencies, no link step\nbeyond per-driver compile.\n\nPhase 3 introduces a real C binary (the pool runner) plus a set of\nlanguage spec `.so` files. They need to compile in the right order\nwith the right flags, and the build needs to be reproducible from a\nclean checkout.\n\n## Concept\n\nA top-level `Makefile` at the project root orchestrates the entire\nphase 3 build. It builds:\n\n1. The pool runner binary: `soramech-pool` (statically links the\n   SoraMech-owned task pool, the vendored JSON parser, the slot\n   store, the graph loader, the dispatch layer, the spec registry).\n2. Each language spec: `langs/<name>/spec.so`, built by a small\n   per-spec Makefile.\n3. (Optional) Unit test binaries.\n\nEach component has its own Makefile if it has non-trivial build\nrules. The top-level Makefile delegates to them via `$(MAKE) -C\n<dir>`. A clean checkout becomes a working build with `make`.\n\n## Directory layout\n\n```\nsoramech/\n├── Makefile                       ← top-level orchestration\n├── soramech-pool                  ← built binary (gitignored)\n├── src/\n│   ├── 008-pool-runner.c          ← main entry, pool lifecycle (issue 301)\n│   ├── slot-store.c / .h          ← per-task slot allocator (issue 302)\n│   ├── graph-loader.c / .h        ← C loader, replaces 003-loader.lua (issue 305)\n│   ├── dispatch.c / .h            ← dispatch action (issue 304)\n│   └── spec-registry.c / .h       ← spec dlopen/registry (issue 303)\n├── libs/\n│   ├── task-pool/                 ← SoraMech-built thread pool\n│   │   ├── pool.h\n│   │   └── pool.c\n│   └── json/                      ← vendored JSON parser (cJSON, jsmn, etc.)\n│       ├── cjson.h\n│       └── cjson.c\n├── langs/\n│   ├── lua/\n│   │   ├── Makefile               ← builds spec.so\n│   │   ├── spec.c\n│   │   └── spec.so                ← built (gitignored)\n│   ├── c/\n│   │   ├── Makefile\n│   │   ├── spec.c\n│   │   ├── soramech-c.h           ← user-facing helper header\n│   │   └── spec.so\n│   └── bash/\n│       ├── Makefile\n│       ├── spec.c\n│       ├── bash-server.sh\n│       └── spec.so\n└── build/                         ← intermediate object files (gitignored)\n```\n\n`build/` holds intermediate `.o` files; binaries land alongside their\nsources or at the project root. `.so` and `.o` files are gitignored;\n`make clean` removes them.\n\n## Top-level targets\n\n```make\n.PHONY: all runner specs clean test\n\nall: runner specs\n\nrunner: soramech-pool\n\nsoramech-pool: $(POOL_OBJECTS)\n\t$(CC) -O2 -Wall -pthread -o $@ $^ -ldl\n\nspecs:\n\t$(MAKE) -C langs/lua\n\t$(MAKE) -C langs/c\n\t$(MAKE) -C langs/bash\n\nclean:\n\trm -f soramech-pool\n\trm -rf build/\n\t$(MAKE) -C langs/lua clean\n\t$(MAKE) -C langs/c clean\n\t$(MAKE) -C langs/bash clean\n\ntest: all\n\t./scripts/run-tests.sh\n```\n\n`POOL_OBJECTS` resolves to the `.o` files for every `src/*.c`,\n`libs/task-pool/*.c`, and `libs/json/*.c`. A pattern rule compiles\neach source into `build/`.\n\n## Per-language spec Makefiles\n\nEach `langs/<name>/Makefile` follows the same shape. Lua's:\n\n```make\nLUA_INCLUDE ?= /usr/include/luajit-2.1\nLUA_LIB    ?= /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu\n\nCFLAGS  = -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -I$(LUA_INCLUDE)\nLDFLAGS = -L$(LUA_LIB) -lluajit-5.1\n\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ $< $(LDFLAGS)\n\nclean:\n\trm -f spec.so\n```\n\nC's spec links `-ldl`. Bash's links nothing beyond libc. The pattern\nis uniform.\n\nLuaJIT's include and lib paths are set via environment variables so\nthe build works on systems where they live elsewhere (macOS via\nhomebrew, Alpine, etc.). Defaults match Debian/Ubuntu.\n\n## Build modes\n\n```\nmake                  ← release: -O2 -Wall\nmake DEBUG=1          ← debug:   -O0 -g -DDEBUG -Wall -Wextra\nmake STRICT=1         ← strict:  release + -Werror -Wextra -Wpedantic\n```\n\n`DEBUG=1` adds `-g` for symbols and `-DDEBUG` for opt-in debug\nprints in the C sources. `STRICT=1` fails the build on any warning;\nuseful in CI.\n\n## Vendoring\n\nVendored libraries live under `libs/` and are checked into the repo\nas plain source — no submodules, no fetches at build time. To\nupdate a vendored library, copy the new sources in and commit. The\nvendored directory carries a small `VENDOR.md` noting the upstream\nsource and the version that was copied.\n\nInitial vendored libraries:\n- `libs/task-pool/` — SoraMech-built thread pool (issue 301)\n- `libs/json/` — JSON parser (issue 305 picks cJSON or similar)\n\nFuture additions land alongside these.\n\n## Spec discovery at runtime\n\nThe pool runner finds language specs by scanning the `langs/`\ndirectory at startup, opening each `langs/<name>/spec.so` via\n`dlopen`, and reading the `soramech_lang_spec` symbol via `dlsym`\n(per issue 303). The path to `langs/` is resolved relative to the\nrunner binary's location: the runner reads `/proc/self/exe`\n(Linux), follows the symlink, and looks for `langs/` next to it.\n\nThis means the binary is location-flexible: the user can drop the\nproject tree anywhere, and `./soramech-pool` finds its specs\nwithout a config file.\n\nIf the user wants to override (custom spec dirs for development),\n`SORAMECH_LANGS_DIR=/path/to/langs ./soramech-pool` overrides the\nauto-detected location.\n\n## Compile and package a map for standalone execution\n\nFolded in from issue 219 (closed). The build system also handles the\n\"package a map for deployment\" step that the editor's Compile button\n(issue 222) and a CLI tool both invoke.\n\nThe compile step turns an editable map directory into a self-contained\ndeployable directory:\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/compiled/\n    pool-runner          ← copy (or symlink) of soramech-pool\n    src/                 ← every source file the map uses\n    bin/                 ← per-box compiled .so files (C boxes)\n    langs/               ← copy of language spec .so files used\n    manifest.json        ← every box, its language, artifact path, build version\n```\n\nRunning `./compiled/pool-runner` executes the map without reference to\nthe editor, the live `src/` outside `compiled/`, or any external\nSoraMech installation.\n\n### Steps the compile step performs\n\n1. **Walk the graph.** Reuse the C loader (issue 305) to enumerate\n   boxes, languages, and source files.\n2. **Copy source.** Every file referenced by `box.ref` plus\n   transitively-required libs lands in `compiled/src/`. The map's\n   local `src/` is the only path `package.path` searches at runtime\n   (issue 306), so all dependencies must be present.\n3. **Compile per-box artifacts.** For each language present, invoke\n   that spec's `compile` callback (issue 303). The C spec emits a\n   wrapper from the box's signature into `compiled/bin/` (issue 307).\n   Lua and Bash have no compile step; their files are copied verbatim.\n4. **Copy spec libraries.** `langs/<name>/spec.so` for every language\n   used in the map is copied to `compiled/langs/<name>/spec.so`. The\n   pool runner's spec discovery (above) finds them relative to the\n   binary location.\n5. **Copy or symlink the runner binary.** `--portable` copies; the\n   default symlinks to save disk on the dev machine.\n6. **Write the manifest.** `compiled/manifest.json` lists every box,\n   its language, its compiled artifact path (or source file for\n   interpreted languages), and the SoraMech build version.\n\n### Incremental compile\n\nmtime comparison per artifact: if the source is newer than the\ncompiled output, recompile that one; otherwise skip. The C spec's\n`compile` callback (issue 307) implements this per-box; the package\nstep inherits it.\n\n### Editor invocation (issue 222)\n\nThe Compile button calls `POST /maps/<name>/compile`. The server\nshells out to a `soramech-compile` CLI (or invokes the same code\nin-process). Output streams back to the editor for display. The\neditor itself never runs the compiled output; the user invokes\n`./compiled/pool-runner` from a terminal.\n\n### CLI invocation\n\nStandalone `soramech-compile <map-dir>` runs the same pipeline\nwithout the server. Used in CI and headless deployment.\n\n### Errors\n\nAny failure aborts the compile and surfaces a precise message:\nwhich box, which file, what failed. Partial output is left in\n`compiled/` for inspection but the manifest is not written, so the\ndeployment is recognizably broken until a clean compile succeeds.\n\n### Open questions (compile step)\n\n- **Multi-architecture**: a directory built on x86_64 won't run on\n  arm64. Out of scope — users compile on the target. Could later\n  add cross-compile if the SoraMind cluster goes mixed-arch.\n- **Source-copy granularity**: copy the file referenced by `box.ref`\n  plus a static-analysis sweep for `require` / `source` /\n  `#include`, or just copy the entire `libs/` tree. Lean toward\n  static analysis with a fallback whole-tree copy if analysis fails.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- macOS: `.so` becomes `.dylib`, and there's no `/proc/self/exe`.\n  Use `_NSGetExecutablePath`. Cross-platform spec discovery is a\n  small platform-#ifdef. Fold into the spec registry implementation.\n- Out-of-tree build (a separate `build/` directory holding all\n  artifacts): nice-to-have, not blocking. Current layout uses\n  in-tree `.o` files in `build/` already — full out-of-tree means\n  the `.so`s live in `build/langs/lua/spec.so` instead of next to\n  the source. Defer.\n- Static vs dynamic linking of vendored libs: vendored sources\n  compile straight into the runner binary. No separate `.so` for\n  the task pool or JSON parser. Right call given how small they are.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Write the top-level Makefile with empty `runner`, `specs`,\n   `clean` targets. Verify `make` succeeds against an empty source\n   tree.\n2. Build the SoraMech thread pool into `libs/task-pool/` (3d-rts\n   referenced as design inspiration). Add a\n   `VENDOR.md`.\n3. Vendor cJSON (or chosen JSON parser) into `libs/json/`. Add a\n   `VENDOR.md`.\n4. Add the pool-runner build rule. Compiles `src/*.c` plus vendored\n   libs into `soramech-pool`. Initially the runner is just `int\n   main() { return 0; }` to verify the link.\n5. Add `langs/lua/Makefile`. Build `spec.so` from a stub `spec.c`.\n6. Add `langs/c/Makefile`. Same shape.\n7. Add `langs/bash/Makefile`. Same shape.\n8. Add `make DEBUG=1` and `make STRICT=1` modes.\n9. Wire `make test` into a placeholder script (real tests come from\n   issue 311).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `Makefile` — top-level (to be created)\n- `langs/lua/Makefile`, `langs/c/Makefile`, `langs/bash/Makefile`\n  — per-spec (to be created)\n- `libs/task-pool/`, `libs/json/` — vendored sources (to be added)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool runner this\n  builds\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec discovery uses\n  `dlopen`/`dlsym`\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md`, `307-c-language-spec.md`,\n  `308-bash-language-spec.md` — per-spec build details\n- `issues/311-integration-tests-and-run-output.md` — `make test`\n  consumers\n- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` (completed) —\n  the editor button this compile step services\n- `issues/completed/219-map-compiler.md` — original issue, folded\n  into this one\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Scaffolding milestone — 2026-05-12\n\nWhat's in place:\n- `Makefile` at the project root with `all` / `runner` / `specs` /\n  `clean` / `test` / `help` targets, and `DEBUG=1` / `STRICT=1`\n  build modes. Source discovery is wildcard-based across\n  `src/*.c`, `libs/task-pool/*.c`, `libs/json/*.c` — additional C\n  sources land as future issues compile them in automatically.\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — minimal `main()` that parses argv,\n  prints usage on `--help`, prints a \"scaffold build\" banner and\n  exits 0 on a map-dir argument. Plus `src/008-pool-runner.info.md`.\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — the public `lang_spec_t` C contract from\n  issue 303 (the four basic callbacks; the fast-path callbacks\n  from issue 312 land later).\n- `langs/{lua,c,bash}/spec.c` + `Makefile` + `spec.info.md` — each\n  builds a `spec.so` that exports `soramech_lang_spec` with all\n  callbacks `NULL`. Verified with `nm -D langs/*/spec.so` — the\n  symbol is exported at `0x4020 D` in every spec.\n- `.clangd` config so the editor LSP resolves the include path the\n  same way the Makefile does.\n- `.file-index-counter` set to `008`.\n\nVerified `make` clean → build → run cycle works in default,\n`DEBUG=1`, and `STRICT=1` modes.\n\nWhat's still ahead inside 309:\n- Vendoring `libs/task-pool/` (lands with 301).\n- Vendoring `libs/json/` (lands with 305 — choice of cJSON / jsmn\n  decided at implementation time).\n- Spec discovery via `/proc/self/exe` (lands with 303's spec\n  registry).\n- Compile / package step for standalone `compiled/pool-runner`\n  (lands with 305 + 307).\n- Real `make test` (lands with 311).\n\nThese follow-ons depend on their respective issues; this issue\nstays open until they're all wired in.\n\n### Compile / package pipeline — 2026-05-19\n\n`scripts/soramech-compile.sh <map>` now produces a portable\n`<map>/compiled/` directory laid out as:\n\n```\ncompiled/\n  meta.json, boxes/, src/, data/, *.txt   # verbatim copies\n  langs/<lang>/spec.so                    # per-language plugin\n  langs/bash/bash-server.sh               # only if bash boxes exist\n  bin/<box>.so                            # pre-compiled C boxes\n  pool-runner                             # *real copy* of soramech-pool\n  manifest.json                           # n_boxes, languages, etc.\n```\n\nTwo subtle correctness points landed alongside the script:\n\n1. **pool-runner must be a real copy, not a symlink.** The runner\n   discovers `langs/` via `readlink(\"/proc/self/exe\")`. A symlink\n   resolves to its target, so a symlinked pool-runner would pick\n   up the project tree's `langs/` instead of the bundled one. A\n   real copy makes the artifact self-describing — `compiled/`\n   stands alone with no reference to the source map directory.\n\n2. **The bash spec self-locates `bash-server.sh`.** Previously\n   the bash spec used a cwd-relative path\n   (`langs/bash/bash-server.sh`), defeating portability. It now\n   uses `dladdr()` on its own symbol to find the loaded `.so`\n   path, takes `dirname()`, and looks for `bash-server.sh` next\n   to itself. SORAMECH_BASH_SERVER still overrides; the\n   cwd-relative path remains as a fallback (with a stderr\n   warning so the fallback isn't silent). This required adding\n   `-ldl` to `langs/bash/Makefile`.\n\nVerified end-to-end: `scripts/run-tests.sh` includes a new\n`compile pipeline (portable run)` integration check that runs\nsoramech-compile on the pipeline fixture, invokes the compiled\nartifact from `/tmp` (so cwd cannot accidentally satisfy any\nrelative path), and asserts both the captured stdout and the\n`file_write` destination match the expected values.\n\nPer-map `compiled/` directories under `tests/maps/*/` are\ngitignored.\n\nThe follow-ons enumerated above are now all in place; the issue\nis effectively done.\n",
```

```json
      "content":"# 310 — Priority queue: wired in, no-op behaviorally\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe SoraMech thread pool's `pool_spawn` (modeled on 3d-rts's API)\ntakes a priority parameter:\n\n```c\ntask_id_t pool_spawn(task_pool_t *pool,\n                     action_fn_t  *actions,\n                     void        **action_args,\n                     int           n_actions,\n                     int           priority);\n```\n\nHigher priority tasks are dispatched ahead of lower priority tasks\nwhen multiple are ready. The pool's queue handles the ordering.\n\nPhase 3 needs to specify what SoraMech does with this knob. The\nsimplest answer is the right one for now: do nothing.\n\n## Decision\n\nEvery dispatch task is submitted at priority `1`. The compile-time\nconstant `MAX_PRIORITY` is set to `1`. There is no graph-level or\nbox-level concept of priority. The runner does not expose any user-\nfacing knob for it.\n\nThe mechanism is wired through the codebase — every `pool_spawn`\ncall passes a priority, the constant is referenced rather than\nhard-coded inline — but the behavior is identical to a single-\npriority pool. Tasks run in submission order (modulo whatever\nordering the pool guarantees within a single priority level).\n\n## Why wire it in if it does nothing\n\nTwo reasons:\n\n1. **Future hooks land as config changes, not refactors.** When a\n   real priority use case appears (allocator cleanup at lowest\n   priority; user-marked urgent boxes; iterator queue draining\n   prioritized over new entry submission), raising `MAX_PRIORITY`\n   and emitting different priorities at the right call sites is a\n   line edit, not a structural change. If the priority parameter\n   were stripped out, adding it later means going back through every\n   `pool_spawn` callsite and threading a new argument.\n\n2. **The pool's API requires it.** `pool_spawn` takes a priority.\n   Callers must pass something. Passing `1` consistently is the\n   straightforward expression of \"no priority concept yet.\"\n\n## Specific call sites\n\n```c\n// src/dispatch.c — every dispatch task\npool_spawn(pool, &dispatch_action, &task_arg, 1, SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT);\n\n// src/008-pool-runner.c — entry-box submission at startup\npool_spawn(pool, &dispatch_action, &task_arg, 1, SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT);\n\n// src/slot-store.c — deferred allocator cleanup task (issue 302)\npool_spawn(pool, &cleanup_action, &cleanup_arg, 1, SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT);\n\n// langs/bash/spec.c — ... none, the spec doesn't spawn pool tasks\n```\n\n`SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT` is `1`. Defined in `src/008-pool-runner.h` (or\na sibling header) so all callers use the same name.\n\n## Future hooks (not in scope, but called out)\n\nWhen `MAX_PRIORITY` is raised, the natural assignments are:\n\n| Future use case                                     | Priority |\n|-----------------------------------------------------|----------|\n| User-marked \"urgent\" boxes (UI / interactive)       | 3        |\n| Iterator continuation when its queue is non-empty   | 2        |\n| Default dispatch task                               | 1        |\n| Allocator cleanup task (deferred coalescing, 302)   | 0        |\n\nThese are speculative. The design conversation about what priorities should mean is\ndeferred until concrete need.)\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Define `SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT` (= 1) and `SM_MAX_PRIORITY` (= 1)\n   in a runner-wide header.\n2. Make every `pool_spawn` call site pass `SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT`.\n3. Set the pool's max priority at `pool_create` time using\n   `SM_MAX_PRIORITY` (if the pool API takes a max-priority hint).\n4. That's it.
```
