      "content":"# 311 — Integration tests & run output (`last-run.json`)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nPhase 2 writes a `last-run.json` after every map run, recording per-\nbox invocations, inputs, outputs, and any errors. The editor reads\nit to display a run summary. Phase 2 testing is ad-hoc: a few maps\nin `maps/` (`hello`, `branch-test`, `classify-demo`, `driver-test`)\nthat the developer runs by hand to verify the synchronous executor\nstill works.\n\nPhase 3 changes the shape of the problem: many concurrent\ninvocations, possibly thousands per run when iterators are in play,\nwritten from multiple worker threads. The phase 2 \"build a single\ntable at end of run\" approach does not survive that. And the\nexisting maps cover only a small slice of the new surface (no\nqueued inputs, no large iterator counts, no fan-in).\n\nThis issue covers two things that go together: the format and\nwriter for the run output, and the integration test plan that\nexercises the phase 3 runtime end-to-end.\n\n## Part A — Run output\n\n### Decoupling from the editor\n\nThe editor (phase 2) is being scoped down to a pure map editor — it\ndoes not know how to run maps and does not display run results.\n`last-run.json` is therefore not a UI feed. It exists for:\n\n- LLM consumption — agents reading the file to understand what a\n  run did\n- CLI-driven inspection — a future viewer utility (out of scope\n  here) that pretty-prints the file\n- Test harness consumption — the integration tests below diff the\n  written file against expected output\n\nDecoupling means the writer's design is driven by these consumers,\nnot by editor rendering needs.\n\n### File format: JSON Lines\n\nThe phase 2 single-document format does not work when the runner is\nstreaming events from many threads. Use JSON Lines instead — one\nJSON object per line, each line is one event, the file grows\nmonotonically as the run proceeds.\n\nEvent types:\n\n```jsonl\n{\"event\":\"run_start\", \"ts\":1234567890.123, \"map\":\"maps/classify-demo\", \"n_workers\":16}\n{\"event\":\"task_submit\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"box_id\":\"classify\", \"worker_idx\":-1}\n{\"event\":\"task_start\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3}\n{\"event\":\"task_end\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3, \"duration_us\":127, \"output_size\":12}\n{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\", \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5, \"size\":256, \"n_cells\":1}\n{\"event\":\"slot_free\", \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5}\n{\"event\":\"run_end\", \"ts\":..., \"duration_us\":1850, \"n_tasks\":7}\n```\n\nJSONL is append-only, which makes thread-safe writing tractable: a\nsingle mutex around the write call serializes the lines, and each\nline is self-contained so a partial line on crash is recoverable\n(reader skips the broken trailing line).\n\nThe reader (LLM, viewer, test harness) parses one line at a time;\ntotal file size doesn't have to fit in memory.\n\n### What gets logged\n\nPer-task: submission, start, end, duration, output size. Inputs\nand outputs are NOT logged by default — for iterator boxes\nproducing thousands of invocations, logging every value bloats\nthe file unbounded. There is a verbosity switch:\n\n- `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1` — log inputs and outputs (truncated past\n  some byte limit, e.g. 4 KB) per task. For debugging.\n- Default: log task lifecycle but not values.\n\nSlot allocator events (alloc, free, coalesce, grow) at a separate\nverbosity level. Off by default; on under `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`.\nFor diagnosing memory issues.\n\n### Writer mechanism\n\nA single dedicated writer thread inside the runner consumes events\nfrom a multi-producer single-consumer ring buffer. Worker threads\npush event records (small fixed-size structs) into the ring; the\nwriter pulls them, serializes to JSON, and writes lines to the\nfile. This avoids per-event mutex contention — the ring buffer is\nthe only shared state, and a well-written MPSC ring is lock-free\non the producer side.\n\nAlternative considered: each worker writes its own log file, merge\nat end. Simpler concurrency, but readers would have to merge by\ntimestamp — and any cross-event reasoning (was task A still\nrunning when task B ended?) requires the merge anyway.\n\nThe writer thread is started after the pool is created and joined\nbefore `pool_destroy`. It also handles `run_end` as the very last\nevent, including the final summary.\n\n### File location\n\n`<map-dir>/last-run.jsonl` (note: `.jsonl` not `.json` — the\nextension reflects the format change). Overwritten on every run.\n\nA rotated archive (`last-run.jsonl.1`, `.2`, …) is out of scope.\nUsers who want history copy the file before re-running.\n\n## Part B — Integration tests\n\n### Scope\n\nEnd-to-end tests of the pool runner against real map directories.\nEach test is:\n\n1. A map directory under `tests/maps/<name>/`\n2. An expected `last-run.jsonl` (or a comparison spec) under\n   `tests/expected/<name>.jsonl`\n3. A test driver script that runs the map and diffs\n\nThe test driver is `scripts/run-tests.sh`. It iterates\n`tests/maps/`, runs each, diffs against expected (with a normalizer\nthat drops timestamps, durations, worker indices — anything non-\ndeterministic), and reports pass/fail.\n\n### Test maps\n\nCoverage targets:\n\n| Test map                  | What it exercises                                    |\n|---------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|\n| `hello`                   | Single Lua box, one input, one output                |\n| `data-only`               | Data box → call box. No inputs, just stored values   |\n| `fan-out-3`               | One output → three consumer boxes (peek, refcount)   |\n| `fan-in-iterator`         | Three producers → iterator with queued input         |\n| `comparator-routing`      | Comparator with all three branches (lt/eq/gt)        |\n| `iterator-100`            | Iterator with 100 input values, round-robin to 3 paths |\n| `multilang`               | One Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all wired      |\n| `large-output`            | Box producing a 1 MB string (variable-size heap)     |\n| `cycle-detector-fail`     | Non-iterator cycle — load must abort                 |\n| `missing-input-fail`      | Connection references a nonexistent box — load aborts|\n| `box-error-fail`          | Box function returns nonzero — runner aborts         |\n\nThe `*-fail` tests verify error behavior — the runner is expected\nto exit nonzero with a precise error message. The driver matches\nexit code and stderr against expected.\n\n### Test driver\n\n```bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh\nfor test_dir in tests/maps/*/; do\n    name=$(basename \"${test_dir}\")\n    expected=\"tests/expected/${name}.jsonl\"\n\n    actual=$( \"${SOURCE_DIR}/soramech-pool\" \"${test_dir}\" )\n    rc=$?\n\n    if [ -f \"${expected}.exit\" ]; then\n        # *-fail tests: assert exit code and stderr substring\n        check_failure \"${name}\" \"${rc}\" \"${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl\"\n    else\n        # success tests: diff normalized last-run.jsonl\n        check_success \"${name}\" \"${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl\" \"${expected}\"\n    fi\ndone\n```\n\n`normalize_jsonl` strips timestamps, durations, worker indices,\nslot ids, and task ids (all non-deterministic) and sorts events by\nevent type. The result should be deterministic across runs.\n\n### Phase 3 demo map\n\nA single map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` that\ndemonstrates everything working together:\n\n- Multiple entry-point data boxes\n- Lua, C, and Bash boxes all wired together\n- An iterator with a queued input\n- A comparator routing into different downstream paths\n- A large-output box (variable-size heap)\n- Non-trivial graph topology (≥ 10 boxes)\n\nRun with `./run.sh` from the demo directory. Prints a short summary\nof what happened (parsing the `last-run.jsonl`) so the demo is\nvisible without a viewer utility.\n\nThis satisfies the standing project rule (CLAUDE.md) that each\nphase produces a runnable demo in `issues/completed/demos/`.\n\n### Test infrastructure constraints\n\n- Tests must not depend on the editor or any HTTP server\n- Tests must not depend on internet access\n- Tests must run in under 60 seconds total on a developer machine\n- Tests must be deterministic when normalized (any\n  non-determinism is normalized out, not papered over with retries)\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Whether to log inputs/outputs by default. Useful for development,\n  noisy for production. Current decision: opt-in via env var,\n  default off.\n- Slot-event logging: also opt-in. Useful for diagnosing memory\n  issues. Off by default.\n- File format: JSON Lines is the choice. An alternative was a\n  protobuf or msgpack binary log, which is faster to write but\n  harder to inspect by hand. JSONL wins on inspectability.\n- Whether to keep timestamps as Unix epoch floats or ISO 8601\n  strings. Epoch floats are smaller and easier to diff. Stick with\n  floats.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n### Run output (Part A)\n1. Define the event struct and JSONL line format. Start with\n   `run_start`, `task_start`, `task_end`, `run_end`.\n2. Implement the MPSC ring buffer for events.\n3. Implement the writer thread: pulls from ring, serializes,\n   appends a line to the output file.\n4. Wire event emission into the pool runner: `run_start` at\n   startup, `task_start` and `task_end` in the dispatch action,\n   `run_end` after quiescence.\n5. Add the verbosity env vars and the optional event types.\n\n### Tests (Part B)\n6. Create `tests/maps/` and `tests/expected/` directory structure.\n7. Write the `hello` test as the first end-to-end smoke check.\n8. Write the test driver `scripts/run-tests.sh` and the JSONL\n   normalizer.\n9. Add tests one at a time as each runtime feature lands. The\n   `*-fail` tests can land before their corresponding successful\n   tests if the failure path is implemented first.\n10. Build the phase 3 demo map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/`\n    once the rest of phase 3 is implemented.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — test driver (to be written)\n- `tests/maps/`, `tests/expected/` — test fixtures (to be created)\n- `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` — phase 3 demo (to be built)\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — emits run_start / run_end\n- `src/dispatch.c` — emits task_start / task_end\n- `src/slot-store.c` — emits slot_alloc / slot_free (verbose mode)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot events\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task lifecycle events\n- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — load-time errors\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — `make test` invokes this\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — blocking semantics relevant to\n  test design\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### JSON writer half — 2026-05-12\n\n`libs/json/json.c` had stub writer bodies left over from 314's\nparser milestone; this pass filled them in. The writer maintains\na small depth stack (capped at 16) where each entry packs two\nbooleans — \"next element is first\" and \"this level is an\nobject.\" That's enough to handle comma placement and pick the\nright close bracket. Overflow of the caller-supplied buffer is\nsticky on `w->err`; `json_writer_finish` reports it.\n\nEight new writer tests in `tests/314-json-test.c` cover the\nprimitives, escape encoding, empty and non-empty containers,\nnesting depth, overflow detection, and a round-trip where the\nwriter emits an object that the parser then decodes and the test\nverifies via the accessor API.\n\nStill ahead for 311: the JSONL event writer (a thin wrapper that\nserializes `task_start` / `task_end` / `run_start` / `run_end`\nrecords using this writer), the MPSC ring buffer the worker\nthreads push events into, and the dedicated writer thread that\ndrains them.\n\n### Event emitters — 2026-05-12\n\n`src/013-jsonl-events.{c,h}` ships the per-event emit functions\non top of issue 314's bounded writer:\n\n- `jsonl_emit_run_start(w, ts, map, n_workers)`\n- `jsonl_emit_task_submit(w, ts, task_id, box_id, worker_idx)`\n- `jsonl_emit_task_start(w, ts, task_id, worker_idx)`\n- `jsonl_emit_task_end(w, ts, task_id, worker_idx, duration_us, output_size)`\n- `jsonl_emit_run_end(w, ts, duration_us, n_tasks)`\n\nEach emit serializes into a fixed 512-byte buffer, appends a\nnewline, and writes to a `FILE *` under a per-writer mutex. The\nMPSC ring + dedicated writer thread aren't there yet — the mutex\nis a placeholder until dispatch is producing events fast enough\nto justify the contention.\n\n`tests/013-jsonl-events-test.c` writes a full sequence, slurps\nthe file back, and parses each line through 314's JSON parser to\nverify the event shape. A concurrent-emit test runs 8 producer\nthreads each emitting 200 events into the same writer and\nverifies every line round-trips.\n\nStill ahead inside 311: slot-event opt-in\n(`SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`), inputs/outputs opt-in\n(`SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1`), the MPSC ring + writer thread, and\nthe integration-test harness map fixtures.\n\n### Multi-producer event queue + writer thread — 2026-05-12\n\n`src/014-event-queue.{c,h}` ships the producer-side queue and the\ndedicated writer thread. Producers (worker threads + the main\nthread) call `event_queue_run_start` / `task_submit` / `task_start`\n/ `task_end` / `run_end`; each emit appends a small fixed-size\nevent record under a brief mutex and signals a CV. The writer\nthread sleeps on the CV, snapshots the queue head into a local\nbatch under the lock, then drains the batch outside the lock —\nJSON encoding + fwrite happen with zero producer contention.\n\nFour unit tests in `tests/014-event-queue-test.c` cover single\nproducer / multi-thread burst (8 producers × 250 events each =\n2000 lines, all round-trip through the JSON parser) / shutdown-\ndrain / pending-count.\n\nThe dispatch action (issue 304) opt-in emits task_start and\ntask_end events with monotonic-clock durations via the queue;\nthe pool runner emits run_start and run_end. `soramech-pool`\nwrites to `map_dir/tmp/last-run.jsonl` when that directory\nexists, falling back to `/tmp/soramech-last-run.jsonl`.\n\nWhat's still ahead inside 311:\n- Lock-free Vyukov MPSC ring with sequence numbers — the\n  architecture doc's preferred design. The mutex queue is a\n  placeholder; upgrade once contention shows up.\n- Opt-in slot events and per-task input/output dumps.\n\n### Integration test runner — 2026-05-12\n\n`scripts/run-tests.sh` runs every fixture map under `tests/maps/`\nthrough `soramech-pool` and asserts the expected box-output\nsubstrings show up in stderr. `make test` invokes the script\nafter the unit tests so a full `make test` covers everything\nfrom slot operations all the way through end-to-end Lua / C /\nBash dispatch via JSONL logging.\n\nSix fixture checks at the moment:\n- `calc`            — single Lua `add → 42`\n- `hello`           — data → Lua, `greet → \"Hello, World!\"`\n- `comparator`      — `high` fires, `low` / `mid` don't\n- `iter-route`      — single-fire iterator picks `out_0` → `a`\n- `pipeline`        — five-box multilang chain\n- `pipeline file`   — verifies the file_write sink wrote\n  `\"11!\"` to `/tmp/soramech-pipeline-out.txt`\n",

```json
{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"148df4a0-1862-4b38-a0d9-b79549b64781",

    "file":{
      "content":"# 312 — Same-language wire fast path: skip JSON for adjacent same-language boxes\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe wire format between boxes is JSON (`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`,\nissue 302's \"no type tags\" — slot store stores opaque bytes; the\nlanguage spec encodes/decodes). Every wire pays the JSON encode +\ndecode cost on every value pass, even when the producer and the\nconsumer are the same language and could use a faster\nlanguage-native serialization.\n\nFor a Lua → Lua wire passing a 10-element table:\n1. Producer's spec: `cjson.encode(table)` → string of N bytes\n2. `slot_push(slot, string, N)`\n3. `slot_peek(slot, buf, N)`\n4. Consumer's spec: `cjson.decode(buf)` → Lua table\n\nSteps 1 and 4 are the cost. They're language-agnostic and unnecessary\nwhen both endpoints share a language.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEach language spec exposes **two invoke paths**:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;\n    const char *file_ext;\n\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int   (*compile)(...);\n\n    // Universal path — JSON bytes in, JSON bytes out\n    int   (*invoke_json)  (void *handle, /* common args */);\n\n    // Fast path — language-native bytes in, language-native bytes out\n    int   (*invoke_native)(void *handle, /* common args */);\n\n    // Bridges used when a value crosses a language boundary\n    int   (*native_to_json)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n    int   (*json_to_native)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\n`invoke_native` is required (every spec implements one). Per-language\n\"native\" format:\n- **Lua**: `lua_dump` for closures, `cjson` or msgpack for tables, raw\n  bytes for strings/numbers. Spec's choice as long as it's\n  symmetric with its own decoder.\n- **C**: raw struct memcpy. The compile-time wrapper (issue 307)\n  knows the types; serialization is `memcpy(slot_buf, &val, sizeof\n  val)`.\n- **Bash**: strings only — Bash has no other native form, so the\n  fast path is identical to the JSON path. Implement as a thin\n  alias.\n\n`invoke_json` is the universal interop format. Required for any\nlanguage that participates in cross-language wires. A spec that\nonly ever talks to itself can skip `invoke_json` (compile error if\na wire crosses to it from another language).\n\n## Compile-time wire classification\n\nEvery wire gets a `fast_path: true | false` flag set at build time\n(issue 309 build step):\n\n```python\nfor wire in graph.wires:\n    src_lang = box_at(wire.from).lang\n    dst_lang = box_at(wire.to).lang\n    wire.fast_path = (src_lang == dst_lang)\n```\n\nThe flag becomes part of the compiled manifest. Runtime never\nre-evaluates language pairing.\n\n## Per-edge format negotiation\n\nClassification is **per edge**, not per box. A box always\nexecutes its user function in native form. The format on the\nwire is decided independently for each input edge and each\noutput edge based on the language pair across that edge:\n\n```\ninput edge native?   = (producer.lang == this_box.lang)\noutput edge native?  = (this_box.lang == consumer.lang)\n```\n\nSo a Lua box sitting in the middle of `[C → Lua → C]` works\nlike this:\n\n- Input edge from the C producer: cross-lang, so the slot\n  carries JSON. On read, the Lua spec calls `json_to_native`\n  to lift it into a Lua value.\n- The box's user function runs natively in Lua. It returns a\n  Lua value.\n- Output edges to the two C consumers: cross-lang, so the spec\n  calls `native_to_json` once and pushes JSON bytes to each\n  consumer's slot.\n\nA Lua box in `[Lua → Lua → C]` works differently *along its\nown edges*:\n\n- Input edge from the Lua producer: same-lang, slot carries\n  native binary. No conversion on read.\n- User function runs.\n- Output edges: one is same-lang (push native), the other is\n  cross-lang (call `native_to_json`, push JSON). The producer\n  pushes once to each consumer's slot in the right format.\n\nThis means **same-lang neighbors get the fast path even when\nsome other neighbor is cross-lang**. The classification doesn't\ncollapse on the first cross-language edge it finds; it stays\nper-edge.\n\n### Why per-edge, not per-box\n\nThe earlier design considered an \"all same-lang or fall back\nto JSON for all\" rule (the simpler classification). It's\nstrictly dominated by the per-edge rule:\n\n- The dominant case is \"a Lua sub-graph occasionally talks to\n  C.\" Per-box would force the Lua-to-Lua interior to round-trip\n  through JSON for every box that has *any* C neighbor.\n- Per-edge keeps the cost local to the actual cross-lang\n  boundary. The interior of any same-lang island skips JSON;\n  only the boundary edges pay.\n- The implementation cost is identical: same number of bits per\n  box, just stored per-port/per-edge instead of per-box.\n\n### What each box records at graph load\n\nFor each box:\n\n- `input_edge_native[i]` — one bit per input port. True iff the\n  producer feeding that port has the same language as this box.\n- `output_edge_native[j]` — one bit per outgoing connection\n  (not per output port — a single output port can fan to\n  multiple consumers, each of which is classified independently\n  because the language pair may differ across consumers).\n\nBoth arrays are computed during `graph_attach_runtime` and live\non the box record. No runtime re-evaluation.\n\n## Runtime dispatch\n\nThe dispatch action calls `invoke_native` always (when the spec\nprovides one). The boundary work is per-edge in two places:\ninput-read and output-push.\n\n### Input-read: per-input-port\n\n```c\nfor (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n    slot_pop(input_slots[i], wire_buf, wire_buf_cap);\n    if (b->input_edge_native[i]) {\n        // wire bytes are native form already; hand to invoke_native as-is\n        native_inputs[i] = wire_buf;\n    } else {\n        // wire bytes are JSON; lift into native form\n        spec->json_to_native(ctx, wire_buf, wire_size,\n                             native_buf, native_cap, &native_size);\n        native_inputs[i] = native_buf;\n    }\n}\nspec->invoke_native(ctx, fn, native_inputs, n_inputs,\n                    native_out, native_out_cap, &native_out_size);\n```\n\n### Output-push: per-outgoing-connection\n\n```c\nfor (int j = 0; j < b->n_connections; j++) {\n    if (b->output_edge_native[j]) {\n        // consumer is same-lang; push native bytes directly\n        slot_push(consumer_slot, native_out, native_out_size, tag);\n    } else {\n        // consumer is cross-lang; serialize to JSON once per such edge\n        spec->native_to_json(ctx, native_out, native_out_size,\n                             json_buf, json_buf_cap, &json_size);\n        slot_push(consumer_slot, json_buf, json_size, tag);\n    }\n}\n```\n\nIf multiple cross-lang consumers share the producer's language,\nthe dispatch can cache the JSON encoding from the first such\nedge and reuse it for the rest (optimization, not required for\ncorrectness).\n\nIf the spec's `invoke_native` is NULL (e.g., bash), the dispatch\nfalls back to the universal `invoke` (JSON-in, JSON-out) and\ntreats every edge as JSON. This is the slow path; it's always\ncorrect.\n\n## Edge cases\n\n- **All-same-language graph**: every wire is fast-path; `invoke_json`\n  never runs. Spec writers can stub it out.\n- **All-different-language graph**: every wire is JSON;\n  `invoke_native` handles bytes that came back from `json_to_native`.\n- **One same-language wire, several cross-language wires from the same\n  producer**: the producer writes JSON. Same-language consumer\n  decodes via `json_to_native` (still cheaper than full encode +\n  decode round-trip — only one direction of conversion is paid,\n  not two).\n- **Type changes mid-development**: a wire that was Lua→Lua becomes\n  Lua→C as the user changes a downstream box's language. Compile\n  flips the flag; the producer now writes JSON. No runtime\n  surprises, no migration.\n\n## Implementation cost\n\nThe two-invoke spec interface adds maybe 30 lines per language\nspec. The compile-time wire classification is one pass over the\ngraph. The dispatch action's input-read branch is one `if` on the\nwire flag. None of this is hot-path complex; the gain is one less\nJSON encode/decode per same-language hop, which is the whole point.\n\n## Future: whole-program same-language compilation\n\nA bigger optimization beyond this issue: at compile time, merge\nall same-language boxes into one translation unit. The C spec\nbecomes whole-program; the Lua spec produces one bytecode chunk\ncovering every Lua function. Box-boundary crossings become regular\nfunction calls — no slot store, no dispatch layer, no spec\ninvocation. Only cross-language wires retain the slot machinery.\n\nThis is a phase-3.5+ optimization and a much bigger lift —\nrequires the spec's `compile` callback to coordinate across all\nboxes of its language, plus a runtime mode that bypasses the\ndispatch layer for fully-merged regions of the graph. The\nwire-level fast path in this issue is the immediate, smaller win.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Spec interface** (issue 303): add `invoke_native`,\n   `invoke_json`, `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` callbacks.\n   Update the contract doc.\n2. **Compile step** (issue 309): walk wires, set `fast_path` flag,\n   set `output_format` per box.\n3. **Dispatch action** (issue 304): branch on `fast_path` /\n   `output_format` when reading inputs and when writing the\n   output.\n4. **Per-language specs** (306, 307, 308): implement both invoke\n   paths. Bash's fast path is a thin alias around the JSON path.\n   C's fast path is `memcpy`. Lua's fast path picks a native\n   encoding (cjson for tables; raw bytes for primitives).\n5. **Tests**: smoke tests confirming a 100k-iteration Lua→Lua\n   pipeline with the fast path runs measurably faster than the\n   same pipeline with the JSON path, and that mixed-language\n   pipelines still work.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — adds the new callbacks\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — branch on fast_path\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — wire-flag enrichment\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md`, `307-c-language-spec.md`,\n  `308-bash-language-spec.md` — per-spec native implementations\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot still stores opaque\n  bytes; the format negotiation is at the spec layer, not the\n  store\n\n## Implementation note: ask the user about type-annotated cross-language encodings\n\nBefore implementing this issue, the implementer must ask the user\nto decide on **type-annotated wire encodings** for cross-language\nhops — primitives go raw bytes (4-byte int as 4 bytes, not as the\nJSON string `\"42\"`), strings go length-prefixed UTF-8, structured\ntypes go JSON. That decision affects the spec interface (whether\n`json_to_native` is enough or whether we need a `decode_wire(type,\nbytes)` shape) and the wire-format byte layout. Don't proceed with\nthe implementation without explicit user direction on this; the\ntwo designs aren't trivially interchangeable later.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Whether a spec must implement `invoke_json`**: leaning yes, so\n  any spec can talk to any other spec. A spec that wants to\n  shortcut can declare cross-language wires unsupported via\n  compile-time error, but that's an opt-out, not the default.\n- **How to share the bridge functions across consumers**: native_to_json\n  on the producer side runs once per output (not per consumer), and\n  the JSON bytes go in the slot. Each cross-language consumer pays\n  json_to_native independently. Same-language consumers pay nothing.\n  Symmetrically: if the producer chose native and there's one\n  cross-language consumer, that consumer pays native_to_json then\n  json_to_native_their_lang. Two conversions for one cross-language\n  hop in this case. Probably fine; it's a corner case.\n\n## Implementation status\n\nWhat's in place (per the round summaries on 2026-05-12 to\n2026-05-19):\n\n- `lang_spec_t` extended with `invoke_native`, `invoke_json`,\n  `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` callback slots (issue 303\n  spec interface).\n- Each of the three specs declares all four callbacks. Today\n  they all alias to the single existing `invoke` implementation;\n  the actual specialization (real native_to_json / json_to_native\n  bodies, real per-language binary native form) is not yet\n  implemented.\n- `graph_attach_runtime` computes a per-box `use_native_invoke`\n  bit (true iff all input producers and all output consumers\n  share this box's language). The dispatch picks\n  `invoke_native > invoke_json > invoke` based on that single\n  bit.\n\nWhat's still ahead:\n\n- **Replace per-box `use_native_invoke` with per-edge\n  classification.** The current bit is the simpler approximation\n  of the per-edge design above. It needs to be split into\n  `b->input_edge_native[i]` and `b->output_edge_native[j]` arrays\n  computed at graph load, with the dispatch's input-read and\n  output-push paths each consulting the relevant array.\n- **Per-language native binary serializations.** Each spec\n  needs a real `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` (also\n  required by issue 317 for data boxes), plus a real\n  `invoke_native` that operates on whatever the spec considers\n  its native handoff format.\n- The type-annotated cross-language encoding decision flagged\n  above is still pending user direction.\n",
      "numLines":332,

Producer's spec: `cjson.encode(table)` → string of N bytes\n17\t2. `slot_push(slot, string, N)`\n18\t3. `slot_peek(slot, buf, N)`\n19\t4. Consumer's spec: `cjson.decode(buf)` → Lua table\n20\t\n21\tSteps 1 and 4 are the cost. They're language-agnostic and unnecessary\n22\twhen both endpoints share a language.\n23\t\n24\t## Intended behavior\n25\t\n26\tEach language spec exposes **two invoke paths**:\n27\t\n28\t```c\n29\ttypedef struct {\n30\t    const char *name;\n31\t    const char *file_ext;\n32\t\n33\t    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n34\t    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n35\t    int   (*compile)(...);\n36\t\n37\t    // Universal path — JSON bytes in, JSON bytes out\n38\t    int   (*invoke_json)  (void *handle, /* common args */);\n39\t\n40\t    // Fast path — language-native bytes in, language-native bytes out\n41\t    int   (*invoke_native)(void *handle, /* common args */);\n42\t\n43\t    // Bridges used when a value crosses a language boundary\n44\t    int   (*native_to_json)(const void *src, int src_size,\n45\t                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n46\t    int   (*json_to_native)(const void *src, int src_size,\n47\t                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n48\t} lang_spec_t;\n49\t```\n50\t\n51\t`invoke_native` is required (every spec implements one). Per-language\n52\t\"native\" format:\n53\t- **Lua**: `lua_dump` for closures, `cjson` or msgpack for tables, raw\n54\t  bytes for strings/numbers. Spec's choice as long as it's\n55\t  symmetric with its own decoder.\n56\t- **C**: raw struct memcpy. The compile-time wrapper (issue 307)\n57\t  knows the types; serialization is `memcpy(slot_buf, &val, sizeof\n58\t  val)`.\n59\t- **Bash**: strings only — Bash has no other native form, so the\n60\t  fast path is identical to the JSON path. Implement as a thin\n61\t  alias.\n62\t\n63\t`invoke_json` is the universal interop format. Required for any\n64\tlanguage that participates in cross-language wires. A spec that\n65\tonly ever talks to itself can skip `invoke_json` (compile error if\n66\ta wire crosses to it from another language).\n67\t\n68\t## Compile-time wire classification\n69\t\n70\tEvery wire gets a `fast_path: true | false` flag set at build time\n71\t(issue 309 build step):\n72\t\n73\t```python\n74\tfor wire in graph.wires:\n75\t    src_lang = box_at(wire.from).lang\n76\t    dst_lang = box_at(wire.to).lang\n77\t    wire.fast_path = (src_lang == dst_lang)\n78\t```\n79\t\n80\tThe flag becomes part of the compiled manifest. Runtime never\n81\tre-evaluates language pairing.\n82\t\n83\t## Per-edge format negotiation\n84\t\n85\tClassification is **per edge**, not per box. A box always\n86\texecutes its user function in native form. The format on the\n87\twire is decided independently for each input edge and each\n88\toutput edge based on the language pair across that edge:\n89\t\n90\t```\n91\tinput edge native?   = (producer.lang == this_box.lang)\n92\toutput edge native?  = (this_box.lang == consumer.lang)\n93\t```\n94\t\n95\tSo a Lua box sitting in the middle of `[C → Lua → C]` works\n96\tlike this:\n97\t\n98\t- Input edge from the C producer: cross-lang, so the slot\n99\t  carries JSON. On read, the Lua spec calls `json_to_native`\n100\t  to lift it into a Lua value.\n101\t- The box's user function runs natively in Lua. It returns a\n102\t  Lua value.\n103\t- Output edges to the two C consumers: cross-lang, so the spec\n104\t  calls `native_to_json` once and pushes JSON bytes to each\n105\t  consumer's slot.\n106\t\n107\tA Lua box in `[Lua → Lua → C]` works differently *along its\n108\town edges*:\n109\t\n110\t- Input edge from the Lua producer: same-lang, slot carries\n111\t  native binary. No conversion on read.\n112\t- User function runs.\n113\t- Output edges: one is same-lang (push native), the other is\n114\t  cross-lang (call `native_to_json`, push JSON). The producer\n115\t  pushes once to each consumer's slot in the right format.\n116\t\n117\tThis means **same-lang neighbors get the fast path even when\n118\tsome other neighbor is cross-lang**. The classification doesn't\n119\tcollapse on the first cross-language edge it finds; it stays\n120\tper-edge.\n121\t\n122\t### Why per-edge, not per-box\n123\t\n124\tThe earlier design considered an \"all same-lang or fall back\n125\tto JSON for all\" rule (the simpler classification). It's\n126\tstrictly dominated by the per-edge rule:\n127\t\n128\t- The dominant case is \"a Lua sub-graph occasionally talks to\n129\t  C.\" Per-box would force the Lua-to-Lua interior to round-trip\n130\t  through JSON for every box that has *any* C neighbor.\n131\t- Per-edge keeps the cost local to the actual cross-lang\n132\t  boundary. The interior of any same-lang island skips JSON;\n133\t  only the boundary edges pay.\n134\t- The implementation cost is identical: same number of bits per\n135\t  box, just stored per-port/per-edge instead of per-box.\n136\t\n137\t### What each box records at graph load\n138\t\n139\tFor each box:\n140\t\n141\t- `input_edge_native[i]` — one bit per input port. True iff the\n142\t  producer feeding that port has the same language as this box.\n143\t- `output_edge_native[j]` — one bit per outgoing connection\n144\t  (not per output port — a single output port can fan to\n145\t  multiple consumers, each of which is classified independently\n146\t  because the language pair may differ across consumers).\n147\t\n148\tBoth arrays are computed during `graph_attach_runtime` and live\n149\ton the box record. No runtime re-evaluation.\n150\t\n151\t## Runtime dispatch\n152\t\n153\tThe dispatch action calls `invoke_native` always (when the spec\n154\tprovides one). The boundary work is per-edge in two places:\n155\tinput-read and output-push.\n156\t\n157\t### Input-read: per-input-port\n158\t\n159\t```c\n160\tfor (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n161\t    slot_pop(input_slots[i], wire_buf, wire_buf_cap);\n162\t    if (b->input_edge_native[i]) {\n163\t        // wire bytes are native form already; hand to invoke_native as-is\n164\t        native_inputs[i] = wire_buf;\n165\t    } else {\n166\t        // wire bytes are JSON; lift into native form\n167\t        spec->json_to_native(ctx, wire_buf, wire_size,\n168\t                             native_buf, native_cap, &native_size);\n169\t        native_inputs[i] = native_buf;\n170\t    }\n171\t}\n172\tspec->invoke_native(ctx, fn, native_inputs, n_inputs,\n173\t                    native_out, native_out_cap, &native_out_size);\n174\t```\n175\t\n176\t### Output-push: per-outgoing-connection\n177\t\n178\t```c\n179\tfor (int j = 0; j < b->n_connections; j++) {\n180\t    if (b->output_edge_native[j]) {\n181\t        // consumer is same-lang; push native bytes directly\n182\t        slot_push(consumer_slot, native_out, native_out_size, tag);\n183\t    } else {\n184\t        // consumer is cross-lang; serialize to JSON once per such edge\n185\t        spec->native_to_json(ctx, native_out, native_out_size,\n186\t                             json_buf, json_buf_cap, &json_size);\n187\t        slot_push(consumer_slot, json_buf, json_size, tag);\n188\t    }\n189\t}\n190\t```\n191\t\n192\tIf multiple cross-lang consumers share the producer's language,\n193\tthe dispatch can cache the JSON encoding from the first such\n194\tedge and reuse it for the rest (optimization, not required for\n195\tcorrectness).\n196\t\n197\tIf the spec's `invoke_native` is NULL (e.g., bash), the dispatch\n198\tfalls back to the universal `invoke` (JSON-in, JSON-out) and\n199\ttreats every edge as JSON. This is the slow path; it's always\n200\tcorrect.\n201\t\n202\t## Edge cases\n203\t\n204\t- **All-same-language graph**: every wire is fast-path; `invoke_json`\n205\t  never runs. Spec writers can stub it out.\n206\t- **All-different-language graph**: every wire is JSON;\n207\t  `invoke_native` handles bytes that came back from `json_to_native`.\n208\t- **One same-language wire, several cross-language wires from the same\n209\t  producer**: the producer writes JSON. Same-language consumer\n210\t  decodes via `json_to_native` (still cheaper than full encode +\n211\t  decode round-trip — only one direction of conversion is paid,\n212\t  not two).\n213\t- **Type changes mid-development**: a wire that was Lua→Lua becomes\n214\t  Lua→C as the user changes a downstream box's language. Compile\n215\t  flips the flag; the producer now writes JSON. No runtime\n216\t  surprises, no migration.\n217\t\n218\t## Implementation cost\n219\t\n220\tThe two-invoke spec interface adds maybe 30 lines per language\n221\tspec. The compile-time wire classification is one pass over the\n222\tgraph. The dispatch action's input-read branch is one `if` on the\n223\twire flag. None of this is hot-path complex; the gain is one less\n224\tJSON encode/decode per same-language hop, which is the whole point.\n225\t\n226\t## Future: whole-program same-language compilation\n227\t\n228\tA bigger optimization beyond this issue: at compile time, merge\n229\tall same-language boxes into one translation unit. The C spec\n230\tbecomes whole-program; the Lua spec produces one bytecode chunk\n231\tcovering every Lua function. Box-boundary crossings become regular\n232\tfunction calls — no slot store, no dispatch layer, no spec\n233\tinvocation. Only cross-language wires retain the slot machinery.\n234\t\n235\tThis is a phase-3.5+ optimization and a much bigger lift —\n236\trequires the spec's `compile` callback to coordinate across all\n237\tboxes of its language, plus a runtime mode that bypasses the\n238\tdispatch layer for fully-merged regions of the graph. The\n239\twire-level fast path in this issue is the immediate, smaller win.\n240\t\n241\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n242\t\n243\t1. **Spec interface** (issue 303): add `invoke_native`,\n244\t   `invoke_json`, `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` callbacks.\n245\t   Update the contract doc.\n246\t2. **Compile step** (issue 309): walk wires, set `fast_path` flag,\n247\t   set `output_format` per box.\n248\t3. **Dispatch action** (issue 304): branch on `fast_path` /\n249\t   `output_format` when reading inputs and when writing the\n250\t   output.\n251\t4. **Per-language specs** (306, 307, 308): implement both invoke\n252\t   paths. Bash's fast path is a thin alias around the JSON path.\n253\t   C's fast path is `memcpy`. Lua's fast path picks a native\n254\t   encoding (cjson for tables; raw bytes for primitives).\n255\t5. **Tests**: smoke tests confirming a 100k-iteration Lua→Lua\n256\t   pipeline with the fast path runs measurably faster than the\n257\t   same pipeline with the JSON path, and that mixed-language\n258\t   pipelines still work.\n259\t\n260\t## Relevant files\n261\t\n262\t- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — adds the new callbacks\n263\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — branch on fast_path\n264\t- `issues/309-build-system.md` — wire-flag enrichment\n265\t- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md`, `307-c-language-spec.md`,\n266\t  `308-bash-language-spec.md` — per-spec native implementations\n267\t- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot still stores opaque\n268\t  bytes; the format negotiation is at the spec layer, not the\n269\t  store\n270\t\n271\t## Implementation note: ask the user about type-annotated cross-language encodings\n272\t\n273\tBefore implementing this issue, the implementer must ask the user\n274\tto decide on **type-annotated wire encodings** for cross-language\n275\thops — primitives go raw bytes (4-byte int as 4 bytes, not as the\n276\tJSON string `\"42\"`), strings go length-prefixed UTF-8, structured\n277\ttypes go JSON. That decision affects the spec interface (whether\n278\t`json_to_native` is enough or whether we need a `decode_wire(type,\n279\tbytes)` shape) and the wire-format byte layout. Don't proceed with\n280\tthe implementation without explicit user direction on this; the\n281\ttwo designs aren't trivially interchangeable later.\n282\t\n283\t## Open questions\n284\t\n285\t- **Whether a spec must implement `invoke_json`**: leaning yes, so\n286\t  any spec can talk to any other spec. A spec that wants to\n287\t  shortcut can declare cross-language wires unsupported via\n288\t  compile-time error, but that's an opt-out, not the default.\n289\t- **How to share the bridge functions across consumers**: native_to_json\n290\t  on the producer side runs once per output (not per consumer), and\n291\t  the JSON bytes go in the slot. Each cross-language consumer pays\n292\t  json_to_native independently. Same-language consumers pay nothing.\n293\t  Symmetrically: if the producer chose native and there's one\n294\t  cross-language consumer, that consumer pays native_to_json then\n295\t  json_to_native_their_lang. Two conversions for one cross-language\n296\t  hop in this case. Probably fine; it's a corner case.\n297\t\n298\t## Implementation status\n299\t\n300\tWhat's in place (per the round summaries on 2026-05-12 to\n301\t2026-05-19):\n302\t\n303\t- `lang_spec_t` extended with `invoke_native`, `invoke_json`,\n304\t  `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` callback slots (issue 303\n305\t  spec interface).\n306\t- Each of the three specs declares all four callbacks. Today\n307\t  they all alias to the single existing `invoke` implementation;\n308\t  the actual specialization (real native_to_json / json_to_native\n309\t  bodies, real per-language binary native form) is not yet\n310\t  implemented.\n311\t- `graph_attach_runtime` computes a per-box `use_native_invoke`\n312\t  bit (true iff all input producers and all output consumers\n313\t  share this box's language). The dispatch picks\n314\t  `invoke_native > invoke_json > invoke` based on that single\n315\t  bit.\n316\t\n317\tWhat's still ahead:\n318\t\n319\t- **Replace per-box `use_native_invoke` with per-edge\n320\t  classification.** The current bit is the simpler approximation\n321\t  of the per-edge design above. It needs to be split into\n322\t  `b->input_edge_native[i]` and `b->output_edge_native[j]` arrays\n323\t  computed at graph load, with the dispatch's input-read and\n324\t  output-push paths each consulting the relevant array.\n325\t- **Per-language native binary serializations.** Each spec\n326\t  needs a real `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` (also\n327\t  required by issue 317 for data boxes), plus a real\n328\t  `invoke_native` that operates on whatever the spec considers\n329\t  its native handoff format.\n330\t- The type-annotated cross-language encoding decision flagged\n331\t  above is still pending user direction.\n332\t"

      "content":"# 313 — Research: whole-program same-language compilation\n\n## Status\nresearch / low priority / blocked until rest of phase 3 is complete\n\n## Concept\n\nInstead of one box = one function call going through the dispatch\nlayer + slot store + spec invocation, **merge all same-language\nboxes at compile time into a single translation unit** for that\nlanguage. Box-to-box transitions within a language region become\nordinary function calls — the optimizer can inline across them, the\nlanguage runtime stays warm, and the slot store and dispatch layer\ndon't run for those transitions at all. Only cross-language wires\nretain the slot machinery.\n\nFor C: every C box becomes a function in one big `.c` file, with\nthe build emitting one `.so`. Wire endpoints become direct calls;\nthe optimizer inlines based on its usual heuristics.\n\nFor Lua: every Lua function gets pre-compiled into one bytecode\nchunk loaded into one shared `lua_State` per worker. Wire\nendpoints become direct `lua_pcall`s into that chunk — no JSON\nencode/decode, no slot push/pop, no spec re-entry per call.\n\nFor Bash: probably no benefit — Bash is already process-per-call;\nfusing scripts doesn't help much. Skip.\n\n## Why this is research, not a feature\n\nThree open questions that need code-level investigation before\nthe design is concrete:\n\n1. **Loop and iterator boundaries**: a same-language region with an\n   iterator inside it has dynamic re-spawning. Is the iterator\n   merged in (a loop in the generated code) or does it remain a\n   spec-mediated boundary? If the latter, the merge buys less.\n2. **Compile time**: whole-program optimization is slow. Either source-map-style mapping or\n   per-function preserved names — both have costs.\n\nThe right way to answer these is to prototype: take a small all-Lua\ngraph (like the hello map) and see what a merged version looks\nlike, both for runtime cost and for build-system complexity. The\nprototype should be able to fall back to the per-box path if the\nmerge fails for any reason.\n\n## Why blocked until rest of phase 3 completes\n\nThe merge optimization piggybacks on the per-box model — same\nspecs, same compile callback, same dispatch layer for cross-language\nwires. Building it before the per-box model is settled risks\ndesigning against a target that's still moving. After phase 3 ships\nand the per-box path is stable, the merge becomes a clean\n\"everything except spec invocation gets shorter for this region.\"\n\nIt's also genuinely lower priority than getting the runtime working\nat all. Inside a merged\n  region, it could become a `while` loop. The\n48\tprototype should be able to fall back to the per-box path if the\n49\tmerge fails for any reason.\n50\t\n51\t## Why blocked until rest of phase 3 completes\n52\t\n53\tThe merge optimization piggybacks on the per-box model — same\n54\tspecs, same compile callback, same dispatch layer for cross-language\n55\twires. Building it before the per-box model is settled risks\n56\tdesigning against a target that's still moving. After phase 3 ships\n57\tand the per-box path is stable, the merge becomes a clean\n58\t\"everything except spec invocation gets shorter for this region.\"\n59\t\n60\tIt's also genuinely lower priority than getting the runtime working\n61\tat all. The same-language fast path (issue 312) captures the\n62\t~2x JSON-skip win without any of this complexity. The merge wins a\n63\tfurther factor only if profile data shows function-call overhead\n64\tmatters at all after 312 ships.\n65\t\n66\t## Scope of the research output\n67\t\n68\tThe deliverable is a written design (not code) with:\n69\t- Concrete answers to the three questions above.\n70\t- A worked example: the merged C generated from a 5-box C-only\n71\t  graph, showing what the build artifact looks like.\n72\t- Estimated runtime cost of the per-box path vs the merged path\n73\t  on that example.\n74\t- A recommendation: ship as a feature, ship as an opt-in flag, or\n75\t  shelve indefinitely.\n76\t\n77\tAfter the design is reviewed, a separate implementation issue\n78\topens (or doesn't, depending on the recommendation).\n79\t\n80\t## Relevant files\n81\t\n82\t- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — the immediate JSON-\n83\t  skip win this builds on\n84\t- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — `compile` callback that would\n85\t  grow whole-program-aware semantics\n86\t- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — Lua-side bytecode pre-compile\n87\t- `issues/309-build-system.md` — how the merge integrates with the\n88\t  compile/package step\n89\t\n90\t## Open questions (for the research, not for now)\n91\t\n92\t- Cross-language wires inside the merged region: the merged region\n93\t  still has cross-language outputs that exit to other regions. The\n94\t  spec interface still applies at those boundaries, so the merge is\n95\t  region-internal optimization, not a global rearchitecture.\n96\t- C ABI for inlined wrappers: with whole-program optimization the\n97\t  wrapper-per-box generation might collapse to nothing. If the\n98\t  optimizer can prove a wire endpoint is always called from the\n99\t  merged region with known types, it can skip the wrapper.\n100\t- Iterators-with-side-effects: an iterator self-rescheduling its\n101\t  own task is normally dispatch-layer machinery. Inside a merged\n102\t  region, it could become a `while` loop. Whether that's safe\n103\t  depends on whether other tasks are blocked on the iterator's\n104\t  output slots — which they shouldn't be in a same-language region,\n105\t  but the analysis has to confirm.\n106\t"

      "content":"# 314 — A small C JSON parser, written for SoraMech\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe phase 3 design assumes a vendored JSON parser sits under\n`libs/json/` — issues 305 (graph loader), 311 (JSONL run output),\nand 309 (build system) all reference it. The original plan was to\ndrop in cJSON / jsmn / similar.\n\nAfter thinking about it: a vendored generic parser is one more\nexternal surface to learn and to debug, with idioms that don't\nmatch the rest of the runtime, and complications around large\ninputs / streaming / arena allocation that we'd want to special-case\nanyway. SoraMech needs JSON in two specific places:\n\n1. **Reading** map files (`meta.json`, `boxes/*.json`,\n   `data/*.json`) at graph load. Inputs are kilobyte-scale, parsed\n   once, validated immediately. The output is a tree that the\n   graph loader walks once.\n2. **Writing** run-log events into `tmp/last-run.jsonl` (issue\n   311). Output is per-event, line-oriented, ASCII-safe; the writer\n   thread serialises one event struct per call.\n\nBoth are narrow enough that a small, opinionated parser tailored to\nthe project beats a general-purpose library on every dimension that\nmatters to us.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA C library under `libs/json/`, vendored as plain source, that\nSoraMech owns end to end. Two halves:\n\n### Parser (DOM, arena-allocated)\n\n```c\ntypedef struct json_arena json_arena_t;\ntypedef struct json_node  json_node_t;\n\ntypedef enum {\n    JSON_NULL, JSON_BOOL, JSON_NUMBER,\n    JSON_STRING, JSON_ARRAY, JSON_OBJECT\n} json_kind_t;\n\njson_arena_t *json_arena_create(void);\nvoid          json_arena_destroy(json_arena_t *a);\n\n/* Parse a NUL-terminated string into a tree owned by the arena.\n * Returns NULL on syntax error; *err_offset and *err_msg are filled\n * with the position and a short diagnostic. */\njson_node_t *json_parse(json_arena_t *a,\n                        const char *src,\n                        int *err_offset, const char **err_msg);\n\n/* Parse a file. Convenience over json_parse + a file read. */\njson_node_t *json_parse_file(json_arena_t *a,\n                             const char *path,\n                             int *err_line, const char **err_msg);\n\n/* Inspect. */\njson_kind_t   json_kind        (const json_node_t *n);\nint           json_is_null     (const json_node_t *n);\nint           json_bool_value  (const json_node_t *n);\ndouble        json_number_value(const json_node_t *n);\nconst char   *json_string_value(const json_node_t *n);   /* NUL-terminated */\nint           json_array_size  (const json_node_t *n);\njson_node_t  *json_array_at    (const json_node_t *n, int i);\nint           json_object_size (const json_node_t *n);\nconst char   *json_object_key  (const json_node_t *n, int i);\njson_node_t  *json_object_value(const json_node_t *n, int i);\njson_node_t  *json_object_get  (const json_node_t *n, const char *key);\n```\n\nAll strings, arrays, and objects are arena-allocated. The whole\nparse tree lives in one `json_arena_t`; destroying the arena\nfrees every node and every string in one go. No per-node `free`.\n\n`json_object_get` is the common path for \"pull the `id` field off\nthis box\" — linear scan over the object's keys; object sizes in\nthis project are < 20, so the simplicity wins over a hash map.\n\n### Writer (streaming, no DOM)\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    char  *buf;\n    int    cap;\n    int    used;\n    int    err;       /* 0 ok; nonzero = truncation / OOM */\n} json_writer_t;\n\nvoid json_writer_init    (json_writer_t *w, char *buf, int cap);\nvoid json_writer_object  (json_writer_t *w);   /* '{' */\nvoid json_writer_end     (json_writer_t *w);   /* '}' or ']' */\nvoid json_writer_array   (json_writer_t *w);\nvoid json_writer_key     (json_writer_t *w, const char *key);\nvoid json_writer_string  (json_writer_t *w, const char *s);\nvoid json_writer_int     (json_writer_t *w, long long v);\nvoid json_writer_number  (json_writer_t *w, double v);\nvoid json_writer_bool    (json_writer_t *w, int v);\nvoid json_writer_null    (json_writer_t *w);\n\n/* Returns the number of bytes written (excludes NUL terminator),\n * or -1 if w->err is set. */\nint  json_writer_finish  (json_writer_t *w);\n```\n\nThe writer maintains a small state stack (depth ≤ 16 is plenty\nfor our event records) so it knows when to emit commas between\nelements. The writer never allocates — the caller hands in a fixed\nbuffer, the writer reports overflow via `w->err`. This matches the\nJSONL event-writer design (issue 311): one record per fixed-size\nstruct, serialised into a per-write buffer of bounded size.\n\n### What the parser supports\n\n- JSON per RFC 8259: objects, arrays, strings, numbers (parsed as\n  `double`), `true`, `false`, `null`.\n- UTF-8 strict. Escape sequences `\\\"`, `\\\\`, `\\/`, `\\b`, `\\f`,\n  `\\n`, `\\r`, `\\t`. `\\uXXXX` for BMP code points; surrogate pairs\n  handled. Decoded strings are NUL-terminated; embedded NULs in\n  source strings are rejected (we don't need them and they make\n  the strings interaction with the rest of the C code awkward).\n- Strict syntax. Trailing commas, comments, unquoted keys: all\n  errors with a precise message.\n\n### What it does NOT support\n\n- **Streaming / SAX**. Our inputs are small and parsed once. If\n  some future use case wants streaming (a 10-MB LLM response that\n  is itself JSON), revisit then.\n- **No integer / no big-number type**. Numbers are `double`. The\n  graph loader's integer-looking fields (`output_capacity`,\n  `n_outputs`) are read via `(int)json_number_value(n)`. Documented\n  in the loader, not in the parser.\n- **No pretty-print**. The writer emits compact JSON only (one\n  whitespace token between primitives, no spaces, no newlines).\n  JSONL needs compact lines anyway.\n- **No mutation API on parsed trees**. Trees are read-only; if a\n  caller wants to construct JSON, it uses the writer.\n\n### Errors\n\n`json_parse` returns NULL on syntax error and fills `*err_offset`\nwith the byte offset where parsing failed, and `*err_msg` with a\nshort static-string description (\"expected ':' after key\",\n\"unterminated string\", \"invalid escape sequence\"). The graph loader\nturns this into a precise diagnostic (\"maps/<name>/boxes/<id>.json:\nline 12: unterminated string\").\n\nOOM during parsing (arena out of memory) is a fatal error — the\narena uses a chunked-buffer allocator that calls `malloc` when it\ngrows; if that fails, the parser reports `*err_msg = \"out of\nmemory\"` and returns NULL. The hard-crash policy of the rest of\nthe runtime (issue 303) applies upstream.\n\n## Why now\n\nThe graph loader (issue 305) is the immediate consumer. The JSONL\nwriter (issue 311) is the next one. Building the parser ourselves\nkeeps the dependency surface to zero and gives us idioms (arenas,\nerror reporting style, allocation policy) that match the slot\nstore and the dispatch layer.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Arena allocator** (`libs/json/arena.c` + `.h`). Chunked\n   bump allocator: each chunk is a `malloc`'d buffer; allocate by\n   advancing an offset; chain chunks when one fills. Free chunks\n   in `json_arena_destroy`.\n2. **Parser** (`libs/json/json.c` + `.h`). Hand-rolled recursive\n   descent. ~600 lines. One internal struct per kind, packed into\n   a `json_node_t` union with a small tag.\n3. **Writer** (in `libs/json/json.c` alongside). State stack for\n   comma placement; bounded buffer; clean error reporting via\n   `w->err`.\n4. **Unit tests** (`tests/314-json-test.c`). Conformance cases:\n   nesting, escapes, surrogate pairs, error positions, writer\n   bracket-comma correctness, round-trip for a meta.json-shaped\n   input.\n5. **Wire into the Makefile.** `libs/json/*.c` is already in the\n   wildcard from issue 309; no Makefile edit needed beyond\n   confirming it picks up.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `libs/json/` — vendored sources (to be created here, not\n  imported from upstream).\n- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — the immediate consumer.\n- `issues/311-integration-tests-and-run-output.md` — the writer's\n  consumer (JSONL events).\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — Makefile already discovers\n  `libs/json/*.c` via wildcard.\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — references the JSON parser in the\n  phase 3 runtime layout.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Comments.** RFC 8259 forbids them; cJSON optionally allows\n  `//` and `/* */`. Box files are produced by the editor, not\n  hand-written, so we don't need them. Stay strict.\n- **`json_node_t` storage layout.** Tagged union (`json_kind_t` +\n  union of payloads) is simplest. Could also pack the kind into\n  low bits of a pointer for size — defer until profiling shows\n  node-count pressure.\n- **Object key lookup performance.** Linear scan is fine for\n  objects with 2–20 keys (every object in a SoraMech map). If\n  data files ever grow to thousands of keys, add an optional\n  hash-table mode.\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Parser milestone — 2026-05-12\n\nWhat shipped:\n- `libs/json/json.h` — full public surface for both halves.\n- `libs/json/json.c` — arena allocator (chunked bump, 16 KB\n  default chunk), recursive-descent parser, every accessor. The\n  parser handles every JSON kind, all escape sequences including\n  BMP `\\uXXXX` and surrogate pairs, with precise error positions.\n  Numbers go through `strtod` after a small NUL-terminated scratch\n  buffer (heap fallback for literals over 64 bytes — exceptionally\n  rare). Arrays and objects build via a temporary linked list in\n  the arena, finalized to fixed-size pointer arrays at close time;\n  the link nodes are abandoned (recovered when the arena is\n  destroyed).\n- `tests/314-json-test.c` — 14 unit tests: every primitive,\n  string escapes, U+00E9 single-escape, U+1F600 surrogate pair,\n  empty / non-empty / nested arrays and objects, whitespace\n  insensitivity, six distinct error-position cases, a realistic\n  meta.json-shaped parse, file loading with line-numbered errors,\n  arena growth across the 16 KB chunk boundary, and accessor\n  safety on the wrong kind.\n- Makefile per-test dependency line for `314-json-test`.\n\nVerified `make STRICT=1` (`-Werror -Wextra -Wpedantic`) builds\ncleanly; 14/14 parser tests and the 12 slot-store tests all pass.\n\nWhat's deferred:\n- **Stricter leading-zero rule.** RFC 8259 disallows `0\\d+`; we\n  currently accept `01` as `1`. None of our inputs produce that\n  shape, so it's a tightening that lands when something needs it.\n\n### Writer half — 2026-05-12\n\nFilled in the writer bodies (object/array open+close+key+\nprimitives) on top of the depth-stack design declared in the\nheader. Eight new writer tests cover comma placement, escape\nemission, empty and non-empty containers, nesting, overflow\ndetection, and a round-trip back through the parser. Done.\n",

The graph loader\n150\tturns this into a precise diagnostic (\"maps/<name>/boxes/<id>.json:\n151\tline 12: unterminated string\").\n152\t\n153\tOOM during parsing (arena out of memory) is a fatal error — the\n154\tarena uses a chunked-buffer allocator that calls `malloc` when it\n155\tgrows; if that fails, the parser reports `*err_msg = \"out of\n156\tmemory\"` and returns NULL. The hard-crash policy of the rest of\n157\tthe runtime (issue 303) applies upstream.\n158\t\n159\t## Why now\n160\t\n161\tThe graph loader (issue 305) is the immediate consumer. The JSONL\n162\twriter (issue 311) is the next one. Building the parser ourselves\n163\tkeeps the dependency surface to zero and gives us idioms (arenas,\n164\terror reporting style, allocation policy) that match the slot\n165\tstore and the dispatch layer.\n166\t\n167\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n168\t\n169\t1. **Arena allocator** (`libs/json/arena.c` + `.h`). Chunked\n170\t   bump allocator: each chunk is a `malloc`'d buffer; allocate by\n171\t   advancing an offset; chain chunks when one fills. Free chunks\n172\t   in `json_arena_destroy`.\n173\t2. **Parser** (`libs/json/json.c` + `.h`). Hand-rolled recursive\n174\t   descent. ~600 lines. One internal struct per kind, packed into\n175\t   a `json_node_t` union with a small tag.\n176\t3. **Writer** (in `libs/json/json.c` alongside). State stack for\n177\t   comma placement; bounded buffer; clean error reporting via\n178\t   `w->err`.\n179\t4. **Unit tests** (`tests/314-json-test.c`). Conformance cases:\n180\t   nesting, escapes, surrogate pairs, error positions, writer\n181\t   bracket-comma correctness, round-trip for a meta.json-shaped\n182\t   input.\n183\t5. **Wire into the Makefile.** `libs/json/*.c` is already in the\n184\t   wildcard from issue 309; no Makefile edit needed beyond\n185\t   confirming it picks up.\n186\t\n187\t## Relevant files\n188\t\n189\t- `libs/json/` — vendored sources (to be created here, not\n190\t  imported from upstream).\n191\t- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — the immediate consumer.\n192\t- `issues/311-integration-tests-and-run-output.md` — the writer's\n193\t  consumer (JSONL events).\n194\t- `issues/309-build-system.md` — Makefile already discovers\n195\t  `libs/json/*.c` via wildcard.\n196\t- `docs/001-architecture.md` — references the JSON parser in the\n197\t  phase 3 runtime layout.\n198\t\n199\t## Open questions\n200\t\n201\t- **Comments.** RFC 8259 forbids them; cJSON optionally allows\n202\t  `//` and `/* */`. Box files are produced by the editor, not\n203\t  hand-written, so we don't need them. Stay strict.\n204\t- **`json_node_t` storage layout.** Tagged union (`json_kind_t` +\n205\t  union of payloads) is simplest. Could also pack the kind into\n206\t  low bits of a pointer for size — defer until profiling shows\n207\t  node-count pressure.\n208\t- **Object key lookup performance.** Linear scan is fine for\n209\t  objects with 2–20 keys (every object in a SoraMech map). If\n210\t  data files ever grow to thousands of keys, add an optional\n211\t  hash-table mode.\n212\t\n213\t## Implementation log\n214\t\n215\t### Parser milestone — 2026-05-12\n216\t\n217\tWhat shipped:\n218\t- `libs/json/json.h` — full public surface for both halves.\n219\t- `libs/json/json.c` — arena allocator (chunked bump, 16 KB\n220\t  default chunk), recursive-descent parser, every accessor. The\n221\t  parser handles every JSON kind, all escape sequences including\n222\t  BMP `\\uXXXX` and surrogate pairs, with precise error positions.\n223\t  Numbers go through `strtod` after a small NUL-terminated scratch\n224\t  buffer (heap fallback for literals over 64 bytes — exceptionally\n225\t  rare). Arrays and objects build via a temporary linked list in\n226\t  the arena, finalized to fixed-size pointer arrays at close time;\n227\t  the link nodes are abandoned (recovered when the arena is\n228\t  destroyed).\n229\t- `tests/314-json-test.c` — 14 unit tests: every primitive,\n230\t  string escapes, U+00E9 single-escape, U+1F600 surrogate pair,\n231\t  empty / non-empty / nested arrays and objects, whitespace\n232\t  insensitivity, six distinct error-position cases, a realistic\n233\t  meta.json-shaped parse, file loading with line-numbered errors,\n234\t  arena growth across the 16 KB chunk boundary, and accessor\n235\t  safety on the wrong kind.\n236\t- Makefile per-test dependency line for `314-json-test`.\n237\t\n238\tVerified `make STRICT=1` (`-Werror -Wextra -Wpedantic`) builds\n239\tcleanly; 14/14 parser tests and the 12 slot-store tests all pass.\n240\t\n241\tWhat's deferred:\n242\t- **Stricter leading-zero rule.** RFC 8259 disallows `0\\d+`; we\n243\t  currently accept `01` as `1`. None of our inputs produce that\n244\t  shape, so it's a tightening that lands when something needs it.\n245\t\n246\t### Writer half — 2026-05-12\n247\t\n248\tFilled in the writer bodies (object/array open+close+key+\n249\tprimitives) on top of the depth-stack design declared in the\n250\theader. Eight new writer tests cover comma placement, escape\n251\temission, empty and non-empty containers, nesting, overflow\n252\tdetection, and a round-trip back through the parser. Done.\n253\t"

{

      "content":"# 315 — Reference-counted compiled-map artifacts\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`scripts/soramech-compile.sh` from issue 309 is destructive at the\ntop:\n\n```bash\nrm -rf \"$COMPILED\"\nmkdir -p \"$COMPILED\" \"$COMPILED/boxes\" \"$COMPILED/src\" ...\n```\n\nWhatever lived in `<map>/compiled/` before the rebuild is gone. If\nanother process — a long-running runner, a different shell, a\nsibling tool that opened the artifact yesterday — had pinned to\nthat exact compiled layout (a particular `pool-runner` binary, a\nparticular `spec.so` ABI, a particular set of pre-compiled C\nboxes), the rebuild yanks the rug. The holder either crashes,\nsilently retains stale `dlopen` handles, or starts reading new\nfiles mid-flight.\n\nThis is fine in single-user development. It stops being fine the\nmoment a SoraMech artifact is the kind of thing other programs\nhold onto across time.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA compiled artifact carries its own reference count. Other\nprograms that depend on a particular build of a map are expected\nto *acquire* a reference on startup and *release* it on shutdown.\nWhen `soramech-compile` is asked to rebuild a map that has any\nlive references, it does NOT clobber the existing directory.\nInstead it builds a sibling directory next door, leaving the\nreferenced one untouched until its holders are done with it.\n\nThe reference count is **expected to be unreliable**. A crashing\nholder doesn't get the chance to release; an SSH session that\ndrops doesn't either. The design accepts that staleness is the\ncommon case, not the exception — every reference entry carries\nenough metadata to be independently validated and (eventually)\nreaped. The reference count is a hint and a courtesy, not a\nguarantee.\n\nThis is conceptually a copy-on-write filesystem for compiled\nartifacts: writes (rebuilds) fork the universe when readers\nexist; readers can keep reading the version they pinned to;\ngenerations get garbage-collected when nothing observable still\npoints at them.\n\n## Concept\n\nA compiled directory contains a `.refs` file (hidden, dot-prefixed\nso it doesn't clutter directory listings). It's append-only by\ndesign — concurrent acquires never need to take a lock; concurrent\nreleases write a separate marker without rewriting the file.\n\nEach reference has three parts:\n\n1. **A date.** When the reference was acquired. Lets a janitor\n   prune references older than some threshold even if their back\n   pointer can't be validated.\n2. **A back-pointer.** The identity of the holder — enough\n   information that an outside observer can ask \"is this holder\n   still alive, and does it still want this reference?\" without\n   trusting the count alone. Concrete candidates:\n   - process PID + start time (PID alone is not enough; PIDs\n     recycle)\n   - a path to a marker file the holder maintains (presence of\n     the marker = the holder is still live and aware of the\n     ref)\n   - some combination (PID + a marker path)\n3. **An opaque ref id.** A short string the holder can use later\n   to identify *its* reference when it wants to release, so it\n   doesn't accidentally release someone else's.\n\nA release writes an entry referencing the original acquire id.\nNet live refs = acquires whose id isn't in the release set.\n\n## Reference file format\n\nA line-oriented log. Each line is one of two record types:\n\n```\nacquire <id> <iso8601-date> <pid> <pid-start-time-ticks> <marker-path>\nrelease <id> <iso8601-date>\n```\n\nAppend-only. Holders open with `O_APPEND` and write a single line\nper operation. Atomic on POSIX as long as the line fits in\n`PIPE_BUF` (4 KB on Linux) — well within budget for these short\nrecords.\n\nReading: tail through the file, build a set of acquire ids,\nsubtract release ids; remaining ids are nominally live. Then\nvalidate each survivor's back pointer.\n\nA `.refs.lock` file is used only for compaction (rewriting the\nlog to drop matched acquire/release pairs) and for the\nfork-to-sibling decision during compile. Steady-state reads /\nwrites don't lock.\n\n## Acquire / release API\n\nA small helper utility, probably a shell script for portability\nsince holders are written in many languages:\n\n```\nscripts/soramech-ref.sh acquire <compiled-dir> [--id <id>] [--marker <path>]\nscripts/soramech-ref.sh release <compiled-dir> --id <id>\nscripts/soramech-ref.sh list    <compiled-dir>          # JSON, including staleness verdicts\nscripts/soramech-ref.sh reap    <compiled-dir>          # compact + drop dead refs\n```\n\n`acquire` prints the assigned id to stdout; the holder is\nresponsible for plumbing it to wherever it'll need to call\nrelease. If no `--id` was supplied, the script generates one\n(timestamp + random suffix).\n\n`list` walks the log and prints a JSON array of `{id, date,\nholder, valid}` entries. Validation reads the back pointer's\nliveness signal (PID exists & start-time matches, or marker file\nexists).\n\n`reap` is destructive — it rewrites the log to remove entries\nwhose holders failed validation. Run periodically; never\nautomatically as part of compile (compile must not destroy state\nits caller might care about).\n\n## Compile-time fork logic\n\n`soramech-compile.sh` consults `<map>/compiled/.refs` (and any\nsibling generation directories' `.refs` files) before deciding\nwhere to write:\n\n1. If `<map>/compiled/` doesn't exist → build there, fresh.\n2. If it exists but has zero live references → build there, after\n   `rm -rf`. Same destructive behavior as today.\n3. If it exists with one or more live references → pick a sibling\n   directory name (see below) and build there. The original\n   `compiled/` stays intact.\n\nAfter a fork-build, the caller has a new directory; `manifest.json`\nin the new directory records the fork relationship (`forked_from`\nfield pointing at the previous generation's path).\n\n### Sibling directory naming\n\nTwo reasonable schemes; pick whichever the implementer prefers:\n\n- **Generation index:** `compiled.0`, `compiled.1`, `compiled.2`...\n  Always pick `compiled.N` where N is one more than the highest\n  existing generation. Easy to grep for; index order = build\n  order.\n- **Timestamp suffix:** `compiled.2026-05-19T2347` (ISO 8601\n  compact). Order-preserving lexicographically; the name itself\n  tells the operator when it was built.\n\nWhichever wins, the script should also leave a `compiled` symlink\npointing at the newest generation, so callers who want \"the\nlatest\" don't have to enumerate.\n\n## Stale reference handling\n\nA reference is stale if any of the following hold:\n\n- The PID no longer exists on the system.\n- The PID exists but its start time (`/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22)\n  doesn't match the recorded value — different process, recycled\n  PID.\n- The marker file path was supplied at acquire and is now\n  missing.\n\nStale refs are *tolerated*: compile-time fork still triggers if\nANY ref exists, stale or otherwise — the caller can run\n`soramech-ref.sh reap` first if they want to consolidate. The\nphilosophy is: the artifact directory belongs to its readers\nuntil proven otherwise, and the cost of an extra build dir is\ntrivial compared to the cost of a use-after-rebuild crash.\n\n## Gitignore considerations\n\nEvery generation (`compiled/`, `compiled.0/`, `compiled.1/`,\n`compiled.2026-05-19T2347/`, the `compiled` symlink) is a derived\nartifact and should never be tracked. The existing\n`.gitignore` line `tests/maps/*/compiled/` covers the canonical\nname; add a sibling pattern to cover generations:\n\n```\ntests/maps/*/compiled/\ntests/maps/*/compiled.*/\n```\n\nThe `.refs` file itself lives *inside* the compiled directory,\nso it inherits the same gitignore.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. Pick the back-pointer format. Recommend PID + start time +\n   optional marker path. Document the choice with a comment at\n   the top of the ref helper.\n2. Write `scripts/soramech-ref.sh` with `acquire`, `release`,\n   `list`, `reap`. Append-only writes for the first two, log\n   rewrite under `.refs.lock` for the last.\n3. Add a small `tests/315-refs-test.sh` that exercises:\n   acquire → list (1 entry, valid) → release → list (0 valid) →\n   acquire → kill the holder process → list (1 entry, stale) →\n   reap → list (0).\n4. Teach `soramech-compile.sh` to read `.refs` and pick the\n   target directory. Implement the sibling-naming scheme.\n   `compiled` becomes a symlink to the newest generation.\n5. Add a `forked_from` field to `manifest.json` when forking.\n6. Update `.gitignore` for the new generation pattern.\n7. Integration check in `scripts/run-tests.sh`: compile the\n   pipeline fixture twice — second time with a live `acquire` —\n   assert a sibling generation was created and the original\n   pinned generation still runs unchanged.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Should the runner (`soramech-pool`) itself acquire a reference\n  when it opens a compiled directory? On the one hand, yes —\n  it's the canonical case the system protects against. On the\n  other, soramech-pool runs are usually short-lived and the\n  acquire/release overhead per run is unwelcome. Possible\n  compromise: only acquire if pool runs longer than N seconds.\n- How does a fork chain end? If `compiled.5` is built while\n  `compiled.4` had live refs but `compiled.4`'s refs are now all\n  stale (caller never released, then died), do we ever prune\n  `compiled.4`? Probably yes, via `soramech-ref.sh reap-all\n  <map>` which walks every generation and drops the ones whose\n  refs all validate as dead.\n- Is the `.refs` log itself something that should be versioned\n  (`.refs.v1`)? If we ever change the line format, in-flight\n  holders won't know how to read it. Versioning the filename\n  avoids the problem.\n- Does the editor (`maps/<x>/` user-facing) want the same\n  mechanism? Probably yes eventually, but out of scope for this\n  issue — start with `compiled/` artifacts only.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — issue 309's compile pipeline,\n  modified here to fork on live references\n- `scripts/soramech-ref.sh` — new helper for acquire / release /\n  list / reap\n- `tests/315-refs-test.sh` — new\n- `.gitignore` — extended pattern for generation directories\n- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — new integration check\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — parent issue; references this\n  one's fork behavior\n\n## Notes (philosophy)\n\nThe unreliability is a feature, not a bug. A reliable reference\ncount would require a kernel-level mechanism (file locks held\nfor the lifetime of the holder), and that's a tower of\noperational complexity for marginal value. By accepting that\nholders sometimes lie and sometimes vanish, we get a system\nthat's robust to crashes, network drops, and SIGKILL — at the\ncost of needing a \"reap\" pass to catch up with reality\noccasionally. The back pointer is what makes that catch-up\npossible: it's the bridge between what the log claims and what\nthe world actually shows.\n\nA reference is a wish, not a contract. The compile pipeline\nhonors wishes by default and only stops honoring them when\nnothing in the world supports the wish anymore. That's how\nrespectful software treats its peers.\n",
