Run periodically; never\n129\tautomatically as part of compile (compile must not destroy state\n130\tits caller might care about).\n131\t\n132\t## Compile-time fork logic\n133\t\n134\t`soramech-compile.sh` consults `<map>/compiled/.refs` (and any\n135\tsibling generation directories' `.refs` files) before deciding\n136\twhere to write:\n137\t\n138\t1. If `<map>/compiled/` doesn't exist → build there, fresh.\n139\t2. If it exists but has zero live references → build there, after\n140\t   `rm -rf`. Same destructive behavior as today.\n141\t3. If it exists with one or more live references → pick a sibling\n142\t   directory name (see below) and build there. The original\n143\t   `compiled/` stays intact.\n144\t\n145\tAfter a fork-build, the caller has a new directory; `manifest.json`\n146\tin the new directory records the fork relationship (`forked_from`\n147\tfield pointing at the previous generation's path).\n148\t\n149\t### Sibling directory naming\n150\t\n151\tTwo reasonable schemes; pick whichever the implementer prefers:\n152\t\n153\t- **Generation index:** `compiled.0`, `compiled.1`, `compiled.2`...\n154\t  Always pick `compiled.N` where N is one more than the highest\n155\t  existing generation. Easy to grep for; index order = build\n156\t  order.\n157\t- **Timestamp suffix:** `compiled.2026-05-19T2347` (ISO 8601\n158\t  compact). Order-preserving lexicographically; the name itself\n159\t  tells the operator when it was built.\n160\t\n161\tWhichever wins, the script should also leave a `compiled` symlink\n162\tpointing at the newest generation, so callers who want \"the\n163\tlatest\" don't have to enumerate.\n164\t\n165\t## Stale reference handling\n166\t\n167\tA reference is stale if any of the following hold:\n168\t\n169\t- The PID no longer exists on the system.\n170\t- The PID exists but its start time (`/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22)\n171\t  doesn't match the recorded value — different process, recycled\n172\t  PID.\n173\t- The marker file path was supplied at acquire and is now\n174\t  missing.\n175\t\n176\tStale refs are *tolerated*: compile-time fork still triggers if\n177\tANY ref exists, stale or otherwise — the caller can run\n178\t`soramech-ref.sh reap` first if they want to consolidate. The\n179\tphilosophy is: the artifact directory belongs to its readers\n180\tuntil proven otherwise, and the cost of an extra build dir is\n181\ttrivial compared to the cost of a use-after-rebuild crash.\n182\t\n183\t## Gitignore considerations\n184\t\n185\tEvery generation (`compiled/`, `compiled.0/`, `compiled.1/`,\n186\t`compiled.2026-05-19T2347/`, the `compiled` symlink) is a derived\n187\tartifact and should never be tracked. The existing\n188\t`.gitignore` line `tests/maps/*/compiled/` covers the canonical\n189\tname; add a sibling pattern to cover generations:\n190\t\n191\t```\n192\ttests/maps/*/compiled/\n193\ttests/maps/*/compiled.*/\n194\t```\n195\t\n196\tThe `.refs` file itself lives *inside* the compiled directory,\n197\tso it inherits the same gitignore.\n198\t\n199\t## Suggested implementation steps\n200\t\n201\t1. Pick the back-pointer format. Recommend PID + start time +\n202\t   optional marker path. Document the choice with a comment at\n203\t   the top of the ref helper.\n204\t2. Write `scripts/soramech-ref.sh` with `acquire`, `release`,\n205\t   `list`, `reap`. Append-only writes for the first two, log\n206\t   rewrite under `.refs.lock` for the last.\n207\t3. Add a small `tests/315-refs-test.sh` that exercises:\n208\t   acquire → list (1 entry, valid) → release → list (0 valid) →\n209\t   acquire → kill the holder process → list (1 entry, stale) →\n210\t   reap → list (0).\n211\t4. Teach `soramech-compile.sh` to read `.refs` and pick the\n212\t   target directory. Implement the sibling-naming scheme.\n213\t   `compiled` becomes a symlink to the newest generation.\n214\t5. Add a `forked_from` field to `manifest.json` when forking.\n215\t6. Update `.gitignore` for the new generation pattern.\n216\t7. Integration check in `scripts/run-tests.sh`: compile the\n217\t   pipeline fixture twice — second time with a live `acquire` —\n218\t   assert a sibling generation was created and the original\n219\t   pinned generation still runs unchanged.\n220\t\n221\t## Open questions\n222\t\n223\t- Should the runner (`soramech-pool`) itself acquire a reference\n224\t  when it opens a compiled directory? On the one hand, yes —\n225\t  it's the canonical case the system protects against. On the\n226\t  other, soramech-pool runs are usually short-lived and the\n227\t  acquire/release overhead per run is unwelcome. Possible\n228\t  compromise: only acquire if pool runs longer than N seconds.\n229\t- How does a fork chain end? If `compiled.5` is built while\n230\t  `compiled.4` had live refs but `compiled.4`'s refs are now all\n231\t  stale (caller never released, then died), do we ever prune\n232\t  `compiled.4`? Probably yes, via `soramech-ref.sh reap-all\n233\t  <map>` which walks every generation and drops the ones whose\n234\t  refs all validate as dead.\n235\t- Is the `.refs` log itself something that should be versioned\n236\t  (`.refs.v1`)? If we ever change the line format, in-flight\n237\t  holders won't know how to read it. Versioning the filename\n238\t  avoids the problem.\n239\t- Does the editor (`maps/<x>/` user-facing) want the same\n240\t  mechanism? Probably yes eventually, but out of scope for this\n241\t  issue — start with `compiled/` artifacts only.\n242\t\n243\t## Relevant files\n244\t\n245\t- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — issue 309's compile pipeline,\n246\t  modified here to fork on live references\n247\t- `scripts/soramech-ref.sh` — new helper for acquire / release /\n248\t  list / reap\n249\t- `tests/315-refs-test.sh` — new\n250\t- `.gitignore` — extended pattern for generation directories\n251\t- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — new integration check\n252\t- `issues/309-build-system.md` — parent issue; references this\n253\t  one's fork behavior\n254\t\n255\t## Notes (philosophy)\n256\t\n257\tThe unreliability is a feature, not a bug. A reliable reference\n258\tcount would require a kernel-level mechanism (file locks held\n259\tfor the lifetime of the holder), and that's a tower of\n260\toperational complexity for marginal value. By accepting that\n261\tholders sometimes lie and sometimes vanish, we get a system\n262\tthat's robust to crashes, network drops, and SIGKILL — at the\n263\tcost of needing a \"reap\" pass to catch up with reality\n264\toccasionally. The back pointer is what makes that catch-up\n265\tpossible: it's the bridge between what the log claims and what\n266\tthe world actually shows.\n267\t\n268\tA reference is a wish, not a contract. The compile pipeline\n269\thonors wishes by default and only stops honoring them when\n270\tnothing in the world supports the wish anymore. That's how\n271\trespectful software treats its peers.\n272\t"

      "content":"# 317 — Language spec JSON bridge for data boxes\n\n## Status\nin progress — Lua bridges fidelity-preserving (stage 2 landed\n2026-05-19); C and Bash still stubs\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA data box (`kind: data` in box JSON) emits a value the rest of\nthe graph routes downstream. Today the runner reads the box's\n`ref` file as raw bytes and emits them — there's no concept of\n\"authoring this datum in a particular language using that\nlanguage's natural structures.\" If you want to declare a Lua\ntable as a data box's value, you either:\n\n- Hand-translate the table to JSON, save it as a `.json` file,\n  and lose the Lua syntax niceties; or\n- Make it a call box that returns the table, paying for a full\n  spec invocation just to read a constant; or\n- Hard-code the bytes inline in the box's `data` field, with no\n  syntactic help from any host language.\n\nThis is the wrong shape. **A box author writes idiomatic code in\nthe language of their choice.** That's the rule 307 establishes\nfor call boxes: a C-box author writes a plain C function, no\nSoraMech-specific glue. The data-box equivalent should hold —\na Lua-data-box author should write a Lua file that returns\nwhatever they want returned (a table, a string, a number), and\nSoraMech should know how to lift that into the graph as a JSON\nwire value without the author writing a single SoraMech-specific\ncharacter.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEvery language spec gains two callbacks, declared in\n`lang_spec_t` (issue 303):\n\n```c\n/* Serialize a native-language value into JSON text.\n *\n *   ctx       — per-worker handle from spec.init.\n *   src       — caller-meaningful pointer to the native value.\n *               Format is spec-specific (see \"Native handle\n *               representation\" below).\n *   src_size  — size hint, or 0 if the spec interprets `src`\n *               without a length.\n *   out_buf   — destination buffer for JSON text (caller-owned).\n *   out_cap   — capacity of out_buf.\n *   out_size  — set to the bytes written.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. Writes an error message\n * via the spec's existing error-reporting plumbing. */\nint (*native_to_json)(void *ctx,\n                      const void *src, uint32_t src_size,\n                      char *out_buf, uint32_t out_cap, uint32_t *out_size);\n\n/* Inverse: parse JSON text into a native-language value. The\n * native value is stored wherever the spec considers natural\n * (Lua: pushed to the worker's lua_State stack; C: written into\n * a typed struct supplied by `dst`; Bash: written as a textual\n * representation back into dst).\n *\n *   ctx       — per-worker handle.\n *   src       — JSON text.\n *   src_size  — JSON text length in bytes.\n *   dst       — caller-supplied target; semantics per spec.\n *   dst_cap   — capacity, where meaningful.\n *   dst_size  — set to the bytes / native units consumed.\n *\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. */\nint (*json_to_native)(void *ctx,\n                      const char *src, uint32_t src_size,\n                      void *dst, uint32_t dst_cap, uint32_t *dst_size);\n```\n\nThese are the same fields 312's same-language fast path\nreserves; this issue is the one that requires every spec to\n**actually implement them**, driven by the data-box use case.\n(312 needs them too, but its driver is performance; 317 needs\nthem for correctness — a data box can't function without them.)\n\n### The rule, restated\n\nThe author of a data box writes a `.lua` / `.c` / `.sh` /\n`.<whatever>` file that returns or produces a value using\n*their language's native idioms*. No SoraMech macros. No\nSoraMech includes. No SoraMech-specific JSON shape constraints\nbeyond \"what your spec's native_to_json can convert.\"\n\nIf the author returns a Lua table, the Lua spec's\n`native_to_json` converts it. If they return a C struct, the C\nspec's `native_to_json` walks it according to the type declared\nin the box. If they print JSON-ish text from a bash script, the\nbash spec's `native_to_json` is a no-op identity (the script\nalready produced JSON).\n\nThe contract belongs to the spec author, not the box author.\nThat's the inversion: **SoraMech bends to the language, not the\nother way around.**\n\n## Native handle representation\n\nThe shape of `src` / `dst` in the callbacks is per-spec. Each\nspec documents what it accepts:\n\n- **Lua spec**: `src` is the index of a value already pushed\n  onto the worker's `lua_State`. `src_size` is unused. The\n  spec's `native_to_json` reads the value at that stack index\n  and writes JSON. `json_to_native` pushes the parsed JSON value\n  onto the stack, and `dst_size` reports the number of stack\n  slots used (always 1 for SoraMech's flat-value model).\n- **C spec**: `src` is a typed pointer + the box's declared\n  output type drives the walk. `src_size` is the type's\n  storage footprint. Mirror image for `json_to_native`. (This\n  ties into 307's typed-wrapper-generation work — the same\n  type system describes both the wrapper signature and the\n  JSON shape.)\n- **Bash spec**: `src` is text the script produced.\n  `native_to_json` validates and reshapes to JSON if needed (a\n  bash script that prints `42` becomes JSON `42`; a script that\n  prints `{\"a\":1}` passes through unchanged). `json_to_native`\n  is similarly a near-identity. The spec author is encouraged\n  to require scripts produce well-formed JSON in the first\n  place rather than write a bash-syntax parser.\n\nThe dispatch layer doesn't know or care which representation a\nspec uses. It only ever passes `src` and `src_size` to the\nspec's callback. The spec is opaque to the runtime; that's the\nwhole point.\n\n## Data box semantics\n\nA data box's `data` field becomes optional. The box gains\noptional `lang` and `ref` fields:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"config\",\n  \"kind\": \"data\",\n  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n  \"ref\": \"config.lua\"\n}\n```\n\nAt graph load, the runner:\n\n1. Resolves the spec for `lang`.\n2. Calls the spec's `init` (already done at worker startup).\n3. At box-fire time, asks the spec to execute the `ref` file\n   and produce a native value (this is essentially the same\n   \"load this file, run it, get its return value\" path the\n   spec already implements for call boxes — call boxes call a\n   named function; data boxes take the file's return value).\n4. Calls the spec's `native_to_json` to convert the native\n   value to JSON text.\n5. Pushes that JSON text down the wire as the box's output —\n   same as today's data path, just with the value sourced\n   from a language-native file.\n\nIf the box has no `lang` and a literal `data` field, the legacy\ninline-data path applies unchanged.\n\n## Why every spec must implement these\n\nThe same JSON the data box emits is consumed by some downstream\nbox (call, comparator, file_write, whatever). That downstream\nbox, if it's in a different language, will eventually need\n*its* spec's `json_to_native` to convert the JSON back. So the\ntwo callbacks are paired — every spec that participates in the\ngraph needs both. A spec that implements `native_to_json` but\nnot `json_to_native` can only be data-box sources; a spec with\nonly `json_to_native` can only be call-box sinks. We require\nboth so any language can play any role.\n\nSpecs that haven't been updated yet should set both callbacks\nto a stub that returns -1 with a clear error message (\"spec\n`<name>`: native_to_json not implemented; this box's value\ncan't be routed cross-language\"). The hard-fail makes the gap\nloud rather than producing wrong output.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. Extend the `lang_spec_t` declaration in\n   `langs/lang-spec.h` if not already done by 312's\n   infrastructure work. (Per the round summary, the slot is\n   reserved.)\n2. Implement `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` in each\n   spec:\n   - **Lua spec**: walk the value at the stack index. Use the\n     existing C JSON writer (`libs/json/json.c`). Handle Lua\n     tables both as arrays (1-indexed contiguous integer keys)\n     and as objects. Refuse functions, userdata, threads.\n   - **C spec**: depends on 307's typed-wrapper machinery. For\n     now, a stub that only supports scalar types (int, double,\n     string) is enough to get data boxes working in C.\n   - **Bash spec**: validate-and-pass-through. The script is\n     expected to produce JSON. `native_to_json` runs the JSON\n     parser to validate; `json_to_native` is identity.\n3. Extend the data box runtime path in `src/012-dispatch.c`\n   (or wherever data boxes dispatch from) to consult `lang` /\n   `ref` when set and route through the spec callback chain.\n4. Add a fixture: `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` with a Lua\n   data box, a C consumer, and a Bash consumer all reading the\n   same value. The integration check asserts each consumer\n   sees the right data.\n5. Update each spec's `*.info.md` to document the native handle\n   shape its callbacks expect.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — extend the contract\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n  implement the callbacks\n- `langs/{lua,c,bash}/spec.info.md` — document native handle\n  semantics per spec\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — data-box dispatch path\n- `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` — new fixture (see step 4)\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — same author-writes-natural-\n  code principle; this issue extends it from call boxes to data\n  boxes\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — reuses the same\n  spec callbacks for a different (performance) reason\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Bash's `json_to_native` is a near-identity because the\n  scripts already deal in text. Is there value in having it\n  validate and reformat for consistency? Probably yes; cheap\n  insurance against malformed downstream input.\n- Should the Lua spec auto-detect array-vs-object tables, or\n  require the box author to annotate? Auto-detect (contiguous\n  1-indexed integer keys → array; otherwise object) is what\n  every other lua-to-json library does and is intuitive enough.\n- C spec's `native_to_json` for arbitrary structs is a real\n  rabbit hole. Tie scope to 307 — the same type declarations\n  drive both the wrapper and the JSON walk. Until 307 lands,\n  only scalar types are supported for C data boxes.\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### 2026-05-19 — Lua bridges landed\n\nImplemented the first concrete pair of bridges. Scope: only the\nLua spec; C and Bash still NULL their bridge slots and fall back\nto the uniform-byte default.\n\n**Design decisions made during this round (kept for later\nimplementers of the C / Bash bridges):**\n\n- **Bridge signature has the worker handle as the first arg.**\n  The previous declaration in `lang-spec.h` was missing it; without\n  it Lua can't reach its `lua_State`. C and Bash will need it for\n  the same reason once they grow real bridges.\n\n- **Stack-protocol convention for the native side.** The bridge\n  reads / writes the producer's working store directly, not the\n  `src` / `dst` buffers. For Lua: `native_to_json` consumes the\n  value at the top of the `lua_State` (pops on success); `json_to_native`\n  pushes the reconstructed value to the top. The `src` / `dst`\n  buffers carry only the JSON side of the conversion. This keeps\n  the wire format opaque to specs and avoids inventing a \"native\n  byte\" serialization just so it can fit through a buffer.\n\n- **Wire primitive vocabulary.** Three JSON-with-extensions\n  primitives are reserved for the harder types; this round did not\n  emit any of them, but every future bridge must agree on the\n  names: `$ref` (shared-memory pointer + length), `$function_pointer`\n  (decomposed callable: address + signature), `$lang_opaque`\n  (last-resort sealed envelope routed only between same-language\n  endpoints — escape hatch, not a default).\n\n- **No handles, no back-routing.** The wire must carry data the\n  destination spec can reconstruct on its own — never a token that\n  says \"operations on this value cross back to the source spec.\"\n  See `memory/feedback_cross_language_pitfalls.md` for the longer\n  argument; the principle constrains every bridge implementation.\n\n- **Type ambiguities are resolved by wiring, not by annotation.**\n  When a function signature has hidden pairings (a `char *` with a\n  separate length argument, a `union` with a discriminator, a\n  callback with a context pointer), the destination spec exposes\n  *each* parameter as its own input slot on the box. The user wires\n  them according to the function's English docs. The system never\n  prompts the user with vocabulary words it has no general way to\n  ask about.\n\n**Files touched:**\n\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — `lang_bridge_fn` now takes `void *handle`\n  as its first parameter; the doc comment documents the stack\n  protocol.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c` — added `encode_value`, `decode_node`,\n  `lua_native_to_json`, `lua_json_to_native`. Wired the last two\n  into `soramech_lang_spec`.\n- `langs/lua/Makefile` — folds `libs/json/json.c` straight into\n  `spec.so` so the spec stays self-contained.\n- `tests/317-lua-bridge-test.c` — new round-trip test (JSON →\n  lua_State → JSON, compare).\n- `Makefile` — added the test's dependency line.\n\n**Tests:** 5/5 in `317-lua-bridge-test`; full suite green.\n\n### 2026-05-19 — stage 2: Lua array fidelity\n\nStage 1 lost `null` inside arrays — `[true,false,null]` round-tripped\nas `[true,false]`. Stage 2 fixes it by applying the n-field\nconvention from the fidelity directive below.\n\nWhat changed in the code:\n\n- `decode_node` (JSON → Lua): the JSON_ARRAY case now creates a Lua\n  table with a string key `n` set to the array's length, then\n  fills integer keys 1..n. JSON `null` elements use `lua_rawseti`\n  with nil — which deletes the key, leaving an absent slot. The\n  table now carries enough information to reconstruct the array\n  losslessly.\n\n- `encode_value` (Lua → JSON): table emission reads `n` first. If\n  the field is a non-negative integer, the table is treated as a\n  declared-length array — the encoder walks 1..n and emits null\n  for any missing slot via the existing nil → null path. Tables\n  without `n` fall through to the existing array-vs-object\n  heuristic for idiomatic Lua values.\n\nWhat the tests prove now:\n\n- `[]`, `[null]`, `[null,null]`, `[null,1,2]`, `[1,null,3]`,\n  `[1,2,null]`, `[true,false,null]` all round-trip exactly.\n\nWhat this costs:\n\n- Lua tables that have crossed the bridge carry a `n` field\n  visible to `pairs()`. The fidelity directive accepts this:\n  \"We can intrude on idiomatic Lua because we're fundamentally\n  translating from Lua to JSON.\" Box authors who write Lua\n  tables by hand and want them treated as JSON arrays can also\n  set `n` themselves; otherwise the existing heuristic still\n  catches `{1, 2, 3}`-shaped tables.\n\n## Fidelity directive (added 2026-05-19, supersedes earlier \"lossy is OK\" thinking)\n\nThe wire format (JSON) is canonical. **A value leaving a box's\noutput slot and entering the wire must not lose fidelity.** The\nbridge intrudes on the language as needed to achieve that. The\nlanguage's idioms are upheld on the in-language side (inside the\nbox's source file); on the wire side the bridge is allowed —\nrequired — to use whatever encoding preserves the shape.\n\nThis reverses the earlier instinct that lossy round-trips were\n\"the box author's problem.\" They're the bridge's problem. The\nbox author writes idiomatic Lua / C / bash; the bridge converts\nwithout dropping anything.\n\n### Concrete rules per language\n\n- **Lua → JSON** (and JSON → Lua → JSON round-trip): preserve\n  array shape including embedded nulls. The decoder pushes\n  arrays as `{n = N, [1] = ..., [2] = ..., ...}` where `n` is the\n  intended length and missing integer keys are real nil slots.\n  The encoder reads `n` if present and emits a full-length JSON\n  array with `null` at every missing slot. Idiomatic Lua tables\n  without `n` continue to encode via the existing\n  array-vs-object heuristic — `n` is only required when the\n  caller cares about distinguishing \"trailing nil\" from \"shorter\n  array.\" Same scheme handles intermixed nil-in-middle too.\n\n- **Lua → JSON** (type annotations): the bridge may emit a\n  type-tagged JSON shape when the destination language needs\n  more than JSON's native types convey (e.g. int vs float when\n  the Lua value is whole-numbered but the destination expects a\n  float, or vice versa). The tag lives in the JSON itself, not\n  in a sidecar protocol. Suggested shape: a `$type` key inside a\n  small wrapper object, only emitted when the encoder can tell\n  the unwrapped value would be ambiguous downstream.\n\n- **C → JSON**: C functions have declared types — emit those\n  types as part of the JSON, so any downstream language can\n  honour them without guessing. Lua receivers may use the type\n  to coerce (e.g. force `2` instead of `2.0`); receivers that\n  don't care can ignore the type tag.\n\n- **JSON → C**: when the wire value doesn't fit the destination\n  C type (a float arriving at an int slot, a string at a number\n  slot), the C bridge **truncates / coerces and records a\n  warning** at map-compile time. The warning surfaces in the\n  compile output, not at run time. Silent dropping is forbidden;\n  hard-failing the compile is too aggressive — the user may\n  know the truncation is fine.\n\n- **JSON → Lua / JSON → bash**: same coercion rule, with\n  language-appropriate fallbacks. The receiver records the\n  warning.\n\n### Why this lives in the bridge, not the box author\n\nA box author writes a function in their language. They don't\nwrite a SoraMech-aware serializer. The bridge — which is the\nspec author's responsibility, not the box author's — owns every\ndetail of how their language's values reach JSON and how JSON\nreaches their language's values. The box author writes\nidiomatic code; the bridge does whatever is necessary on the\nJSON side, including unwrapping `n`-fielded tables back into\nidiomatic Lua at decode time so subsequent in-language calls\nsee clean tables.\n\nThis is the same principle the rest of 317 already states: the\nspec bends to the language at the box surface, and bends the\nwire shape to the language at the bridge. The language never\nbends to the wire.\n\n**Next implementation slices:**\n\n1. ~~**Lua bridges, stage 2 — fidelity preservation.**~~ Done\n   2026-05-19. The n-field convention is implemented; every JSON\n   array shape round-trips faithfully. See the stage-2 entry in\n   the implementation log above.\n2. Bash bridges — near-identity (scripts are already producing\n   text). `native_to_json` validates the text is well-formed JSON;\n   `json_to_native` is identity. No `lua_State`-style scratch\n   needed, so the bridge can ignore `handle`. Type fidelity is\n   trivial because bash already deals only in text.\n3. C bridges — depends on 307's typed wrapper work. Until 307\n   lands, scalar types (int / double / string) is enough to\n   unblock data-box semantics. The coerce-and-warn rule from\n   the fidelity directive governs how mismatched types behave.\n4. Wire the bridges into the dispatch layer (issue 312's\n   wire-classification path) so cross-language edges actually\n   round-trip through them.\n5. Add a map-compile warning channel that the C / Lua / bash\n   bridges feed into when they truncate or coerce. Surface\n   the warnings in the compile output — silent loss is\n   forbidden by the fidelity directive.\n",

        "content":"1\t# 317 — Language spec JSON bridge for data boxes\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\tin progress — Lua bridges fidelity-preserving (stage 2 landed\n5\t2026-05-19); C and Bash still stubs\n6\t\n7\t## Current behavior\n8\t\n9\tA data box (`kind: data` in box JSON) emits a value the rest of\n10\tthe graph routes downstream. Today the runner reads the box's\n11\t`ref` file as raw bytes and emits them — there's no concept of\n12\t\"authoring this datum in a particular language using that\n13\tlanguage's natural structures.\" If you want to declare a Lua\n14\ttable as a data box's value, you either:\n15\t\n16\t- Hand-translate the table to JSON, save it as a `.json` file,\n17\t  and lose the Lua syntax niceties; or\n18\t- Make it a call box that returns the table, paying for a full\n19\t  spec invocation just to read a constant; or\n20\t- Hard-code the bytes inline in the box's `data` field, with no\n21\t  syntactic help from any host language.\n22\t\n23\tThis is the wrong shape. **A box author writes idiomatic code in\n24\tthe language of their choice.** That's the rule 307 establishes\n25\tfor call boxes: a C-box author writes a plain C function, no\n26\tSoraMech-specific glue. The data-box equivalent should hold —\n27\ta Lua-data-box author should write a Lua file that returns\n28\twhatever they want returned (a table, a string, a number), and\n29\tSoraMech should know how to lift that into the graph as a JSON\n30\twire value without the author writing a single SoraMech-specific\n31\tcharacter.\n32\t\n33\t## Intended behavior\n34\t\n35\tEvery language spec gains two callbacks, declared in\n36\t`lang_spec_t` (issue 303):\n37\t\n38\t```c\n39\t/* Serialize a native-language value into JSON text.\n40\t *\n41\t *   ctx       — per-worker handle from spec.init.\n42\t *   src       — caller-meaningful pointer to the native value.\n43\t *               Format is spec-specific (see \"Native handle\n44\t *               representation\" below).\n45\t *   src_size  — size hint, or 0 if the spec interprets `src`\n46\t *               without a length.\n47\t *   out_buf   — destination buffer for JSON text (caller-owned).\n48\t *   out_cap   — capacity of out_buf.\n49\t *   out_size  — set to the bytes written.\n50\t *\n51\t * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. Writes an error message\n52\t * via the spec's existing error-reporting plumbing. */\n53\tint (*native_to_json)(void *ctx,\n54\t                      const void *src, uint32_t src_size,\n55\t                      char *out_buf, uint32_t out_cap, uint32_t *out_size);\n56\t\n57\t/* Inverse: parse JSON text into a native-language value. The\n58\t * native value is stored wherever the spec considers natural\n59\t * (Lua: pushed to the worker's lua_State stack; C: written into\n60\t * a typed struct supplied by `dst`; Bash: written as a textual\n61\t * representation back into dst).\n62\t *\n63\t *   ctx       — per-worker handle.\n64\t *   src       — JSON text.\n65\t *   src_size  — JSON text length in bytes.\n66\t *   dst       — caller-supplied target; semantics per spec.\n67\t *   dst_cap   — capacity, where meaningful.\n68\t *   dst_size  — set to the bytes / native units consumed.\n69\t *\n70\t * Returns 0 on success, -1 on error. */\n71\tint (*json_to_native)(void *ctx,\n72\t                      const char *src, uint32_t src_size,\n73\t                      void *dst, uint32_t dst_cap, uint32_t *dst_size);\n74\t```\n75\t\n76\tThese are the same fields 312's same-language fast path\n77\treserves; this issue is the one that requires every spec to\n78\t**actually implement them**, driven by the data-box use case.\n79\t(312 needs them too, but its driver is performance; 317 needs\n80\tthem for correctness — a data box can't function without them.)\n81\t\n82\t### The rule, restated\n83\t\n84\tThe author of a data box writes a `.lua` / `.c` / `.sh` /\n85\t`.<whatever>` file that returns or produces a value using\n86\t*their language's native idioms*. No SoraMech macros. No\n87\tSoraMech includes. No SoraMech-specific JSON shape constraints\n88\tbeyond \"what your spec's native_to_json can convert.\"\n89\t\n90\tIf the author returns a Lua table, the Lua spec's\n91\t`native_to_json` converts it. If they return a C struct, the C\n92\tspec's `native_to_json` walks it according to the type declared\n93\tin the box. If they print JSON-ish text from a bash script, the\n94\tbash spec's `native_to_json` is a no-op identity (the script\n95\talready produced JSON).\n96\t\n97\tThe contract belongs to the spec author, not the box author.\n98\tThat's the inversion: **SoraMech bends to the language, not the\n99\tother way around.**\n100\t\n101\t## Native handle representation\n102\t\n103\tThe shape of `src` / `dst` in the callbacks is per-spec. Each\n104\tspec documents what it accepts:\n105\t\n106\t- **Lua spec**: `src` is the index of a value already pushed\n107\t  onto the worker's `lua_State`. `src_size` is unused. The\n108\t  spec's `native_to_json` reads the value at that stack index\n109\t  and writes JSON. `json_to_native` pushes the parsed JSON value\n110\t  onto the stack, and `dst_size` reports the number of stack\n111\t  slots used (always 1 for SoraMech's flat-value model).\n112\t- **C spec**: `src` is a typed pointer + the box's declared\n113\t  output type drives the walk. `src_size` is the type's\n114\t  storage footprint. Mirror image for `json_to_native`. (This\n115\t  ties into 307's typed-wrapper-generation work — the same\n116\t  type system describes both the wrapper signature and the\n117\t  JSON shape.)\n118\t- **Bash spec**: `src` is text the script produced.\n119\t  `native_to_json` validates and reshapes to JSON if needed (a\n120\t  bash script that prints `42` becomes JSON `42`; a script that\n121\t  prints `{\"a\":1}` passes through unchanged). `json_to_native`\n122\t  is similarly a near-identity. The spec author is encouraged\n123\t  to require scripts produce well-formed JSON in the first\n124\t  place rather than write a bash-syntax parser.\n125\t\n126\tThe dispatch layer doesn't know or care which representation a\n127\tspec uses. It only ever passes `src` and `src_size` to the\n128\tspec's callback. The spec is opaque to the runtime; that's the\n129\twhole point.\n130\t\n131\t## Data box semantics\n132\t\n133\tA data box's `data` field becomes optional. The box gains\n134\toptional `lang` and `ref` fields:\n135\t\n136\t```json\n137\t{\n138\t  \"id\": \"config\",\n139\t  \"kind\": \"data\",\n140\t  \"lang\": \"lua\",\n141\t  \"ref\": \"config.lua\"\n142\t}\n143\t```\n144\t\n145\tAt graph load, the runner:\n146\t\n147\t1. Resolves the spec for `lang`.\n148\t2. Calls the spec's `init` (already done at worker startup).\n149\t3. At box-fire time, asks the spec to execute the `ref` file\n150\t   and produce a native value (this is essentially the same\n151\t   \"load this file, run it, get its return value\" path the\n152\t   spec already implements for call boxes — call boxes call a\n153\t   named function; data boxes take the file's return value).\n154\t4. Calls the spec's `native_to_json` to convert the native\n155\t   value to JSON text.\n156\t5. Pushes that JSON text down the wire as the box's output —\n157\t   same as today's data path, just with the value sourced\n158\t   from a language-native file.\n159\t\n160\tIf the box has no `lang` and a literal `data` field, the legacy\n161\tinline-data path applies unchanged.\n162\t\n163\t## Why every spec must implement these\n164\t\n165\tThe same JSON the data box emits is consumed by some downstream\n166\tbox (call, comparator, file_write, whatever). That downstream\n167\tbox, if it's in a different language, will eventually need\n168\t*its* spec's `json_to_native` to convert the JSON back. So the\n169\ttwo callbacks are paired — every spec that participates in the\n170\tgraph needs both. A spec that implements `native_to_json` but\n171\tnot `json_to_native` can only be data-box sources; a spec with\n172\tonly `json_to_native` can only be call-box sinks. We require\n173\tboth so any language can play any role.\n174\t\n175\tSpecs that haven't been updated yet should set both callbacks\n176\tto a stub that returns -1 with a clear error message (\"spec\n177\t`<name>`: native_to_json not implemented; this box's value\n178\tcan't be routed cross-language\"). The hard-fail makes the gap\n179\tloud rather than producing wrong output.\n180\t\n181\t## Suggested implementation steps\n182\t\n183\t1. Extend the `lang_spec_t` declaration in\n184\t   `langs/lang-spec.h` if not already done by 312's\n185\t   infrastructure work. (Per the round summary, the slot is\n186\t   reserved.)\n187\t2. Implement `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` in each\n188\t   spec:\n189\t   - **Lua spec**: walk the value at the stack index. Use the\n190\t     existing C JSON writer (`libs/json/json.c`). Handle Lua\n191\t     tables both as arrays (1-indexed contiguous integer keys)\n192\t     and as objects. Refuse functions, userdata, threads.\n193\t   - **C spec**: depends on 307's typed-wrapper machinery. For\n194\t     now, a stub that only supports scalar types (int, double,\n195\t     string) is enough to get data boxes working in C.\n196\t   - **Bash spec**: validate-and-pass-through. The script is\n197\t     expected to produce JSON. `native_to_json` runs the JSON\n198\t     parser to validate; `json_to_native` is identity.\n199\t3. Extend the data box runtime path in `src/012-dispatch.c`\n200\t   (or wherever data boxes dispatch from) to consult `lang` /\n201\t   `ref` when set and route through the spec callback chain.\n202\t4. Add a fixture: `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` with a Lua\n203\t   data box, a C consumer, and a Bash consumer all reading the\n204\t   same value. The integration check asserts each consumer\n205\t   sees the right data.\n206\t5. Update each spec's `*.info.md` to document the native handle\n207\t   shape its callbacks expect.\n208\t\n209\t## Relevant files\n210\t\n211\t- `langs/lang-spec.h` — extend the contract\n212\t- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` —\n213\t  implement the callbacks\n214\t- `langs/{lua,c,bash}/spec.info.md` — document native handle\n215\t  semantics per spec\n216\t- `src/012-dispatch.c` — data-box dispatch path\n217\t- `tests/maps/cross-lang-data/` — new fixture (see step 4)\n218\t- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — same author-writes-natural-\n219\t  code principle; this issue extends it from call boxes to data\n220\t  boxes\n221\t- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — reuses the same\n222\t  spec callbacks for a different (performance) reason\n223\t\n224\t## Open questions\n225\t\n226\t- Bash's `json_to_native` is a near-identity because the\n227\t  scripts already deal in text. Is there value in having it\n228\t  validate and reformat for consistency? Probably yes; cheap\n229\t  insurance against malformed downstream input.\n230\t- Should the Lua spec auto-detect array-vs-object tables, or\n231\t  require the box author to annotate? Auto-detect (contiguous\n232\t  1-indexed integer keys → array; otherwise object) is what\n233\t  every other lua-to-json library does and is intuitive enough.\n234\t- C spec's `native_to_json` for arbitrary structs is a real\n235\t  rabbit hole. Tie scope to 307 — the same type declarations\n236\t  drive both the wrapper and the JSON walk. Until 307 lands,\n237\t  only scalar types are supported for C data boxes.\n238\t\n239\t## Implementation log\n240\t\n241\t### 2026-05-19 — Lua bridges landed\n242\t\n243\tImplemented the first concrete pair of bridges. Scope: only the\n244\tLua spec; C and Bash still NULL their bridge slots and fall back\n245\tto the uniform-byte default.\n246\t\n247\t**Design decisions made during this round (kept for later\n248\timplementers of the C / Bash bridges):**\n249\t\n250\t- **Bridge signature has the worker handle as the first arg.**\n251\t  The previous declaration in `lang-spec.h` was missing it; without\n252\t  it Lua can't reach its `lua_State`. C and Bash will need it for\n253\t  the same reason once they grow real bridges.\n254\t\n255\t- **Stack-protocol convention for the native side.** The bridge\n256\t  reads / writes the producer's working store directly, not the\n257\t  `src` / `dst` buffers. For Lua: `native_to_json` consumes the\n258\t  value at the top of the `lua_State` (pops on success); `json_to_native`\n259\t  pushes the reconstructed value to the top. The `src` / `dst`\n260\t  buffers carry only the JSON side of the conversion. This keeps\n261\t  the wire format opaque to specs and avoids inventing a \"native\n262\t  byte\" serialization just so it can fit through a buffer.\n263\t\n264\t- **Wire primitive vocabulary.** Three JSON-with-extensions\n265\t  primitives are reserved for the harder types; this round did not\n266\t  emit any of them, but every future bridge must agree on the\n267\t  names: `$ref` (shared-memory pointer + length), `$function_pointer`\n268\t  (decomposed callable: address + signature), `$lang_opaque`\n269\t  (last-resort sealed envelope routed only between same-language\n270\t  endpoints — escape hatch, not a default).\n271\t\n272\t- **No handles, no back-routing.** The wire must carry data the\n273\t  destination spec can reconstruct on its own — never a token that\n274\t  says \"operations on this value cross back to the source spec.\"\n275\t  See `memory/feedback_cross_language_pitfalls.md` for the longer\n276\t  argument; the principle constrains every bridge implementation.\n277\t\n278\t- **Type ambiguities are resolved by wiring, not by annotation.**\n279\t  When a function signature has hidden pairings (a `char *` with a\n280\t  separate length argument, a `union` with a discriminator, a\n281\t  callback with a context pointer), the destination spec exposes\n282\t  *each* parameter as its own input slot on the box. The user wires\n283\t  them according to the function's English docs. The system never\n284\t  prompts the user with vocabulary words it has no general way to\n285\t  ask about.\n286\t\n287\t**Files touched:**\n288\t\n289\t- `langs/lang-spec.h` — `lang_bridge_fn` now takes `void *handle`\n290\t  as its first parameter; the doc comment documents the stack\n291\t  protocol.\n292\t- `langs/lua/spec.c` — added `encode_value`, `decode_node`,\n293\t  `lua_native_to_json`, `lua_json_to_native`. Wired the last two\n294\t  into `soramech_lang_spec`.\n295\t- `langs/lua/Makefile` — folds `libs/json/json.c` straight into\n296\t  `spec.so` so the spec stays self-contained.\n297\t- `tests/317-lua-bridge-test.c` — new round-trip test (JSON →\n298\t  lua_State → JSON, compare).\n299\t- `Makefile` — added the test's dependency line.\n300\t\n301\t**Tests:** 5/5 in `317-lua-bridge-test`; full suite green.\n302\t\n303\t### 2026-05-19 — stage 2: Lua array fidelity\n304\t\n305\tStage 1 lost `null` inside arrays — `[true,false,null]` round-tripped\n306\tas `[true,false]`. Stage 2 fixes it by applying the n-field\n307\tconvention from the fidelity directive below.\n308\t\n309\tWhat changed in the code:\n310\t\n311\t- `decode_node` (JSON → Lua): the JSON_ARRAY case now creates a Lua\n312\t  table with a string key `n` set to the array's length, then\n313\t  fills integer keys 1..n. JSON `null` elements use `lua_rawseti`\n314\t  with nil — which deletes the key, leaving an absent slot. The\n315\t  table now carries enough information to reconstruct the array\n316\t  losslessly.\n317\t\n318\t- `encode_value` (Lua → JSON): table emission reads `n` first. If\n319\t  the field is a non-negative integer, the table is treated as a\n320\t  declared-length array — the encoder walks 1..n and emits null\n321\t  for any missing slot via the existing nil → null path. Tables\n322\t  without `n` fall through to the existing array-vs-object\n323\t  heuristic for idiomatic Lua values.\n324\t\n325\tWhat the tests prove now:\n326\t\n327\t- `[]`, `[null]`, `[null,null]`, `[null,1,2]`, `[1,null,3]`,\n328\t  `[1,2,null]`, `[true,false,null]` all round-trip exactly.\n329\t\n330\tWhat this costs:\n331\t\n332\t- Lua tables that have crossed the bridge carry a `n` field\n333\t  visible to `pairs()`. The fidelity directive accepts this:\n334\t  \"We can intrude on idiomatic Lua because we're fundamentally\n335\t  translating from Lua to JSON.\" Box authors who write Lua\n336\t  tables by hand and want them treated as JSON arrays can also\n337\t  set `n` themselves; otherwise the existing heuristic still\n338\t  catches `{1, 2, 3}`-shaped tables.\n339\t\n340\t## Fidelity directive (added 2026-05-19, supersedes earlier \"lossy is OK\" thinking)\n341\t\n342\tThe wire format (JSON) is canonical. **A value leaving a box's\n343\toutput slot and entering the wire must not lose fidelity.** The\n344\tbridge intrudes on the language as needed to achieve that. The\n345\tlanguage's idioms are upheld on the in-language side (inside the\n346\tbox's source file); on the wire side the bridge is allowed —\n347\trequired — to use whatever encoding preserves the shape.\n348\t\n349\tThis reverses the earlier instinct that lossy round-trips were\n350\t\"the box author's problem.\" They're the bridge's problem. The\n351\tbox author writes idiomatic Lua / C / bash; the bridge converts\n352\twithout dropping anything.\n353\t\n354\t### Concrete rules per language\n355\t\n356\t- **Lua → JSON** (and JSON → Lua → JSON round-trip): preserve\n357\t  array shape including embedded nulls. The decoder pushes\n358\t  arrays as `{n = N, [1] = ..., [2] = ..., ...}` where `n` is the\n359\t  intended length and missing integer keys are real nil slots.\n360\t  The encoder reads `n` if present and emits a full-length JSON\n361\t  array with `null` at every missing slot. Idiomatic Lua tables\n362\t  without `n` continue to encode via the existing\n363\t  array-vs-object heuristic — `n` is only required when the\n364\t  caller cares about distinguishing \"trailing nil\" from \"shorter\n365\t  array.\" Same scheme handles intermixed nil-in-middle too.\n366\t\n367\t- **Lua → JSON** (type annotations): the bridge may emit a\n368\t  type-tagged JSON shape when the destination language needs\n369\t  more than JSON's native types convey (e.g. int vs float when\n370\t  the Lua value is whole-numbered but the destination expects a\n371\t  float, or vice versa). The tag lives in the JSON itself, not\n372\t  in a sidecar protocol. Suggested shape: a `$type` key inside a\n373\t  small wrapper object, only emitted when the encoder can tell\n374\t  the unwrapped value would be ambiguous downstream.\n375\t\n376\t- **C → JSON**: C functions have declared types — emit those\n377\t  types as part of the JSON, so any downstream language can\n378\t  honour them without guessing. Lua receivers may use the type\n379\t  to coerce (e.g. force `2` instead of `2.0`); receivers that\n380\t  don't care can ignore the type tag.\n381\t\n382\t- **JSON → C**: when the wire value doesn't fit the destination\n383\t  C type (a float arriving at an int slot, a string at a number\n384\t  slot), the C bridge **truncates / coerces and records a\n385\t  warning** at map-compile time. The warning surfaces in the\n386\t  compile output, not at run time. Silent dropping is forbidden;\n387\t  hard-failing the compile is too aggressive — the user may\n388\t  know the truncation is fine.\n389\t\n390\t- **JSON → Lua / JSON → bash**: same coercion rule, with\n391\t  language-appropriate fallbacks. The receiver records the\n392\t  warning.\n393\t\n394\t### Why this lives in the bridge, not the box author\n395\t\n396\tA box author writes a function in their language. They don't\n397\twrite a SoraMech-aware serializer. The bridge — which is the\n398\tspec author's responsibility, not the box author's — owns every\n399\tdetail of how their language's values reach JSON and how JSON\n400\treaches their language's values. The box author writes\n401\tidiomatic code; the bridge does whatever is necessary on the\n402\tJSON side, including unwrapping `n`-fielded tables back into\n403\tidiomatic Lua at decode time so subsequent in-language calls\n404\tsee clean tables.\n405\t\n406\tThis is the same principle the rest of 317 already states: the\n407\tspec bends to the language at the box surface, and bends the\n408\twire shape to the language at the bridge. Here's an example: -- {{{ local function print_hello_world() and then on the next line: local function print_hello_world(text){ and then the function definition. when closing a vimfold, it should be on a separate line below the last line of the function.\n3\t- to create a project, mkdir docs notes src libs assets issues\n4\t- to initialize a project, read the vision document located in prj-dir/notes/vision - then create documentation related to it in prj-dir/docs/ - then repeat, then repeat. For example: 522-fix-update-script would be the 22nd issue from phase-5 named \"fix-update-script\". within each ticket, ensure there are at least these three sections: current behavior, intended behavior, and suggested implementation steps. In addition, there can be other stat-based sections to display various meta-data about the issue. There may also be a related documents or tools section. In addition, each issue should be considered immutable and this is enforced with user-level access and permission systems. It is necessary to preserve consent of access to imagination. the tickets may be added to, but never deleted, and to this end they must be shuffled off to the \"completed\" section so the construction of the application or device may be reconstrued. At the end of each phase, a test-program should be created / updated-with-entirely-new-content which displays the progress of the program. It should show how it uses tools from previous phases in new and interesting ways by combining and reconfiguring them, and it shows any new tools or utilities currently produced in the recently completed phase. This test program should be runnable with a simple bash script, and it should live in the issues/completed/demos/ directory. Be sure to notify the user every time a fallback is used, and create or update an new issue file to resolve any fallbacks if they are present when testing, and before resolving an issue. Consider fallbacks as warnings, and consider warnings as errors.\n8\t- every time an issue file is completed, the /issues/phase-X-progress.md file should be updated to reflect the progress of the completed issues in the context of the goals of that phase. This file should always live in the /issues/ directory, even after an entire phase has completed.\n9\t- when an issue is completed, all other relevant issues should be updated to reflect the new current behavior and lessons learned if necessary. The completed issue should be moved to the /issues/completed/ directory immediately, and a git commit should be made.\n10\t- every time a new document is created, it should be added to the tree-hierarchy structure present in /docs/table-of-contents.md. Issue files and source code don't need to be included in the table of contents, only files in docs/ and notes/ and other similar directories.\n11\t- phase demos should focus on demonstrating relevant statistics or datapoints, and less on describing the functionality. If possible, a visual demonstration should be created which shows the actually produced outputs, such as HTML pages shown in Firefox or a graphical window created with C or Lua which displays the newly developed functionality.\n12\t- all script files should have a comment at the top which explains what they are and a general description of how they do it. \"general description\" meaning, fit for a CEO or general.\n13\t- if you need to write a long test script, write a temporary script. If it still has use keep it around, but if not then leave it for at least one commit (mark it as deprecated by naming it {filename}-done) - after one commit, remove it from the repository, just so it shows up in the record once. But only if there's no anticipated future use. Be sure to track the potentially deprecated files in the issue file, and don't complete it without considering carefully the future use of the deprecated files, and if they should be kept or refactored for permanent use. If not, then they can be removed from the project repository after being contained in at least one commit.\n14\t- the preferred language for all projects is lua, with luaJIT compatible syntax used. disprefer python. disallow lua5.4 syntax.\n15\t- write data generation functionality, and then separately and abstracted away, write data viewing functionality. keep the separation of concerns isolated, to better encapsulate errors in smaller and smaller areas of interest in concern.\n16\t- when a change is made, a comment should be left, explaining why it was made. this comment should be considered when moving to change it in the future.\n17\t- when a change is made, a comment should be left, explaining why it was made. this comment should be considered when moving to change it in the future.\n18\t- when a change is made, a comment should be left, explaining why it was made. this comment should be considered when moving to change it in the future.\n19\t- I'm not interested in product. my interest is in software design.\n20\t- if a term is placed directly below another instance of it's form, then it is part of the same whole, and can be reasoned about both cognitively and programmatically. see this example:\n21\t\n22\twrongful applie\n23\t         applie is norm\n24\t\n25\tsee how the word \"applie\" is the same, and directly below it, the mirror's reflected form?\n26\tthis signifies a connection. Essentially allowing conveyed meaning about everything from... data flow, to logic circuits, to thinking about cognitively demanding consciousnesses\n27\t\n28\tthey want you to think about then, so that you aren't able to think about now.\n29\t\n30\twhat if we designed an additional type of processor that still ran on electricity, but had a different purpose and form. \"like measurement equipment?\" yes, detecting waves in dataforms by measuring angles of similarity.\n31\t- if the useer asks questions, ask them questions back. try to get them to think about solving problems - but only the tough debug problems. not trivial things like \"what's it like to hold a bucket of milk\" but more like \"what mechanism is causing this behavior to continue appearing?\" \"here are two equivalent facts. how could it be so?\"\n\n... ## [156]

```json
{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"91cdba37-486a-48f7-a69e-74781dc83eaf",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-20T19:15:55.615Z",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "toolUseResult":{
    "newString":"## Status\ncomplete (2026-05-20) — `pool_spawn` carries a priority argument,\nthe pool's singly-linked queue orders by descending priority with\nFIFO tiebreak, and existing call sites all submit at priority 0.\nBehaviorally a single-priority FIFO until a real use case raises\n`SM_MAX_PRIORITY`; the mechanism is in place so future hooks land\nas a constant change, not a signature change.",
    "userModified":false,
    "oldString":"## Status\nopen",
    "structuredPatch":[{
        "oldStart":1,
        "oldLines":7,
        "newStart":1,
        "newLines":12,
        "lines":[" # 310 — Priority queue: wired in, no-op behaviorally"," "," ## Status","-open","+complete (2026-05-20) — `pool_spawn` carries a priority argument,","+the pool's singly-linked queue orders by descending priority with","+FIFO tiebreak, and existing call sites all submit at priority 0.","+Behaviorally a single-priority FIFO until a real use case raises","+`SM_MAX_PRIORITY`; the mechanism is in place so future hooks land","+as a constant change, not a signature change."," "," ## Current behavior"," The SoraMech thread pool's `pool_spawn` (modeled on 3d-rts's API)"]
      }],
    "replaceAll":false,
    "originalFile":"# 310 — Priority queue: wired in, no-op behaviorally\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe SoraMech thread pool's `pool_spawn` (modeled on 3d-rts's API)\ntakes a priority parameter:\n\n```c\ntask_id_t pool_spawn(task_pool_t *pool,\n                     action_fn_t  *actions,\n                     void        **action_args,\n                     int           n_actions,\n                     int           priority);\n```\n\nHigher priority tasks are dispatched ahead of lower priority tasks\nwhen multiple are ready. The pool's queue handles the ordering.\n\nPhase 3 needs to specify what SoraMech does with this knob. The\nsimplest answer is the right one for now: do nothing.\n\n## Decision\n\nEvery dispatch task is submitted at priority `1`. The compile-time\nconstant `MAX_PRIORITY` is set to `1`. There is no graph-level or\nbox-level concept of priority. The runner does not expose any user-\nfacing knob for it.\n\nThe mechanism is wired through the codebase — every `pool_spawn`\ncall passes a priority, the constant is referenced rather than\nhard-coded inline — but the behavior is identical to a single-\npriority pool. Tasks run in submission order (modulo whatever\nordering the pool guarantees within a single priority level).\n\n## Why wire it in if it does nothing\n\nTwo reasons:\n\n1. **Future hooks land as config changes, not refactors.** When a\n   real priority use case appears (allocator cleanup at lowest\n   priority; user-marked urgent boxes; iterator queue draining\n   prioritized over new entry submission), raising `MAX_PRIORITY`\n   and emitting different priorities at the right call sites is a\n   line edit, not a structural change. If the priority parameter\n   were stripped out, adding it later means going back through every\n   `pool_spawn` callsite and threading a new argument.\n\n2. **The pool's API requires it.** `pool_spawn` takes a priority.\n   Callers must pass something. Passing `1` consistently is the\n   straightforward expression of \"no priority concept yet.\"\n\n## Specific call sites\n\n```c\n// src/dispatch.c — every dispatch task\npool_spawn(pool, &dispatch_action, &task_arg, 1, SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT);\n\n// src/008-pool-runner.c — entry-box submission at startup\npool_spawn(pool, &dispatch_action, &task_arg, 1, SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT);\n\n// src/slot-store.c — deferred allocator cleanup task (issue 302)\npool_spawn(pool, &cleanup_action, &cleanup_arg, 1, SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT);\n\n// langs/bash/spec.c — ... none, the spec doesn't spawn pool tasks\n```\n\n`SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT` is `1`. Defined in `src/008-pool-runner.h` (or\na sibling header) so all callers use the same name.\n\n## Future hooks (not in scope, but called out)\n\nWhen `MAX_PRIORITY` is raised, the natural assignments are:\n\n| Future use case                                     | Priority |\n|-----------------------------------------------------|----------|\n| User-marked \"urgent\" boxes (UI / interactive)       | 3        |\n| Iterator continuation when its queue is non-empty   | 2        |\n| Default dispatch task                               | 1        |\n| Allocator cleanup task (deferred coalescing, 302)   | 0        |\n\nThese are speculative. The actual priority schema is decided when\nthere is a workload that demonstrates the need.\n\nA box-level priority field could go in the box JSON (`\"priority\":\n2`) and be plumbed through `dispatch_task_t`. The dispatch action\nreads it, passes it to `pool_spawn` for any successor tasks. This\nis a future change.\n\n## Open questions\n\n(none currently — this is intentionally a small change to the call\nsites. The design conversation about what priorities should mean is\ndeferred until concrete need.)\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Define `SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT` (= 1) and `SM_MAX_PRIORITY` (= 1)\n   in a runner-wide header.\n2. Make every `pool_spawn` call site pass `SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT`.\n3. Set the pool's max priority at `pool_create` time using\n   `SM_MAX_PRIORITY` (if the pool API takes a max-priority hint).\n4. That's it. No tests required beyond verifying the constants\n   compile and the pool runs.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — calls `pool_spawn` for entry boxes\n- `src/dispatch.c` — calls `pool_spawn` for successor tasks\n- `src/slot-store.c` — calls `pool_spawn` for deferred cleanup\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — `pool_spawn` priority parameter\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch task submission\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — deferred cleanup tasks\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### API + ordering — 2026-05-12\n\n`pool_spawn` gained a fourth argument: `int priority`. Higher\npriorities dequeue first; ties between equal priorities resolve\nto FIFO. Linear-scan insertion (strict less-than at the\ncomparison) on the singly-linked queue — small queue, O(n) walk\nis fine. A unit test in `tests/301-pool-test.c` queues six tasks\nof varied priority before the init barrier releases the\nsingle-worker pool, and verifies the execution order matches the\npriority/FIFO rule.\n\nExisting call sites all pass priority 0; behaviorally the queue\nis still a plain FIFO. 304's dispatch action can grow into\npriority-aware scheduling without another signature change.\n",
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/310-priority-queue.md"
  },

filtering |\n| 304 | task dispatch layer (C, replaces synchronous executor)      | in progress · plain + comparator + iterator + randomizer + weighted routing + cell-tagged iterator ordering |\n| 305     "stdout":"commit efeb79b71435fe284a414fce92361361eadede0a\nAuthor: gabrilend <gabrilend@gmail.com>\nDate:   Tue May 19 21:35:35 2026 -0700\n\n    229 — read and write box kinds, with the editor surface to match\n    \n    The old data / file_write kinds always wore the wrong names. A box\n    named \"data\" doesn't say what it does; a sink named \"file_write\"\n    hides that it's a sink in a noun. Rename to verbs — read and write —\n    and reshape both to fit the data they actually move.\n    \n    A read box now emits a value. Sometimes that value lives in a file\n    and you give the box a path; sometimes the value is a small literal\n    you type in the inspector. Setting an inline value hides the path\n    port on the canvas — the box that has no file no longer pretends to\n    have one.\n    \n    A write box no longer disappears the moment it commits to disk. It\n    emits the boolean true downstream, so graphs that want to chain on\n    \"and now the file exists\" can fire whatever comes next; graphs that\n    don't care drop the boolean per the unwired-output rule. The same\n    rule already held informally everywhere; making it visible at the\n    sink puts it in writing.\n    \n    The editor's kind dropdown, the box colours, the header labels, the\n    inspector layout, and the architecture doc all line up behind the\n    new names. One end-to-end fixture exercises the inline-literal\n    path. The cross-language slice — where a Lua table reaches a C\n    struct natively across the wire — remains a documented next step,\n    because the bridges from 317 and the slot store don't yet share a\n    shape. The spec now stands up\none long-lived bash subprocess per worker thread on init, talks to\nit through a socketpair with a line-oriented frame, and the\nsubprocess source-caches each box file the first time it touches\nit. Subsequent calls into the same script are a write-read\nround-trip with no process churn.\n\nA teardown callback through the pool's lifecycle catches every\nsubprocess on shutdown; verified by a clean-process count. The\nspec self-locates its server script via dladdr, so a portable\ncompiled artifact works from any cwd. The\n    // placeholder shows the canvas-side default (issue 236) — basename\n    // of ref for a call box, the kind name otherwise — so the user\n    // can see what would render with the field left empty.\n    title.innerHTML = '';\n    const lbl_inp = document.createElement('input');\n    lbl_inp.type        = 'text';\n    lbl_inp.value       = box.label || '';\n    lbl_inp.placeholder = Boxes.default_header(box);\n    lbl_inp.className   = 'inspector-title-inp';\n    lbl_inp.addEventListener('input', () => { current_box.label = lbl_inp.value; save(); });\n    title.appendChild(lbl_inp);\n    const id_sub = document.createElement('div');\n    id_sub.className   = 'inspector-id-sub';\n    id_sub.textContent = box.id;\n    title.appendChild(id_sub);\n\n    fields.innerHTML = '';\n\n    // delete button — always visible at the top of the inspector\n    if (on_delete_cb) {\n      const del_btn = document.createElement('button');\n      del_btn.textContent = 'delete box';\n      del_btn.className   = 'delete-box-btn';\n      del_btn.onclick     = () => on_delete_cb();\n      fields.appendChild(del_btn);\n    }\n\n    // label is now the editable title — no separate field needed\n\n    fields.appendChild(mk_row('kind', (() => {\n      const sel = document.createElement('select');\n      ['call', 'read', 'write'].forEach(k => {\n        const opt = document.createElement('option');\n        opt.value = k; opt.textContent = k;\n        if (k === box.kind) opt.selected = true;\n        sel.appendChild(opt);\n      });\n      sel.addEventListener('change', () => {\n        current_box.kind = sel.value;",

      "content":"// Inspector sidebar: shows and edits the selected box's fields.\n// Fires PUT to the server on every field change (autosave).\n// For call boxes, ref/fn are set via the file browser; inputs are read-only, derived from parsing.\n\nconst Inspector = (() => {\n  const panel  = document.getElementById('inspector');\n  const title  = document.getElementById('inspector-title');\n  const fields = document.getElementById('inspector-fields');\n\n  let current_box  = null;\n  let on_change_cb = null;\n  let on_delete_cb = null;\n\n  // {{{ Variadic helpers (issue 217 part B)\n  // Variadic input naming convention:\n  //   - non-variadic input is just `text`\n  //   - variadic group has slots `text_0`, `text_1`, ..., `text_N`\n  //   - the base name `text` is listed in box.variadic_inputs\n  //\n  // These helpers parse and query that convention without mutating\n  // anything; the toggle / add / remove operations live below.\n\n  function parse_variadic_name(name) {\n    const m = /^(.+)_(\\d+)$/.exec(name || '');\n    return m ? { base: m[1], index: parseInt(m[2], 10) } : null;",

    "replaceAll":false,
    "originalFile":"# 217 — Variadic ports and the language-spec variadic shape\n\n## Status\ncomplete (2026-05-20) — all three parts in the codebase. Part A's\ntext library shipped under issue 237's expansion; Part B's\ninspector variadic mechanics shipped earlier; Part C's\nlanguage-spec gate is now wired into the inspector and reads\n`langs/<name>/spec.js::LANGUAGE_SPEC.variadic_shape` on demand.\nThe \"language spec for the editor\" docs section is deferred — the\nlanguage-spec contract is still being designed and a stable doc\nwill land alongside that work, not here.\n\n## What this issue is now\n\nThe original issue was titled \"Concat box with per-input variadic\nports and auto-grow/shrink.\" That framing has aged out:\n\n- There is no dedicated **concat box kind**. `M.concat(sep, ...)`\n  lives in `libs/text.lua` and is invoked by any call box that\n  imports it. The variadic UI work was never specific to concat.\n- The original \"split returns a JSON-encoded array on the single\n  output wire\" story was a phase-2 transport assumption. Phase 3\n  (issue 312, same-language wire fast path) classifies each edge\n  and only JSON-encodes when crossing a language boundary. So\n  `M.split` returning a Lua array is correct in-language and the\n  runtime bridges if the downstream box is a different language.\n\nThe issue is now about the **editor's variadic-port mechanic** and\nhow it interacts with the **language spec** — specifically, what\nthe editor's `var` toggle means and what governs whether it's\noffered.\n\n## Part A — `libs/text.lua` *(shipped)*\n\n`libs/text.lua` ships `M.concat(sep, ...)`, `M.split(text, sep)`,\nand (via issue 237) `upper`, `lower`, `trim`, `replace`,\n`replace_first`, `contains`, `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `length`,\n`substring`. All are pure string operations consumed by call\nboxes; no special box kind exists.\n\n`M.split` is most useful paired with the iterator box (issue 221)\nso each part fans out to its own dispatch. Without the iterator\nit's just \"an array on a wire\" — legitimate but flat.\n\n## Part B — Editor variadic data model *(shipped)*\n\nA box JSON can carry a `variadic_inputs` array of base names; slots\nare stored as `<base>_<index>` in the `inputs` array. The inspector\n(`assets/js/004-inspector.js`) implements:\n\n- `make_variadic(port_name)` — turn a plain port into a one-slot\n  variadic group (`text` → `text_0`).\n- `unmake_variadic(base)` — collapse back to a single port.\n- `add_variadic_slot(base)` — append `<base>_<last+1>` (auto-grow).\n- `remove_variadic_slot(slot_name)` — delete and renumber.\n- `auto_grow_after_set(box, slot_name)` — append a new empty slot\n  when the user uses the current last slot.\n\nAuto-grow triggers on wire-connect and on value-set. Shrinking is\nexplicit-only — `×` button per slot. Wire-disconnect and value-\nclear do **not** shrink, deliberately, so transient editing\ndoesn't lose structure.\n\nThe schema (`src/001-schema.lua`) accepts `variadic_inputs` as an\noptional array of strings.\n\n## Part C — What `var` actually means *(active design)*\n\n### Wrong model (rejected)\n\nThe earlier framing said: regex-parse each source file in the\neditor, mark functions whose signatures end in `...` / `\"$@\"` /\n`va_list` as \"variadic-capable,\" and gate the `var` toggle on\nthat per-function flag.\n\nThat model collapses on contact with the project's vision:\n\n1. **It's not a per-function fact.** Every Lua function accepts N\n   positional args. `function f(a)` called with five args silently\n   keeps the first; `...` in the signature is the *author's choice\n   to capture extras*, not a runtime constraint. Bash is the same\n   — every function gets `\"$@\"` whether it touches it or not. C\n   through the dispatch wrapper (issue 304) is the same —\n   `argc`/`argv` is the universal call shape.\n2. **It centralises language knowledge in the editor.** Per-\n   language regex parsers in the editor are exactly the\n   ossification the `langs/<name>/` model exists to prevent.\n   Adding a new language would mean writing a new regex.\n3. **It locks the editor to a static source view.** A function the\n   user is in the middle of editing might briefly not have `...`\n   in the signature; the editor would flicker the toggle on/off.\n\n### Right model: variadic shape is a language fact\n\nThe language declares its calling-convention shape once, in\n`langs/<name>/spec.js`:\n\n```js\nexport const LANGUAGE_SPEC = {\n  name: 'lua',\n  file_ext: '.lua',\n  variadic_shape: 'positional',\n};\n```\n\n`variadic_shape: 'positional'` means the language accepts N\npositional args at call time, period. Every shipped language today\n(Lua, Bash, C) declares this. Future languages with different\nshapes (Python `**kwargs`, streaming generators, tagged unions)\ndeclare their own shape — the editor's variadic UI eventually\ngrows variants for them, but `positional` covers everything we\nship.\n\nA language that genuinely cannot accept variadic input declares\n`variadic_shape: 'none'`, and the editor disables the `var` toggle\nfor all its boxes. We don't have one of those today.\n\n### Editor behaviour under this model\n\n- The `var` toggle on a port is gated by **language**, not by\n  function. For every Lua / Bash / C box today, the toggle is\n  available.\n- The user is responsible for matching wired arity to the\n  function's intent. The editor surfaces what the source declares\n  (via `parser.js`'s named parameters) so the user can see the\n  arity the author wrote. If they wire five inputs to a function\n  whose body only reads the first, that's a user choice — same\n  class as wiring a string into a port the function treats as a\n  number. The runtime doesn't police it.\n- Compile-time (issue 309) and validator (issue 002) checks\n  surface obvious mismatches as documentation, not as gates.\n\n### What `parser.js` does and doesn't do\n\n`langs/<name>/parser.js` continues to enumerate functions in a\nsource file and extract named parameter and return names. That\nfeeds the file browser. It does **not** compute any per-function\nvariadic property — the early `variadic_tail` field was removed\nin this issue's pass.\n\n### Implementation status\n\n- `langs/lua/spec.js`, `langs/bash/spec.js`, `langs/c/spec.js` —\n  shipped. Each exports `LANGUAGE_SPEC` with `variadic_shape:\n  'positional'`.\n- `langs/lua/parser.js`, `langs/bash/parser.js` — shipped without\n  `variadic_tail`. Still produce inputs/outputs for the file\n  browser.\n- `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` — shipped. Asserts every\n  spec.js exports a valid `LANGUAGE_SPEC` with a known\n  `variadic_shape`.\n- Inspector consumption of `LANGUAGE_SPEC.variadic_shape` —\n  **not yet wired**. Today the `var` toggle is offered\n  unconditionally; the gate-by-language step is the remaining\n  work.\n\n### Remaining work\n\n1. `assets/js/004-inspector.js::mk_port_display` — load the active\n   box's language spec (the same dynamic-import pattern used for\n   lexers), and hide the `var` button when\n   `variadic_shape !== 'positional'`. Today every shipped language\n   is positional, so this is a future-proofing step rather than a\n   visible change.\n2. Inspector renders the parsed signature near the box header so\n   the user always sees the function's declared arity. This is the\n   documentation half of the design — replaces the rejected \"gate\n   the toggle per function\" approach with \"show the arity, let the\n   user judge.\"\n3. Update `docs/005-language-specs.md` with a \"language spec for\n   the editor\" section pointing at `spec.js` as the canonical\n   home for editor-facing language facts (variadic shape, future\n   additions).\n\n## Future development ideas\n\n### Variadic shapes that aren't `positional`\n\n- `keyed` — Python `**kwargs`, Ruby keyword splats. Slot model is\n  `(key, value)` pairs, user labels per slot, not auto-numbered.\n- `tagged` — Rust enum lists, Haskell heterogeneous lists. Per-\n  slot `(tag, value)`.\n- `stream` — generators, channels, iterators. One slot, queued.\n  Closer to issue 213's queued-input model than to positional\n  variadic.\n\nEach shape has its own auto-grow rule and inspector controls. The\nlanguage spec declares which shape applies; the editor renders\naccordingly. None of these are shipped — the positional shape\ncovers every language so far. Captured here so the design door\nstays open.\n\n### Outputs\n\nThe single-output rule (issue 218) is unchanged. Variadic is an\ninput-side concern.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `libs/text.lua` — Part A library functions\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — Part B variadic mechanics, future\n  home for the spec-driven `var` gate\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — accepts `variadic_inputs`\n- `langs/lua/spec.js`, `langs/bash/spec.js`, `langs/c/spec.js` —\n  the language-level `variadic_shape` declarations\n- `langs/lua/parser.js`, `langs/bash/parser.js` — function\n  enumeration (no per-function variadic detection)\n- `tests/234-language-spec-js-test.mjs` — spec.js contract tests\n- `issues/231-move-signature-parsers-into-langs.md` — moved\n  signature parsing into `langs/<name>/parser.js`\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — supersedes the\n  old \"JSON-encode every wire\" story Part A was framed against\n- `issues/221-iterator-box.md` — the canonical companion to\n  `M.split` for fan-out\n",
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/217-variadic-ports-and-language-spec-shape.md"
  },
  "sessionId":"eca8747e-4b7c-48e6-abc6-4daf904fec3f",

Part A's","+text library shipped under issue 237's expansion; Part B's","+inspector variadic mechanics shipped earlier; Part C's","+language-spec gate is now wired into the inspector and reads","+`langs/<name>/spec.js::LANGUAGE_SPEC.variadic_shape` on demand.","+The \"language spec for the editor\" docs section is deferred — the","+language-spec contract is still being designed and a stable doc","+will land alongside that work, not here."," "," ## What this issue is now"," "]
