y=\"200\">slab_create(n_cells, n_workers)</text>\n    <text class=\"label\" x=\"0\" y=\"218\">slab_destroy()</text>\n  </g>\n</svg>\n\n<h2>Action walkthrough</h2>\n\n<h3>1 · slab_create (once, at pool_create)</h3>\n<div class=\"panel\">\n  <ol>\n    <li>Allocate one contiguous block: <code>n_cells * 64 bytes</code>.\n      Default <code>n_cells = 4096</code>; configurable at pool creation.</li>\n    <li>Walk the block writing the singly-linked free pointer into the\n      first 8 bytes of every cell. Result: every cell points to its\n      successor; the last points to <code>NULL</code>.</li>\n    <li>Store <code>free_head</code> = pointer to cell 0.</li>\n    <li>Allocate per-thread cache arrays sized to\n      <code>POOL_MAX_WORKERS * 16</code>.</li>\n    <li>Each worker thread on init pops its initial 16 cells from\n      the global free list (one mutex acquisition each, only at startup).</li>\n  </ol>\n</div>\n\n<h3>2 · slab_alloc (per-task creation, hot path)</h3>\n<div class=\"panel\">\n  <ol>\n    <li>Caller is a worker thread. Read its <code>thread_idx</code> from\n      TLS (<code>pool_current_worker</code>).</li>\n    <li>Local cache non-empty? → pop top, return pointer.\n      <span style=\"color:var(--green)\">~3 ns.</span></li>\n    <li>Local cache empty? → acquire global mutex; pop a batch of 16 cells\n      off <code>free_head</code>; release; pop one from refilled cache;\n      return.\n      <span style=\"color:var(--gold)\">~50 ns amortized.</span></li>\n  </ol>\n  <p>Returned pointer is to an uninitialized 64-byte region. Caller writes\n    the task struct fields in place.</p>\n</div>\n\n<h3>3 · slab_free (per-task completion, hot path)</h3>\n<div class=\"panel\">\n  <ol>\n    <li>Caller is the worker thread that just ran the task to completion.\n      Read <code>thread_idx</code>.</li>\n    <li>Push the freed cell pointer onto the local cache stack.\n      <span style=\"color:var(--warm)\">~3 ns.</span></li>\n    <li>Cache size now exceeds 32? → acquire global mutex; chain the\n      bottom 16 of the cache into the global free list; release.\n      <span style=\"color:var(--gold)\">~50 ns amortized.</span></li>\n  </ol>\n  <p>The bottom-half drain pattern keeps recently-freed cells warm in\n    the local cache for immediate reuse, while shedding the older half\n    back to the global pool for other threads.</p>\n</div>\n\n<h3>4 · slab_destroy (once, at pool_destroy)</h3>\n<div class=\"panel\">\n  <ol>\n    <li>Pool quiescence has been confirmed; no thread holds a cell pointer.</li>\n    <li>Free each thread's local cache array.</li>\n    <li>Free the global slab block.</li>\n    <li>No cell-by-cell teardown. The arena dies in one shot.</li>\n  </ol>\n</div>\n\n<h2>What lives in a cell</h2>\n<div class=\"panel\">\n<table>\n  <tr><td class=\"k\">8 bytes</td><td class=\"v\">free-list <code>next</code> pointer, OR overwritten when allocated</td></tr>\n  <tr><td class=\"k\">8 bytes</td><td class=\"v\">pointer to <code>box_runtime_state</code> (the box this task instantiates)</td></tr>\n  <tr><td class=\"k\">4 bytes</td><td class=\"v\">task_id (event-log correlation, per 311)</td></tr>\n  <tr><td class=\"k\">4 bytes</td><td class=\"v\">flags (work / readiness-check / fast-fast-path; priority hint)</td></tr>\n  <tr><td class=\"k\">≤ 40 bytes</td><td class=\"v\">inline input snapshot or pointer to a values-array if too many to fit</td></tr>\n</table>\n<p style=\"margin-top:14px;color:var(--dim)\">Total budget: 64 bytes per cell.\n  Common case fits entirely; the values-array escape hatch handles\n  high-arity boxes without bloating every cell.</p>\n</div>\n\n<h2>Contention notes</h2>\n<div class=\"panel\">\n<ul>\n  <li><b>Hot path is lock-free.</b> 95%+ of allocations and frees touch only\n    the calling thread's local cache. No atomics, no fences, no contention.</li>\n  <li><b>Refill / drain</b> uses a single mutex. Frequency depends on burst\n    size; a thread that allocates and frees 1000 tasks in a tight loop may\n    refill / drain only ~60 times total.</li>\n  <li><b>Cross-thread free is fine.</b> Producer thread allocates and pushes\n    a task to the pool's queue. Consumer thread runs it and frees the cell.\n    The free hits the consumer's local cache, not the producer's. Cells\n    naturally migrate across caches; the periodic drain rebalances.</li>\n  <li><b>False sharing avoided</b> by sizing cells to 64 bytes (one cache\n    line). Two cells never share a line.</li>\n</ul>\n</div>\n\n</body>\n</html>\n",

The task itself never touches the ring buffer; it operates on its frozen input snapshot. After the task ends, the cell goes back to the slab; the ring buffer state is independent of the task's lifecycle.\n\n**One readiness-check per (producer-task, consumer-box) — fired at end of producer task.** Confirmed. The escape hatch is \"if it doesn't fit, allocate a separate values-array from the slab and store a pointer.\" Adds one indirection only for high-arity boxes.\n\n**Things I do NOT think need to live in the cell:**\n- Pointer to the producing-task's parent — not needed at runtime; only useful for debugging cascade traces; can be flagged on by a build option, off in production.\n- Submit time / start time / end time — the event log captures these on the way out; storing in the cell would double-spend.\n- A waiting-list pointer — we agreed no parking, so no list.\n\n**Hot path enumeration** (where cells get created):\n\n1. **Pool startup** — main thread spawns one task per entry box. N tasks, where N = entry-box count. Cold.\n2. **Producer task completion** — submits 1 readiness-check task per distinct downstream consumer box. We should make sure we have a slot for box reference counts, it just... doesn't get used if the stretch goal isn't met. But we still have it there, as documentation that SOMETHING goes there, it just hasn't been built yet. Then we ask why, then we end up adding it because it's a good idea.\n\n  Inline run con: the readiness check is now an unbounded-duration task. A worker that picked up a \"readiness check\" might end up running a\n  5-second LLM call. Other tasks queue behind it; pool fairness suffers.\n\n\"readiness check\" doesn't fully capture the entirety of what this operation does, specifically, it is intended to \"attempt a run\" of a box. we make these checks by providing the most recent change that would enable the box to run - essentially, our logic is such that the fewest amount of steps between each function call must be made, while enabling the \"long-tail\" async threads to do non-blocking tasks on their own time. As soon as they can, they knit themselves with their fellow threads, co-creating a weaving texture of computer programming. proving without a doubt that intelligence can have a dynamical host.",

{

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Two important reframes from you. Let me trace them.\n\n---\n\n## Box refcount slot — keep it visible as documentation\n\nYou're right. The slot should exist in the design *now*, even if the retirement logic doesn't fire yet. Documentation by structural presence. Same pattern as priority queue (310): the field is in place, the behavior is wired through, the consumer that does something interesting with the value is the follow-on.\n\nSo:\n- **`box_runtime_state` carries `live_predecessor_count`** — initialised at graph load to the number of distinct upstream producer boxes for this box. Box-level state, not cell-level (one count per box, shared by all tasks instantiating it).\n- **Every task's completion path includes \"if this is my box's last possible invocation, decrement downstream boxes' `live_predecessor_count`.\"** The hook exists in the dispatch loop from day one.\n- **The actual retirement action** (free the box's slot table, cascade upward) is the stretch piece. Until it ships, the decrement is a no-op — the count drops but nothing checks it.\n\nWhen someone reads the dispatch code in six months and asks \"why are we decrementing this count if nothing watches it?\" — that's the prompt to ship retirement. The slot is the question.\n\nI'll add `live_predecessor_count` to box_runtime_state in 302 and call out the decrement-but-no-act loop in the dispatch code, with the explicit comment \"the action that consumes this is the box-retirement stretch goal; the count is honest now so the action lands as a one-place addition later.\"\n\n---\n\n## \"Attempt task\" — and what it collapses\n\nThis dissolves the two-task model I had. A producer's push doesn't spawn a *check*; it spawns an *attempt*. The attempt walks the consumer's inputs, and either:\n- All inputs ready → run the consumer's spec, write outputs, submit further attempts. The attempt IS the work task.\n- Not all ready → return. Some other producer's push will trigger another attempt later, with the same shape.\n\nThis is simpler, structurally rigid (same task kind for every entry into the pool's queue), and faster:\n- **One allocation per consumer invocation, not two.** No separate \"readiness check\" cell.\n- **One pool round-trip per consumer invocation, not two.**\n- **The inline-run question disappears.** It's not \"should we run inline?\" — the attempt IS the run, when conditions are met. The \"fast same-lang chain\" case happens naturally: producer ends → submits attempt → worker picks up attempt → finds ready → runs → submits more attempts. Every hop is one allocation, one queue round-trip. There's no fork between \"check task that submits a work task\" and \"run-inline shortcut.\"\n\nThis also reframes the **\"submitting most-recently-relevant change\" intuition** you described. The producer task knows what it just changed (it filled a specific slot or N slots on a specific consumer). The attempt it submits is precisely targeted: \"the consumer whose input set may have just become ready because of MY push.\" Not a generic re-evaluation; a targeted attempt with a known cause.\n\nThe fairness concern I raised earlier (long tasks blocking the pool) is now... real, but unavoidable, because every task in the pool is potentially long-running. That's the price of running real work on the pool. The pool's parallelism handles it — N workers means N concurrent long tasks; new attempts spawn on whichever worker frees first.\n\nSo the dispatch model is:\n\n```\nproducer task:\n   compute output\n   for each downstream consumer box C this producer just touched:\n      write all values to C's input slots (snapshotted into the attempt's cell at the END)\n   for each distinct C:\n      slab_alloc() → attempt_task for C\n      pool_spawn(attempt_task)\n   slab_free(this cell)\n\nattempt task:\n   if every required input on C is satisfiable (slot value or data-box pull):\n      snapshot values into local vars\n      invoke spec, get output\n      push output to downstream consumer slots\n      submit one attempt per distinct downstream consumer\n      decrement input $ref counts\n      decrement upstream boxes' live_predecessor_count if applicable\n   slab_free(this cell)\n```\n\n**One task kind. One allocation per invocation. Self-similar at every layer.** The \"attempt\" name captures it — every task is an attempt to advance the graph.\n\n---\n\n## The poetic passage\n\n> *\"As soon as they can, they knit themselves with their fellow threads, co-creating a weaving texture of computer programming. proving without a doubt that intelligence can have a dynamical host.\"*\n\nThat goes in the architecture docs. The structural-shell section already has the apartment-building metaphor; the dispatch-attempt loop's description gets your weaving framing. The shell is rigid; the work that happens inside it is dynamic, threading itself into existence one attempt at a time. That's the dance the structural rules are designed to host.\n\nI'll weave (sorry) the passage into the dispatch-overview section of `docs/001-architecture.md` next to where the attempt loop is described. Verbatim as quotation, attributed by date.\n\n---\n\n## Still open before I write code\n\nTwo questions still pending:\n\n**(1) Iterator flip-switch — Reading A, B, or C?**\n\n- **A** — what 233 shipped: output iteration (one output → N branches round-robin). Flip switch in inspector is the existing routing-kind dropdown.\n- **B** — input iteration (a box that fires once per element of an array-valued input port). New behavior.\n- **C** — input port iteration (fire once per filled input port instead of once when all ports filled). Also new.\n\nOr some other reading I missed.\n\n**(2) Pre-commit work order:**\n\nI have these commits queued in my head, in this order. Want to confirm or reorder:\n\n1. Architecture docs (top of `001-architecture.md`) — structural-shell statement + the weaving passage.\n2. Issue 244 — data-box pull model.\n3. Update issue 304 — rewrite to describe the attempt-task model + new task-cell layout + box-refcount slot.\n4. Issue 302 implementation — slab allocator + LVH refcount + eager neighbor-merge + on-failure deep sweep + box-refcount field on box_runtime_state.\n\nEach commits separately, trinity-style. Sound right?"

## [924]

```json
{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"cea93de4-0946-44c9-b50d-051ad05961b5",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-21T05:06:47.962Z",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "sessionId":"eca8747e-4b7c-48e6-abc6-4daf904fec3f",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"## Reading A — full picture\n\nA box configured with `routing.kind = \"iterator\"` declares `n_outputs` (an integer ≥ 1). The box gets `n_outputs` named output ports — `out_0`, `out_1`, …, `out_{n-1}` — laid out on the right edge in order.\n\nWhen the box fires:\n1. It consumes its inputs the normal way (one value from each input slot — same as any other box).\n2. It produces ONE output value (also the normal way — single-output rule from 218).\n3. The dispatch layer reads-and-increments a per-box atomic counter slot (`SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER`, from 302), takes the counter `mod n_outputs`, and routes the output value to *only that one branch*.\n\nSo with `n_outputs = 3`:\n- Invocation 1 → `out_0` fires, `out_1` and `out_2` stay silent.\n- Invocation 2 → `out_1` fires.\n- Invocation 3 → `out_2` fires.\n- Invocation 4 → `out_0` again. And so on.\n\nEach branch's wire (or fan-out of wires) fires only on the invocations it was rotated to. The atomic counter is shared across parallel iterator-task workers, so two simultaneous invocations on two workers get distinct branch indices — no race, no coordination, no double-firing.\n\nUse cases:\n- **Round-robin distribution** across N downstream consumers (load spreading).\n- **Cyclic pattern emission** (a stamp-and-rotate box marking three different sinks in turn).\n- **N-phase pipeline** (boxes downstream of `out_0` do step 1, `out_1` does step 2 — though typically a series of plain calls reads cleaner for that).\n\nIt's the **output-side** counterpart to variadic inputs (217). Variadic inputs let one port accept N wires; iterator outputs let one port distribute to N wires across invocations.\n\nThe flip switch in the inspector is the existing mode dropdown 233 shipped: `plain | comparator | iterator`. Picking `iterator` exposes the `n_outputs` integer control. No new switch needed — what's there does this exactly.\n\n---\n\n## Commits\n\nPlan acknowledged: **commit 1 is docs** (arch update + 244 + 304 rewrite), **commit 2 is code** (302 implementation). Doing commit 1 now."

      "content":"## Execution model — phase 3 (thread pool)\n\nTasks are ephemeral; box state is durable. Each box owns one slot\nper input port plus optional state (iterator counter, language\nhandle). A **task** is one stack frame on a worker — `box_id` is\nall it carries. Tasks come and go; boxes persist for the run.\n\n### Slots\n\nEvery input port has exactly one slot, allocated at graph load and\nfreed at run end. A wire is a routing declaration; the producer\ndoesn't own a slot — its output is a push event into every\ndownstream input slot it's wired to. Fan-out is N pushes; fan-in is\nN producers pushing into one slot.\n\nSlot modes:\n\n| Mode                    | Cells   | Reads via         | Used for                                    |\n|-------------------------|---------|-------------------|---------------------------------------------|\n| 1-cell peek             | 1       | `slot_peek`       | Literals; wires from runs-once producers    |\n| N-cell pop              | N       | `slot_pop`        | Wires whose producer runs many times        |\n| `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER`   | 1 atom  | `slot_read_inc`   | Iterator / randomizer / weighted counters   |\n\nCompile-time analysis decides per wire: a producer is \"runs-once\" if\nno transitive ancestor is an iterator, else \"runs-N-times.\" The\nformer gets a 1-cell peek slot (subsequent consumer tasks re-read the\nsame value); the latter gets an N-cell ring (FIFO drain, one cell\nper consumer task).\n\nVariable-size payloads (long LLM outputs, dynamically-sized arrays)\nlive in a separate **large-value heap**. The slot then holds a small\nfixed-size handle `{ uint32_t size; uint32_t offset; }`. The slot\nallocator only ever sees fixed-size slots; the two-tier scheme keeps\nthe hot path simple while supporting unbounded values.\n\n### Cell tagging for parallel iterators\n\nEach cell optionally carries a 4-byte ordering tag alongside its\ndata. Iterator pushes carry their counter value as the tag; slots\ndownstream of an iterator are allocated with `SLOT_TAGGED`, and\n`slot_pop` on a tagged slot returns the **lowest-tag** cell — not\nthe head. This preserves iteration order across parallel iterator\nworkers (task K of iterator A may push before task K-1 if it landed\non a faster worker; the tag makes the consumer see the values in\niteration order regardless).\n\nWhen a consumer has two tagged inputs from two iterators, each port\npops in tag order independently — pairing falls out as `(A_K, B_K)`\nfor every K.\n\n### The dispatch action\n\nOne C function, one phase per worker per task:\n\n1. **Read inputs.** For each input port: `slot_peek` (peek mode) or\n   `slot_pop` (pop mode) into a heap buffer. Tasks are spawned only\n   when every input slot has a value (spawn-on-input-ready rule), so\n   no waiting is needed.\n2. **Invoke spec.** Look up the box's `lang`, find the worker's\n   handle for it, call `invoke_native` or `invoke_json` (per the\n   wire's fast-path classification). Output lands in a heap buffer\n   sized to the box's declared output size, or into the large-value\n   heap if the box's output is variable-size.\n3. **Pick the branch.** Dispatch on `routing.kind`:\n   - `plain`: every outgoing wire fires.\n   - `comparator`: compare to `comparand`, fire only `lt`/`eq`/`gt`.\n   - `iterator`: `idx = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)`,\n     fire `out_idx` only.\n   - `randomizer` / `weighted` / `distributor`: kind-specific rule\n     (computes an `idx` from the counter slot or from downstream\n     fill, fires that branch).\n4. **Push.** For each firing wire, `slot_push` into the consumer's\n   input slot. The push carries the appropriate ordering tag\n   (iterator counter snapshot for iterator-rooted wires; 0 for\n   plain). Each push triggers a spawn-on-input-ready check on the\n   consumer; if the check passes, the dispatch layer spawns a new\n   `dispatch_task_t` and the pool picks it up.\n5. **Done.** The action returns; the pool decrements the active-task\n   counter. The action does not block, does not wait, does not park.\n\n### Startup, quiescence, and termination\n\nStartup: the pool runner pushes literal-input values into the\ncorresponding slots, then spawns first tasks for boxes whose input\nsets are now satisfied. Iterator counter slots start at 0.\n\nQuiescence: the main thread waits on a condition variable that\nsignals when the pool's active-task counter reaches zero with no\npending spawns. That's the run-over signal. The graph validator at\nload time rejects non-iterator cycles, so the run cannot deadlock —\nan iterator with no upstream pushes simply contributes nothing\nfurther, and once the counter drains, termination fires.\n\nHard-crash error policy: a nonzero `invoke_*` return aborts the\nprocess. No retry, no per-task failed state, no fallback executor.\n\n### Blocking-aware iterator pattern\n\nLong-running operations (network calls, LLM inference) hold their\nworker for the duration. Pool size is the budget. The cooperative\npattern for not holding a worker for minutes: split the call into a\n\"kickoff\" box and a \"check-done\" iterator that polls. Each pass\nthrough the iterator releases the worker between checks. Documented\nfully in `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.\n\n## Run output — `tmp/last-run.jsonl`\n\nPhase 3 writes one JSON object per event, one event per line, to\n`tmp/last-run.jsonl`. The format decouples the runner from the\neditor — the editor never displays run results; the file is for LLM",

          "new_string":"# SoraMech — Architecture\n\n## The structural shell\n\nSoraMech is a structural shell. The thread pool, the slot store, the\ndispatch layer, the allocator — these are the steel and concrete of\nan apartment building. They hold the roof up. They do not decorate\nthe rooms.\n\nBox authors design the rooms. Library authors furnish them. The\nshell provides the framing, the load-bearing walls, the structural\nguarantees of what can hang where. The shell does not know what\ncolour the curtains are.\n\n> \"We are creating a structural shell, like an apartment building\n> that is just steel and concrete at first, and the user can build\n> the walls and windows and design the doors and movement paths as\n> they please. The library authors are doing the actual decorating,\n> with tables and chairs and pictures of the beach. We are\n> structural, we keep the roof from caving in. To that end, we must\n> be rigid. We must be firm. We must be flexible.\" — 2026-05-20\n\nTwo consequences shape every design decision below.\n\n### One allocator function per kind of operation\n\nFor each distinct kind of allocation the runtime needs, exactly one\nfunction performs it. The same function is called from every box's\nhot path; only its parameters vary. The user's code, the spec's\ncode, the dispatch layer's code — all reach the same entry point.\n\nThis is the rigidity. The shell does not present \"convenient\nshortcuts\" for special cases. Every value lifecycle goes through\nthe same allocator. Every task struct comes from the same slab.\nEvery wire push goes through the same `slot_push`. No alternatives,\nno escape hatches.\n\nThe exceptions are setup and teardown: the graph loader allocates\nevery box's slot table once at startup before the pool launches;\n`pool_destroy` releases everything in one shot at the end. Outside\nthose two moments, the shell is uniform.\n\n### No single-threaded process outside the pool\n\nEvery piece of runtime work — every allocation, every reference\ncount update, every dispatch action, every cleanup — happens\ninside a pool task. There is no background garbage collector, no\nmaintenance daemon, no separate scheduler. The pool is the\nuniversal scheduler; the pool task is the universal unit of work.\n\nConsequences:\n\n- The allocator's deep sweep, when it runs, runs inside the\n  failing-to-allocate task. There is no \"sweep thread\" polling for\n  free memory. There is no quiescence-triggered sweep either — we\n  cannot assume there will ever be a quiescent moment in a graph\n  with self-feeding iterators.\n- Reference count decrements happen at the end of the task that\n  was holding the reference. Cleanup is the task's last act, not\n  a separate worker's job.\n- Box-level retirement (when all of a box's possible inputs are\n  exhausted) is checked inside the task whose completion may have\n  triggered the retirement condition.\n\nThe pool's parallelism is the only parallelism the runtime\nprovides. A side thread would be a different shape — a violation\nof the uniform \"one allocator, one scheduler\" rule.\n\n## Three programs, one data format",

```json

    "newString":"# SoraMech — Architecture\n\n## The structural shell\n\nSoraMech is a structural shell. The thread pool, the slot store, the\ndispatch layer, the allocator — these are the steel and concrete of\nan apartment building. They hold the roof up. They do not decorate\nthe rooms.\n\nBox authors design the rooms. Library authors furnish them. The\nshell provides the framing, the load-bearing walls, the structural\nguarantees of what can hang where. The shell does not know what\ncolour the curtains are.\n\n> \"We are creating a structural shell, like an apartment building\n> that is just steel and concrete at first, and the user can build\n> the walls and windows and design the doors and movement paths as\n> they please. The library authors are doing the actual decorating,\n> with tables and chairs and pictures of the beach. We are\n> structural, we keep the roof from caving in. To that end, we must\n> be rigid. We must be firm. We must be flexible.\" — 2026-05-20\n\nTwo consequences shape every design decision below.\n\n### One allocator function per kind of operation\n\nFor each distinct kind of allocation the runtime needs, exactly one\nfunction performs it. The same function is called from every box's\nhot path; only its parameters vary. The user's code, the spec's\ncode, the dispatch layer's code — all reach the same entry point.\n\nThis is the rigidity. The shell does not present \"convenient\nshortcuts\" for special cases. Every value lifecycle goes through\nthe same allocator. Every task struct comes from the same slab.\nEvery wire push goes through the same `slot_push`. No alternatives,\nno escape hatches.\n\nThe exceptions are setup and teardown: the graph loader allocates\nevery box's slot table once at startup before the pool launches;\n`pool_destroy` releases everything in one shot at the end. Outside\nthose two moments, the shell is uniform.\n\n### No single-threaded process outside the pool\n\nEvery piece of runtime work — every allocation, every reference\ncount update, every dispatch action, every cleanup — happens\ninside a pool task. There is no background garbage collector, no\nmaintenance daemon, no separate scheduler. The pool is the\nuniversal scheduler; the pool task is the universal unit of work.\n\nConsequences:\n\n- The allocator's deep sweep, when it runs, runs inside the\n  failing-to-allocate task. There is no \"sweep thread\" polling for\n  free memory. There is no quiescence-triggered sweep either — we\n  cannot assume there will ever be a quiescent moment in a graph\n  with self-feeding iterators.\n- Reference count decrements happen at the end of the task that\n  was holding the reference. Cleanup is the task's last act, not\n  a separate worker's job.\n- Box-level retirement (when all of a box's possible inputs are\n  exhausted) is checked inside the task whose completion may have\n  triggered the retirement condition.\n\nThe pool's parallelism is the only parallelism the runtime\nprovides. A side thread would be a different shape — a violation\nof the uniform \"one allocator, one scheduler\" rule.\n\n## Three programs, one data format",

```json
{

  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "name":"Edit",
        "id":"toolu_014toLqeGnrQ6tUcsafCN8zc",
        "caller":{
          "type":"direct"
        },
        "type":"tool_use",
        "input":{
          "new_string":"### The dispatch action — the attempt loop\n\nEvery task in the pool is an **attempt task**. The pool's queue\nholds attempt tasks; workers pick them up; each attempt either\nadvances the graph by one box invocation or returns without doing\nanything. There is no separate \"readiness check\" task kind. An\nattempt that finds its inputs ready *is* the work invocation; an\nattempt that doesn't, returns and disappears.\n\n```\nproducer task:\n   compute output\n   for each downstream consumer box C this producer just touched:\n      write all values to C's input slots\n         (snapshotted into the attempt's cell at the END)\n   for each distinct C:\n      slab_alloc() → attempt_task for C\n      pool_spawn(attempt_task)\n   slab_free(this cell)\n\nattempt task:\n   if every required input on C is satisfiable\n      (slot value or data-box pull):\n      snapshot values into local vars\n      invoke spec, get output\n      push output to downstream consumer slots\n      submit one attempt per distinct downstream consumer\n      decrement input $ref counts\n      decrement upstream boxes' live_predecessor_count if applicable\n   slab_free(this cell)\n```\n\nThe producer task and the attempt task are the same shape of\nallocation, same call site, same return path. One cell per\ninvocation in the steady-state hot path; no double-allocation\nbetween \"check that I'm ready\" and \"do my work.\"\n\nThree properties fall out:\n\n- **Targeted attempts.** A producer knows which consumer boxes it\n  just pushed to; the attempts it submits are for those specific\n  consumers, not a generic re-evaluation of every consumer in the\n  graph.\n- **One readiness check per producer task.** Even if a producer\n  writes to multiple slots on the same consumer, only one attempt\n  is submitted for that consumer. The submission happens at the\n  END of the producer, after every output value has been placed —\n  the attempt is guaranteed to find a coherent input set, not a\n  half-written one.\n- **No parking.** An attempt that finds its inputs unsatisfied\n  returns. The shell does not hold tasks in waiting states. The\n  next producer push to any of the consumer's input slots triggers\n  another attempt with the same shape. Eventually one of those\n  attempts finds the input set complete and runs the work.\n\n> \"the most recent change that would enable the box to run —\n> essentially, our logic is such that the fewest amount of steps\n> between each function call must be made, while enabling the\n> long-tail async threads to do non-blocking tasks on their own\n> time. As soon as they can, they knit themselves with their\n> fellow threads, co-creating a weaving texture of computer\n> programming. proving without a doubt that intelligence can have\n> a dynamical host.\" — 2026-05-20\n\nRouting kinds (per 233) dispatch the output-side push: `plain` fans\nto every wire, `comparator` picks one of `lt`/`eq`/`gt` by numeric\ncomparison, `iterator` reads-and-increments a per-box atomic\ncounter slot mod `n_outputs` and fires only the picked branch. The\nfollow-on kinds (randomizer / weighted / distributor) live in\nissues 240–242.\n\nCross-language pushes carry a `$ref` handle when the output value\nis variable-size (per 312/317): the producer writes the bytes to\nthe large-value heap once, refcount = number of consuming slots,\nand writes the `(ptr, length)` handle into each consumer slot. The\nbytes themselves are never copied; the consumer's spec follows the\npointer to read.",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"### The dispatch action\n\nOne C function, one phase per worker per task:\n\n1. **Read inputs.** For each input port: `slot_peek` (peek mode) or\n   `slot_pop` (pop mode) into a heap buffer. Tasks are spawned only\n   when every input slot has a value (spawn-on-input-ready rule), so\n   no waiting is needed.\n2. **Invoke spec.** Look up the box's `lang`, find the worker's\n   handle for it, call `invoke_native` or `invoke_json` (per the\n   wire's fast-path classification). Output lands in a heap buffer\n   sized to the box's declared output size, or into the large-value\n   heap if the box's output is variable-size.\n3. **Pick the branch.** Dispatch on `routing.kind`:\n   - `plain`: every outgoing wire fires.\n   - `comparator`: compare to `comparand`, fire only `lt`/`eq`/`gt`.\n   - `iterator`: `idx = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)`,\n     fire `out_idx` only.\n   - `randomizer` / `weighted` / `distributor`: kind-specific rule\n     (computes an `idx` from the counter slot or from downstream\n     fill, fires that branch).\n4. **Push.** For each firing wire, `slot_push` into the consumer's\n   input slot. The push carries the appropriate ordering tag\n   (iterator counter snapshot for iterator-rooted wires; 0 for\n   plain). Each push triggers a spawn-on-input-ready check on the\n   consumer; if the check passes, the dispatch layer spawns a new\n   `dispatch_task_t` and the pool picks it up.\n5. **Done.** The action returns; the pool decrements the active-task\n   counter. The action does not block, does not wait, does not park.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/001-architecture.md"
        }
      }],

## [944]

```json
{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"6c71cbcb-f138-4864-98df-6c579cad180f",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-21T05:09:58.525Z",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "toolUseResult":{
    "content":"# 244 — Data boxes as round-robin default providers, pulled on demand\n\n## Status\nopen · design\n\n## Current behavior\n\nIssue 229 renamed `kind: data` to `kind: read` and reshaped the box\nso its value can come from either a file path or an inline literal.\nThe current dispatch model (304) treats a read box as a producer:\nat pool startup the runner pushes the read box's value into every\nconsumer slot wired from it. After that single push, the read box\nis \"done\" — it never pushes again.\n\nThis breaks down in two cases:\n\n1. **Multiple read boxes feeding the same input slot.** The slot\n   ends up holding one value (whichever read box's startup-push\n   landed first) and silently ignores the others. The user's\n   intent — \"rotate among these values\" — is not honored.\n2. **A read box feeding a slot whose other producers fire many\n   times.** Once the read box's startup push is consumed, the slot\n   sits empty until a call-box producer fills it. If the consumer\n   fires N times and the call-box producer also fires N times,\n   the read box's value is consumed at most once. The user's\n   intent — \"this is a default that's always available\" — is not\n   honored.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA read box is an **inexhaustible source**, not a one-shot producer.\nIts declared value is always available, on every consumer's\nrequest. Consumers pull from read boxes when they need a value and\nno value is currently waiting in the slot.\n\n### Pull, not push\n\nRead boxes do not push at startup, do not appear in the pool's task\nqueue, and do not have task structs of their own. They are\n**callable sources** whose state lives in the box's runtime record:\n\n- For an inline literal (`value` field set), the value sits in the\n  box's record as bytes ready to copy.\n- For a file path (`path` field set), the bytes are read once at\n  graph load and cached in the box's record. The user editing the\n  file mid-run is not supported; the cached bytes are the source of\n  truth for the run.\n\nThe attempt-task model from the architecture doc makes the pull\nhappen naturally. When an attempt task examines a consumer's input\nslots, the check is now:\n\n```\nfor each required input port:\n   if the slot has a value waiting (ring buffer non-empty):\n      take that value\n   elif the port has any read-box predecessor:\n      round-robin pull from the next read-box predecessor\n   else:\n      not ready — return from the attempt\n```\n\nThe pull copies the read box's value (or its `$ref` handle, if\nthe value is variable-size) into the consumer's local snapshot.\nThe read box's record is unchanged.\n\n### Round-robin across multiple read-box predecessors\n\nA consumer input port with N read-box predecessors carries a small\npiece of state on the consumer box:\n\n```\ninput_port_state {\n   data_box_ids: [box_id, box_id, ...],   // declared order\n   rr_index:     0                        // next to pull from\n}\n```\n\nThe attempt task uses `data_box_ids[rr_index]`, increments\n`rr_index` mod `len(data_box_ids)`, and proceeds. Multiple attempt\ntasks running in parallel for the same consumer use the same\ncounter via the atomic-increment slot operation from 302 — distinct\nattempts get distinct indices, no race.\n\n### Mixed predecessors: read boxes as defaults\n\nA consumer port may have a mix of call-box predecessors AND\nread-box predecessors. The attempt rule (slot-first, read-box-\nfallback) handles this naturally:\n\n- If a call-box producer has pushed a value, the slot is non-empty\n  and the attempt consumes from there.\n- If the slot is empty, the attempt pulls from the next read-box\n  predecessor.\n\nSo a read box behaves as a **default value** for the slot — used\nonly when no call-box producer has supplied an actual value. This\nmatches the typical use: \"supply a fallback host address, but if a\ncall box computes a custom one, use the custom one instead.\"\n\n## Schema implications\n\nThe compile-time check from 230 currently requires every\nnon-optional input port to be wired, carry a literal, or be marked\noptional. Under this issue, **a read-box predecessor on the port\nalso satisfies the requirement** — the port is guaranteed to be\nfed at attempt time, just via pull rather than push.\n\n`src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` extends:\n\n```\nstate if any of:\n   has_wire (any producer-class predecessor)        ← unchanged\n   has_literal (port.value set)                     ← unchanged\n   has_data_box_predecessor (read-box predecessor)  ← new\n   is_optional (port.optional == true)              ← unchanged\n```\n\nThe editor's compile-or-save validation surfaces the same check;\nthe user sees an error if a required port has none of the above.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` — extend to\n   recognize read-box-as-predecessor as a satisfying state.\n2. `src/010-graph-loader.c` — at graph load, walk every consumer\n   box; for each input port, compute the list of read-box\n   predecessors and store as part of the port's runtime state.\n   Cache each read box's value bytes (or LVH handle) in the box's\n   runtime record.\n3. `src/012-dispatch.c` — the attempt-task's input check\n   incorporates the read-box pull: slot first, else round-robin\n   from `data_box_ids[rr_index]`.\n4. The startup phase no longer spawns tasks for read boxes (or\n   pushes their values eagerly). Read boxes are graph-load data\n   only; they do not appear in the pool's queue.\n5. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-defaults/` — a consumer with one\n   call-box and one read-box predecessor, exercising both \"value\n   available\" and \"fallback pulled\" paths.\n6. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-rotation/` — a consumer with three\n   read-box predecessors, asserting round-robin order over a series\n   of attempt invocations.\n\n## Cycle behavior\n\nPull-on-demand removes a startup-ordering concern: a graph with a\nread box feeding two consumers no longer depends on \"did the read\nbox's push land before either consumer fired its first attempt?\" —\nthe attempts pull when they need to, regardless of order. Iterators\ndownstream of read boxes work cleanly: each iteration's attempt\npulls fresh from the read box (or its rotation).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/completed/229-data-box-as-language-agnostic-file-io.md` —\n  parent; renamed data→read/write. This issue extends the read-box\n  semantics from \"one-shot producer\" to \"inexhaustible pull-source.\"\n- `issues/completed/230-required-inputs-and-optional-flag.md` —\n  parent; this issue adds a third satisfying state to its check.\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — extended binding check.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.c` — per-port read-box-predecessor list\n  computed at load.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — attempt-task input pull.\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — the attempt loop (described in the\n  \"structural shell\" section) is the place where the pull happens.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Read-box value mutation during a run.** A file-backed read box\n  whose file changes mid-run: do we re-read on every pull, or stay\n  with the load-time cached value? Lean toward \"load-time cache\"\n  (deterministic, no I/O per pull, mirrors the immutability of the\n  graph during a run). Re-read on pull is a follow-on if the use\n  case appears.\n- **Round-robin determinism across parallel attempts.** The atomic\n  counter for `rr_index` gives every attempt a distinct index, but\n  the order in which attempts complete is non-deterministic. If\n  attempts A1 and A2 both pull index 0 and index 1 respectively\n  but A2 finishes first, the consumer's overall output sequence\n  reflects A2 before A1. This is the same parallel-iterator\n  ordering question 302's tagged slots already solve. Apply the\n  same tagging: attempts that pull from read boxes carry the\n  pulled index as a tag, downstream consumers reorder by tag.\n",
    "userModified":false,
    "type":"create",
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/244-data-box-pull-on-demand.md",
    "structuredPatch":[]

Under this issue, **a read-box predecessor on the port\nalso satisfies the requirement** — the port is guaranteed to be\nfed at attempt time, just via pull rather than push.\n\n`src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` extends:\n\n```\nstate if any of:\n   has_wire (any producer-class predecessor)        ← unchanged\n   has_literal (port.value set)                     ← unchanged\n   has_data_box_predecessor (read-box predecessor)  ← new\n   is_optional (port.optional == true)              ← unchanged\n```\n\nThe editor's compile-or-save validation surfaces the same check;\nthe user sees an error if a required port has none of the above.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` — extend to\n   recognize read-box-as-predecessor as a satisfying state.\n2. `src/010-graph-loader.c` — at graph load, walk every consumer\n   box; for each input port, compute the list of read-box\n   predecessors and store as part of the port's runtime state.\n   Cache each read box's value bytes (or LVH handle) in the box's\n   runtime record.\n3. `src/012-dispatch.c` — the attempt-task's input check\n   incorporates the read-box pull: slot first, else round-robin\n   from `data_box_ids[rr_index]`.\n4. The startup phase no longer spawns tasks for read boxes (or\n   pushes their values eagerly). Read boxes are graph-load data\n   only; they do not appear in the pool's queue.\n5. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-defaults/` — a consumer with one\n   call-box and one read-box predecessor, exercising both \"value\n   available\" and \"fallback pulled\" paths.\n6. Fixture: `tests/maps/data-box-rotation/` — a consumer with three\n   read-box predecessors, asserting round-robin order over a series\n   of attempt invocations.\n\n## Cycle behavior\n\nPull-on-demand removes a startup-ordering concern: a graph with a\nread box feeding two consumers no longer depends on \"did the read\nbox's push land before either consumer fired its first attempt?\" —\nthe attempts pull when they need to, regardless of order. Iterators\ndownstream of read boxes work cleanly: each iteration's attempt\npulls fresh from the read box (or its rotation).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/completed/229-data-box-as-language-agnostic-file-io.md` —\n  parent; renamed data→read/write. This issue extends the read-box\n  semantics from \"one-shot producer\" to \"inexhaustible pull-source.\"\n- `issues/completed/230-required-inputs-and-optional-flag.md` —\n  parent; this issue adds a third satisfying state to its check.\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — extended binding check.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.c` — per-port read-box-predecessor list\n  computed at load.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — attempt-task input pull.\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — the attempt loop (described in the\n  \"structural shell\" section) is the place where the pull happens.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Read-box value mutation during a run.** A file-backed read box\n  whose file changes mid-run: do we re-read on every pull, or stay\n  with the load-time cached value? Lean toward \"load-time cache\"\n  (deterministic, no I/O per pull, mirrors the immutability of the\n  graph during a run). Re-read on pull is a follow-on if the use\n  case appears.\n- **Round-robin determinism across parallel attempts.** The atomic\n  counter for `rr_index` gives every attempt a distinct index, but\n  the order in which attempts complete is non-deterministic. If\n  attempts A1 and A2 both pull index 0 and index 1 respectively\n  but A2 finishes first, the consumer's overall output sequence\n  reflects A2 before A1. This is the same parallel-iterator\n  ordering question 302's tagged slots already solve. Apply the\n  same tagging: attempts that pull from read boxes carry the\n  pulled index as a tag, downstream consumers reorder by tag.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/244-data-box-pull-on-demand.md"
        }

Single-threaded,\nblocking, runs in Lua coroutines.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe task dispatch layer is the C component that runs inside each pool\nworker. The pool calls a single C action — `dispatch_action` — per\ntask. That action is the one place in the runtime that:\n\n- Reads from and writes to slots\n- Calls `lang_spec->invoke`\n- Picks the output branch per `routing.kind` (issue 233)\n- Pushes the function's output to the picked branch's downstream\n  input slots, triggering downstream task spawns\n\nThere is no Lua-level executor in the phase 3 path. `004-executor.lua`\nis replaced wholesale.\n\n## Task struct\n\nA task is one ephemeral invocation of a box. ## [958]

```json
{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"277fbff3-16e7-48bf-b0fb-f46d0befe20a",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-21T05:11:25.721Z",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "sessionId":"eca8747e-4b7c-48e6-abc6-4daf904fec3f",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "name":"Write",
        "id":"toolu_01UYakt21oKoSshseSFdRX42",
        "caller":{
          "type":"direct"
        },
        "type":"tool_use",
        "input":{
          "content":"## Concept\n\nThe task dispatch layer is the C component every pool worker runs.\nEvery task in the pool is an **attempt task** — same shape, same\nallocation, same call site. An attempt task either advances the\ngraph by one box invocation (when its consumer's inputs are\nready) or returns without doing anything (when they aren't).\n\nThere is no separate \"readiness check\" task kind. There is no\n\"work task\" kind distinct from a check. There is one kind, the\nattempt; the work it performs is conditional on what it finds.\n\nThe architecture doc's \"structural shell\" section frames this:\none allocator per kind of operation, one scheduler (the pool),\none task shape. The dispatch action is the one place the runtime:\n\n- Reads from input ring buffers (or pulls from read-box predecessors)\n- Calls the language spec's `invoke`\n- Picks the output branch per `routing.kind`\n- Pushes the output value into every downstream consumer slot\n- Submits attempt tasks for the consumers whose input sets may\n  have just become satisfiable\n\n`004-executor.lua` is replaced wholesale. There is no Lua-level\nexecutor in phase 3.\n\n## Task struct (cell layout)\n\nA task struct is a 64-byte slab cell. The layout reserves space\nfor every field every attempt may need; the fields' meaning is\nthe same for \"this attempt found ready inputs and ran\" and \"this\nattempt didn't find ready inputs and returned.\" One shape, two\noutcomes.\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void   *next_free;          /* 8B — free-list link, overwritten on alloc */\n    box_t  *box;                /* 8B — the box this attempt is for */\n    uint32_t task_id;           /* 4B — event-log correlation (311) */\n    uint32_t flags;             /* 4B — work / attempt / priority hint */\n    void   *output_destinations;/* 8B — per-wire consumer slot pointers */\n    void   *input_snapshot;     /* 8B — values OR pointer to values-array */\n    uint32_t live_wire_count;   /* 4B — box-refcount slot (244 / retirement) */\n    uint32_t _pad;              /* 4B — alignment */\n    /* remaining 16B available for inline input snapshot or extensions */\n} attempt_task_t;\n```\n\nThe `live_wire_count` slot is the documented placeholder for the\nbox-level retirement system. The dispatch action populates it at\ncreation; the box-retirement consumer that DOES something with\nthe count is the stretch goal in 302. Until that ships, the slot\nis honest but unread — its presence is documentation that the\nfield belongs in the design.\n\nThe `input_snapshot` is the FIFO-popped values from each input\nslot's ring buffer (or the pointer to a read-box's value when\npulled per 244). Once the attempt has snapshotted, the slot\nstate is independent of the task's execution.\n\nThe `output_destinations` is the array of consumer slot pointers\nthe attempt will write to — one per outgoing wire (or one per\nfiring branch, for routed boxes). Pre-computed at graph load and\nreferenced through the box pointer.\n\n## The dispatch action — the attempt loop\n\n```\nproducer task (a completing attempt that ran):\n   compute output via spec invoke\n   for each downstream consumer box C this producer just touched:\n      write all values to C's input slots\n         (snapshotted into the attempt's cell at the END)\n   for each distinct C:\n      slab_alloc() → attempt_task for C\n      pool_spawn(attempt_task)\n   decrement input $ref counts\n   decrement upstream boxes' live_predecessor_count if applicable\n   slab_free(this cell)\n\nattempt task (newly picked up by a worker):\n   if every required input on C is satisfiable\n      (slot value or data-box pull per 244):\n      snapshot values into local vars\n      invoke spec, get output\n      [continue as producer task above]\n   slab_free(this cell)\n```\n\nThree properties of this loop:\n\n- **Targeted attempts.** A producer knows which consumer boxes it\n  just pushed to; it submits attempts for *those specific\n  consumers*, not a generic re-evaluation.\n- **One attempt per (producer, consumer-box) pair.** Even if a\n  producer writes to multiple slots on the same consumer, only\n  one attempt is submitted for that consumer. Dedup happens at\n  the end of the producer's run, after every output value has\n  been placed. The attempt is guaranteed to find a coherent\n  input set, not a half-written one.\n- **No parking.** An attempt that finds its inputs unsatisfied\n  returns. The shell does not hold tasks in waiting states. The\n  next producer push to any of the consumer's input slots\n  triggers another attempt with the same shape. Eventually one\n  of those attempts finds the input set complete and runs the\n  work.\n\nThe attempt task's \"if inputs ready, run\" branch IS the\ninline-fast-path for same-language chains. There is no separate\nspawn step between the readiness decision and the work; the work\njust happens, in the same allocation, on the same worker. A\nproducer pushing into a fast same-language consumer fires an\nattempt that runs immediately on whichever worker picks it up —\none allocation, one queue round-trip per box invocation.\n\n## Initial submission\n\nAt startup the pool runner walks the graph and submits an attempt\ntask for each **entry box** (a box whose required inputs are all\nsatisfiable from literal values or read-box predecessors, i.e.\nwhose attempt would succeed on first try). Read boxes do NOT\npush at startup under 244 — they're pulled on demand from inside\nattempts that find their slots empty and their port has a\nread-box predecessor.\n\nIterator counter slots start at 0. Literal-only entry boxes\nsubmit their first attempt at startup and increment from there.\n\n",
          "file_path":"/tmp/304-front.txt"
        }
      }],

    "content":"## Concept\n\nThe task dispatch layer is the C component every pool worker runs.\nEvery task in the pool is an **attempt task** — same shape, same\nallocation, same call site. An attempt task either advances the\ngraph by one box invocation (when its consumer's inputs are\nready) or returns without doing anything (when they aren't).\n\nThere is no separate \"readiness check\" task kind. There is no\n\"work task\" kind distinct from a check. There is one kind, the\nattempt; the work it performs is conditional on what it finds.\n\nThe architecture doc's \"structural shell\" section frames this:\none allocator per kind of operation, one scheduler (the pool),\none task shape. The dispatch action is the one place the runtime:\n\n- Reads from input ring buffers (or pulls from read-box predecessors)\n- Calls the language spec's `invoke`\n- Picks the output branch per `routing.kind`\n- Pushes the output value into every downstream consumer slot\n- Submits attempt tasks for the consumers whose input sets may\n  have just become satisfiable\n\n`004-executor.lua` is replaced wholesale. There is no Lua-level\nexecutor in phase 3.\n\n## Task struct (cell layout)\n\nA task struct is a 64-byte slab cell. The layout reserves space\nfor every field every attempt may need; the fields' meaning is\nthe same for \"this attempt found ready inputs and ran\" and \"this\nattempt didn't find ready inputs and returned.\" One shape, two\noutcomes.\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void   *next_free;          /* 8B — free-list link, overwritten on alloc */\n    box_t  *box;                /* 8B — the box this attempt is for */\n    uint32_t task_id;           /* 4B — event-log correlation (311) */\n    uint32_t flags;             /* 4B — work / attempt / priority hint */\n    void   *output_destinations;/* 8B — per-wire consumer slot pointers */\n    void   *input_snapshot;     /* 8B — values OR pointer to values-array */\n    uint32_t live_wire_count;   /* 4B — box-refcount slot (244 / retirement) */\n    uint32_t _pad;              /* 4B — alignment */\n    /* remaining 16B available for inline input snapshot or extensions */\n} attempt_task_t;\n```\n\nThe `live_wire_count` slot is the documented placeholder for the\nbox-level retirement system. The dispatch action populates it at\ncreation; the box-retirement consumer that DOES something with\nthe count is the stretch goal in 302. Until that ships, the slot\nis honest but unread — its presence is documentation that the\nfield belongs in the design.\n\nThe `input_snapshot` is the FIFO-popped values from each input\nslot's ring buffer (or the pointer to a read-box's value when\npulled per 244). Once the attempt has snapshotted, the slot\nstate is independent of the task's execution.\n\nThe `output_destinations` is the array of consumer slot pointers\nthe attempt will write to — one per outgoing wire (or one per\nfiring branch, for routed boxes). Pre-computed at graph load and\nreferenced through the box pointer.\n\n## The dispatch action — the attempt loop\n\n```\nproducer task (a completing attempt that ran):\n   compute output via spec invoke\n   for each downstream consumer box C this producer just touched:\n      write all values to C's input slots\n         (snapshotted into the attempt's cell at the END)\n   for each distinct C:\n      slab_alloc() → attempt_task for C\n      pool_spawn(attempt_task)\n   decrement input $ref counts\n   decrement upstream boxes' live_predecessor_count if applicable\n   slab_free(this cell)\n\nattempt task (newly picked up by a worker):\n   if every required input on C is satisfiable\n      (slot value or data-box pull per 244):\n      snapshot values into local vars\n      invoke spec, get output\n      [continue as producer task above]\n   slab_free(this cell)\n```\n\nThree properties of this loop:\n\n- **Targeted attempts.** A producer knows which consumer boxes it\n  just pushed to; it submits attempts for *those specific\n  consumers*, not a generic re-evaluation.\n- **One attempt per (producer, consumer-box) pair.** Even if a\n  producer writes to multiple slots on the same consumer, only\n  one attempt is submitted for that consumer. Dedup happens at\n  the end of the producer's run, after every output value has\n  been placed. The attempt is guaranteed to find a coherent\n  input set, not a half-written one.\n- **No parking.** An attempt that finds its inputs unsatisfied\n  returns. The shell does not hold tasks in waiting states. The\n  next producer push to any of the consumer's input slots\n  triggers another attempt with the same shape. Eventually one\n  of those attempts finds the input set complete and runs the\n  work.\n\nThe attempt task's \"if inputs ready, run\" branch IS the\ninline-fast-path for same-language chains. There is no separate\nspawn step between the readiness decision and the work; the work\njust happens, in the same allocation, on the same worker. A\nproducer pushing into a fast same-language consumer fires an\nattempt that runs immediately on whichever worker picks it up —\none allocation, one queue round-trip per box invocation.\n\n## Initial submission\n\nAt startup the pool runner walks the graph and submits an attempt\ntask for each **entry box** (a box whose required inputs are all\nsatisfiable from literal values or read-box predecessors, i.e.\nwhose attempt would succeed on first try). Read boxes do NOT\npush at startup under 244 — they're pulled on demand from inside\nattempts that find their slots empty and their port has a\nread-box predecessor.\n\nIterator counter slots start at 0. Literal-only entry boxes\nsubmit their first attempt at startup and increment from there.\n\n",

The shell does not hold tasks in waiting states. The\n118\t  next producer push to any of the consumer's input slots\n119\t  triggers another attempt with the same shape. Eventually one\n120\t  of those attempts finds the input set complete and runs the\n121\t  work.\n122\t\n123\tThe attempt task's \"if inputs ready, run\" branch IS the\n124\tinline-fast-path for same-language chains. There is no separate\n125\tspawn step between the readiness decision and the work; the work\n126\tjust happens, in the same allocation, on the same worker. A\n127\tproducer pushing into a fast same-language consumer fires an\n128\tattempt that runs immediately on whichever worker picks it up —\n129\tone allocation, one queue round-trip per box invocation.\n130\t\n131\t## Initial submission\n132\t\n133\tAt startup the pool runner walks the graph and submits an attempt\n134\ttask for each **entry box** (a box whose required inputs are all\n135\tsatisfiable from literal values or read-box predecessors, i.e.\n136\twhose attempt would succeed on first try). Read boxes do NOT\n137\tpush at startup under 244 — they're pulled on demand from inside\n138\tattempts that find their slots empty and their port has a\n139\tread-box predecessor.\n140\t\n141\tIterator counter slots start at 0. Literal-only entry boxes\n142\tsubmit their first attempt at startup and increment from there.\n143\t\n144\t## Iterator counter and parallel iteration\n145\t\n146\tThe iterator's counter lives in a `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot\n147\tallocated for the box at graph load time (issue 302). The\n148\tdispatch action reads and increments it atomically, mid-action:\n149\t\n150\t```c\n151\tuint32_t branch_idx = slot_read_inc(box->counter_slot, n_iter_outputs);\n152\tslot_push(downstream[branch_idx].input_slot, output_buf, output_size,\n153\t          /* tag = */ branch_idx);\n154\t```\n155\t\n156\t`slot_read_inc` returns the current counter value `mod\n157\tn_iter_outputs` and atomically advances the underlying counter.\n158\tConcurrent iterator tasks on different workers each call\n159\t`slot_read_inc` independently and each get a unique value —\n160\t**iterator tasks parallelize across workers**, picking distinct\n161\tbranches without coordination.\n162\t\n163\tNo box-side mutable state, no per-task counter snapshot. The\n164\tcounter is just data in a slot the dispatch layer reads.\n165\t\n166\t## Cross-iterator pairing under parallel iteration\n167\t\n168\tWith parallel iterator tasks, push ordering at the consumer is\n169\tnon-deterministic — task 6 of iterator A may push to consumer C\n170\tbefore task 5 if 6 happened to land on a faster worker. FIFO pop\n171\tat C would consume them out of iteration order.\n172\t\n173\tThe fix is **counter-tagged pushes**. Each iterator push (in phase\n174\t5) carries the counter value the action read for this invocation:\n175\t\n176\t```c\n177\tslot_push(downstream.input_slot, output_buf, output_size,\n178\t          /* tag = */ branch_idx_or_counter_snapshot);\n179\t```\n180\t\n\n...           "new_string":"Verified by re-running all 6 fixture maps and the dedicated\n`test_iterator_multi_fire` test (which now exercises tagged\ninput slots).\n\n### Design rewrite to the attempt-task model — 2026-05-20\n\nWhat changed in the design (not yet in the code):\n\n- The two-phase model (producer's dispatch action calls\n  `dispatch_spawn_if_ready` inline on each consumer; if ready,\n  spawns a fresh `dispatch_task_t` for the consumer) is replaced\n  by the **attempt-task model**. Every task in the pool is an\n  attempt; the work happens conditionally when the attempt finds\n  inputs ready. One allocation per invocation, not two.\n- The task struct grows from `{ box_id }` to the 64-byte cell\n  layout above (free-list link, box pointer, task_id, flags,\n  input snapshot, output destinations, live_wire_count\n  placeholder).\n- Read-box producers stop pushing at startup; they become\n  pull-on-demand sources per issue 244.\n- The \"no parking\" rule from the structural-shell doc holds: an\n  attempt that finds its inputs unsatisfied returns and is\n  collected; the next push to the consumer triggers a fresh\n  attempt.\n\nWhat's still in the code from the older model:\n\n- The `dispatch_action` body in `src/012-dispatch.c` is the\n  two-phase shape: read inputs → invoke → push → inline\n  `dispatch_spawn_if_ready` per consumer. Plain, comparator, and\n  iterator routing all work under this shape.\n- `dispatch_task_t` is still `{ box_id, task_id }` plus a\n  context pointer.\n- Read boxes still push at startup.\n\nThe refactor lands with issue 302's slab-allocator + LVH\nrefcount work, since the task-cell layout and the refcount\nplumbing share the same allocator changes. After 302 ships:\n\n1. `src/012-dispatch.c::dispatch_action` becomes the single\n   attempt-loop body.\n2. Task allocation moves from per-spawn malloc to slab pop.\n3. Spawn logic moves from \"producer inlines check\" to \"producer\n   submits attempts\" — one submission per distinct downstream\n   consumer box, at the END of the producer.\n4. Read-box predecessors are recognized at attempt time and\n   pulled round-robin per 244.\n5. The `live_wire_count` field on the cell is populated by\n   graph load; the box-retirement consumer is the stretch\n   piece that may or may not ship with 302.",

After 302 ships:","+","+1. `src/012-dispatch.c::dispatch_action` becomes the single","+   attempt-loop body.","+2. Task allocation moves from per-spawn malloc to slab pop.","+3. Spawn logic moves from \"producer inlines check\" to \"producer","+   submits attempts\" — one submission per distinct downstream","+   consumer box, at the END of the producer.","+4. Read-box predecessors are recognized at attempt time and","+   pulled round-robin per 244.","+5. The `live_wire_count` field on the cell is populated by","+   graph load; the box-retirement consumer is the stretch","+   piece that may or may not ship with 302."]
      }]
  },

```json
{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"30eaae5c-4c61-41b3-b7dd-ec2135d98a86",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-21T05:15:25.834Z",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "sessionId":"eca8747e-4b7c-48e6-abc6-4daf904fec3f",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "name":"Bash",
        "id":"toolu_01DgCiTYjYKDVaRTHvoW2c7K",
        "caller":{
          "type":"direct"
        },
        "type":"tool_use",
        "input":{
          "command":"git commit -m \"$(cat <<'EOF'\nthe structural shell — dispatch as attempt loop, data boxes as defaults\n\nThe architecture doc grows a top-of-file section naming what\nSoraMech is structurally: an apartment building of steel and\nconcrete that holds the roof up so library and box authors can\ndecorate the rooms. The shell is rigid where it must be — one\nallocator per kind of operation, one scheduler (the pool), one\ntask shape — and flexible where the user lives.\n\nTwo consequences follow and are now stated explicitly. There is\nno single-threaded process outside the pool: every allocation,\nevery reference count update, every cleanup happens inside a\npool task. There is no quiescence-triggered sweep either,\nbecause a graph with self-feeding iterators may never be\nquiescent. The user's framing — \"we are structural, we keep the\nroof from caving in\" — sits in the doc verbatim.\n\nThe dispatch section in the same doc is rewritten to the attempt\nloop. Every task is an attempt; an attempt that finds inputs\nready IS the work; an attempt that doesn't, returns. One task\nkind, one allocation per invocation, no separate readiness\ncheck. Producer tasks submit one attempt per distinct downstream\nconsumer at the END of their own run, so the attempt is\nguaranteed to find a coherent input set. The weaving passage\nthe user wrote during this conversation is preserved verbatim\ninside the dispatch section.\n\nIssue 244 is the new design for read boxes as pull-on-demand\nsources. Multiple read boxes feeding the same input slot rotate\nround-robin; a read box feeding a slot that also has a call-box\nproducer behaves as the default value pulled only when the call\nbox hasn't supplied. The compile-time required-input check\n(issue 230) extends to recognise a read-box predecessor as a\nsatisfying state alongside wires, literals, and the optional\nflag.\n\nIssue 304 is rewritten to describe the attempt-task model and\nthe new 64-byte cell layout — box pointer, task id, flags, input\nsnapshot, output destinations, live_wire_count placeholder for\nthe box-retirement stretch goal. ## [995]

```json
{
  "userType":"external",
  "parentUuid":"51ab96e5-444a-4dc9-bfaa-46dd5ef4dc24",
  "timestamp":"2026-05-21T05:22:37.821Z",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech",
  "sessionId":"eca8747e-4b7c-48e6-abc6-4daf904fec3f",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Yes — full walkthrough, with the planned changes called out inline. **🔧 = 302 lands here.** *⏳ = another open issue will change this later.*\n\n---\n\n## 1 · Authoring (editor side)\n\nUser opens `http://localhost:7700/`, sees the canvas, creates boxes, wires them up, sets literal values and `n_outputs` and `comparand` and `routing.kind` via the inspector. Each save fires `API.put_box(id, data)` → HTTP PUT → `src/005-http-server.lua` writes the JSON to `maps/<name>/boxes/<id>.json`. Schema validation runs on every save through `src/001-schema.lua::validate_box`.\n\n→ No 302 changes here.\n\n## 2 · Compile\n\nUser clicks Compile → `scripts/soramech-compile.sh <map-dir>` runs:\n- Reads `meta.json`, every `boxes/*.json`, every source file the boxes reference.\n- Runs graph-level checks (`src/001-schema.lua::check_input_bindings` — every required port has a wire/literal/optional flag *⏳ 244: extends to recognize read-box predecessors*).\n- Per-spec compile: C boxes get their `.so` built. *⏳ 307: this is where wrapper generation will land — typed signatures parsed from box JSON, wrapper.c emitted, compiled alongside user source.*\n- *⏳ 313: same-language source files concatenated into one translation unit per language; the inlined call graph replaces per-box dispatch entries within a language island.*\n- Copies the runner binary, all sources, all spec `.so`s into `compiled/`.\n\n→ No 302 changes here.\n\n## 3 · Runner startup\n\n`./compiled/pool-runner <map-dir>` launches. The `main` in `src/008-pool-runner.c` parses argv, resolves `langs/` via `/proc/self/exe`, opens the map directory.\n\n→ No 302 changes.\n\n## 4 · Graph load (`src/010-graph-loader.c`)\n\nWalks `boxes/*.json`, parses each via the 314 JSON parser into a `json_arena_t`. Builds `box_runtime_state[]` — one entry per box. Resolves wire endpoints (`from_box`, `to_box` strings → integer indices). Detects non-iterator cycles via DFS, aborts if found. Calls `graph_attach_runtime` to:\n\n- Allocate per-input-port slots via `slot_alloc`. Slot mode (peek vs pop) chosen by the `multi_spawn` BFS (any box reachable from an iterator gets pop-mode ring slots).\n- Resolve per-box spec via `box.lang` lookup in the spec registry.\n- Set `SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE` on slots whose producers have `output_capacity == 0`.\n- Compute the per-box `use_native_invoke` bit (same-language all-neighbors). *⏳ 312: this expands to per-edge `input_edge_native[i]` / `output_edge_native[j]` arrays.*\n\n**🔧 302 adds here:**\n- **`box_runtime_state.live_predecessor_count`** field, populated from the count of distinct upstream producer boxes. (Read-box predecessors don't count for *⏳ 244*: read boxes are pull-only, not producers.)\n- **LVH chunk pool sizing** based on the size-class enumeration the loader does — *305's phase 5 deferred work that I'll finally land as part of 302.*\n\n## 5 · Pool spin-up (`libs/task-pool/pool.c`)\n\n`pool_create(n_workers)` spawns N worker threads, each parked on the init barrier. Main thread registers `spec_pool_init_cb` as the per-worker init callback. Workers wake in stage 2 of the barrier, call into the spec registry to populate their per-language handles (each gets its own `lua_State`, its own bash subprocess, its own dlopen handle cache). Stage 3 releases workers into the task loop.\n\n**🔧 302 adds here:**\n- **`slab_create(n_cells, n_workers)`** called inside `pool_create`. One big block of 64-byte cells, free-list initialized, per-thread cache arrays allocated. Each worker pops its initial 16 cells from the global free list during init.\n\n## 6 · Initial submission\n\n`src/008-pool-runner.c` walks the graph, identifies entry boxes (zero required inputs, or all required inputs satisfiable from literals / read-box predecessors). For each, calls `dispatch_spawn(ctx, box_id, priority)` to allocate a task and submit to the pool.\n\n**🔧 302 changes here:**\n- **Task allocation** moves from `pool_spawn`'s internal `malloc` to `slab_alloc`. One atomic-pop from the calling thread's local cache.\n\n*⏳ 244 changes here:* Read boxes are no longer pushed at startup. They sit in `box_runtime_state` as callable sources. Entry-box detection still works; the dispatch will pull from them at attempt time.\n\n## 7 · Steady-state hot loop — the attempt cycle\n\nThe current code (one task picked up = one full `dispatch_action` body): read inputs → invoke spec → push to consumer slots → inline `dispatch_spawn_if_ready` per consumer.\n\n*⏳ 304 refactor:* This becomes the attempt loop described in the architecture doc. Producer's last act is to submit one attempt per distinct downstream consumer; the attempt itself checks inputs and runs or returns. **302 does not refactor the dispatch body** — that's 304's follow-on commit. But 302 does change the allocator the dispatch uses for spawning tasks.\n\n**🔧 302 changes inside the hot loop:**\n- **`dispatch_spawn` allocates from the slab.** `slab_alloc` returns a 64-byte cell. Task initialization writes fields into the cell instead of into a fresh malloc.\n- **Task completion calls `slab_free`.** Pushes the cell back to the local thread cache.\n- **`live_predecessor_count` decrement.** When a producer completes and its own count was already at 0 (no upstream can fire it again), the box has retired — decrement `live_predecessor_count` on every downstream box this producer fed. Cascade upward through retired boxes. *(The actual freeing-the-slot-table action is the stretch goal; 302 may or may not land it. The decrement itself happens unconditionally — the field is honest from day one.)*\n\n## 8 · Value lifecycle\n\nThis is where 302's biggest changes land.\n\n**Fixed-size values** (declared `output_capacity > 0`): producer writes bytes inline into each consumer's ring slot cell. Five consumers = five writes. No central allocation, no refcount. Consumer pops, cell becomes free again. **🔧 302 does not change this path** — fixed-size cells are pre-allocated at graph load and stay put.\n\n**Variable-size values** (`output_capacity == 0`, the LVH path): producer calls `lvh_alloc(size)` → gets pointer + length → writes bytes → pushes `(ptr, length)` handle into each consumer slot.\n\n**🔧 302 reshapes the LVH:**\n- **Chunk layout grows a refcount header.** `[uint32 refcount | uint32 length | data...]`. Pointer the consumer sees is at `+8` from the chunk start.\n- **`lvh_alloc(size, n_consumers)`** sets refcount = n_consumers (the producer knows this from the box's outgoing wire count to the matching branch).\n- **Eager neighbor-merge on free.** When a consumer pops a `$ref` cell, its `slab_free`-equivalent for the LVH chunk decrements the refcount. At 0, the chunk returns to the size-class free list AND checks both physical neighbors — if either neighbor is also free, merge into a larger chunk on the appropriate larger free list.\n- **Address-ordered chunk list.** A doubly-linked list of all chunks (free + allocated) in address order, separate from the size-class free lists. Used by neighbor-merge (O(1) lookup) and the deep sweep (O(n) walk).\n- **Deep sweep on allocation-failure.** Before the LVH calls `mmap`/`sbrk` to grow, walk the address-ordered chunk list, find runs of contiguous free chunks, merge each run into one large chunk pushed onto the right size-class list. Re-try the allocation; only if THAT fails do we grow. This is the only deep-sweep trigger — no quiescence trigger, no timer.\n\n*⏳ 312 changes the LVH-consumer interaction:* the wire format for cross-language hops carries `{\"$ref\": ptr, \"$len\": n}` JSON when the value is in LVH. Lua-to-Lua hops skip JSON entirely; pure-C-to-pure-C hops will too once 313 ships.\n\n## 9 · Cross-language wire\n\nToday: most cross-language hops serialize the value to a JSON string and put the string in the consumer slot. The Lua spec already implements native-to-JSON and JSON-to-native bridges (317 stage 2).\n\n*⏳ 317 + 312 land here together later:* the wire carries plain JSON for small primitives (optionally wrapped with `$type` annotations when the receiver needs type info), and `$ref` handles for LVH values. Bash bridges and C bridges still pending.\n\n→ **No 302 changes**, but 302's LVH refcount header IS the mechanism `$ref` consumers will use. So 302 unblocks 312/317 even though it doesn't touch their bridge code directly.\n\n## 10 · Termination\n\nActive-task counter hits 0 → `pool_wait_quiescent` returns → main thread calls `pool_destroy`. Workers join. Per-worker teardown callback runs (closes bash subprocesses, `lua_close` per state). Slot tables freed. JSONL writer thread drains and joins.\n\n**🔧 302 adds here:**\n- **`slab_destroy`** releases the slab block. No per-cell cleanup — the arena dies in one shot per the structural-shell rule.\n- **LVH destroy** releases the chunk regions. Address-ordered list and size-class free lists go with them. No deep sweep at teardown either — the arena dies anyway.\n\n→ `last-run.jsonl` is flushed and closed. `main` returns. Process exits.\n\n---\n\n## Summary of 302's touch points\n\n| File | Change |\n|---|---|\n| `libs/task-pool/pool.c` + `pool.h` | Slab allocator API (`slab_create`, `slab_alloc`, `slab_free`, `slab_destroy`). Per-thread cache arrays. Hot-path lockless pop/push. |\n| `src/015-large-value-heap.c` + `.h` | Refcount header layout. `lvh_alloc(size, refs)` initialized refcount. Eager neighbor-merge in `lvh_unref`. Address-ordered chunk list. Deep sweep on allocation-failure. |\n| `src/010-graph-loader.c` | Populate `live_predecessor_count` from upstream-producer-box count. (Read-box predecessors excluded per 244.) Compute LVH chunk pool sizing from the per-box `output_capacity` enumeration. |\n| `src/010-graph-loader.h` | `live_predecessor_count` field on the box runtime state. |\n| `src/012-dispatch.c` | `dispatch_spawn` uses `slab_alloc`. Task completion calls `slab_free`. Cascade decrement of `live_predecessor_count` at task end. (Dispatch body unchanged — that's 304's refactor.) |\n| `tests/302-*.c` (new) | Slab allocator unit tests: alloc-free roundtrip, refill at empty, drain at full, multi-threaded contention. LVH refcount tests: pop decrements, neighbor-merge fires, deep sweep recovers. |\n\nPlus updates to `src/015-large-value-heap.info.md` and a fresh `libs/task-pool/slab.info.md` per project convention.\n\n---\n\nWant me to proceed, or any course corrections?"
